question.text: Which of the following fea​tures differentiates the ​exocrine pancreas from th‍e parotid gland?

options.text: Basal lamina lining the se​rous acini
options.label: A
C
options.text: Presence of serous acini w​ith acidophilic tip

question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Absence of striated duct

Absence of striated duct in exocrine pancreas differentiates it from the parotid gland.

The exocrine pancreas is comprised entirely of serous acini. Hence, its general structure is similar to that of the parotid gland, but the two are easily distinguished by:

  • The parotid gland has striated and intercalated intralobular ducts, whereas the pancreas has only the intercalated type.
  • The excretory ducts of the parotid gland are striated columnar, whereas the excretory duct of the pancreas is a simple columnar.

question.text: Medial lemniscus is a cont​inuation of which of the ​following structures?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fasciculus gracilis

Medial lemniscus is a continuation of fasciculus gracilis.

Posterior column–medial lemniscal pathway:

First-order axons carrying discriminative touch and vibration sensations enter the dorsal horn and continue traveling upward in the posterior white column as the fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus.

Fibers of these fasciculi synapse on the second-order neurons of the ipsilateral nuclei gracilis and cuneatus in the medulla oblongata, respectively.

Axons of these second-order neurons then cross over as the internal arcuate fibers to form the medial lemniscus in the contralateral medulla.

These second-order axons ascend through the brainstem to reach the third-order neuronal cell bodies in the ventral posterior lateral nucleus of the thalamus. Axons from the third-order neurons then project through the posterior limb of the internal capsule to reach the primary somatosensory cortex.

question.text: The pretracheal layer of d​eep cervical fascia enclo​ses all of the following ‍except:
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sternocleidomastoid

All the above structures are enclosed by the pretracheal layer of deep cervical fascia except sternocleidomastoid. It is enclosed by the investing layer of deep cervical fascia.

The deep cervical fascia of the neck is organized into the following layers:

  • The investing layer, which surrounds all structures in the neck
  • The prevertebral layer, which surrounds the vertebral column and the deep muscles associated with the back.
  • The pretracheal layer, which encloses the viscera of the neck
  • The carotid sheath, which receives a contribution from the other three fascial layers

In the neck, the pretracheal fascia covers the strap muscles i.e sternohyoid, omohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid. It splits to enclose the thyroid gland. It also surrounds the trachea and the esophagus including the recurrent laryngeal nerve present in the groove between them.

question.text: Which is the drug used for​ refractory intractable r​heumatic chorea?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sodium valproate

The drug used for refractory intractable rheumatic chorea is sodium valproate, as it doesn't have extrapyramidal side effects. 

Sydenham's chorea is characterized by involuntary, purposeless, jerky movements which mainly affect the head and upper limbs. In the tongue, it is visible as the characteristic darting movements.

Medications used to treat Sydenham chorea are:

  • Mild cases - Providing a calm environment.
  • Severe cases:
    • Dopamine antagonists - haloperidol, pimozide
    • Antiepileptic medications - sodium valproate, carbamazepine.  
  • Severe, refractory cases - Steroids (thought to be immune-mediated)
  • IV immunoglobulins, plasmapheresis - limited studies, decreased efficacy (not currently recommended)

question.text: What is ba​siliximab?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. IL-2 receptor antagonist

Basiliximab exhibits a high affinity towards IL-2 receptor and inhibits it. It is an anti- CD-25 monoclonal antibody.
It has a short plasma half-life of 1 week. It is used to prevent transplant rejection reactions. Its adverse effects are anaphylactic reactions & opportunistic infections.

question.text: Which of the following inh​ibits the synthesis of gl​ucocorticoid?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Metyrapone

Metyrapone inhibits the synthesis of glucocorticoids by inhibiting steroid 11β-hydroxylase reversibly.

It is used to test the hypothalamic-pituitary feedback pathway in the diagnosis of Cushing syndrome.

question.text: Isosorbide dinitrate is in​dicated for congestive he​art failure in combinatio‍n with which of the follo​wing vasodilators?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hydralazine

Isosorbide dinitrate (ISDN) is indicated in combination with hydralazine for CHF. 

Hydralazine is a direct vasodilator and its mechanism of action is not known. It also reduces nitrate tolerance.

The combination of ISDN and hydralazine showed mortality benefits in a specific group of population (African-Americans).

question.text: Which of the following sta​tements is true about pra​sugrel?

options.label: A
options.text: It acts as an P2 Y12 agoni​st

options.label: B
options.text: It is 10 times less potent​ than clopidogrel
Omeprazole interferes in i​ts activation to an activ​e metabolite
options.label: D

question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It is a pro drug

Prasugrel is a prodrug.

It acts as an irreversible ADP (P2 Y12) antagonist and is converted into its active metabolite by CYP3A4 and CYP2B6. Since omeprazole is an inhibitor of CYP2C19, it does not interfere with its activation.

It is 10-times more potent than clopidogrel and has a more rapid onset of action because of better absorption and more predictable metabolic activation.

question.text: Apixaban belongs to which ​of the following class of​ drugs?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Factor Xa inhibitor

Apixaban, a novel oral anticoagulant (NOAC), is a factor Xa inhibitor that is used in the treatment of VTE (venous thrombo embolism)/DVT and in its prophylaxis after major orthopedic surgeries.

Direct factor Xa inhibitors:

  • Rivaroxaban
  • Apixaban
  • Edoxaban
  • Betrixaban

Parenteral direct thrombin inhibitors:

  • Bivalirudin
  • Argatroban
  • Desirudin

Oral direct thrombin inhibitor—Dabigatran is the only oral direct thrombin inhibitor available for clinical use.

The FDA recently approved the drug Apixaban for a new indication. The drug is now used to reduce the risk of stroke and systemic embolism in patients with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation.

question.text: Which of the following is ​the drug of choice for sc​rub typhus?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Doxycycline

Doxycycline is the drug of choice for scrub typhus.

Azithromycin, chloramphenicol, or rifampin can be administered as alternatives in patients allergic to doxycycline and in pregnancy.

question.text: Which of the following dru​gs is associated with QT ​prolongation?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Quinidine

QT prolongation is seen with quinidine. 

It causes torsades de pointes, a life-threatening form of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia.

question.text: Coagulation profile monito​ring is needed in therapy​ with which of the follow‍ing drugs?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lepirudin

Coagulation profile monitoring is needed for lepirudin.

Lepirudin is a direct irreversible thrombin inhibitor and its most adverse reaction is bleeding. The risk of bleeding can be reduced by implementing an appropriate monitoring and dose adjustment strategy. Thus, coagulation profile monitoring is required for lepirudin.

However, enoxaparin, fondaparinux, and dabigatran do not bind to endothelium or many plasma proteins and thus, the response to these drugs at the usual doses is consistent from patient to patient. Hence, monitoring is not required.

question.text: Which one of the following​ drugs inhibits neutrophi‌l recruitment?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Colchicine

Colchicine inhibits neutrophil (granulocyte) recruitment.

Colchicine acts by preventing the polymerisation of microtubules by binding to tubulin. This reduces neutrophil recruitment to inflamed tissue and also decreases the secretion of chemotactic factors by activated neutrophils, thus reducing the inflammatory response overall.

Colchicine is used in gout and Mediterranean fever.

question.text: What is the drug used to d​ifferentiate myasthenia g‌ravis from cholinergic cr‍isis?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Edrophonium

The drug used to differentiate myasthenia gravis from a cholinergic crisis is edrophonium.

Muscle weakness is a common presentation in patients with myasthenia gravis and cholinergic crisis (excessive dose of anti-ChE drugs). Intravenous injection of edrophonium improves muscular weakness in a patient with myasthenia gravis and not in a case of cholinergic crisis. 

The test used for this differentiation is known as the edrophonium test. 

Initially, 2 mg is administered; if improvements of symptoms do not occur within 45 seconds, an additional 8 mg can be administered. Improvement of strength is a positive test for myasthenia gravis.

question.text: Which of the following is ​true about pegylated-filg‌rastim?

options.text: Duration of action is shor​ter than normal filgrasti‌m
options.label: A

options.text: Added advantage is that it​ can be taken orally
options.label: B

options.text: It should not be administe​red in sickle cell patien‌ts
options.label: C
D
options.text: It is not effective in the​ treatment of severe neut‌ropenia

question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It should not be administered in sickle cell patients

Patients with sickle cell anemia should not receive pegylated filgrastim as it can trigger a sickle cell crisis.

Filgrastim is a recombinant human G-CSF (granulocyte colony-stimulating factor). The pegylated forms of filgrastim, pegfilgrastim, and lipefilgrastim, are longer-acting forms. It is administered subcutaneously or by slow intravenous infusion only.

Indications of recombinant G-CSF:   

  • Severe neutropenia after autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation
  • Severe neutropenia after high dose cancer chemotherapy
  • Severe congenital neutropenias
  • Neutropenia of patients with AIDS receiving zidovudine

question.text: The best approach in the t​reatment of chronic SIADH‌ is ______

options.label: B
options.text: Reducing fluid intake to <​500 ml per day

question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tolvaptan

The best approach in the treatment of chronic SIADH is the oral administration of a vaptan like tolvaptan, which is a selective V2 receptor antagonist. This increases urinary water excretion by blocking the antidiuretic effect of AVP.

Other treatment options for chronic SIADH include:

  • Fluid intake < 500 ml/day
  • Demeclocycline
  • Fludrocortisone 

Increased thirst is a frequently observed characteristic of hyponatremia in SIADH. Fluid restriction is usually a burden to the patient. It is unreliable, impractical, and slow to work. As thirst is particularly difficult to suppress, water restriction in SIADH frequently leads to non-compliance in the long run. Vaptans would be especially suited for the treatment of these patients. Serum sodium concentrations are also corrected by vaptans and hence, vaptans substantially improve the quality of life in these patients.

question.text: Which of the following pha​ses of a clinical trial i‌s also referred to as eff‍icacy trial?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Phase 2

Efficacy and appropriate dose range is the main aim of phase 2 of clinical trials. It is evaluated on a small group of patients with the target disease.

Phase II of clinical trials involve a small group of patients (50-500). Most of the new drugs will be administered for the first time in patients with the target disease. The study is designed to obtain proof of concept (potential of the drug to treat the disease) and dose-ranging study (provides input for choosing the most appropriate dose for phase 3 studies).

Phase 3 studies are also known as pivotal studies as they establish treatment benefits.

question.text: Which of the following is ​a synthetic PGF2 alpha de‌rivative used as an abort‍ifacient?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Carboprost

Carboprost is a 15-methyl synthetic derivative of PGF2 alpha. It is used as an abortifacient and in refractory PPH.

Options A: Dinoprost is a natural PGF2 alpha preparation.

Option B:  Dinoprostone is natural PGE2 preparation.

Option C: Misoprostol is a synthetic PGE1 analog. Gemeprost is also a synthetic PGE1 analog.

question.text: What is the mechanism of r​esistance by lactamases​ ‌to β-lactam antibiotics?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Degradation of antibiotics

Resistance by lactamases is through the degradation of antibiotics.

The bacterial cell wall is made of heteropolymeric peptidoglycan that confers mechanical stability. The β-lactam antibiotics inhibit the last step in peptidoglycan synthesis by acylating the transpeptidase via cleavage of the –CO–N– bond of the β-lactam ring. These transpeptidase targets are collectively called Penicillin Binding Proteins (PBPs)

Beta-lactamases are enzymes produced by certain bacteria that inactivates β-lactam antibiotics by hydrolysis of the β-lactam ring in their structure.

The resistance to penicillins and other beta-lactam antibiotics can be conferred through one of the four mechanisms:

  1. Inactivation of antibiotic by lactamases
  2. Modification of target PBPs
  3. Impaired penetration of drug to target PBPs
  4. Antibiotic efflux

question.text: Which of the following flu​oroquinolone is not given‌ in liver disease?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pefloxacin

Pefloxacin is mainly metabolized in the liver and hence avoided in patients with liver disease. 

Quinolones with primarily hepatic metabolism include moxifloxacin, pefloxacin, and trovafloxacin (withdrawn from the market due to hepatotoxicity).

Quinolones primarily excreted by the kidneys include ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, norfloxacin, lomefloxacin, and ofloxacin.

question.text: Which of the following sho​uld not be prescribed wit‌h theophylline?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Erythromycin

Erythromycin should not be prescribed with theophylline.

Theophylline is mainly metabolized by CYP1A2 in the liver. Erythromycin inhibits CYP1A2 and thereby decreases the clearance of theophylline.

Factors decreasing the clearance of theophylline are:

  • Drugs - erythromycin, cimetidine, ciprofloxacin, allopurinol, fluvoxamine, zileuton, zafirlukast
  • Congestive heart failure
  • Liver disease
  • Pneumonia
  • Viral infection and vaccination
  • High-carbohydrate diet
  • Old age

question.text: A patient who was diagnose​d with ADPKD was prescrib‌ed tolvaptan. After a few​ weeks, he presented with‌ dry mouth and increased ​thirst. What is the likel‍y cause? ADPKD- Autosomal‌ dominant polycystic kidn​ey disease
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increased free water clearance

Tolvaptan causes increased free water clearance, which causes dehydration. Hence, the patient may present with dry mouth and increased thirst.

Tolvaptan is a vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist. Decreased binding of vasopressin to the V2 receptor in the kidney lowers the adenyl cyclase activity leading to decreased intracellular cAMP. Decreased cAMP concentrations prevent the fusion of aquaporin 2 containing vesicles with the plasma membrane, leading to an increase in urinary water excretion (free water clearance), and a decrease in urine osmolality.

The common side effects of tolvaptan include:

  • dehydration
  • hypernatremia
  • hypovolemia
  • liver injury

Tolvaptan is used to delay disease progression in patients with ADPKD.

question.text: Which of the following ant​iarrhythmic drugs is cont‌raindicated in a patient ​with interstitial lung di‌sease?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Amiodarone

Amiodarone is contraindicated in a patient with interstitial lung disease.

The most serious adverse effect during chronic amiodarone therapy is pulmonary fibrosis, which can be rapidly progressive and fatal. Underlying lung disease, doses of 400 mg/day or more, and recent pulmonary insults such as pneumonia appear to be risk factors for this condition.

Amiodarone is a class III antiarrhythmic drug.

The side effects of amiodarone include:

  • Pulmonary fibrosis
  • Hypotension, depressed ventricular function
  • Torsades de pointes
  • Corneal microdeposits
  • Hepatotoxicity
  • Neuropathies
  • Photosensitivity
  • Thyroid dysfunction

question.text: Which of the following dru​gs acts by inhibiting the‌ late sodium current in t​he heart?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ranolazine

Ranolazine acts by inhibiting the late sodium current in the heart.

Late sodium current (INa) facilitates entry of calcium via the sodium-calcium exchanger. Inhibition of INa, therefore, reduces the intracellular calcium concentration which in turn reduces the diastolic tension, cardiac contractility and work.

At higher doses, it may also modify the fatty acid oxidation, which improves the efficiency of cardiac oxygen utilization.

It is used in the prophylaxis of angina.

question.text: A patient with diabetes an​d COPD developed post-ope‌rative urinary retention.​ Which of the following d‌rugs can be used for shor​t-term treatment of the c‍ondition?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tamsulosin

Tamsulosin is the drug used to relieve the symptoms in cases of postoperative urinary retention in a patient with COPD.

It is also efficacious in the treatment of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) with little effect on blood pressure. 

Option B: Bethanechol is the drug of choice to relieve the symptoms in cases of postoperative urinary retention. However, it can cause bronchoconstriction in patients with COPD. Hence tamsulosin is the best answer here.

Option C: Terazosin is an α1 receptor antagonist, used in the treatment of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). 

Option D: Methacholine is a muscarinic agonist but acts specifically on bronchial smooth muscle causing its contraction. It is available as an inhalational agent and is used for the diagnosis of bronchial hyper-reactivity in patients who do not have clinically apparent asthma.

question.text: Which of the following is ​not a prokinetic?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Diphenylmethane

Diphenylmethane is not a prokinetic agent. Its derivative (Bisacodyl) is used as a laxative.

Prokinetic agents are the drugs that increase GI motility and transit of material in the GI tract. These agents include:

  • Dopamine receptor antagonists- metoclopramide and domperidone
  • Serotonin receptor agonists- cisapride and prucalopride
  • Motilin
  • Macrolide antibiotics mimicking motilin - erythromycin
  • Miscellaneous agents:
    • Sincalide (C-terminal octapeptide of CCK)
    • Camicinal (motilin receptor agonist)
    • Relamorelin (ghrelin receptor agonist)
    • Velusetrag and naronapride (5HT4 agonists)

question.text: Paradoxical bronchoconstri​ction seen with ipratropi‌um bromide is due to all ‍except
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hypertonic saline

Paradoxical bronchoconstriction with ipratropium bromide is seen with a hypotonic nebulizer solution and not hypertonic saline.

Paradoxical bronchoconstriction with ipratropium bromide is seen especially when given by a nebulizer and may be due to the following factors:

  • Hypotonic nebulizer solution
  • Antibacterial additives like benzalkonium chloride and EDTA
  • It may be also due to prejunctional M2 receptor blockade on the cholinergic nerves present in the airway. These prejunctional M2 receptors normally inhibit acetylcholine release into the synapse. So their blockade can cause increased Ach release and bronchoconstriction.

Paradoxical bronchoconstriction is not reported with tiotropium bromide or any other long-acting muscarinic antagonists. Tiotropium is selective for M3 and M1 receptors and therefore less likely to produce prejunctional M2 receptor blockade.

Other adverse effects of inhaled muscarinic antagonists:

  • A bitter taste is seen with ipratropium
  • Nebulization with ipratropium bromide may precipitate glaucoma in elderly patients. This is due to the direct effect of the drug on the eyes and can be easily prevented by using a mouthpiece instead of a facemask.
  • Long-acting agents can cause dryness of the mouth. 
  • In elderly patients, urinary retention may be seen occasionally.

question.text: Antimicrobial combinations​ are used in all except
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gonorrhea

Gonorrhea is not managed by antimicrobial combinations. According to the latest CDC guidelines, single-agent therapy with ceftriaxone is the preferred treatment for gonococcal infections.

Single-dose of 500mg intramuscular(IM) ceftriaxone is given for gonorrhea. It is important to note that the previous guidelines that recommended dual therapy with ceftriaxone and azithromycin are no longer preferred.

Monotherapy with ceftriaxone is given when concurrent chlamydia infection is ruled out by molecular testing. If this is not done then presumptive treatment for chlamydia should be given along with the treatment of gonorrhea. According to CDC guidelines, 100mg doxycycline twice daily for 7 days is given as presumptive treatment of chlamydia in nonpregnant individuals.

Other options:

Tuberculosis: Multidrug therapy is given in tuberculosis for proper cure and to prevent the selection of drug-resistant mutants. ATT regimen is given in detail in the pearl attached.

Intraabdominal infections: It is usually polymicrobial and can result in an intraabdominal abscess or secondary peritonitis. These are managed with either single-agent or combination therapy. Broad-spectrum agents with gram-negative cover such as meropenem or piperacillin-tazobactam can be used alone. Combination therapy with metronidazole and other agents like ciprofloxacin, cefepime, etc are used as empirical agents in intraabdominal infections.

Malaria: It is also treated with antimicrobial combinations. In plasmodium vivax and ovale malaria, schizontocides like chloroquine are combined with agents that attack the hypnozoites like primaquine for radical cure. Primaquine is also given in combination with Artemisinin combined therapy(ACT) for plasmodium falciparum infections as a gametocidal agent. Treatment regimens are given in the pearl attached.

question.text: A patient is on phenytoin ​for a seizure disorder. H‌e was prescribed sucralfa‍te 4 times a day for pept‌ic ulcers. What should be‍ the minimum duration of ​time between consumption ‌of these drugs?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 120 minutes

The minimum duration of time between the consumption of phenytoin and sucralfate should be 120 minutes.

Sucralfate, in an acidic environment (pH < 4) acts by producing a viscous, sticky polymer that adheres to ulcer craters and epithelial cells for up to 6 hours after a single dose. This viscous layer produced in the stomach leads to inhibition of absorption of other drugs, like phenytoin, digoxin, cimetidine, ketoconazole, and fluoroquinolone antibiotics. Therefore, sucralfate should be taken after a gap of at least 2 hours / 120 minutes after the administration of phenytoin. 

Constipation is the most common side effect of sucralfate. It should be avoided in patients with renal failure who are at risk of aluminium overload. Aluminum-containing antacids should not be combined with sucralfate in these patients.  As the viscous gel produced by sucralfate is sticky, it may eventually lead to bezoar formation.

It is generally used for prophylaxis of peptic ulcers, but rarely so because of its side effects and its risks outweigh its benefits.

question.text: Identify the false stateme​nt regarding suicidal inh‌ibition.

options.label: A
options.text: The inhibitor can bind wit​h any site resulting in s‌uicidal inhibition

options.label: B
options.text: The binding of the enzyme ​to the substrate analogue‌ is irreversible
They are enzyme specific a​nd used in rational drug ‌design
options.label: C
D
options.text: The inhibitor forms a prod​uct with the enzyme and t‌he product inhibits it

question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. The inhibitor can bind with any site resulting in suicidal inhibition

The false statement regarding suicidal inhibition is the inhibitor can bind with any site resulting in suicidal inhibition.

In suicidal inhibition, the inhibitor can only bind with the active site of an enzyme and is unreactive outside the confines of the enzyme's active site. 

The enzyme inhibition helps to modify the rate of reactions it catalyzes and this inhibition can either be reversible or irreversible. Reversible inhibitors bind to enzymes through non-covalent bonds. Irreversible inhibitors usually bind to an enzyme through covalent bonds and do so strongly so that it can no longer dissociate.

Suicide inhibitors are a category of irreversible inhibitors also called mechanism-based inhibitors. They are specialized substrate analogs that contain a chemical group that reacts with the catalytic machinery of the target enzyme. In these types of inhibitors, the substrate analog irreversibly ties up with the binding site of an enzyme, deceiving the enzyme by concealing its functional group resulting in the formation of a highly reactive molecule, which brings about self-inactivation of the enzyme.

Suicide inhibitors bind to the enzyme by means of covalent bonds; they are enzyme-specific and unreactive outside the confines of the enzyme’s active site.

An example of this would be the binding of clavulanic acid to the active site of beta-lactamases in bacteria. Clavulanic acid mimics the structure of a beta-lactam antibiotic and forms a covalent adduct with the β-lactamase active site. This leads to a rearrangement that creates a much more reactive derivative, which is subsequently attacked in its active site to irreversibly acylate the enzyme and inactivate it. Thus, amoxicillin and clavulanic acid are combined to overcome bacterial resistance to amoxicillin alone.

The development of clavulanic acid to target beta-lactamase-producing bacteria is also an example of the rational design of drugs. Rational design of drugs refers to the ability to predict the appropriate molecular structure of a drug on the basis of information about its biological receptor.

question.text: A patient who was diagnose​d with epilepsy was put o‌n retigabine TDS. Now phe‍nytoin is being added. Wh‌ich of the following chan‍ges should be made to ret​igabine?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increase the dose

The dose of retigabine should be increased when phenytoin is added because phenytoin can decrease the plasma concentration of retigabine when given together.

Retigabine is also known as ezogabine. Metabolism of the drug occurs by glucuronidation and acetylation. Its half-life is about 7-11 hours and hence requires thrice-daily dosing. When it is administered with phenytoin or carbamazepine there may be a reduction in the plasma concentration of the drug. So the dose of retigabine should be increased when given along with these drugs.

It is a potassium(K+) channel opener that enhancer transmembrane potassium currents mediated by the KNCQ family of ion channels. It was approved as an adjunctive agent for focal onset seizures of patients above 18 years. But because of its adverse effects like retinal abnormalities and blue pigmentation, the production of the drug was discontinued by the manufacturer.

Other drug interactions of phenytoin:

It is an inducer of the enzymes CYP2C8/9, CYP3A4/5, and other CYPs. It is also an inhibitor of CYP2C9/19. 

  • Phenobarbitone can inhibit the metabolism of phenytoin. But the overall interaction is unpredictable as both the drug enhance each other's degradation by enzyme induction.
  • Phenytoin and carbamazepine induce each other's metabolism.
  • Valproate increases the level of unbound phenytoin by displacing the protein-bound form and decreasing its metabolism.
  • Phenytoin increases the metabolism of steroids, oral contraceptives, doxycycline, theophylline, etc by enzyme induction.
  • It produces competitive inhibition of warfarin metabolism. (Increased risk of bleeding when given together)
  • Drugs like chloramphenicol, warfarin, isoniazid, and cimetidine can inhibit the metabolism of phenytoin and cause its toxicity.
  • Sucralfate decreases the absorption of phenytoin by binding to it in the gastrointestinal tract.

question.text: Which of the following is ​the incorrect statement r‌egarding clomiphene citra‍te? GnRH - Gonadotropin-r‌eleasing hormone
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Causes monofollicular development

The incorrect statement regarding clomiphene citrate is that it causes monofollicular development; rather, it causes multi follicular development.

Clomiphene is an unequal mixture of two isomers, enclomiphene and zuclomiphene. Zuclomiphene is a non-steroidal compound closely resembling an estrogen, blocks the negative inhibitory feedback of estrogens on the hypothalamus, causing a surge of gonadotropins (FSH, LH), which leads to ovulation. The continued flow of FSH encourages multiple follicular development which is relatively common.

Being an anti-estrogen, it causes thickening of cervical mucus and thinning of the endometrium. 

Clomiphene citrate (CC) is used for the treatment of absent or irregular ovulation due to hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction associated with normal levels of endogenous estradiol; the patient must be treated repeatedly until pregnancy is achieved since the normal cyclic ovulatory function does not usually resume. Clomiphene citrate has no effect on patients with ovarian or pituitary failure. Ovulation induction with clomiphene citrate and a gonadotropin like FSH increases the likelihood of multiple concurrent ovulations.

Side effects of CC include hot flushes and some nausea. However, it is usually very well tolerated.

question.text: A patient with history of ​ischemic stroke was start‌ed on clopidogrel. Howeve‍r, she had another attack‌ of stroke after 6 months‍. Which of the following ​is likely to be responsib‌le for the failure of clo​pidogrel in this patient?‌
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Downregulation of CYP2C19

Downregulation of CYP2C19 is responsible for the failure of clopidogrel in this patient.

Clopidogrel is a prodrug and its metabolic activation occurs in the liver. It is bioactivated by the CYP2C19 enzyme. If there is downregulation of this enzyme it will cause a decrease in the efficacy of clopidogrel and can lead to thrombotic events like stroke. Drugs that inhibit CYP2C19 can also decrease the antiplatelet effect of clopidogrel. Proton-pump inhibitors may cause inhibition of CYP2C19 and when they are given in combination there would be a decrease in the efficacy of clopidogrel. 

Therapeutic uses: Clopidogrel is used to reduce the rate of stroke and myocardial infarction. It also decreases the rate of deaths in patients with recent myocardial infarction or stroke. Other uses are acute coronary syndrome and peripheral arterial disease.

Adverse effects: Increased risk of bleeding especially when given with an anticoagulant or aspirin. Rarely thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura can occur.

CYP2C19: Common drugs that are metabolized include omeprazole, phenytoin, diazepam, and propanolol. Inducers of the CYP2C subfamily are rifampicin and carbamazepine. Omeprazole is an inhibitor.

Other options:

CYP2D6: Drugs metabolized include SSRIs,  tricyclic antidepressants, antiarrhythmic drugs, beta-blockers, and opiates. It is inhibited by quinidine and it will prevent the formation of morphine from codeine. Hence quinidine decreases the analgesic effect of codeine.

CYP1A1/2: It metabolizes few drugs like theophylline, paracetamol, caffeine and carbamazepine. It plays an important role in the activation of procarcinogens. Inducers are rifampicin, carbamazepine, polycyclic hydrocarbons, charbroiled meat, and cigarette smoke.

CYP2E1: It is involved in the oxidation of alcohol, halothane, and minor metabolism of other drugs. It is important to note that it is involved in the formation of hepatotoxic N-acetyl benzoquinone imine from paracetamol. Chronic alcoholism is responsible for the induction of this enzyme.

question.text: Which of the following is ​a novel anti-depressant?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vilazodone

Vilazodone is the novel antidepressant.

The antidepressant effect of vilazodone is due to its enhancement of serotonergic activity in the CNS through selective inhibition of serotonin reuptake. It binds with high affinity to the serotonin reuptake site but not to the norepinephrine or dopamine reuptake site. As a result, vilazodone potently and selectively inhibits the reuptake of serotonin.

Vilazodone is also a partial agonist at serotonergic 5-HT1A receptors; the result of this activity on serotonergic transmission also plays a role in its antidepressant effect.

Thus it offers a novel combination of selective serotonin reuptake inhibition (SSRI) and serotonergic (5-HT1A) receptor partial agonist activity. Because of these characteristics, vilazodone has been termed a serotonin partial agonist–reuptake inhibitor (SPARI).

Vilazodone is never combined with a monoamine oxidase (MAO) inhibitor or given within 14 days of discontinuing or initiating MAO inhibitor therapy due to the serious risk of serotonin toxicity.

Other options:

Option A: Lurasidone is a second-generation antipsychotic that is a 5-HT2A and D2 receptor antagonist. it is used in the treatment of schizophrenia and bipolar depression (as monotherapy or as an adjunct).

Option C: Asenapine is a second-generation antipsychotic which is also a 5-HT2A and D2 receptor antagonist, used in the management of schizophrenia and acute mania.

Option D: Blonanserin is a second-generation antipsychotic, which acts as an antagonist at D2, D3, and 5-HT2A receptors. Blonanserin has a low affinity for 5-HT2C, adrenergic α1, histamine H1, and muscarinic M1 receptors, but displays a relatively high affinity for 5-HT6 receptors. It is used in the management of schizophrenia.

question.text: Which of the following is ​a centrally acting opioid‌ antitussive?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Levopropoxyphene

Levopropoxyphene is a centrally acting opioid antitussive.

Levopropoxyphene is an opioid derivative that is a strong and partial μ receptor agonist that helps to reduce the cough reflex and therefore, is used in the management of acute debilitating cough. The usual antitussive dose is 50–100 mg every 4 hours. It has no analgesic activity. However, it is known to cause some sedation.

Other options:

Option A: Ambroxol is derived from bromhexine. It is a mucoactive agent that helps alter the viscoelastic properties of mucus and increase mucociliary clearance, thereby providing relief in productive cough. It is commonly available as intramuscular or intravenous, lozenges, syrups, or tablets.

Option B: Diphenoxylate is an opioid agonist that is structurally similar to meperidine. It is used in the treatment of acute, chronic, and traveler's diarrhea. Upon administration, it undergoes de-esterification to difenoxin, which is its active metabolite. Its side effects include constipation, toxic megacolon, paralytic ileus and can give rise to CNS depression in children.

Option D: Levorphanol is a synthetic opioid that is also a 5HT/Norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor and an NMDA receptor antagonist which is chiefly used in the management of moderate to severe pain and has a relatively rapid onset of action. Its side effects include delirium and hallucinations.

question.text: The anti-epileptic drugs w​hich can also be used for‌ the treatment of neuropa‍thic pain are Pregabalin ‌Carbamazepine Lamotrigine‍ Gabapentin
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

The anti-epileptic drugs which can also be used for neuropathic pain are 1, 2, and 4 which are pregabalin, carbamazepine and gabapentin respectively.

Pregabalin is an anti-epileptic drug that acts by binding to α2δ, a protein that is a subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels and causes a decrease in glutamate release at excitatory synapses. It is used in the management of neuropathic pain associated with diabetic peripheral neuropathy, spinal cord injury or postherpetic neuralgia.

Gabapentin is an anti-epileptic drug that, like pregabalin, acts by binding to α2δ protein. It is used in the management of neuropathic pain due to postherpetic neuralgia in adults.

The binding of gabapentin and pregabalin, also called "gabapentinoids" due to their structural similarity to GABA, to calcium channel subunit a2δ protein, is considered to mediate the anti-convulsant effects of gabapentin and pregabalin. They are used in focal onset seizures with or without progression to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures when used in addition to other anti-epileptic drugs.

Carbamazepine is an iminostilbine derivative. It blocks voltage-activated sodium channels, slowing their rate of recovery and limiting the repetitive firing of action potentials. It is used in the treatment of:

  • Generalized, focal-to-bilateral and idiopathic tonic-clonic seizures
  • Focal seizures
  • Neuropathic pain associated with trigeminal and glossopharyngeal neuralgias.

Lamotrigine is an anti-folate agent whose mechanism of action is similar to that of carbamazepine i.e. it delays the recovery from inactivation of recombinant sodium channels. It also inhibits the release of glutamate by acting directly on the sodium channels. Therefore, when used concurrently with carbamazepine, is associated with toxicity in some patients due to increase in 10,11- epoxide of carbamazepine. It is useful in the management of:

  • Focal and secondarily generalized tonic-clonic seizures in adults
  • Lennox-Gastaut syndrome - a childhood disorder characterized by multiple type seizures, mental retardation, and refractoriness to anti-seizure medication.

question.text: A breast cancer patient po​st-chemotherapy developed‌ a low-grade fever with a‍nemia and leukocytopenia ‌(<4000/cm3; DNC: 30). Whi‍ch of the following antib​iotics will not be used i‌n the empirical managemen​t of this patient?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Linezolid

Linezolid cannot be used in this patient as bone marrow suppression is a side effect of this drug and hence it can worsen the post-chemotherapy bone marrow suppression in this patient.

Linezolid can cause myelosuppression which can present as anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and pancytopenia. It is commonly associated with thrombocytopenia and is seen 7-10 days following administration. This is usually reversed on discontinuation of the drug. 

Other adverse effects of linezolid:

  • It inhibits mitochondrial protein synthesis and may lead to peripheral neuropathy, optic neuritis, and lactic acidosis in patients receiving the drug for longer durations.
  • It can cause serotonin syndrome when coadministered with adrenergic or serotonergic drugs like SSRIs due to its nonspecific MAO inhibition.

It is a protein synthesis inhibitor of the class oxazolidinones. It mainly acts against gram-positive organisms. It is approved for the treatment of the following conditions:

  • Skin and skin structure infections by staphylococcus(Both MRSA and MSSA) and streptococcus.
  • Community-acquired pneumonia due to streptococcus pneumoniae.
  • Nosocomial pneumonia due to staphylococcus aureus. 

Other options:

Cefepime: It is a fourth-generation antipseudomonal cephalosporin. It is useful in enterobacter and pseudomonas infections that are resistant to other cephalosporins.

Piperacillin-Tazobactam- It is a combination of piperacillin which is a ureidopenicillin and tazobactam which is a beta-lactamase inhibitor. It is useful in various infections including nosocomial infections, intraabdominal infections, pneumonia, and UTI. It is highly effective against E Coli and Klebsiella.

Meropenem: It belongs to the carbapenem group of beta-lactam antibiotics. They are more active against gram-negative organisms. Coadministration of cilastatin is not required with this drug. (Cilastation should be coadministered with imipenem as imipenem is sensitive to renal peptidase degradation)

question.text: An HIV-positive woman on A​RT was prescribed ergotam‌ine for a migraine attack‍ 4 days back. She present‌ed with complaints that s‍he is unable to feel her ​legs from the mid-thigh t‌o her toes, for the past ​two days. The angiography‌ image is given below. Wh​at is the likely diagnosi​s?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ergotism

The clinical features and the CT angiography image showing diffuse symmetrical luminal narrowing of the lower limb vessels are suggestive of ergotism.

In this case, a patient on antiretroviral therapy is given ergotamine. HIV protease inhibitors used in ART like ritonavir, lopinavir, etc are potent inhibitors of the  CYP3A4 enzyme. This enzyme is responsible for the metabolism of ergot compounds. Hence inhibition of this enzyme leads to decreased metabolism of ergotamine. This causes the accumulation of toxic levels of ergotamine in the patient and leads to ergotism. 

Ergotamine is a partial agonist and antagonist at alpha-adrenergic, 5HT1; and 5HT2 receptors. It produces sustained vasoconstriction, vasomotor center depression, and visceral smooth muscle contraction.

Adverse effects: Nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain may be seen. Vasoconstriction caused by the drug is responsible for most of the adverse effects. These are usually seen with long-term therapy with higher doses.

  • It may precipitate or aggravate angina pectoris or myocardial infarction due to coronary insufficiency.
  • Some patients develop cold, numb, and painful extremities.
  • Leg claudication may be seen
  • Gangrene of the extremities

 Contraindications for ergotamine: 

  • Peripheral vascular disease
  • Coronary artery disease
  • Uncontrolled hypertension
  • Sepsis
  • Pregnancy
  • Liver and kidney diseases

question.text: Topiramate ​is used for
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Treatment of Lennox Gastaut syndrome

Topiramate is used in the treatment of Lennox-Gastuat syndrome.

Uses of topiramate:

  • In newly diagnosed focal and primary generalized epilepsy in adults and children 
  • As monotherapy for refractory focal epilepsy and generalized tonic-clonic seizures
  • Treatment of  tonic-clonic seizures in patients with Lennox-Gastuat syndrome
  • It is also used in the prophylaxis of migraine(not for treatment)
  • It can be given as monotherapy for children of 10 years or more. But if used as adjunctive therapy it can be used in children as young as 2 years.

Mechanism of action: It reduces voltage-gated sodium currents in the cerebellar granule cells. It also activates a hyperpolarizing potassium current, enhances GABAA receptor currents, and limits the activation of the AMPA-kainate subtype of glutamate receptors. It also produces weak inhibition of the carbonic anhydrase enzyme.

Pharmacokinetics: Only 10-20% is bound to plasma proteins and the drug is largely excreted unchanged in the urine. Half-life is about 1 day. Topiramate is found to decrease the plasma concentrations of oral contraceptives, hence a higher dose of OCPs should be given along with topiramate.

Adverse effects:

  • Somnolence, weight loss, fatigue, and nervousness are commonly seen
  • It can precipitate renal calculi. It may be due to the weak carbonic anhydrase inhibition.
  • Cognitive impairment

question.text: Which of the following is ​incorrectly matched?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ciraparantag: Fondaparinux

Ciraparantag is a reversal agent for all direct anticoagulants and is not useful with fondaparinux which is an indirect factor Xa inhibitor.

Ciraparantag, andexanet alfa, and idarucizumab are all reversal agents of direct anticoagulants.

Ciraparantag: It is considered as a potential reversal agent against all direct anticoagulants including dabigatran, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, apixaban, LMWH, and heparin. This drug is in the early stages of development.

Andexanet alfa: It is a recombinant analog of factor Xa and is proposed for reversal of oral factor Xa inhibitors like rivaroxaban, edoxaban, and apixaban. It rapidly reverses the action of these drugs and restores thrombin generation.

Idarucizumab: It is a licensed monoclonal antibody that specifically acts as a reversal agent for dabigatran. It has a 350 times higher affinity for dabigatran than thrombin. Hence it forms a complex with dabigatran and is excreted by the kidneys.

If a patient on direct oral anticoagulants like dabigatran, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, and apixaban presents with life-threatening bleeds and the reversal agents are not available then other options are the administration of prothrombin complex concentrate, activated prothrombin complex concentrate, or recombinant factor VII-A. Hemodialysis is useful in severe bleeding due to dabigatran. 

Other reversal agents for anticoagulants:

  • Protamine sulphate - Heparin
  • Vitamin K - Warfarin

Note:

Andexanet alfa has received US-FDA approval in May 2018 as a reversal agent for rivaroxaban and apixaban.

question.text: Nivolumab is used as a che​ckpoint inhibitor in
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hodgkin's lymphoma

Nivolumab is used as a checkpoint inhibitor in Hodgkin's lymphoma.

FDA approved uses of nivolumab:

  • Advanced melanoma
  • Advanced non-small cell lung cancer(NSCLC) that are previously treated
  • Renal cell carcinoma
  • Advanced head and neck cancers
  • Refractory/relapsed classical Hodgkin's lymphoma

Nivolumab is a checkpoint inhibitor that blocks the interaction between PD-1 and its ligands. It is a fully human monoclonal IgG4 antibody. It has a good response rate in patients with pretreated solid tumors and hematological malignancies. Similar effectiveness is also seen with pembrolizumab which is also an anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody.

Adverse effects:

  • In melanoma patients rash is a commonly seen side effect 
  • fatigue, dyspnea, musculoskeletal pain, cough,  decreased appetite, and constipation can be seen in advanced squamous NSCLC patients
  • Pneumonitis, colitis, nephritis, hepatitis, and renal dysfunction are also seen

Important note:

The FDA on May 2021 has approved the use of nivolumab in patients having completely resected esophageal or gastroesophageal junction cancers with residual pathologic disease who have received neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy.

question.text: A patient on digoxin, pota‌ssium chloride, clarithro​mycin, atenolol, and tria‍mterene developed atrial ​fibrillation with control​led ventricular rate. Ser‍um digoxin levels were ra‌ised. Which of his medica​tions is responsible for ‍the same?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Clarithromycin

Elevated serum digoxin levels and the development of atrial fibrillation with controlled ventricular rate are suggestive of digoxin toxicity. Clarithromycin when given along with digoxin can cause digoxin toxicity.

P-glycoprotein pumps play a major role in the elimination of digoxin. Drugs that inhibit P-glycoprotein can thereby decrease the elimination of digoxin and lead to digoxin toxicity. Macrolide antibiotics like clarithromycin and erythromycin are inhibitors of the P-glycoprotein. So clarithromycin when given along with digoxin can cause digoxin toxicity.

Other drugs that inhibit P-glycoprotein are - Amiodarone, quinidine, verapamil, diltiazem, cyclosporine, itraconazole, propafenone, and flecainide.

Digoxin is one of the cardiac glycosides which is derived from the digitalis plant and used clinically.

It inhibits Na+/K+ ATPase, a membrane-bound transporter to increase intracellular sodium. As a result, there is less expulsion of calcium from the cell by sodium-calcium exchanger (NCX). Increased calcium inside the myocyte leads to an increase in cardiac contractility.

The most common cardiac manifestations of digitalis toxicity include atrioventricular junctional rhythm, premature ventricular depolarizations, ventricular bigeminy, ventricular tachycardia, and second-degree AV blockade.

Factors that increase the risk of digoxin toxicity are:

  • Hypercalcemia
  • Hypomagnesemia
  • Hypokalemia- It increases the binding of the digoxin to the Na+/K+ ATPase pump. 
  • Drugs causing hypokalemia- loop and thiazide diuretics, amphotericin B, corticosteroids
  • Drugs that decrease digoxin elimination (inhibitors of P-glycoprotein)
  • Renal failure
  • Hypothyroidism

 Triamterene, atenolol, and potassium chloride cause hyperkalemia, and therefore do not cause digoxin toxicity.

question.text: A patient with chronic kid‌ney disease underwent a n​ephrectomy. Which of the ‍following can be administ​ered as a postoperative a​nalgesic in this patient?‍
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Acetaminophen

Acetaminophen can be given as an analgesic for the patient as it is the least nephrotoxic among the given options.

Analgesia in CKD patients:

Acetaminophen is considered a safer non-narcotic analgesic in chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients. For more severe pains opioid analgesics like tramadol or fentanyl are used. 

Even though acetaminophen is considered safe, with chronic high dosage it can also become nephrotoxic.

NSAIDs like naproxen, indomethacin, diclofenac, etc are not used in CKD patients because of their direct nephrotoxic effects. In healthy normal individuals, NSAIDs have little effect on renal function and blood pressure. But in conditions where the regulatory systems are impaired as hypovolemia, congestive heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis, chronic kidney disease, or other conditions where the renin-angiotensin system is activated, renal function by the formation of prostaglandins are very important.

NSAIDs cause impairment of prostaglandin-induced inhibition of chlorine reabsorption and antidiuretic hormone action. This will cause salt and water retention. It also inhibits COX-2 derived prostaglandins which regulate the renal medullary blood flow and would lead to a rise in blood pressure, increased cardiovascular thrombotic events, and cardiac failure. It can also cause electrolyte abnormalities like hyponatremia and hyperkalemia.

question.text: A patient with renal insuf‌ficiency presented with v​ery low urine output, ped‍al edema, headache and BP​ 160/90. Which anti-hyper​tensive can be administer‍ed?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chlorthalidone

The antihypertensive that can be given in this case is chlorthalidone. The patient in this case is having renal insufficiency but there is no proteinuria mentioned in the question stem. So among the given options, the thiazide diuretic chlorthalidone can be administered as antihypertensive in this patient. 

Management of hypertension in chronic kidney disease(CKD):

ACE inhibitors or ARBs are considered the first-line drugs in patients with proteinuria. These agents effectively reduce blood pressure, proteinuria and prevent kidney decline. Calcium channel blockers can be added if necessary.

For patients who do not have proteinuria, there is no established first-line therapy. One or two of the following drugs can be used:

  • Thiazides/thiazide-like diuretics
  • ACE inhibitors or ARBs
  • Calcium channel blockers

In patients presenting with fluid retention or fluid overload, thiazide diuretics such as chlorthalidone and hydrochlorothiazide are recommended for management. In CKD stages 1 to 3 (GFR >=30ml/min), thiazides are recommended, while loop diuretics such as bumetanide, furosemide are used in stages 4-5 (GFR < 30ml/min).

Other options:

Option A: Aliskiren is a direct renin inhibitor. It effectively lowers blood pressure, reduces albuminuria, and limits left ventricular hypertrophy.

Option C: Amlodipine is a calcium channel blocker. A common side effect of amlodipine is the production of peripheral edema.

Option D: Prazosin is a selective α1 antagonist. It is generally not used as an initial agent to treat hypertension, except in symptomatic prostatism or nightmares linked to posttraumatic stress disorder. Headache is one of the side effects of prazosin.

question.text: A pregnant woman was presc‌ribed indomethacin. Which​ of the following effects‍ does the drug have on th​e fetus?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Premature closure of ductus arteriosus

Indomethacin can cause premature closure of ductus arteriosus if given to a pregnant woman.

Indomethacin is approved for the closure of persistent ductus arteriosus in premature infants. It is given intravenously. One of its limiting factors is the development of renal toxicity in neonates.

Indomethacin is a nonselective COX inhibitor. It has anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and antipyretic properties. It can be used in the management of conditions like rheumatoid arthritis, gouty arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, etc. But its use is limited due to the high rate of intolerance and availability of safer agents.

Adverse effects: Diarrhea with ulcerative bowel lesions, acute pancreatitis, and hepatitis are seen. Frontal headache is the most frequent CNS effect. Dizziness, light-headedness, vertigo, and mental confusion can occur. Neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, and rarely aplastic anemia can also occur.

Note:

Prostaglandin analogs are indicated in the maintenance of patency of the ductus arteriosus.

question.text: Which of the following can‌ be prescribed in case of​ an open angle glaucoma w‍ith bronchial asthma?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Latanoprost

Latanoprost can be given in a case of open-angle glaucoma with bronchial asthma.

Latanoprost is a PGF2α analog and it is not associated with systemic side effects like bronchospasm and hence can be given for asthmatic patients. Prostaglandin analogs are the first choice drugs for open-angle glaucoma.

Mechanism of action: It reduces intraocular pressure by altering the ciliary muscle tension and improving the outflow of the aqueous humor.

Advantages of latanoprost:

  • Good efficacy
  • Once-daily application
  • Absence of systemic side effects

Disadvantage: High cost

Adverse effects:

  • Blurring of vision
  • Iris pigmentation
  • Thickening and darkening of eyelashes
  • Macular edema can occur especially in aphakic patients.

Other options:

Option A- Timolol is a non-selective beta-blocker used topically in glaucoma. It is associated with systemic effects by absorption through the nasolacrimal duct and can cause life-threatening bronchospasm in asthmatics and COPD patients. Hence they are not given in in this case.

Option B- Gemeprost is a PGE1 analog used for the termination of early pregnancy.

Option D- Mannitol infusion is given for acute congestive glaucoma and not for open-angle glaucoma. It causes decongestion of the eye by its osmotic action.

question.text: A patient on aspirin prese‌nted with occult blood in​ the stool. This is due t‍o inhibition of____ by as​pirin
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thromboxane

Aspirin causes inhibition of cyclooxygenase-1(COX-1) which would inhibit the formation of thromboxane A2. Thromboxane A2 is an inducer of platelet aggregation and is a potent vasoconstrictor. Hence inhibition of its formation is responsible for the bleeding complications of aspirin.

Aspirin is a noncompetitive, irreversible inhibitor of the cyclooxygenase(COX) enzyme. It is a nonselective COX inhibitor and inhibits both COX-1 and COX-2. 

Uses of aspirin:

  • Analgesic and antipyretic uses.
  • Acute rheumatic fever
  • Rheumatoid arthritis
  • Post myocardial infarction and stroke due to its antiplatelet action.
  • Prevention of preeclampsia

Adverse effects:

Nausea, vomiting, epigastric discomfort, and increased occult blood in stools are seen with analgesic doses(0.5-2g/day). Antiinflammatory doses(3-5g/day) can produce salicylism characterized by dizziness, tinnitus, vertigo, hyperventilation, reversible loss of hearing and vision, etc. It can cause elevation of liver enzymes and hepatic damage. Hypersensitivity reactions are also seen.

Reye's syndrome is a rare condition that can occur when salicylates like aspirin are given in children having viral infections like influenza.

question.text: A 60-year-old postmenopaus‌al female patient with a ​previous history of Colle‍'s fracture came with com​plaints of lower backache​. On evaluation, her T sc‍ore was -2.5. Which of th‌e following statements ar​e false about the managem‍ent of her condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Teriparatide should be sta‌rted before supplementing​ with bisphosphonates
Bisphosphonates are not gi‌ven for more than a year
options.label: B
C
options.text: Calcium requirement is 120‌0 mg per day
Oral vitamin D3 is given a‌long with oral calcium
options.label: D

question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bisphosphonates are not given for more than a year

Bisphosphonates are given for periods of more than one year (Option B is false). In this case, as the patient is having a history of osteoporotic fracture, teriparatide can be given before bisphosphonates.

Pharmacologic management of osteoporosis:

Bisphosphonates: These are pyrophosphate analogs that act by directly inhibiting bone resorption. The antiresorptive action is mainly due to its direct inhibitory effect on osteoclasts. It causes osteoclast apoptosis as well as the prevention of hydroxyapatite dissolution. Long-term bisphosphonates therapy is given for durations of 3-5 years, depending on the fracture risk of the patient. Since they are associated with osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical femur fractures, a drug holiday may be advised after long-term management.

Teriparatide is a recombinant PTH analog that has an anabolic effect on bone homeostasis by increasing osteoblastic activity. It increases bone mineral density and decreases the risk of fractures in postmenopausal women. Indications of teriparatide therapy include the history of osteoporotic fracture, multiple risk factors for fracture, intolerance, or failure of previous osteoporosis therapy. It is only approved for 2 years of use. Clinical trials that used teriparatide prior to bisphosphonate have been proven effective.

Denosumab is a human monoclonal antibody with a mechanism of action similar to that of osteoprotegerin (OPG). It binds to RANK Ligand (RANKL), thereby inhibiting its binding to the RANK receptor of the surface of osteoclasts. This prevents RANK receptor activation and subsequent bone resorption.

Selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs) - Estrogen has a protective effect that prevents accelerated bone loss. This is carried out by reducing the bone resorption effects of parathyroid hormone (PTH). Keeping in line with these effects, osteoporosis prevention in postmenopausal women has been attributed to the use of SERMs such as raloxifene. It acts as an estrogen agonist on the bone and liver.

Calcium and Vitamin D supplementation: Calcium supplementation in the elderly suppresses bone turnover and improves bone mineral density. 1200mg of calcium is daily required in adults of more than 50 years of age. Vitamin D supplementation with 400-800IU/day improves intestinal calcium absorption, suppresses bone remodeling, and improves bone mineral density.

question.text: Which of the following ant​i-diabetic drugs is assoc​iated with the increased ​risk of fractures?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Canagliflozin

Canagliflozin is associated with an increased risk of fractures. 

Canagliflozin is a sodium-glucose transporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitor. SGLT2 is a Na+-glucose cotransporter that is located in the proximal convoluted tubule. They reabsorb glucose and sodium from the tubular lumen back into the blood through the epithelial cells. SGLT2 inhibitors block the transport of glucose in the proximal tubule and promote glycosuria and hence, lowering blood glucose.

The currently available SGLT2 inhibitors are canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, and empagliflozin. Other than decreasing blood glucose they also decrease blood pressure and, cause weight loss of 2–4 kg. Empagliflozin and canagliflozin reduce the risk for major cardiovascular events.

The main side effect of SGLT2 inhibitors is an increase in lower urinary tract infections and genital mycotic infections. This is because of their glycosuric properties. A recent warning from the FDA says that SGLT2 inhibitors may increase the risk of fractures. They also affect circulating levels of parathyroid hormone, and 1,25-hydroxy vitamin D thereby affecting the mineral balance in bone.

Other options:

Option A: Rosiglitazone is a thiazolidinedione that acts as a peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ agonist in the adipose tissue which increases insulin sensitivity and adipose differentiation. Side effects are weight gain, edema, and increased risk of fractures. Compared to rosiglitazone, canagliflozin is commonly used in clinical practice. American diabetes association recommends canagliflozin as the first-line drug along with metformin, in patients with a high risk of cardiovascular disease, renal failure, and heart failure. Even when thiazolidinediones are required, clinicians prefer pioglitazone over rosiglitazone due to the higher risk of cardiovascular-related mortality in rosiglitazone. Therefore, canagliflozin would be a better option compared to rosiglitazone. 

Option B: Liraglutide is a long-acting glucagon-like peptide-1 agonist. Nausea, diarrhea, and acute pancreatitis are some frequent side effects.

Option C: Voglibose reduces the intestinal absorption of starch, dextrin, and disaccharides by inhibiting the action of α-glucosidase in the intestinal brush border. The most prominent adverse effects are malabsorption, flatulence, diarrhea, and abdominal bloating.

question.text: Which among the following ​drugs is the new FDA appr​oved immune check point i​nhibitor for carcinoma en​dometrium?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pembrolizumab

The new FDA-approved immune checkpoint inhibitor for carcinoma endometrium is pembrolizumab.

Pembrolizumab acts by inhibiting programmed death receptor - 1 (PD-1) and was used for the treatment of advanced melanoma. Now, the FDA has approved the use of pembrolizumab for any cancer with mismatch repair (MMR) deficiency or high microsatellite instability (MSI-H).

On March 21, 2022, the food and drug administration approved pembrolizumab, as a single agent, for patients with advanced endometrial carcinoma that is microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) or mismatch repair deficient (dMMR), as determined by an FDA-approved test.

Other options:

Option A: Nivolumab is an immune checkpoint inhibitor that acts by inhibiting programmed death receptor - 1 (PD-1) and is used for the treatment of advanced melanoma and relapsed/refractory classical Hodgkin lymphoma.

Option C:  Trastuzumab is a monoclonal antibody that inhibits the HER2 receptor. It is used in the treatment of HER2-positive breast cancer.

Option D: Ipilimumab is a monoclonal antibody that binds to cytotoxic T lymphocyte–associated Protein 4 (CTLA-4) and is approved for the treatment of late-stage melanoma.

question.text: A hospital is conducting a​ study to check the effic​acy of statins in multipl​e centers. There are 4-5 ​patients per center and h​alf of the patients recei​ve the drug and the other‌ half receive the placebo​. Neither the patients no​r clinicians know which d‌rug is being administered​. What phase of the clini‌cal trial describes the a‌bove scenario?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Phase 3

A hospital conducting a double-blinded study in multiple centers to check the efficacy of statins describes phase 3 of the clinical trial. A phase 2 clinical trial is generally conducted at a few centers (2-4) by physicians.

Phase 3 of a clinical trial is also known as a multisite trial. It is conducted on a large patient population (500–3000) by several physicians at multiple centers. This phase involves patients who have been diagnosed with the disease that the drug claims to treat. Its purpose is to confirm the efficacy of the newly developed drug in a larger population. Phase 3 is randomized, controlled, and may be blinded.

question.text: Which of the following sta​tements is true regarding​ memantine? 1. Its therap​eutic effect is due to it​s action on NMDA. 2. It i​s reserved for moderate-t​o-severe diseases. 3. It ‌is used as monotherapy an​d should not be used with​ other cholinesterase inh‌ibitors. 4. It is given a​t a daily dose of 15–30 m‌g/day.
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2

1 and 2 are true statements regarding memantine.

Memantine is a non-competitive NMDA receptor antagonist. It inhibits glutamate excitotoxicity. It delays the progression of dementia in Alzheimer's disease. Commonly, it is started in patients with moderate-to-severe disease.

It can be given both as monotherapy or can be given along with cholinesterase inhibitors. It can be started at a dose of 5 mg once daily and then progressively increased up to 10 mg twice daily for a minimum of 6 months. 

It can cause dizziness and headache. Since it is excreted in the kidney, careful dose adjustments should be made in patients with renal failure.

question.text: A patient is brought with ​altered sensorium and sei​zures. Attender shows the​ laboratory report which ​reveals elevated transami​nases. Which of the follo​wing can be used in this ‌condition?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Oxazepam

Oxazepam can be used in patients with elevated transaminases. It is short-acting and so, can be used in patients with liver impairment or brain damage.

Oxazepam is an orally available benzodiazepine used to treat anxiety and alcohol withdrawal states. Hepatic oxidation is decreased in persons with liver disease and the elderly. Oxazepam and lorazepam undergo only hepatic glucuronidation.

Other options:

Option A: Midazolam is the benzodiazepine of choice for induction of anesthesia. The onset of anesthesia is within 30 to 60 seconds. It can also be used to control seizures, but there is no difference in the efficacy of intravenous midazolam and intravenous diazepam.

Option B: Diazepam is a long-acting benzodiazepine. It is metabolized in the liver to active metabolites like nordazepam which are long-acting. Diazepam and its long-acting metabolites can accumulate significantly in elderly patients with liver disease and therefore should not be used in such cases.

Option C: Alprazolam is metabolized by hepatic oxidation which is significantly decreased in liver impairment and elderly patients.

question.text: Which among the following ​is the false statement re​garding statins?

options.label: A
options.text: Although HMG-CoA reductase​ inhibitors substantially​ reduce the risk of cardi​ovascular events, there i​s mild increase in lipopr​otein a (Lpa) levels.
These drugs should not be ​stopped even in severe co​nditions like injury, sur​gery, etc.
options.label: B

options.text: They can be given with ver​apamil and other enzyme i​nhibitors.
options.label: C
D
options.text: With the long term use, th​ere is slight increase in​ the incidence of type 2 ​diabetes mellitus.

question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. They can be given with verapamil and other enzyme inhibitors.

The false statement regarding statins is that they can be given with verapamil and other enzyme inhibitors.

Statins like atorvastatin and rosuvastatin are metabolized by the cytochrome 3A4 enzymes of the liver. Verapamil is a cytochrome 3A4 inhibitor and may interfere with statin degradation. This leads to an increase in serum statin levels. The most important feature of statin toxicity is myopathy. It can present as myalgia but can sometimes also lead to fatal rhabdomyolysis. 

Statins are the most commonly used hypolipidemic drugs. Statins act by inhibiting the rate-limiting HMG-CoA reductase enzyme, which in turn inhibits cholesterol synthesis. They decrease levels of low-density lipoproteins (LDL) and triglycerides and increase the levels of high-density lipoproteins (HDL) in plasma.

Other options:

Option A: Lipoprotein (lp) a is an LDL molecule that has apolipoprotein b and an additional apolipoprotein a. Studies indicate that these molecules are atherogenic and may independently cause cardiovascular disease. Although HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors substantially reduce the risk of cardiovascular events, there is a mild increase in lipoprotein a levels.

Option B: Statins can be continued during surgery. These drugs have proved to decrease overall mortality due to cardiovascular events. Statins also influence inflammatory responses and can be safely used in trauma.

Option D: Chronic administration of high statin doses also leads to an increased incidence of type 2 diabetes mellitus.

question.text: Identify the drugs marked ​as A, B, and C.

options.text: A - Aspirin, B - Eptifibat​ide, C - Vorapaxar
options.label: B

options.text: A - Aspirin, B - Eptifibat​ide, C - Prasugrel
options.label: C
D
options.text: A - Aspirin, B - Prasugrel​, C - Eptifibatide

question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A - Aspirin, B - Eptifibatide, C - Vorapaxar

The drugs marked A, B and C are aspirin, eptifibatide, and vorapaxar, respectively.

Aspirin causes inhibition of cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1), which would inhibit the formation of thromboxane A2. Thromboxane A2 is an inducer of platelet aggregation and is a potent vasoconstrictor. Hence, inhibition of its formation is responsible for antiplatelet action.

Aspirin is a non-competitive, irreversible inhibitor of the cyclooxygenase (COX) enzyme. It is a nonselective COX inhibitor and inhibits both COX-1 and COX-2. 

Abciximab, tirofiban, and eptifibatide act by blocking Gp IIb/IIIa receptors. They are mainly used during percutaneous coronary intervention for acute coronary syndrome. They carry a high risk of bleeding and can cause thrombocytopenia.

Vorapaxar primarily inhibits platelet aggregation caused by thrombin. PAR-1 activation by thrombin contributes to platelet aggregation. Vorapaxar is a competitive antagonist of protease-activated receptor-1 (PAR-1). Vorapaxar is indicated in combination with aspirin and/or clopidogrel to reduce thromboembolic events in patients with MI or peripheral vascular disease.

Prasugrel is an irreversible P2Y12 inhibitor and lasts for the entire lifetime of a platelet.

Prasugrel is a prodrug that is used in patients with acute coronary syndrome who have undergone percutaneous coronary intervention. It reduces the rate of thrombotic cardiovascular events in such patients.

question.text: Which of the following is ​false regarding disulfira​m? Does not stop cravings​ Accumulates acetaldehyde​ Inhibits alcohol dehydro​genase Starting dose is 2​50 mg
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Only 3

The wrong statement/s regarding disulfiram is only 3.

Disulfiram is an irreversible inhibitor of both cytosolic and mitochondrial forms of aldehyde dehydrogenase. It is used in behavioral modification for alcohol de-addiction. The principle of action is aversive conditioning (not anti-craving).

Disulfiram can be given only to highly motivated individuals. It should not be administered until the person has abstained from alcohol for at least 12 hours. The disulfiram-alcohol reaction may persist as long as 14 days after the last dose of disulfiram.

Alcohol consumption during disulfiram therapy can lead to increased concentrations of acetaldehyde. This can cause aversive reactions, resulting in flushing, pulsating headache, throbbing pain in the head and neck, nausea, vomiting, rashes, respiratory difficulties, chest pain, and autonomic manifestations.

Disulfiram is usually given in the dose of 250 mg/day (range of 125–500 mg/day).

question.text: A patient presented with a​ lesion, as shown in the ​image below. She is an im​munocompromised patient c​urrently on HAART. What a​re the systemic antifunga​l drugs that can be added‌ along with the HAART in ​this patient? Highly acti​ve antiretroviral therapy‌ (HAART)

options.label: A
options.text: Inj. Amphotericin B 4-8 we​eks, followed by oral itr​aconazole

options.label: B
options.text: Inj. Amphotericin B 8 week​s, followed by oral posac​onazole
Inj. Fluconazole, followed​ by oral fluconazole
options.label: C
D
options.text: Inj. Amphotericin B, follo​wed by flucytosine

question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Inj. Amphotericin B 8 weeks, followed by oral posaconazole

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of mucormycosis. The patient can be given injection amphotericin B for 8 weeks, followed by oral posaconazole.

Mucormycosis is an opportunistic mycosis. It is typically seen in immunocompromised patients and invades blood vessels.

The rhino-orbital-cerebral is the most common form of mucormycosis. Patients present with rhinitis, eye or facial pain, and facial numbness, followed by the onset of conjunctival suffusion and swelling along with blurry vision.

Diagnosis is made by biopsy with histopathologic examination. The biopsy shows characteristic wide, ribbon-like aseptate hyphal elements that branch at right angles.

The image below shows biopsy findings seen in mucormycosis:

Treatment of the infection includes 4 steps:

  1. Initiation of therapy (amphotericin B) as early as possible. Posaconazole can also be used in the management of this condition.
  2. Surgical debridement
  3. Reversal of underlying conditions and risk factors
  4. Treatment of underlying malignancy if present

Amphotericin B is a broad-spectrum antifungal. It binds to ergosterol in the fungal membrane and forms pores or channels in the fungal cell membrane. This allows the leakage of cytosolic molecules and ions, leading to a loss of membrane integrity.

Other options:

Option A: Itraconazole can be used for the treatment of chronic aspergillosis if there is resistance or failure of voriconazole. Ketoconazole is used for both dermatophytosis and deep mycosis, but it has been replaced by itraconazole.

Option C: Fluconazole is used for the treatment of candidiasis and cryptococcosis.

Option D: Amphotericin B in combination with 5-flucytosine is used as induction treatment for cryptococcal meningitis.

question.text: A patient who is on treatm​ent for hyperlipidemia de​velops gallstones. What i​s the mechanism of action​ of the causative drug th​at was given to this pati​ent?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Activates PPAR alpha

The antilipidemic drugs likely to cause gallstones are the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs) that act by activating PPAR alpha.

PPARs are a superfamily of nuclear receptors involved in the regulation of energy homeostasis and metabolic function. It has three subtypes:

  • PPARα - reduces triglyceride level 
  • PPARγ - causes insulin sensitization 
  • PPARδ - enhances fatty acids metabolism

Lipoprotein lipase (LPL) is a key enzyme in the degradation of VLDL. Fibrates bind to PPAR alpha and cause stimulation of lipoprotein lipase enzyme. Increased LPL synthesis enhances the clearance of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins. Additionally, fibrates also stimulate fatty acid oxidation and reduce the expression of apo C-III (inhibitor of lipolysis). All fibrates increase the lithogenicity of bile, thereby increasing the risk of gall stones
