question.text: A 25-year-old male present​ed with abdominal pain. O​n examination, a painful ​growing mass is felt in t‌he right hypochondrium. A​spiration of the cyst is ‍shown below. Identify the​ organism.
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Echinococcus granulosus

The patient presenting with abdominal pain and a growing mass in the right hypochondrium has a hydatid cyst of the liver. Aspirate of the cyst shows Echinococcus granulosus (with hooks).

Echinococcus granulosus is the most common causative agent in hydatid cysts, while Echinococcus multilocularis and Echinococcus ligartus account for a small number of cases.

Dogs are the definitive hosts of E. granulosus. Sheep are the usual intermediate hosts, but humans are accidental intermediate hosts. Humans are end-stage hosts of the parasite since there is no human-to-human transmission.

Approximately 75% of hydatid cysts are located in the right lobe of the liver and are solitary. The clinical presentation of a hydatid cyst is largely asymptomatic until complications occur. The most common presenting symp­toms are abdominal pain, dyspepsia, and vomiting. The most frequent sign is hepatomegaly.

The life cycle of Echinococcus is depicted in the image below:

The hydatid cyst wall consists of 3 layers:

  • Pericyst- the outer dense fibrous capsule that is formed as a result of host inflammatory response.
  • Ectocyst - the intermediate layer consisting of acellular, chitinous, laminated hyaline material.
  • Endocyst - the inner germinal layer that is cellular and consists of several nuclei embedded in protoplasmic mass and is extremely thin. It is the vital layer of the cyst, and it is the site of asexual reproduction, giving rise to brood capsules with scolices.

The brood capsules are cellular masses in the hydatid fluid, which consists of scoleces. In a definitive host, these scoleces develop into adult tapeworms, while in the intermediate hosts, these develop into new hydatid cysts. The brood capsules are attached to the endocyst by a pedicle or stalk. 

The brood capsules may mature and detach from the mother cyst and become the daughter cysts, which are replicas of the mother cysts. The freed brood capsules and scoleces present in the hydatid fluid are called hydatid sand.

Other options:

Option B: Hymenolepis nana (dwarf tapeworm) is the smallest tapeworm. Humans are the definitive host. It has no intermediate host. It occurs more commonly in children, and the patient acquires this infection by ingesting food or water contaminated with eggs. The egg attaches to the intestine and develops into the larva and adult worm. The adult worm resides in the small intestine. Patients are usually asymptomatic. However, in heavy infections, they present with nausea, anorexia, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, and irritability. Pruritus may also be present due to an allergic response.

Option C: Taenia solium is a parasitic tapeworm transmitted through undercooked pork, causing intestinal infection (taeniasis) or more severe cyst formation in tissues, including the brain (cysticercosis). It's prevalent in regions with poor sanitation and where pork is consumed.

Option D: Taenia saginata is a parasitic tapeworm transmitted through undercooked beef containing cysticerci (“measly” beef). Humans are the definitive host, and cows are the intermediate hosts. Taenia solium and Taenia saginata eggs are morphologically indistinguishable.

question.text: A 16-month-old boy is foun​d to weigh 8kg. A WHO gro​wth chart(weight-for-age)​ is provided below. Plot ‍the growth chart for this​ child. What is the most ‌appropriate advice based ​on the plotted graph?

options.label: C
options.text: Severe malnutrition - refe​r to nutrition rehabilita​tion center
Moderate malnutrition - te​ach the mother on how to ​feed
options.label: D

question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Moderate malnutrition - teach the mother on how to feed

The weight for age of the child falls in between -2SD and -3SD as shown in the growth chart below, which is suggestive of moderate malnutrition and the mother should be taught to feed the baby properly. 

The primary treatment in mild and moderate malnutrition involves providing sufficient protein and energy intake, with a recommended minimum of 150 kcal/kg/day. Nutritious home food is advised, and frequent feeding (up to 7 times a day) may be required to achieve the necessary energy intake. High-fat foods are often used to increase energy in therapeutic diets. 

Animal-source foods, such as milk and eggs, are recommended by WHO as they provide necessary amino acids and nutrients. Plant-source foods like legumes and cereals can also be good protein sources. A slight increase in protein intake (3g/kg/day) is sufficient for catch-up growth with high energy intake. Milk and vegetable protein mixtures can be used as a protein source and adequate minerals and vitamins are also added.

Weight gain is the best measure of treatment efficacy for mild and moderate malnutrition. 

Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) should be referred to a hospital for proper management. Uncomplicated SAM can be managed at home under supervision. Complicated SAM should be treated as an inpatient. 

Management of SAM is summarized in the image below. 

The World Health Organization(WHO) has established international standards for normal child growth from birth to 5 years of age. The normalization of the anthropometric measures is done in terms of z-scores (standard deviation scores). The anthropometric indicators are marked in a growth chart which is compared with a reference curve.

The anthropometric measures used are weight for age, height for age, weight for height, BMI, and mid-upper arm circumference.

  • Low weight for height, or wasting, indicates acute malnutrition. 
  • High weight-for-height indicates overweight.
  • Low height-for-age, or stunting, indicates chronic malnutrition. This is the best indicator of long-term nutritional status in the pediatric population.
  • Low weight for the age indicates acute or chronic malnutrition. It does not differentiate between wasting and stunting. Hence, it has limited clinical significance.

Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) is used for the screening of wasting in children between 6 months to 5 years. In children aged 6 months to 5 years, MUAC <11.5cm is considered as severe malnutrition.

question.text: Which of the following fea​tures differentiates the ​exocrine pancreas from th‍e parotid gland?

options.label: A
C

question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Absence of striated duct

Absence of striated duct in exocrine pancreas differentiates it from the parotid gland.

The exocrine pancreas is comprised entirely of serous acini. Hence, its general structure is similar to that of the parotid gland, but the two are easily distinguished by:

  • The parotid gland has striated and intercalated intralobular ducts, whereas the pancreas has only the intercalated type.
  • The excretory ducts of the parotid gland are striated columnar, whereas the excretory duct of the pancreas is a simple columnar.

question.text: Pacemaker generating the r‌hythm for breathing is __‍______

options.label: B
options.text: Dorsal group of neurons in‌ the medulla

question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pre-Bőtzinger complex

Pre-Botzinger complex generates the rhythm for automated breathing.

  • These are also known as pacemaker cells located in the medulla.
  • These are the first set of neurons that initiate inspiration.
  • These neurons discharge rhythmically, and they produce rhythmic discharges in the phrenic motor neurons.

Breathing is under the control of both the following:

  • Voluntary control: Located in the cerebral cortex (via corticospinal tract)
  • Automatic control: Driven by pacemaker cells in the medulla (Pre-Botzinger complex). These activate motor neurons via cervical (Phrenic nerve innervating diaphragm) and thoracic spinal cord (external intercostal muscle).

There is a reciprocal innervation to expiratory and inspiratory muscles in that motor neurons supplying expiratory muscles are inactive when motor neurons supplying inspiratory muscles are active, and vice versa.

 

Inspiration
Initiation Pre-Botzinger complex (Pacemaker cells) in Medulla
Maintenance Apneustic center in lower Pons stimulates Dorsal group of neurons in the medulla
Termination  Apneustic center inhibited by Vagus and Pneumotaxic center

Regulation of expiration: During quiet breathing, expiration is a passive process; there is no firing of neurons. Ventral respiratory group of neurons are involved in forceful expiration like during exercise.

Mnemonic DIVE: Dorsal respiratory group for Inspiration and Ventral respiratory group for Expiration.

question.text: A person who had dinner at​ 8 pm the previous night,​ tested his blood glucose‍ levels at 7 am the next ​morning. What is the sour​ce of blood glucose in th​is case?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hepatic glycogenolysis

The source of blood glucose in a person fasting overnight for 11 hours (8 pm to 7 am) is hepatic glycogenolysis.

First stage of fasting: The fasting state begins two to four hours after the absorptive/well-fed state. In early fasting i.e; 4-18 hours after the well-fed state, the blood glucose level is maintained by hepatic glycogenolysis. The glycogen stores are sufficient for around 18 hours after a meal following which they start to deplete. So the source of blood glucose in a person fasting for 11 hours will be liver glycogenolysis.

Second stage of fasting: Gluconeogenesis begins 4–6 hours after the last meal but becomes fully active only after stores of liver glycogen are depleted (after 18 hours). They can serve as a source of glucose for up to 2 days.

Substrates for gluconeogenesis are:

  • Glucogenic amino acids ( mainly alanine) from the muscle and
  • Glycerol from adipose tissue 

During fasting, the glucogenic amino acids are transported to the liver, transaminated into pyruvate, and converted to glucose.

Third stage of fasting:

  • Lipolysis occurs in the adipose tissue due to the activity of hormone-sensitive lipase, stimulated by increased glucagon:insulin ratio.
  • Free fatty acids are the source of energy in this stage and not glucose. Triacylglycerols will be hydrolyzed to fatty acids and glycerol. 
  • Beta oxidation of fatty acids takes place which provides acetyl CoA. 
  • In prolonged starvation (>3 days), acetyl CoA is converted to ketone bodies in the liver which will act as the main fuel source for skeletal and heart muscle and can meet up to 20% of the brain’s energy needs.

Final stage of fasting: After several weeks of starvation, ketone body synthesis will not take place due to depleted triacylglycerol stores. Proteins remain the only source of fuel. Protein degradation increases, and death results from a loss of heart, liver, or kidney function.

Role of insulin and glucagon:

When blood glucose falls during fasting, there is increased secretion of glucagon and decreased release of insulin. Hence glucagon:insulin ratio is increased.

Effects of increased glucagon:insulin ratio on enzymes of glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis:

  1. It activates glycogen phosphorylase, the key enzyme of glycogenolysis, and deactivates glycogen synthase. This causes a rapid mobilization of liver glycogen stores to be utilized as fuel.
  2. It favors the synthesis of glucose-6-phosphatase which converts glucose-6-phosphate to glucose. The resulting glucose is used by red blood cells (lack mitochondria) and the brain as they are largely dependant on glucose in the fasting state.
  3. Phosphoenol pyruvate carboxykinase and fructose-1, 6-bisphosphatase are induced, leading to increased gluconeogenesis.
Metabolic process         Fasting state      Fed state
Glucagon: insulin   Increased              Decreased
Gluconeogenesis    Increased                Decreased            
Glycogenolysis  Increased                Decreased
Ketogenesis  Increased                Decreased
Glycogen storage  Decreased  Increased             

Other options:

Option C: Muscle glycogen cannot contribute directly to plasma glucose, since muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase. So glycogen cannot be converted to glucose to be used as fuel during starvation. 

Option D: In the well-fed state/ absorptive state of two to four hours after a meal, dietary glucose is the main source of fuel.

Lente insulin is an intermediate-acting insulin and is a combination of Ultralente and Semilente in the ratio of 7:3

question.text: A 3-year-old toxic child p​resents with tachypnea, h‍igh-grade fever, inspirat​ory stridor, and develope​d difficulty in swallowin‌g with drooling of saliva​ within 4-6 hours of feve‌r. Along with airway mana​gement which of the follo​wing needs to be given?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. IV ceftriaxone

The clinical presentation of a toxic-looking child with high-grade fever, tachypnea, inspiratory stridor, dysphagia, and salivary drooling strongly suggests acute epiglottitis. Once the airway is secured, empirical antimicrobial therapy with intravenous ceftriaxone is recommended in the management of acute epiglottitis. 

The most common causative agents of epiglottitis in vaccinated children are Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus pneumoniae, non-typeable Haemophilus influenzae, and Staphylococcus aureus. The incidence of Haemophilus influenzae type B has decreased significantly due to vaccination. 

The child presents with a high fever, sore throat, dyspnea, dysphagia, and progressive respiratory obstruction. The child may exhibit a toxic appearance, with salivary drooling and assuming a tripod position. The presence of stridor indicates near-complete obstruction of the airway.

Laryngoscopy should be promptly conducted in a controlled setting, such as an operating room or intensive care unit when the diagnosis of epiglottitis is certain or likely based on clinical evaluation. 

Acute epiglottitis is a medical emergency due to unpredictable clinical course and sudden airway obstruction. Immediate airway management through endotracheal or nasotracheal intubation or tracheostomy is crucial, regardless of the severity of respiratory distress. Empiric treatment with antibiotics like ceftriaxone, cefepime, or meropenem is recommended until culture and susceptibility results are available. Dexamethasone may also be administered to reduce pharyngeal edema. 

Other options: 

Option A: Nebulisation with racemic adrenaline is given in moderate to severe croup.

question.text: Which among the following ​is the false statement re​garding statins?

options.label: A
options.text: Although HMG-CoA reductase​ inhibitors substantially​ reduce the risk of cardi​ovascular events, there i​s mild increase in lipopr​otein a (Lpa) levels.
These drugs should not be ​stopped even in severe co​nditions like injury, sur​gery, etc.
options.label: B

options.text: They can be given with ver​apamil and other enzyme i​nhibitors.
options.label: C
D
options.text: With the long term use, th​ere is slight increase in​ the incidence of type 2 ​diabetes mellitus.

question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. They can be given with verapamil and other enzyme inhibitors.

The false statement regarding statins is that they can be given with verapamil and other enzyme inhibitors.

Statins like atorvastatin and rosuvastatin are metabolized by the cytochrome 3A4 enzymes of the liver. Verapamil is a cytochrome 3A4 inhibitor and may interfere with statin degradation. This leads to an increase in serum statin levels. The most important feature of statin toxicity is myopathy. It can present as myalgia but can sometimes also lead to fatal rhabdomyolysis. 

Statins are the most commonly used hypolipidemic drugs. Statins act by inhibiting the rate-limiting HMG-CoA reductase enzyme, which in turn inhibits cholesterol synthesis. They decrease levels of low-density lipoproteins (LDL) and triglycerides and increase the levels of high-density lipoproteins (HDL) in plasma.

Other options:

Option A: Lipoprotein (lp) a is an LDL molecule that has apolipoprotein b and an additional apolipoprotein a. Studies indicate that these molecules are atherogenic and may independently cause cardiovascular disease. Although HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors substantially reduce the risk of cardiovascular events, there is a mild increase in lipoprotein a levels.

Option B: Statins can be continued during surgery. These drugs have proved to decrease overall mortality due to cardiovascular events. Statins also influence inflammatory responses and can be safely used in trauma.

Option D: Chronic administration of high statin doses also leads to an increased incidence of type 2 diabetes mellitus.

question.text: An autopsy was performed t‌o find the cause of death‍ of a person brought dead‍ to the casualty and it s‌howed a fracture of the t‍hyroid cartilage and brui​sing around the neck. The‌ cause of death is?

Both bruising around the neck and the fracture of the thyroid cartilage are findings seen in throttling. Throttling/manual strangulation is when bare hands are used to compress the neck and strangulate.


Mechanism of death:

  • Occlusion of blood vessels supplying blood to the brain (carotid arteries).
  • Occlusion to airway probably plays a minor role if any, in causing death
  • Carotid sinus pressure may result in vagus nerve stimulation, resulting in cardiac arrest (vagal inhibition)

Autopsy findings:

  • Abrasions on the neck: fingernail marks from assailant or victim
  • Fracture of thyroid cartilage
  • Inward fracture of greater cornu of the hyoid bone.

question.text: Identify the virus given i​n the following replicati​on cycle.
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Herpes simplex virus

The given image shows the life cycle of the herpes simplex virus (HSV).

The herpes virus capsid is icosahedral and encloses a core containing a linear double-stranded DNA genome. The nucleocapsid is surrounded by a lipid envelope derived from the modified host cell nuclear membrane. The envelope carries glycoprotein spikes.

Steps of HSV replication:

The virus enters the cell by fusing with the plasma membrane, and viral DNA is released from the capsid at the nuclear pore. This is followed by circularization of the genome and transcription of immediate-early genes.

α-Proteins are products of immediate-early genes. These proteins stimulate the transcription of early genes. β-proteins are products of early genes. These proteins function in DNA replication, to yield concatemeric DNA. Transcription of late genes gives rise to γ-proteins. These primarily consist of viral structural proteins and participate in virion assembly.

Viral DNA is cleaved from concatemers and then packaged into capsids. Enveloped viral particles collect in the endoplasmic reticulum and are then transported by a vesicular movement to the cell surface.

Image shows replication cycle of herpes simplex virus.

Other options:

Option A) The human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) virus is spherical, enveloped RNA virus. The nucleocapsid has an icosahedral shell and a cone-shaped core, enclosing the ribonucleoproteins. The genome icomprises two identical single-stranded, RNA copies, with the reverse transcriptase enzyme, which is a characteristic feature of retroviruses.

The images below show the structure of the HIV virus and its life cycle.

Option C: The hepatitis B virus is a DNA virus with an outer envelope and an inner nucleocapsid. The viral genome consists of two linear strands of DNA in a circular configuration. One of the strands (the plus strand) is incomplete resulting in partially double stranded and partially single-stranded DNA. The images below show the structure and life cycle of the hepatitis B virus.

Option D: Coronavirus are enveloped RNA viruses with a genome consisting of positive sense unsegmented single-stranded RNA. They have petal-shaped surface projections. Coronavirus nucleocapsids develop in the cytoplasm and mature by budding into cytoplasmic vesicles. The images below show the structure and life cycle of coronaviruses.

question.text: In conventional oxygen the​rapy, which device will d​eliver highest FiO2?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Non rebreathing mask

Non rebreathing masks provide highest FiO2 during conventional oxygen therapy.

The non-rebreather mask is a low flow device that can be used to deliver oxygen at higher concentrations (FiO2 80-95%). It uses a reservoir bag to let the oxygen get concentrated while a one-way valve doesn't allow to breathe in expired air.

 This type of masks are used in patients with significant hypoxia, with relatively normal ventilation, such as victims of trauma or carbon monoxide exposure.

Other options:

A) Venturi mask:

  • Venturi mask is a high-flow, fixed-performance oxygen delivery system and the highest oxygen concentration (FiO2) delivered is 60% at a flow rate of 15 L/min.
  • It is based on the Bernoulli Principle, which states that in order to maintain a constant flow, a fluid must increase its velocity as it flows through a constriction.
  • It is available in different colors, with the green valve venturi mask providing 60% FiO2. 
  • This is useful with patients who require greater FiO2 such as COPD patients, where it is important to provide controlled oxygenation.

 

 

B) Hudson mask:

  • Also known as simple face mask
  • Low-flow, variable performance device 
  • They provide an oxygen flow rate of up to 5-10 L/min and provide a variable FiO2.
  • The body of the mask functions as reservoir for both oxygen and expired carbon dioxide.
  • Used in patients who require oxygen therapy for shorter periods of time.

D) Nasal cannula:

  • They are low-flow, variable performance devices, with flow rate of 1-4 L/min.
  • Used in patients who require low supplemental oxygen.
  • Nasopharynx acts as the reservoir in such cannulas.

Indications of a nasal cannula and other low-flow oxygen delivery systems include 

  • Minute ventilation < 8–10 L/min
  • Breathing frequencies < 20 breaths/min
  • Normal inspiratory flow (10–30 L/min).

question.text: A forest worker developed ‌skin lesions over the for​earm, which initially sta‍rted as macules but then ‌became nodules. Histology‌ of the nodules shows the​ following findings. Whic‍h of the following is tru​e regarding this conditio​n?

options.label: A
options.text: The organism does not inva‌de underlying fascia, ten​don, muscle, or joints.
Angioinvasion is common, e‌specially in people with ​hemolytic anemia.
options.label: B

options.text: It is a dimorphic organism‌, and yeast forms are see​n in clinical sample.
options.label: C

options.text: These bodies are formed by‌ engulfment of the dead f​ungi by the macrophages.
options.label: D

question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. The organism does not invade underlying fascia, tendon, muscle, or joints.

The most likely diagnosis based on the clinical vignette and the histopathology showing sclerotic bodies is chromoblastomycosis. It is primarily a subcutaneous mycosis and does not commonly invade underlying tissue, tendon, or joints.

Chromoblastomycosis is caused by dematiaceous fungi, primarily Fonsecaea spp and Cladophialophora spp. Not all species of dematiaceous fungi are known to be thermally dimorphic fungi (Option C)

Chromoblastomycosis, the most common chromomycosis, is more commonly seen in tropical areas among agricultural workers and woodcutters who walk barefoot. Traumatic implantation is the mode of infection. Most often, the infection occurs in trauma-prone sites, such as exposed areas of the lower and upper limbs.

Patients present with warty cauliflower-like cutaneous nodules on the feet and lower legs. The disease generally remains localized, with slow peripheral extension. Lymphatic spread can occur.

Diagnosis is made by the demonstration of sclerotic bodies, also called copper-penny bodies, in tissue sections. Sclerotic bodies appear as round or irregular, dark brown bodies with septae.

First-line management includes itraconazole or terbinafine. Flucytosine used on its own or combined with amphotericin B may also be effective. For small lesions, surgical excision is the therapy of choice.

question.text: The most common site of br‌anchial cyst is ______.

options.text: Junction of upper and midd‌le third of the sternomas​toid muscle
options.label: A

options.text: Junction of middle and low‌er third of the sternomas​toid muscle
options.label: B

options.text: Between the two heads of t‌he sternomastoid muscle
options.label: D

question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Junction of upper and middle third of the sternomastoid muscle

The most common site of a branchial cyst is at the junction of the upper and middle third of the sternomastoid muscle at its anterior border.

The below image shows a large right-sided branchial cyst.

Branchial cyst develops due to the persistence of the cervical sinus. The cervical sinus is formed when the 2nd arch mesoderm overgrows the succeeding arches and overhangs them as shown in the image. The space between the overhanging 2nd pharyngeal arch and the 3rd, 4th, and 6th arches is called the cervical sinus. The cavity of the cervical sinus is lined by ectoderm and normally gets obliterated.

Branchial cysts are usually lined by squamous epithelium and contain thick, turbid fluid full of cholesterol crystals. It is fluctuant and may transilluminate when it contains clear fluid.

A branchial fistula may be acquired or congenital. The congenital fistula is seen at the junction of the middle and lower third of the sternomastoid (option B). An acquired fistula is usually seen in cases of incomplete surgery for the branchial cyst or spontaneous rupture, and it is seen at the same site as the cyst.

question.text: What is nutritional therapy in inflammatory bowel disease used for?
question.explanation:
Nutritional therapy is used for inducing remission in Crohn's disease.

Dietary antigens may stimulate an immune response. Hence, nutritional therapies like total parenteral nutrition, enteral nutrition (peptide-based preparations), etc. can be used to provide bowel rest in active Crohn's disease. These interventions cannot be used for maintaining remission.

Ulcerative colitis does not respond to dietary intervention.

Drugs used in treatment of Crohn’s disease:
  • Oral budesonide (mainly for mild to moderate)
  • Oral prednisolone
  • Methotrexate
  • Anti TNF alpha
  • Azathioprine
  • 6-mercaptopurine
  • Monoclonal antibodies
  • Antibiotics

question.text: Which of the following DPP-4 inhibitors requires the dose to be decreased when used concomitantly with ketoconazole?

Correct answer: C. Saxagliptin

The DPP-4 inhibitor that requires dose reduction when used with ketoconazole is saxagliptin.

Ketoconazole is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor, and saxagliptin is primarily metabolized by CYP. Co-administration increases saxagliptin plasma levels significantly

Among DPP-4 inhibitors, saxagliptin uniquely undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism via CYP3A4, making it particularly susceptible to drug–drug interactions with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors. Other DPP-4 inhibitors are renally excreted or have minimal CYP involvement, so interactions are clinically insignificant.

DPP-4 inhibitors (gliptins) act by inhibiting the enzyme dipeptidyl peptidase-4, which normally degrades incretin hormones such as GLP-1 and GIP. By prolonging incretin activity, they enhance glucose-dependent insulin secretion, suppress glucagon, and improve postprandial glucose control without causing hypoglycemia or weight gain.

question.text: All of the following are t‌he core clinical features​ for the diagnosis of Lew‍y body dementia except:

Orthostatic hypotension is not a core clinical feature of Lewy body dementia (LBD) as per DSM-5.

LBD also known as dementia with Lewy bodies is the second most type of progressive dementia after Alzheimer’s disease. Protein deposits, called Lewy bodies, deposit in nerve cells in the brain region involved in thinking, memory, and movement (motor control)

Core features of LBD as per DSM-5 are fluctuating cognition, attention, alertness, recurrent visual hallucination, and Parkinsonian symptoms. Suggestive features are REM sleep behavior disorder and severe neuroleptic sensitivity.
Orthostatic hypotension, erectile dysfunction, and constipation are other features of LBD.

Treatment of LBD includes rivastigmine and donepezil which may improve cognition, and reduce hallucinosis and delusion. Pimavanserin may be used to treat psychosis.

question.text: Which of the following is ​not a hepatic porphyria?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Erythropoietic protoporphyria

Erythropoietic protoporphyria is not a type of hepatic porphyria. 

Porphyrias are classified into erythropoietic and hepatic porphyrias, based on the location of accumulation of heme pathway intermediates:

  1. Erythropoietic porphyrias:
    1. The overproduction of heme pathway intermediates occurs primarily in bone marrow erythroid cells.
    2. They are characterized by cutaneous symptoms and appear in early childhood.
    3. Examples: Congenital erythropoietic porphyria, erythropoietic protoporphyria, X-linked protoporphyria
  2. Hepatic porphyrias:
    1. The overproduction of heme pathway intermediates occurs primarily in the liver.
    2. Acute hepatic porphyrias are characterised by neurologic symptoms and present acutely. Examples: Acute intermittent porphyria, hereditary coproporphyria, variegate porphyria, ALA dehydratase deficient porphyria
    3. Chronic hepatic porphyrias present in adulthood with photosensitivity. Example: Porphyria cutanea tarda

question.text: A young patient came with ‌complaints of acute abdom‍inal pain on and off and ​tingling sensation of lim‌bs and at times weakness ‌of limbs. She had a histo‌ry of eating paint from t​he wall of a newly built ​house. Which of the follo​wing enzyme defect will b‌e the cause of her condit​ion?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. ALA dehydratase

A child with acute abdominal pain, tingling sensation and weakness of limbs with history of eating paint likely has lead poisoning. It is characterized by impaired ALA dehydratase enzyme activity.

Lead is a potent inhibitor of both ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase/ heme synthase (option C). However, it has the greatest inhibitory action on ALA dehydratase. Lead poisonining thus leads to the buildup of protoporphyrin and ALA. Lead also substitutes for calcium in many fundamental cellular processes. It can cross red blood cell membranes as well as the blood-brain barrier and enter the neuroglial cells which support brain function. The fatal dose of lead is 20g of lead acetate and the fatal period is 1 to 2 days.

Other options: 

Option A: ALA synthase 2 defect causes X-linked protoporphyria. 
Option C: Heme synthase, or ferrochelatase, defect causes erythropoeitic protoporphyria. 
Option D: Coproporphyrinogen oxidase defect causes hereditary corproporphyria.

question.text: The given condition is cau‍sed by which drug?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bleomycin

The given image shows flagellate dermatitis. It is caused by bleomycin.

Flagellate dermatitis starts as bands of pruritic, flagellate, erythema over the trunk, and extremities within few hours to 6 months after administration. The rash heals with persistent flagellate hyperpigmentation.

No treatment is necessary since the lesions usually disappear when bleomycin is discontinued. If the patient is itchy, managing pruritus with an antihistamine may limit trauma to the skin, and thus avoid further hyperpigmentation.

Another side effect that one needs to watch out for with the use of bleomycin is the development of pulmonary fibrosis.

question.text: Which of the following is ​not a post-transcriptiona​l modification?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Glycosylation

Glycosylation is not a post-transcriptional modification; it is a post-translational modification.

A primary transcript is the initial, linear, RNA copy of a transcription unit. The collection of all the primary transcripts synthesized in the nucleus by RNA polymerase II is known as heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA). The pre-mRNA components of hnRNA undergo extensive co- and posttranscriptional modification in the nucleus and become mature mRNA. These modifications usually include the following :

  • Addition of a 5′ cap - This is the first of the processing reactions for pre-mRNA. The cap is a 7-methylguanosine attached to the 5′ terminal end of the mRNA and is resistant to most nucleases. Creation of the cap requires the removal of the γ-phosphoryl group from the 5′ triphosphate of the pre-mRNA, followed by the addition of guanosine monophosphate. Methylation of this terminal G occurs in the cytosol and is catalyzed by guanine- 7-methyltransferase. Additional methylation steps may occur (options A and B).
  • Addition of a 3′-poly-A tail - Most eukaryotic mRNA have a chain of 40 to 250 adenylates (adenosine monophosphates) attached to the 3′ end. This poly-A tail is added by the nuclear enzyme, polyadenylate polymerase. The poly-A tail terminates eukaryotic transcription. In addition, it helps stabilize the mRNA, facilitates its exit from the nucleus, and aids in translation. 
  • Splicing - Maturation of eukaryotic mRNA usually involves removal from the primary transcript of RNA sequences (introns) that do not code for protein (endonuclease cleavage). The remaining coding (expressed) sequences, the exons, are joined together to form the mature mRNA. The process of removing introns and joining exons is called splicing. The molecular complex that accomplishes these tasks is known as the spliceosome (option D).

The APL valve typically opens at pressures of 30-40 cm H₂O to allow for safe ventilation without causing barotrauma to the lungs. This range is appropriate for manual ventilation to prevent high airway pressures that could lead to lung injury.

question.text: While conducting a health ‍camp, you host an awarene​ss campaign on healthy di‍etary practices. Which of‌ the following substances‌ would you say has the hi‌ghest respiratory quotien​t immediately after consu‍mption?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mixed diet

The food item with the highest respiratory quotient (RQ) immediately after consumption is a mixed diet. 

This is because, immediately after a mixed meal (containing carbohydrates, protein, and fat), carbohydrates is the most commonly metabolized component, so the RQ reaches 1. But, a few hours after, the body would have used up the readily available carbohydrates, and the RQ reaches 0.70, due to fat metabolism.

The respiratory quotient is the ratio of carbon dioxide produced/oxygen consumed. The respiratory quotient for various substances:

Substance RQ
Carbohydrate 1.00 
Protein (option D) 0.81 
Fat (option B) 0.71  
Alcohol (option C) 0.66 

In diabetes, the rate of utilization of carbohydrates reduces in relation to fats, hence RQ falls (approximately 0.7). The RQ is lowest when ketosis is very active.

Note: For all metabolic fuels, the energy produced is the same (20 kJ/L of oxygen).

question.text: A 30-year-old male patient‌ on multiple drugs develo​ped a well-defined, round​ reddish-brown lesion on ‌his lips. He gives a hist​ory of taking an over-the​-counter drug recently an‌d mentions that he had a ‍similar lesion on his lip‍s in the past that resolv‌ed spontaneously. Which o​f the following drugs is ​the most likely cause?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ibuprofen

The clinical scenario of a well-defined, round reddish-brown lesion on the lips along with the history of similar episodes in the past which resolved spontaneously suggests a likely diagnosis of fixed drug eruption and the most likely cause is ibuprofen.

Fixed drug eruptions (FDE) are cutaneous adverse reactions to certain drugs. They are characterized by sharply demarcated dull red to brown lesions. They occur in lips, hands, legs, face, genitalia, and oral mucosa, and cause a burning sensation. The lesion recurs in the same locations upon re-exposure to the offending drug.

Drugs that are commonly known to cause fixed drug eruptions include co‐trimoxazole, NSAIDs, tetracyclines, barbiturates, phenolphthalein in laxatives, etc. Drug-specific clinical patterns may also occur. These include lesions on the lips and genitals due to NSAIDs and lesions on genitals due to tetracyclines.

Oral provocation of the implicated drug is the gold standard to confirm drug causality. A patch test can help in diagnosis. 

Treatment involves stopping the offending drug and the use of topical corticosteroids.

The image below shows a sharply demarcated red-brown macule of a fixed drug eruption.

question.text: Which of the following tes‌ts would you use to diffe‌rentiate between nevus an‍emicus and vitiligo in a ‌patient?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diascopy

Diascopy is a test that helps to differentiate between nevus anemicus and vitiligo.

Nevus anemicus is secondary to a localized area of vasoconstriction, and diascopy of the adjacent skin reveals a color identical to that of the ‘depigmented’ area, since other pigments are unaltered. In vitiligo, the lesion appears paler, since there is a loss of melanin.

Diascopy is a clinical maneuver performed to assess superficial erythema in dermatological conditions. In this procedure, a glass slide or a stiff, clear, colorless piece of plastic is pressed onto the skin to compress blood out of small vessels, in order to allow evaluation of other colors. Vessels can be seen to blanch and fill, by varying the amount of pressure on the skin, which is different for different conditions.

The purpose of this procedure is to empty blood from the superficial vessels to determine if skin redness is due to blood present within the vessels or extravasated onto the skin.

Diascopy is of particular value in the following conditions:

  • Granulomatous conditions: A translucent brownish color is seen on diascopy, known as ‘apple jelly’ nodules. They are seen in all 3 of sarcoidosis, granuloma annulare, and lupus vulgaris.
  • Differentiation between nevus anemicus and nevus depigmentosus: On diascopy, nevus anemicus (congenital white patch of vasoconstriction) becomes indistinguishable with the merging of the lesion into the surrounding skin. However, the border of nevus depigmentosus remains unaltered after diascopy.
  • Spider nevus: Application of medium pressure to a spider nevus can compress radiating arterioles and allow visualization of pulsatile flow in the feeding vessel.
  • Differentiation between erythema (vasodilation) and purpura (extravasated blood): Erythema blanches on compression of vessels, while purpura and petechiae do not blanch on compression.

question.text: From a crime scene, you re​cover a fingerprint that ‍is of a loop pattern. Whi​ch of the following patte‌rns most likely represent‌s the same?

Fingerprint first develops in 12–16 weeks of intrauterine life and is complete by 24 weeks. They are the impressions of patterns produced by the papillary or epidermal ridges present on the fingertips. The arrangement and distribution of the ridges not only remain unchanged throughout life but are unique for each individual. The study of this ridge pattern in the skin is called dermatoglyphics or dactylography and helps in the identification of an individual.

Edgeoscopy is the study of edges of friction ridges, which normally show seven characteristic features. Ridgeology is the study of friction ridges, which are composed of the edges of ridge units that vary in size, shape, and alignment.

question.text: A middle-aged woman presen​ted with bilateral propto​sis, restriction of eye m​ovements, and chemosis. H‌er thyroid profile showed​ she was euthyroid. What ​is the most probable caus‍e?

question.text: Which of the following con‌nects the structures mark​ed as 'A' and 'B'?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Foramen of Monro

The structure marked as 'A' in the given image is lateral ventricle, and 'B' is third ventricle. The structure connecting these two is foramen of Monro.

The ventricular system is derived from the inner lumen of the developing neural tube. Lining the ventricles is the choroid plexus, consisting of modified ependymal cells responsible for producing the CSF. From the lateral ventricles, CSF flows through the interventricular foramen of Monro to the third ventricle. The third ventricle communicates with the fourth ventricle via the cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius (option A), which courses through the midbrain. Surrounded by the pons and medulla anteriorly and the cerebellum posteriorly, the fourth ventricle sends CSF out of the ventricular system and into the subarachnoid space via the lateral foramina of Luschka (option C) and midline foramen of Magendie (option D).

question.text: A young woman presents wit‍h a 2-week history of pro​gressive severe headache ‍and blurry vision. Examin‌ation showed bilateral pa‌pilledema.   • Liver: Hepatomegaly and hyperlipidemia

question.text: A 12-year-old male child f‌rom a remote area is bein​g examined for a defect i​n his legs. The parents o‌f the child give a histor​y his legs were plastered‍ for a few months after b‌irth. However, there was ​a lapse in further follow‌-up. On examination, the ‌child is suffering from u‌ncorrected Congenital tal‌ipes equinovarus (CTEV). ​Which of the following is​ the best treatment optio‌n for the child?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Triple arthrodesis

As the child is having Congenital talipes equinovarus (CTEV) and his age is 12, Triple arthrodesis is the best treatment option for this child.

Triple arthrodesis consists of a fusion of the three joints of the foot-Talo-navicular joint, Talo-calcaneal joint, and Calcaneo-cuboid joint. It is done after 10-12 years of age when there is complete skeletal maturation. Of the three talonavicular joint fusion is the most difficult to achieve.

CTEV is a congenital malformation of the foot. It is predominately seen in male children. The components of deformity are as follows:

  • Cavus: This deformity occurs due to exaggerated arching of the foot at the mid-tarsal joint.
  • Adduction: This deformity occurs at the talonavicular joint.
  • Inversion: This deformity occurs at the subtalar joint. The calcaneum is inverted and along with it, the whole foot is inverted. This leads to a medially facing sole. 
  • Equinus: This deformity occurs at the ankle joint and tarsal joints.

question.text: A female patient with hear​ing loss is examined and ‌is found to be Rinne nega‍tive at 256 Hz and 512 Hz‌, while Rinne positive at​ 1024 Hz. What is the exp​ected air conduction and ‌bone conduction gap?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 30-45 dB

The given clinical scenario of hearing loss with a negative Rinne at 256 Hz and 512 Hz and positive Rinne at 1024 Hz indicates air conduction and bone conduction gap of 30-45 dB.

Tuning fork tests are performed commonly with tuning forks of frequencies such as 128, 256, 512, and 1024. The tuning fork of 512 Hz is considered ideal as forks of lower frequencies produce a sense of bone vibration, while those of higher frequencies have a shorter decay time. 

Rinne’s test is done by placing a vibrating tuning fork on the patient’s mastoid and when he stops hearing, it is brought beside the external auditory meatus (EAC). If he still hears the sound, air conduction (AC) is better than bone conduction (BC).

The inferences are as follows:

  • Rinne's test is considered positive (normal) when the air conduction AC>BC is seen in normal people and people with sensorineural deafness.
  • It is considered negative when the BC>AC, and is seen in patients with conductive deafness. It suggests a minimum hearing loss of 15-20 dB.

 A prediction of the air-bone gap can be made using tuning forks of 256, 512, and 1024 Hz:

  • A Rinne test negative for 256 Hz but positive for 512 Hz indicates an air-bone gap of 20-30 dB.
  • A Rinne test negative for 256 and 512 Hz but positive for 1024 Hz indicates an air-bone gap of 30-45 dB.
  • A Rinne negative for 256, 512, and 1024 Hz indicates an air-bone gap of 45-60 dB.

question.text: Which of the following is ‌not an immature defense m​echanism?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sublimation

Sublimation is a mature defense mechanism, unlike introjection, regression, and somatization, which are immature defense mechanisms.

Sublimation is a mature defense mechanism. It means to gratify an impulse by changing the end goal from a socially objectionable one to a socially valued one. Sublimation of aggressive impulses generally takes place through games or sports. Sublimation allows instincts to be channelled and not dammed up or diverted. Hence, in sublimation, feelings are acknowledged, modified, and directed toward a socially valued/acceptable goal so that modest instinctual satisfaction is achieved.

Mature defense mechanisms are healthy and adaptive throughout the life cycle. They are socially adaptive and useful in the integration of personal needs and motives, social demands, and interpersonal relations. They can underlie seemingly admirable and virtuous patterns of behaviour.

Other mature defense mechanisms are:

  • Anticipation
  • Humor
  • Altruism
  • Asceticism
  • Suppression

Immature defense mechanisms are usually triggered due to anxieties related to intimacy or its loss. These mechanisms are fairly common in preadolescent years and adult character disorders. Although they are regarded as socially awkward and undesirable, improvement in interpersonal relationships and personal maturity can alleviate it. Some of the immature defense mechanisms are:

Option B. Introjection involves taking up features from the external world and making them a part of oneself. Introjection of a loved object involves internalizing the characteristics of the object to ensure closeness and constant presence of the object in order to reduce the anxiety associated with separation from or loss of the object. Similarly, the introjection of a feared object involves internalizing the aggressive characteristics of the object and using it defensively to have the aggression under their control. Introjection can also take place from a sense of guilt.

Option C. Regression involves a return to a previous stage of development or functioning to avoid the anxieties or hostilities involved in later stages. This reflects a basic tendency to achieve instinctual gratification or to escape instinctual tension by returning to earlier modes and levels of gratification when later and more differentiated modes fail or involve intolerable conflict.

Option D. In somatization, psychic derivatives are converted into bodily symptoms and tend to react to somatic symptoms rather than psychic ones.

Other immature defenses include:

  • Acting out
  • Blocking
  • Hypochondriasis
  • Passive–aggressive behaviour
  • Projection (non-psychotic)
  • Schizoid fantasy

Neurotic Defenses include:

  • Controlling
  • Displacement
  • Exterternalization
  • Inhibition
  • Intellectualization
  • Isolation
  • Rationalization
  • Reaction formation
  • Repression
  • Sexualization

Narcissistic-Psychotic Defenses include Projection, Denial, and Distortion.

question.text: While examining the visual‌ fields in a 52-year-old ​male in the ophthalmology​ OPD, You noticed that th​e patient is unable to se‍e the upper fourth portio‌ns of the same side of hi‌s superior visual field. ‍Such visual field defects‌ are seen in which of the​ following lesions?
question.explanation:

The "Pie in the sky" field defect refers to superior quadrantic hemianopia due to the involvement of the inferior fibers of the optic radiations in the temporal lobe (Meyer’s loop).

The term "pie in the floor" defects refers to inferior quadrantic hemianopia. They are produced when the superior fibers of the optic radiations in the parietal lobe (Baum's loop) are involved.

question.explanation:

Functional MRI is based on the technique called BOLD i.e., blood oxygen level-dependent technique.

During a particular activity, the corresponding brain area will have increased oxygen consumption. Thus, this type of MRI helps in the detection of functions of different brain parts.

question.text: A chronic alcoholic who ha‌dn’t consumed alcohol for‍ the past 3 days was brou​ght to the emergency depa‌rtment. He had features o​f disorientation, poor at‍tention span, and agitati​on. On examination, he ha‌d fever, tachycardia, and‍ diaphoresis. Identify th​e condition.
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Delirium tremens

The given clinical scenario of disorientation with features of autonomic hyperactivity (tachycardia, diaphoresis, fever) in a patient who stopped alcohol 3 days back is suggestive of delirium tremens.

Delirium tremens is the most severe alcohol withdrawal syndrome. It occurs usually within 3-4 days of alcohol withdrawal.

Characteristic features are:

  • Clouding of consciousness with disorientation to time and place
  • Poor attention and distractibility
  • Visual hallucination and illusions which are often vivid and frightening
  • Autonomic disturbances like tachycardia, fever, hypertension, sweating, and pupillary dilatation
  • Psychomotor agitation and ataxia

Benzodiazepines such as chlordiazepoxide and lorazepam are used in the treatment and prevention of delirium tremens.

Option A: Korsakoffs psychosis is characterized by impaired mental abilities (especially recent memory) and anterograde amnesia in an alert and responsive patient. The patient may have symptoms of confabulation.

Option B: Wernicke's encephalopathy is characterized by ataxia (affecting primarily the gait), vestibular dysfunction, confusion, and ocular motility abnormalities.

Option D: Alcohol-induced dementia is characterized by the development of multiple cognitive deficits (e.g., memory problems, language impairment, and an inability to perform complex motor tasks) that are judged to be a direct consequence of alcohol use. This persists beyond the usual duration of alcohol intoxication or acute withdrawal.

question.text: Where are the ossification‌ centers resulting in bip​artite patella most commo‍nly located?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Superolateral angle

The ossification centers resulting in a bipartite patella are most commonly located in the superolateral angle of the patella.

A bipartite patella (two-part patella) is a patella with an unfused accessory ossification center, typically at the superolateral aspect. It usually is asymptomatic and is noted incidentally, however pain, when present, can be caused by overuse (such as in a cyclist or climber).

There are three types of bipartite patella.

  • Type I (5%) occurs at the inferior pole.
  • Type II (20%) occurs along the entire lateral border of the patella.
  • Type III (75%) the most common type, occurs as an elliptical area in the superolateral portion of the patella.


Depending on the number of fragments they may be classified as bipartite, tripartite or multipartite.

For diagnosis, a conventional skyline view is followed by a skyline view with the patient in a squatting weight-bearing position to assess if pain is caused by a nonunion at the bipartite site. If the gap is higher in the squatting weight-bearing posture than in the standard skyline view, the test result is considered positive.

MRI is not required to diagnose the condition.

Treatment:

If pain occurs with a bipartite patella, limiting and restricting activity, correcting the activity that is causing an overuse syndrome, and prescribing nonsteroidal antiinflammatory agents can result in improvement in 3 weeks. 

Operative treatment with the Ogata technique is rarely necessary.

question.text: A boy presents with compla‌ints of intermittent low-​grade fever and membrane ​over the left tonsil, whi‌ch appeared insidiously. ‌On examination of the ora‌l cavity, the surgeon tri‌ed to remove the membrane‌, which came off easily r​evealing an irregular ulc‌er over the tonsil. What ​is the most probable diag​nosis?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vincent’s angina

The given clinical history of low-grade fever, easily removable membrane over tonsil revealing irregular ulcers is suggestive of Vincent’s angina.

The condition presents with low-grade fever and sore throat, and a membrane over the tonsil. The membrane is easily removed to reveal irregular ulcers over the tonsil. A throat swab will show both the organisms typical of the disease, namely fusiform bacilli and spirochaetes, specifically Borrelia vincentii.

Other Options:

Option A: Diphtheria is slower in onset with less local discomfort. In the above case, the membrane is removed easily but in diphtheria, the membrane is adherent and its removal leaves a bleeding surface. The membrane in diphtheria extends beyond the tonsils, onto the soft palate, and is dirty grey in color. The smear and culture of the throat swab will reveal Corynebacterium diphtheriae.


Option C: In Infectious mononucleosis, pharyngitis is the most prominent sign, with an exudate resembling that of streptococcal pharyngitis. Both tonsils are very much enlarged, congested, and covered with an exudative membrane. There is marked local discomfort. Lymph nodes are enlarged in the posterior triangle of the neck along with splenomegaly. There is the failure of antibiotic treatment. A blood smear may show more than 50% lymphocytes, of which about 10% are atypical. Paul-Bunnell test will show high tires of heterophile antibody.

Option D: Aphthous ulcer are shallow ulcers that are often multiple and separated by normal intervening mucosa. They may involve any part of the oral cavity or oropharynx. Sometimes, it is solitary and may involve the tonsil and the pillars. It is very painful. 

Other differential diagnoses for membrane over the tonsil:

  • Membranous tonsillitis
  • Malignancy of tonsil
  • Agranulocytosis
  • Leukemia
  • Traumatic ulcer
  • Candidal infection of the tonsil

question.text: The CT abdomen of a patien​t presenting with abdomin‍al pain and vomiting is s​hown below. What is the p‍robable diagnosis?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cholelithiasis

A patient presenting with abdominal pain and vomiting, with CT showing a Mercedes-Benz sign, is characteristic of cholelithiasis.

Mercedes–Benz sign (triradiate sign), is seen when a gallstone contains central radiolucent gas. The fissures may be tri-radiate or bi-radiate (seagull sign). These fissures appear dark on CT or radiographs, giving the sign its characteristic appearance. 

Gallbladder stones or cholelithiasis are the most common condition affecting the gallbladder. They are often discovered incidentally and typically remain asymptomatic. However, they become symptomatic when the stones obstruct the cystic duct. In such cases, patients may experience dull or colicky right upper quadrant or epigastric pain radiating to the back, along with symptoms like nausea and vomiting. 

Only about 10% of gallstones are radiopaque. Ultrasonography (USG) is the most accurate initial imaging modality of choice for the diagnosis of gallbladder stones. These stones appear as echogenic foci producing acoustic shadows. The sensitivity of USG for gallstones is >95%.

question.text: Inferior thyroid artery su​pplies which of the follo‌wing structures? Thyroid ‍Parathyroid Esophagus Thy​mus
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 3, and 4

All the given 4 structures are supplied by the Inferior thyroid artery.

Inferior thyroid artery is a branch of the thyrocervical trunk, which in turn, is a branch of the first part of the subclavian artery. The inferior thyroid artery loops upwards anterior to the medial border of the scalenus anterior, turns medially just below the sixth cervical transverse process, and then descends on longus colli to the lower border of the thyroid gland.

Branches:

  • Pharyngeal branches: These supply the lower part of the pharynx.
    • Tracheal branches supply the trachea and anastomose with the bronchial arteries;
    • Oesophageal branches supply the oesophagus and anastomose with the oesophageal branches of the thoracic aorta; and
    • Inferior and ascending glandular branches supply the posterior and inferior regions of the thyroid gland, and anastomose with the contralateral inferior and ipsilateral superior thyroid arteries.
    • The ascending branch also supplies the parathyroid glands.
  • Ascending cervical artery
  • Inferior laryngeal
  • Muscular branches

Note: Thymic branches originating from the internal thoracic, inferior thyroid artery, and sometimes superior thyroid arteries supply the thymus and the surrounding mediastinal connective tissue.

question.text: A 58-year-old patient with​ a history of cardiovascu​lar disease presents with‍ sudden, painless loss of‍ vision in one eye. Fundu​s examination reveals a p‍ale retina with a cherry-‌red spot at the macula an​d segmentation of the blo‌od column in the retinal ​veins. Which of the follo‌wing steps can be taken w‌ithin 24 hours to potenti​ally improve the patient'​s outcome?

options.text: Perform immediate paracent​esis of the anterior cham​ber
options.label: B

question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Perform immediate paracentesis of the anterior chamber

A 58-year-old patient with a history of cardiovascular disease presenting with sudden, painless loss of vision in one eye and a fundus examination showing a pale retina with a cherry-red spot is indicative of central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO). Immediate intervention to reduce IOP, including paracentesis of the anterior chamber, ocular massage or intravenous acetazolamide is critical to potentially improve the outcome.

Central retinal artery occlusion is a medical emergency where rapid restoration of blood flow is essential to prevent permanent vision loss. Paracentesis of the anterior chamber helps lower intraocular pressure, which can facilitate dislodging the embolus causing the occlusion. 

Other options:

Option A. Prescribe oral anticoagulants: Anticoagulants do not provide the immediate reduction in intraocular pressure or quick restoration of retinal blood flow necessary in acute CRAO.

Option C. Administer intravitreal steroids: Intravitreal steroids are used for inflammatory conditions and certain retinal disorders but are not effective in the acute management of CRAO.

Option D. Refer for retinal detachment surgery: Retinal detachment surgery is not relevant in the management of CRAO and requires immediate vascular intervention rather than surgical repair of retinal tissue.

question.text: A slit-lamp examination re‌veals the following findi​ng. It is also noted that​ these yellow-white vitre‌ous opacities do not sett​le down when the eye is i‌mmobile. All of the follo​wing statements about thi​s condition are true exce​pt:
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Common in myopes

The examination findings are suggestive of asteroid bodies/hyalosis. It is not common in myopes.

Asteroid hyalosis is a common degenerative process in which calcium pyrophosphate particles collect within the vitreous gel. It is seen clinically as numerous tiny round yellow-white opacities of varying size and density. These move with the vitreous during eye movements but do not sediment inferiorly when the eye is immobile.

Only one eye is affected in 75% of patients; it rarely causes visual problems and the majority of patients are asymptomatic. The cause of asteroid hyalosis is unknown, but it has been associated with diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and hypercholesterolemia. The prevalence of asteroid hyalosis increases with age and affects 3% of those aged 75–86 years. It is more common in men than in women. While treatment of asteroid hyalosis is usually unnecessary, vitrectomy may occasionally be indicated.

question.text: What is the most common ca​use of ophthalmia neonato​rum in developed countrie‌s?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chlamydia

Chlamydia is at present the most common cause of ophthalmia neonatarum in developed countries.

Ophthalmia neonatarum also called neonatal conjunctivitis is inflammation of the conjunctiva occurring in an infant <30 days after birth.It should be ruled out in any infant having discharge or watering within the first week of birth.

Causes include:

  1. Chlamydia(Option A): neonatal inclusion conjunctivitis caused by serotypes D-K is at present the most common cause in developed countries. 
  2. Gonorrhoea(Option B): effective prophylaxis against gonococcal infection and its subsequent decline has almost eliminated it's incidence in developed countries.
  3. Staphylococcus aureus(Option D), Haemophilus species, Streptococcus haemolyticus, and Streptococcus pneumoniae are other less commonly seen causes of ophthalmia neonatarum
  4. Herpes simplex ophthalmia neonatrum rarely occurs and is caused by Herpes simplex type 2 virus from the mother.
  5. Chemical conjunctivitis(Option C) is caused by the application of prophylactic antibiotics or silver nitrate at the time of birth.

48–72 h

Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae

Prophylactic treatment: 1% tetracycline or erythromycin eye ointment is applied to the eyes, if the mother is suspected to have gonococcal or chlamydia infection.

question.text: A histologist is studying ‌the structure of lymphoid​ tissue. The histological‍ features shown in the im‍age below are seen in:
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Palatine tonsil

The given slide shows the histology of tonsils with non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium and lymphoid nodules in the center.

The tonsil consists of lymphoid nodules, which are surrounded by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium on its oropharyngeal surface. The epithelium dips into the substance of the gland and forms tonsillar crypts.

The following image shows the histology of the tonsils:

 

Histology of thymus (option A):

The thymus is a lymphoid tissue that is arranged in the form of lobules. The lobules are separated from each other by connective tissue. 

Each lobule is made up of an outer darker staining cortex and an inner pale-staining medulla. The medulla contains pink rounded masses called Hassell's corpuscles.

 

Structure of a lymph node (option B):

Each lymph node is bean-shaped. The concave part consists of the hilum, through which the blood vessels enter and leave the node. Microscopy shows the following features:

Each lymph node is surrounded by a thin capsule. Below the capsule is the clear space, which is called the subcapsular sinus. 

The lymph node contains the outer cortex and an inner medulla. The cortex consists of densely packed lymphocytes and therefore stains dark. Numerous follicles can be seen in the cortex. Each nodule has a pale-staining germinal center surrounded by a zone of densely packed lymphocytes. The medulla consists of lymphocytes arranged in the form of anastomosing cords. It appears pale. Numerous blood vessels can be seen in this area.

The image below shows the histology of the lymph node:

 

Structure of spleen (Option D):

The spleen is the largest lymphoid organ of the body.

Microscopic features of the spleen:

It is surrounded by a thick capsule. This capsule extends into the organ forming trabeculae. The substance of the spleen consists of red pulp and white pulp. In red pulp, the lymphocytes are diffusely distributed and contain numerous sinusoids. In white pulp, the lymphocytes are densely packed and arranged in the form of cords around the arterioles.

When cut transversely, the cords are similar to the nodules in the lymph nodes. They have a pale germinal center surrounded by a ring of densely packed lymphocytes. However, there is an eccentrically placed arteriole within the germinal center.

The image below shows the spleen: WP- white pulp, RP- Red pulp, CR- central arteriole.

Structure of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue:

The aggregations are in the form of lymphatic follicles. Germinal centers may be present. Between the nodules, there is diffuse lymphoid tissue, which is called a parafollicular zone. The nodules predominantly consist of B lymphocytes with T lymphocytes in the diffuse areas.

They lie close to the epithelium. They are not surrounded by a capsule and also do not have connective tissue septa. They have a supporting network of reticular fibers. Examples are palatine tonsils, Peyer's patches, and lymphoid nodules in the vermiform appendix.

The image below shows Peyer's patches.

question.text: Triad of tenosynovitis, de‌rmatitis and migratory as‌ymmetric polyarthralgia i‍s _________
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Disseminated gonococcal infection

Disseminated gonococcal infection is a triad of tenosynovitis, dermatitis and migratory asymmetric polyarthralgia.

It occurs as a result of hematogenous spread following genital infection. The skin lesions appear in crops of 5-50. They are small, tender and initially maculopapular. A central vesicle or pustule appears and progresses to hemorrhage and necrosis. It is most commonly seen peripherally near affected joints. They may also occur on the torso and the palms and soles.

Skin lesion in disseminated gonococcal infection.

Tenosynovitis often affects the hands and fingers. Migratory polyarthralgia affects the knees, elbows, wrists, metacarpophalangeal joints and ankle joints.

Reiter’s syndrome:  Triad of arthritis, conjunctivitis, and nonspecific urethritis. It may follow infection with Chlamydia, Campylobacter, Salmonella or Yersinia.

Behcet’s disease: Triad of recurrent aphthous ulcers, genital ulcerations, and uveitis. It is an autoimmune disease of unknown etiology.

Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome: Perihepatic inflammation and adhesions with pelvic inflammatory disease. It is a rare disease seen following gonococcal infection.

question.text: Match the following tests ​with the ligament injurie​s they are used to examin‍e. 1)Apley test a)Medial ​collateral ligament 2)Lac​hman test b)Posterior cru​ciate ligament 3)McMurray​ test c)Anterior cruciate‍ ligament 4)Valgus stress‌ test d)Menisci

2)Lachman test c)Anterior cruciate ligament
3)McMurray test  d)Menisci
4)Valgus stress test  a)Medial collateral ligament

It is to be noted here that both Apley grinding test and McMurray test are done to test meniscal injuries.

Apley test: This test is performed with a prone patient, the knee is flexed to 90  degrees and rotated while a compression force is applied, which is called the grinding test. Reproduction of symptoms indicates a torn meniscus. The distraction test involves repeated rotation while the leg is pulled upwards by the examiner, holding the thigh down. This produces increased pain only if there is ligament damage.

The Lachman test is also done to detect injuries to the anterior cruciate ligament. Here the leg is in slight external rotation and the knee is flexed 20 degrees. One hand is placed to stabilize the femur and another hand applies the anterior force to the proximal tibia to look for any abnormal movement.

McMurray test: Done to detect menisci injuries. The patient's knee is completely flexed while he lies supine. One hand is used to stabilize and palpate the knee joint and the leg is internally and externally rotated with the other hand. The leg is then slowly extended. Meniscal injury presents as a palpable or audible click.

The valgus stress test is performed with the knee extended by placing one hand along the lateral thigh and pressing inward while the other hand is placed on the medial aspect of the ankle and pushed outward as shown in the image below. It is positive in medial collateral ligament injury.

question.text: Which of the following conditions is associated with a spongy appearance with sunburst calcification on the CT abdomen?
question.explanation:
The spongy appearance with central sunburst calcification on the CT abdomen is seen in serous cystadenoma of the pancreas.

CT findings of serous cystadenoma of the pancreas:
  • Typically demonstrates a multicystic, lobulated mass in the pancreatic head sometimes described as a ‘bunch of grapes’.
  • A characteristic enhancing central scar may be present which can show associated stellate calcification (present in ~20% of cases)

question.text: While performing a PET-CT scan, uptake in which of the following areas is likely to be a false positive?
question.explanation:
On 18F-FDG PET-CT scan, the urinary bladder shows normal physiological uptake and is a potential source of false-positive in oncologic imaging.

The following are areas of normal physiological uptake on PET CT:
  • Brain tissue
  • Skeletal muscle, especially after strenuous activity and laryngeal muscles following speech
  • Myocardium
  • Gastrointestinal tract - intestinal wall
  • Genitourinary tract - as FDG is excreted via the renal system and passes into the collecting systems
  • Brown fat - FDG accumulates here as glucose and ATP are required for heat production
  • Thymus
  • Bone marrow
The following image shows supraclavicular uptake on a PET scan, due to the presence of brown adipose tissue.

question.text: What is the maximum recommended cuff pressure for inflating the cuff of an endotracheal tube?
question.explanation:
The cuff pressure should ideally be maintained between 20-30 cm H2O (standard target is 25 cm H2O).

Excessive pressure (>30 cm H2O) can cause tracheal mucosal injury, while inadequate pressure (<20 cm H2O) increases the risk of micro-aspiration and VAP (Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia). If nitrous oxide is used, pressures must be monitored as it can diffuse into and over-inflate the cuff.

question.text: A patient with chronic alcoholism presented with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. His lab reports showed elevated serum amylase and lipase levels. Which of the following signs is unlikely to be seen in the radiograph of this patient?
question.explanation:
The given clinical scenario with elevated serum amylase and lipase suggests acute pancreatitis.

Grey Turner's sign, seen in this condition, is a clinical sign, not a radiological finding, characterized by flank discolouration due to retroperitoneal haemorrhage.

Acute hemorrhagic pancreatitis can present clinically with certain named signs like Cullen’s sign, Grey Turner’s sign, Fox sign, and Bryant’s sign (discolouration of the scrotum).

Radiological signs in acute pancreatitis include:
  • colon cut-off sign
  • preserved renal halo sign
  • sentinel loop sign (upper abdomen)

Note: The sentinel loop sign may aid in localizing the source of inflammation. For example, the sentinel loop sign in the right lower quadrant may be due to appendicitis.

question.text: All of the following are useful to reduce CIN in patients with diabetic nephropathy except:
question.explanation:
Ans. D) Doing CE-MRI instead of CECT

Explanation:

  • • Explanation:
  • • Contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN) is a potential complication of contrast administration in patients with renal impairment, such as diabetic nephropathy. Effective strategies to reduce the risk of CIN include using safer contrast agents, optimizing hydration, and stopping nephrotoxic medications.
  • • Doing CE-MRI instead of CECT:
  • • Doing CE-MRI instead of CECT:
  • • CE-MRI uses gadolinium-based contrast agents , which are not safer alternatives in patients with renal dysfunction. Gadolinium can cause nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF) , a severe systemic condition, especially in patients with impaired renal function. Hence, using CE-MRI with gadolinium is not an appropriate strategy to reduce CIN.
  • • CE-MRI uses gadolinium-based contrast agents , which are not safer alternatives in patients with renal dysfunction.
  • • gadolinium-based contrast agents
  • • Gadolinium can cause nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF) , a severe systemic condition, especially in patients with impaired renal function.
  • • nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF)
  • • Hence, using CE-MRI with gadolinium is not an appropriate strategy to reduce CIN.
  • • Other Options:
  • • Other Options:
  • • Option A. Iodixanol:
  • • Option A. Iodixanol:
  • • Iodixanol is a non-ionic, dimeric iodinated contrast agent , which is considered the safest among iodinated contrasts. Non-ionic dimers, such as iodixanol, have a lower osmolality compared to ionic monomers, reducing the risk of nephrotoxicity. It is an effective strategy to reduce CIN risk.
  • • Iodixanol is a non-ionic, dimeric iodinated contrast agent , which is considered the safest among iodinated contrasts.

  • • Option B. Hydration before contrast administration:
  • • Option B. Hydration before contrast administration:
  • • IV hydration is the most evidence-backed method to prevent CIN. Adequate hydration ensures proper renal perfusion and dilutes the contrast agent, minimizing nephrotoxicity.
  • • IV hydration is the most evidence-backed method to prevent CIN.
  • • IV hydration

  • • Option C. Stopping nephrotoxic drugs before contrast:
  • • Option C. Stopping nephrotoxic drugs before contrast:
  • • Discontinuing nephrotoxic medications (e.g., NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, metformin) before contrast administration reduces the burden on the kidneys and helps prevent CIN.

question.text: The CT nephrogram of a patient with loin pain is given below. All of the following can be included in the differential diagnoses except:
question.explanation:
The given image shows linear bands of contrast extending from the medulla of the kidney towards the cortex of the kidney, called a striated nephrogram seen on plain film and CT nephrography.

Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) shows swiss cheese nephrogram, not striated nephrogram.

Conditions which show striated nephrogram include:
  • Unilateral:
    • Acute ureteric obstruction
    • Acute pyelonephritis
    • Acute renal vein thrombosis
    • Acutely following renal contusion
    • Acute radiation therapy to the kidney
  • Bilateral:
    • Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD)
    • Acute pyelonephritis (if it is bilateral)
    • Acute tubular obstruction
    • Acute tubular necrosis
    • Hypotension

options.text: It is used to assess the oral cavity before intubation

B
options.text: In class II, tonsillar pillars cannot be visualized
Higher scores are associated with higher risk of sleep apnea
options.label: C
D
options.text: In class III, only the hard palate is visible

question.explanation:
In Mallampati Class III, the soft palate and the base of the uvula are visible. If only the hard palate is visible, it is classified as Class IV.

Modified Mallampati Classes:
  • Class I: Soft palate, fauces, uvula, and pillars are visible.
  • Class II: Soft palate, fauces, and portion of uvula are visible.
  • Class III: Soft palate and base of uvula are visible.
  • Class IV: Only the hard palate is visible.

question.text: What is the earliest sign of left atrial enlargement on a chest x-ray?

options.label: D
options.text: Elevation of left main bronchus and widening of carina

question.explanation:
Enlargement of the left atrial appendage is the earliest sign of left atrial enlargement (LAE) on a chest x-ray. It is seen as a fullness below the pulmonary artery.

Other radiographic signs seen in LAE include:
  • The third mogul sign represents an enlargement of the left atrial appendage along the upper left cardiac border, leading to straightening of the left heart border.
  • Posterior displacement of the oesophagus - seen on the lateral view of the barium swallow study.
  • Elevation of left main bronchus and widening of the carina.
  • Double density sign or double atrial shadow - the enlarged LA extends towards the right cardiac border, hence, both RA and LA borders can be seen distinctly over the right heart border (as shown below):

The X-ray below demonstrates straightening of the left cardiac border and widening of the carina, with the carinal angle becoming more obtuse, reflecting left atrial enlargement.

The causes of left atrial enlargement are as follows:
  • Congenital: Ventricular septal defect, Patent ductus arteriosus
  • Acquired: Mitral valvular disease, left ventricular failure, left atrial myxoma

Here, the patient leans forward in the sitting position, over a basin, and spits any blood oozing into the mouth while breathing through it. Merocel is a non-absorbable nasal packing material that increases in size on rehydration with normal saline. This compresses the bleeding vessel.

Epistaxis is bleeding from inside the nose and is commonly seen in all age groups. It can be due to trauma, infections, foreign bodies, or local neoplasms. Some systemic conditions like thrombocytopenia, liver diseases, and hemophilia can result in the condition.

Management of Epistaxis:

  1. Pinching of the nose with thumb and index finger for about 5 minutes compresses the vessels of the Little’s area.
  2. Cauterisation of the bleeding point with silver nitrate or electrocautery. This is done under topical anesthesia.
  3. Anterior nasal packing.
  4. Posterior nasal packing for which patients should be hospitalized.
  5. Endoscopic cauterization of the bleeding point. 
  6. Elevation of the mucoperichondrial flap and submucosal resection operation- for persistent and recurrent bleeds from the septum.
  7. Ligation of vessels.
  8. Transnasal endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation (TESPAL) is done under topical anesthesia with sedation or under general anesthesia. It is effective in controlling refractory posterior bleeds.
  9. Embolization of the internal maxillary artery by an interventional radiologist, via femoral artery catheterization. 

The image below depicts nasal packing.

Other options:

Option A: Systemic and not topical antibiotics are indicated if the nasal pack is planned to stay for 2-3 days. It prevents sinus infections and toxic shock syndrome.

Option B: Intermittent oxygen may be required in patients with bilateral nasal packs and not unilateral because of increased pulmonary resistance from naso-pulmonary reflex.

Option D: Patients requiring postnasal packs should always be hospitalized. It is important to evaluate the cause of epistaxis.
