question.text: What does Ribot’s law deal‌ with?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Retrograde amnesia

Ribot's law deals with retrograde amnesia.

During incidents of retrograde amnesia, most recently acquired memories are the most vulnerable to disruption from brain damage. This temporal gradation of retrograde amnesia that preferentially spares the more distant memories is known as Ribot's law.

E.g: If an incident causing retrograde amnesia occurs at 30 years of age, the memories acquired at 25 years of age may be more severely affected than those memories acquired at 20 years of age or earlier.

question.text: Which of the following is ​not included in the major‍ diagnostic triad of fat ​embolism syndrome (FES)?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fat globules in urine

Fat globules in urine is a minor criterion in diagnosing fat embolism syndrome.

Fat embolism syndrome is caused by the release of fat globules from the bone marrow into the bloodstream. It usually occurs following long bone or pelvic fractures, and multiple fractures.

Along with platelet aggregates, the globules result in the following manifestations which make up the major diagnostic triad:

  • Respiratory insufficiency
  • Neurological impairment
  • Petechial rash

question.text: A 35-year-old woman is dia​gnosed with rheumatoid ar​thritis. What associated ‌complication is shown in ‌the image?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Scleromalacia perforans

Scleromalacia perforans is the associated complication of rheumatoid arthritis that is shown in the image.

Scleromalacia perforans is a specific type of necrotizing scleritis without inflammation, characterized by progressive scleral thinning. The uveal tissue appears to shine through it. Spontaneous perforation is a rare complication of the condition. It is typically seen in elderly women with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis. A yellowish patch of melting sclera can be seen. This is due to the obliteration of blood supply.

Clinical features include pain, photophobia, and lacrimation. The affected eye appears red. Medical management includes steroids and immunosuppressants. In severe cases, surgical treatment by scleral patch graft may be done. 

Other options:

Option B - Ciliary staphyloma is used to describe the bulge of an area of weak sclera lined by the ciliary body. Common causes include scleritis, developmental glaucoma, and end-stage primary or secondary glaucoma. Thinning of the sclera, secondary to perforating injury, can also result in the condition.

Option C - Coloboma is a congenital anomaly, that develops due to a defect in the closure of the embryonic cleft. It is characterized by poorly developed uveal tissue. In some cases, it might be deficient. The lens, choroid, and retina may also be involved. 

The image below shows coloboma of the right eyelid.

Option D - Malignant melanoma of the conjunctiva appears as a mass near the limbus. It can be pigmented or non-pigmented. It is usually seen in elderly patients. The choroid, iris, ciliary body, and eyelids can also develop the tumor.

The image below shows malignant melanoma of the choroid.

question.text: An HIV-positive patient wa‌s started on antiretrovir​al therapy. These drugs b‌elong to which category?

Schedule J contains a list of diseases that a drug may not prevent or cure. E.g. - HIV & Atherosclerosis.

The Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 are the set of rules under The Drugs and Cosmetics Act,1940 which contains provisions for the classification of drugs under given schedules and there are guidelines for the storage, sale, display, and prescription of each schedule.

question.text: The empty delta sign is a ‌radiological feature of w‍hich of the following con​ditions?

Correct answer: A. Cerebral venous thrombosis

The empty delta sign is a characteristic finding of superior sagittal sinus thrombosis, seen on contrast-enhanced CT(CECT) or MRI. It appears as a triangular filling defect(clot) outlined by contrast. This sign is not observed on non-contrast imaging.

question.text: A 70-year-old male patient​ presents with decreased ​hearing in higher frequen‍cies. It was noted that t‌he basilar membrane was a‍ffected. Which of the fol‍lowing structures lie nea​r the affected structure?​
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Oval window

The affected structure in high-frequency hearing loss is the basal turn of the cochlea. Among the given options, the structure that lies near it is the oval window. 

The traveling wave theory of von Bekesy states that a sound wave, depending on its frequency, reaches maximum amplitude at a segment on the basilar membrane and stimulates that segment. The high frequencies are represented in the basal turn of the cochlea and the progressively lower ones towards the apex.
 
The cochlea has a bony core called the modiolus, and a spiral canal that runs around it. At the base of the canal, the two main openings are the oval window and the round window. The footplate of stapes rests against the oval window. The base of the modiolus transmits nerves and vessels to the cochlea. (option A)
 
The inner ear consists of a bony labyrinth and a membranous labyrinth. The bony labyrinth consists of the vestibule, semicircular canals, and the cochlea. The membranous labyrinth consists of the cochlear duct, the utricle and saccule, semicircular ducts, and the endolymphatic duct and sac.
 
The cochlear duct has three walls- the basilar membrane, Reissner's membrane, and the stria vascularis. The basilar membrane supports the organ of Corti, which is the sensory hearing epithelium. The length of the basilar membrane increases from the base to the apex. As a result of this, higher frequency sound is heard at the basal coil while lower frequencies are heard at the apex.
 
The stria vascularis is involved in the secretion of endolymph and contains vascular epithelium. (Option B)

 

The helicotrema (option D) is an opening at the apex of the cochlea, at which the scala vestibuli and scala tympani communicate. The scala vestibuli, tympani, and media are three compartments of the bony cochlea.

question.text: Marshall's triad (punctate​ lacerations, bruises, an‍d abrasions) is seen in w​hich type of blast injury​?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Secondary blast injury

Marshall's triad in a bomb explosion is seen due to secondary blast injuries.

Marshall described the characteristic injuries associated with bomb explosions. It includes:

  • Abrasions
  • Bruises/ contusions
  • Puncture lacerations

Blast injuries are classified as:

  • Primary injuries- effect of transmitted blast waves on gas-containing structures. External injuries are absent and are characterized by internal injuries. The middle ear, lungs, and gastrointestinal tract are the most susceptible to this.
  • Secondary injuries- injuries caused by shrapnel and other airborne debris propelled by the explosion. These injuries may affect any part of the body and sometimes result in penetrating trauma. Most casualties are caused by secondary injuries.
  • Tertiary injuries- are caused by blast wind that can throw victims against solid objects.
  • Quaternary injuries- all other injuries caused by explosions are not included in the above three categories. eg, flash burns, crush injuries, respiratory effects due to toxic dust, gas, etc.

question.text: Malignant Otitis Externa i‌s______
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Infective condition

Malignant Otitis Externa/ necrotizing Otitis Externa is an infective and locally invasive condition.

It is caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa in immunocompromised individuals like elderly, diabetics, patients on immunosuppressants and steroids.

It presents as severe ear pain with discharge.

Diagnosis:

  • Biopsy to exclude carcinoma.
  • Tc 99 scan helps in early diagnosis before radiological changes appear.
  • Gallium citrate 67 scan, Indium 111 labeled leukocyte scan are used to test resolution of infection.
  • MRI to see intracranial spread and CT scan to detect bone erosion.

Treatment:

  • Antipseudomonal antibiotics, debridement of necrotic material.

question.text: Methemoglobinemia is cause‍d by:
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Prilocaine

Methemoglobinemia is caused by prilocaine.

It is due to the metabolism of the aromatic ring of prilocaine to o-toluidine which is an oxidizing agent and oxidizes hemoglobin to methemoglobin. Methemoglobinemia risk is directly associated with the total dose administered, usually appearing when doses exceed 8 mg/kg.

Intravenous administration of methylene blue is the treatment for methemoglobinemia.

Benzocaine can also cause methemoglobinemia similar to prilocaine.

question.text: Which of the following is ​the shortest and narrowes‌t segment of the facial n‍erve?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Labyrinthine segment

The shortest and narrowest segment of the facial nerve is the labyrinthine segment (length 4.0 mm, diameter 0.61–0.68 mm).

The labyrinthine segment is from the fundus of meatus to the geniculate ganglion where the nerve takes a turn posteriorly forming a genu. The nerve in the labyrinthine segment has the narrowest diameter  and the bony canal in this segment is also the narrowest. Thus edema or inflammation can easily compress the nerve and cause paralysis.

question.text: Arrange in sequence the st​ructures involved in the ​direct pathway: 1. Striat‍um 2. Globus pallidus 3. ‌Substantia nigra 4. Thala​mus 5. Cortex
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 5,1,2,3,4

The sequence of structures involved in the direct pathway is cortex > striatum > globus pallidus > substantia nigra > thalamus.

There are five parallel circuits that connect the frontal cortex to the striatum, pallidum, substantia nigra, and thalamus. These circuits have both direct and indirect pathways. The direct pathway stimulates the cortex to produce movement, whereas the indirect pathway inhibit it. 

The cerebral cortex projects into the striatum. The striatum is seen projected into the pallidum and substantia nigra pars reticularis. Fibres originate from different striatal cells according to their endings in the external and internal pallidum. In the direct pathway, striatal neurones project directly to the internal pallidum.  Whereas some other fibres that arise from the neurons project to the external pallidum. This is called the indirect pathway.  

The sequence of structures involved in the indirect pathway is cortex > striatum > globus pallidus externa > subthalamic nucleus > globus pallidus interna and substantia nigra >Thalamus

The striatal activity in the direct pathway is mediated by D1 dopamine receptors and in the indirect pathway by D2 dopamine receptors. 

Putamen lies lateral and the internal capsule lies medial to the pallidum. It receives fibres from the striatum and subthalamic nuclei. It acts as the main output of the basal ganglia to the thalamus and superior colliculus. The substantia nigra is seen in each cerebral peduncle of the midbrain located deep to the crus cerebri. The levels of dopamine in the substantia nigra and striata are seen reduced in parkinsonism disease.

In parkinsonism disease, due to the death of neurons in substantia nigra activity of the direct pathway is reduced and the indirect pathway is increased. This results in bradykinesia in parkinsonism disease. Whereas in Huntington's disease, the activity of the indirect pathway is affected resulting in choreic involuntary movements.

question.text: Which of the following mus​cles is not involved in t​he overhead abduction of ‍the arm?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pectoralis major

Pectoralis major is mainly involved in adduction and medial rotation of the arm and is not involved in the abduction of the arm.

Glenohumeral abduction is about 120° or more. The glenohumeral arthrodesis restricts the abduction at about 45°. Further abduction occurs at the sterno­ and acromiocla­vicular articulations, and contralateral vertebral flexion.

Muscles involved in the abduction of the shoulder:

  • The first 15° of abduction is initiated by the supraspinatus muscle.
  • 15° to 90° of abduction is carried out mainly by the middle fibers of the deltoid muscle.
  • Abduction of the arm, beyond 90°, is carried out by the movement of the shoulder girdle caused by the action of trapezius and serratus anterior.

question.text: A 36-year-old female patie‌nt is posted for laparosc​opic cholecystectomy. She​ forgot the instruction o‍f being nil per oral and ​had breakfast a few hours‍ back. The anesthetist de​cides to use the device s​hown below to reduce the ‍risk of gastric aspiratio​n. Identify the device us‍ed. LMA - Laryngeal mask ​airway
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. LMA Supreme

The image shown above is the LMA Supreme.

The LMA Supreme (SLMA) is a single-use, second-generation supraglottic airway device, identified by the presence of a modified cuff design, a drainage tube that allows for gastric access, an integrated bite block, and a fixation tab.

The fixation tab should rest 1-2.5 cm above the upper lip and help in the determination of the proper size of SLMA to be used. It helps in an improved perilaryngeal seal when the cheek is taped across the fixation tab. SLMA is based on the LMA ProSeal (PLMA) variant. Studies suggest that second-generation LMAs such as the SLMA and PLMA reduced the risk of gastric aspiration. 

The property of preventing gastric aspiration along with the improved airway seal and higher leak pressures have enabled supraglottic airway devices to be used in various applications where the classic LMAs (cLMA) are potentially unsuitable. Such situations include non-supine positions, laparoscopic surgeries like cholecystectomy, and in patients who are obese. The successful, routine use of the SLMA in fasted, nonobese patients for cesarean section has also been reported.

question.text: A 43-year-old male present‌s with complaints of unil​ateral blurring of vision​ and photophobia. On fund​oscopic examination, the ‍following picture is seen‌. The most probable diagn‌osis is:
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Toxoplasmosis

The characteristic “headlight in the fog” appearance is suggestive of Toxoplasmosis. It is called so because of the white inflammatory retinal nidus appearing as a headlight when viewed through an inflamed vitreous that resembles a fog.

Ocular toxoplasmosis

  • Toxoplasmosis is caused by Toxoplasma gondii, an obligate intracellular protozoan.
  • The cat is the definitive host, with intermediate hosts including mice, livestock, birds, and humans.
  • Ocular features
    • Toxoplasmosis constitutes 20–60% of all cases of posterior uveitis in immunocompetent individuals.
    • Reactivation at previously inactive cyst-containing scars is the rule in the immunocompetent.
    • A single inflammatory focus of fluffy white retinitis or retinochoroiditis associated with a pigmented scar ("satellite lesion") is typical.
    • "Headlight in the fog" is the classic description of a white retinal inflammatory nidus viewed through vitritis.
    • "Spill-over" anterior uveitis is common.
  • Treatment
    • Prednisolone (1 mg/kg) is given initially and tapered according to clinical response
    • Pyrimethamine is a folic acid antagonist, is administered as a loading dose of 75–100 mg for 1–2 days followed by 25–50 mg daily for 4 weeks in combination with oral folinic (not folic) acid 5 mg three times a week to retard thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and folate deficiency.
    • Sulfadiazine 1 g four times daily for 3–4 weeks is usually given in combination with pyrimethamine.
    • Intravitreal therapy with clindamycin (1 mg) and dexamethasone (400 μg) may be as effective as triple therapy in reactivated infection.

question.text: A patient diagnosed with c‌arcinoid syndrome excrete‌s a large amount of a cer‍tain metabolite of seroto‌nin in the urine. Which e​nzyme is involved in the ‌production of this metabo‌lite?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Monoamine oxidase

In carcinoid syndrome, 5-hydroxy indole acetic acid (5-HIAA) is excreted in large amounts in the urine and the enzyme monoamine oxidase is responsible for its production.

A carcinoid tumor is a tumor of argentaffin cells that produces an excessive amount of serotonin and is characterized by cutaneous flushing, abdominal cramps, and diarrhea. Serotonin is a specialized product of tryptophan metabolism (as shown below).

Urinary metabolites of serotonin in patients with carcinoid syndrome include N-acetylserotonin glucuronide and 5-hydroxy indole acetic acid. 

5-HIAA testing is a 24-hour urine test that is specific for carcinoid tumors. This test is the most common biochemical test for carcinoid tumors associated with carcinoid syndrome.

 Other options:

Option A: Aminotransferase is involved in the conversion of GABA to Succinate.

Option B: PLP-dependent amino acid decarboxylase is involved in the second step of the synthesis of serotonin, where 5-hydroxy tryptophan is decarboxylated to 5-hydroxy tryptamine/serotonin.

Option D: Tryptophan is first acted on by tryptophan hydroxylase in serotonin synthesis.

question.text: Match the following radiog‌raph images with their vi‍ews. Submentovertical vie​w Caldwell view Water's v‌iew Towne's view
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1-c, 2-b, 3-d, 4-a

The correctly matched pair is 1-c, 2-b, 3-d, 4-a.

Waters' view (also known as the Occipitomental view or nose-chin position) is a radiographic view, where an X-ray beam is angled at 37° to the orbitomeatal line. The rays are passed from behind the head and are perpendicular to the radiographic plate.

  • It is commonly used to get a better view of the maxillary sinuses.

Structures observed:

  • Maxillary sinuses
  • Frontal sinuses
  • Sphenoid sinus (through open mouth)
  • Zygoma
  • Zygomatic arch
  • Nasal bone

Caldwell's view (also known as the occipitofrontal view or nose-forehead position) is a radiographic view of the skull, where the X-ray plate is angled at 15° to the orbito-meatal line. The rays pass from behind the head and are perpendicular to the radiographic plate.

  • It is commonly used to get a better view of frontal sinuses.

Structures seen are: 

  • Frontal sinuses 
  • Ethmoid sinuses
  • Maxillary sinuses
  • Frontal process of the zygoma and the zygomatic process of the frontal bone
  • Superior margin of orbit and lamina papyracea
  • Superior orbital fissure
  • Foramen rotundum (inferolateral to superior orbital fissure)

The image below shows Caldwell's view 

Towne's view: 

It is taken with the patient in the supine position and lying on his back with the chin often depressed into the neck. The X-ray camera is angled at 30 degrees towards the feet so that the rays enter the head at the level of the hairline.

  • This is usually taken for acoustic neuroma and apical petrositis.
  • Bilateral petrous pyramids are visible in this view and hence can be compared.
Structures seen are:
  • Arcuate eminence and superior semicircular canal.
  • Mastoid antrum.
  • Internal auditory canal.
  • Tympanic cavity.
  • Cochlea.
  • External auditory canal.

The image below shows Towne's view 

Submentovertical view (also known as the basal view or Hirtz view) is taken with vertex near the film and X-ray beam projected at right angles to the film from the submental area.

 Structures seen are:
  • Sphenoid, posterior ethmoid, and maxillary sinuses (seen best in that order).
  • Zygoma.
  • Zygomatic arch.
  • Mandible along with coronoid and condyloid processes.
  • External auditory canal.
  • Middle ear cleft, i.e. mastoid cells, middle ear, and eustachian tube.
  • Internal auditory canal.

question.text: Fracture shown in the radi​ograph is:
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Aviator’s fracture

The above radiograph shows Aviator’s fracture. 

An aviator fracture is a coronal-plane fracture of the neck of the talus resulting from forced dorsiflexion of ankle. 

It is the second most common talar fracture, after talar dome fractures.

question.text: A 33-year-old patient pres​ented with myalgia, difﬁc‌ulty in climbing stairs, ​getting up from squatting‌ position, and combing hi​s hair for 3 months. An e‍dematous purplish-red per‌iorbital rash was seen. I​nvestigations revealed el​evated creatinine kinase ​levels. Muscle biopsy rev‌ealed perifascicular and ​perivascular lymphocytic ​infiltrates with muscle f​iber degeneration. Which ​of the following is not t‌rue regarding this condit​ion?

options.label: A

options.text: 20 to 40% of patients have​ an underlying malignancy‌
options.label: C
D
options.text: Dilated capillary loops in​ nail fold can be seen

question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Muscle tenderness is common

The above clinical scenario is suggestive of dermatomyositis. Muscle tenderness is not common in this disorder.

It is an autoimmune disorder affecting, predominantly, the skin and skeletal muscle and usually presents initially with a facial rash especially around eyelids which can be pruritic and sore. Myositis symptoms are usually weakness and fatigue especially while climbing stairs, raising arms, and standing from sitting due to proximal muscle weakness.

The presence of dysphagia points to a poorer prognosis.

The clinical signs seen in dermatomyositis are as follows:

  • Heliotrope rash around eyelids with a lilac hue.
  • Gottron papules - flat-topped lichenoid eruption on the proximal and distal interphalangeal joint
  • Shawl sign or V sign - fixed erythematous macular erythema)
  • Nail fold changes with periungal erythema with visible dilated capillary loops in the proximal nail fold
  • Proximal myopathy
  • Poikiloderma atrophicans vasculare
  • Calcinosis cutis

Approximately 20 to 40% of patients have an underlying malignancy (eg, lung, ovarian, breast) and hence screening should be done at the time of diagnosis.

question.text: A girl presented with itch‌ing and oozing from an ea‌rlobe lesion after wearin‍g nickel earrings. What t‌est will you do to confir‍m the diagnosis?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Patch test

This is a case of allergic contact dermatitis and the diagnosis is made by a patch test.

Allergic contact dermatitis is a reaction to a substance (allergen) that causes an eruption only in those individuals previously sensitized by the same molecule. It is a delayed-type of hypersensitivity (Type IV) reaction. It presents as pruritis and an eczematous eruption in sites where contact has taken place with the etiological agent/allergen.

Nickel is the most frequent contact allergen. Most of its salts, for example, nickel chloride and nickel sulfate, are readily soluble in water and sweat and have strong sensitizing properties. Jewelry and metal components of clothing are the usual sources of nickel in prolonged contact with the skin. 

Patch tests are used to identify the etiologic agent(s) of allergic contact dermatitis. Patches are usually applied to the back and removed 48 hours after application. The skin where the patch was applied is examined with readings taken 1 hour after removal and again 48 hours later.

The image below shows a picture of a skin patch allergy test:

 

Treatment of includes

  • Avoidance of the allergen (for example, further use of nickel‐plated objects should be avoided in this case)
  • A topical clioquinol–steroid combination can be considered as a treatment (clioquinol is known to chelate nickel)

question.text: Select the correct stateme‌nt:

options.text: Damage to the left hemisph‌ere leads to loss of insi‌ght
options.label: A
B
options.text: Damage to the right hemisp‌here can trigger depressi‌on
Patients with left tempora‌l lobe epilepsy maybe phi‌losophical and humorless
options.label: C
D
options.text: Patients with left tempora‌l lobe epilepsy may displ‌ay excessive emotions

question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Patients with left temporal lobe epilepsy maybe philosophical and humorless

Patients with left Temporal Lobe Epilepsy may generate references to personal destiny and philosophical themes and display a humorless approach to life.

The left hemisphere is responsible for analysis. The right hemisphere is responsible for affect, humor, socialization, and body image. Within the hemispheres, the temporal and frontal lobes play a prominent role in emotion.

Dysfunctions of Right Hemisphere:

  • Lesion in the right hemisphere:
    • Because the left hemisphere is intact, which is analytical and not emotional, and the damaged right hemisphere is unable to emote, the patient will show an indifference to the illness and therefore portray a lack of insight, which is called anosognosia.
    • There will be a loss of right hemispheric functions.
    • Eg: If a patient is unable to move his left hand, but denies to have any problem and is humorless, it is a case of right hemisphere injury.
  • Overactivation of the right hemisphere: As  seen in right Temporal Lobe Epilepsy, will lead to an excessive emotionality.

Dysfunction of Left Hemisphere:

  • Lesion in the left hemisphere:
    • The intact right hemisphere will struggle with the loss as it is highly emotional and left unchecked by the damaged left hemisphere, which will lead to a catastrophic depression.
    • There will be a loss of left hemispheric functions (intellectual disorder, aphasia).
  • Overactivation  of the left hemisphere: As seen in left Temporal Lobe Epilepsy, will lead to the patient being overanalytical and referring to thoughts of personal destiny and philosophy and having a humorless approach to life.

question.text: Which of the following con‌ditions is treated using ‍gamma knife?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Arterio-venous malformation

The arterio-venous malformation is treated using a gamma knife. 

Stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) is a reasonable alternative for people who refuse or cannot tolerate surgery. Here, beams are modified and focused only to concentrate on the tumor and have little effect on surrounding tissue. It can be done by using: 

  • X-knife using a linear accelerator (LINAC)
  • Gamma-knife using Cobalt 60 
  • CyberKnife - image-guided linear accelerator using real-time image guidance to deliver radiation from multiple angles.

The patient wears a specialized helmet that is surgically fixed to the skull. Gamma knife aims gamma radiation through a target point in the patient’s brain. An ablative dose of radiation is thereby sent through the tumour in one treatment session while surrounding brain tissues are relatively spared. 

SRS has been used in the treatment of almost every intracranial lesion but is commonly used in the treatment of acoustic schwannoma, pituitary adenoma, meningioma, and trigeminal neuralgia but not glioblastoma.

question.text: A 65-year-old postmenopaus​al female patient comes w​ith persistent backache n​ot responding to conserva‌tive treatment. She has a‌ history of lifting heavy​ weights 4 months back an‍d progressively increasin​g pain that worsens on wa‌lking. The pain starts ra​diating down her legs aft‍er walking for a distance​ of around 100 m. However‌, she feels no pain on wa‌lking uphill. What is the​ most probable diagnosis?​
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lumbar stenosis

The given clinical scenario of an old woman with back pain that worsens on walking and relieves walking uphill points to the diagnosis of lumbar stenosis. 

Walking uphill may be preferred as it flexes the spine and maximizes the spinal canal capacity, relieving the pain. 

Spinal stenosis is the narrowing of the spinal canal, causing nerve compression. It can be congenital or acquired, with degeneration being the most common cause. Other factors include conditions like spondylolysis, trauma, infection, and metabolic disorders. 

Degenerative spinal stenosis involves disc degeneration, facet joint hypertrophy, and ligamentum flavum calcification. These changes lead to reduced spinal canal dimensions and compression of the nerves resulting in neurogenic claudication. 

They present with symptoms such as back pain (most common), sciatica, sensory disturbances in the legs, motor weakness, and sometimes urinary disturbances. Pain typically occurs after standing or walking for a few minutes and is relieved by sitting, squatting, or flexing the spine. 

MRI is the imaging method of choice for the investigation of spinal stenosis. Conservative treatment is the first line for spinal stenosis, including reassurance, pain relief, exercise, and activity modification.

Surgery is considered if conservative measures fail and there is significant functional impairment and severe neurological symptoms. Posterior decompression is the surgical method. Laminectomy is performed for central stenosis.

question.text: A middle-aged man is poste‌d for an open cholecystec‌tomy. He has a medical hi​story of hypercholesterol‌emia. The pre-anesthetic ‌evaluation revealed abnor​mal liver function tests ‌and mild hepatomegaly. Wh​ich of the following musc​le relaxants can be safel‍y used in this patient?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Atracurium

Atracurium can be safely used in this patient with liver disease because of non-hepatic metabolism.

Atracurium and cis-atracurium undergo plasma ester hydrolysis and Hofmann elimination at physiological pH and temperature. Hofmann elimination is a spontaneous, non-enzymatic, chemical degradation. So, the clearance of atracurium and cis-atracurium is independent of liver or kidney function. Hence, they are the agents of choice in patients with liver disease and/or renal failure.

The metabolites of atracurium and cis-atracurium are monoquaternary acrylate and laudanosine.

Some of the adverse effects of atracurium are hypotension, tachycardia, and allergic reactions (bronchospasm) due to a dose-dependent histamine release. On the other hand, these adverse effects are not seen with cis-atracurium and so it is preferred over the former.

Pancuronium, rocuronium, and vecuronium are dependent on the liver for excretion.

Histology of lymph node:

question.text: A young man is diagnosed w‌ith hypertension. His lab​oratory studies reveal hy‌pokalemia and metabolic a‍lkalosis. He says that hi​s mother was also diagnos‍ed with hypertension at a​ younger age. Genetic tes​ting revealed the presenc​e of a mutation in ENaC g​ene. Which of the followi‌ng drugs is commonly used‍ in the treatment of the ‌given condition?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Amiloride

The clinical, laboratory, and genetic features are suggestive of Liddle's syndrome. It occurs due to the increased function of epithelial sodium channels. Amiloride blocks these channels and is therefore commonly used in the treatment of Liddle's syndrome.

Amiloride is a potassium-sparing diuretic that blocks epithelial sodium channels in collecting tubules. Therefore, it reduces sodium retention and potassium wasting. Triamterene acts similar to amiloride. However, it is less potent and more toxic than amiloride.

It is used to treat Liddle's syndrome, hypokalemia due to other diuretics, and lithium-induced polyuria. Its toxicity can cause hyperkalemic metabolic acidosis.

Liddle's syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition that is caused due to the gain of function mutation in the ENaC gene which codes for the epithelial sodium channels present in the kidney. Due to increased sodium retention, patients present with hypertension and hypokalemic alkalosis. They have normal aldosterone levels. They respond to treatment with amiloride.

Other options:

Option A: Furosemide is a loop diuretic and acts by inhibiting Na+/K+/2Cl- transporter in the ascending loop of Henle. Therefore it is not used in the treatment of Liddle's syndrome. A condition that mimics overdose loop diuretic is Bartter's syndrome. This syndrome occurs due to a defect in the Na+/K+/2Cl- transporter in the ascending loop of Henle. Patients will have low blood pressure, polyuria, polydipsia, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, and normal to increased calcium excretion. 

Option B: Spironolactone is an aldosterone antagonist. Since the levels of aldosterone are normal in Liddle's syndrome, it cannot be used in the treatment of the condition. The toxicity of spironolactone can cause hyperkalemia and gynecomastia.

Option D: Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide diuretic and acts by the inhibition of the Na+/Cl- transporter in the distal convoluted tubule. Therefore it is not commonly used in the treatment of Liddle's syndrome. A condition that mimics an overdose of thiazide diuretics is Gitelman syndrome. It is an autosomal recessive disease that causes a defect in the Na+/Cl- transporter in the distal convoluted tubule. Patients present with low blood pressure, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, hypomagnesemia, and hypocalciuria.

question.text: Which of the following act​s by suicide inhibition? ​1-Ethinyl estradiol 2- Sp​ironolactone 3- Ritonavir​ 4- Benzbromarone
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 3,4

Ritonavir and benzbromarone are both suicide inhibitors. 

Suicide inhibition is when an inhibitor binds to an enzyme and then undergoes a reaction to form an irreversible complex with the enzyme, inactivating it permanently. Ritonavir is a protease inhibitor used in HIV treatment and benzbromarone is a uricosuric agent used to treat gout by increasing uric acid excretion. It also inhibits CYP2C9 via mechanism-based (suicide) inhibition.

Other options: 

Ethinyl estradiol is a synthetic estrogen used in oral contraceptives and hormone replacement therapy. It acts through receptor-mediated mechanisms, not through suicide inhibition.

Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic and aldosterone antagonist. It works by competitively inhibiting aldosterone receptors in the distal tubules of the kidney, not through suicide inhibition.

question.text: In case of a meniscal tear‌ repair, which of the fol​lowing zones heals best?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Red zone

The red zone heals best in case of a meniscal tear due to its rich blood supply.

The menisci are divided into three zones depending on the perfusion of blood. The menisci are supplied by perimeniscal blood vessels from superior and inferior branches of medial and lateral genicular vessels.

Following birth, the menisci become increasingly avascular. By adulthood, only the peripheral 10% to 25% of the tissue is perfused. This gives rise to 3 distinct regions of the menisci:

  • The peripheral relatively vascularised region called the red-red zone (Zone 1)
  • A zone of transition between the 2 zones, which is called the red-white zone (Zone 2)
  • The completely avascular inner zone known as the white-white zone (Zone 3)

There is a direct relationship between the vascularization and capacity of the tissue to heal, predisposing the white-white zone to permanent post-traumatic and degenerative lesions.

Pemphigus vegetans is a rare form of pemphigus, it has two types, a severe Neumann type, and a milder Hallopeau type. Eosinophilic abscesses can be seen in the epidermis of older lesions.

question.text: A patient presents to you ‌with a history of ingesti​on of one uncrushed seed ​similar to that shown in ​the image below. He is as‌ymptomatic at presentatio​n. Which of the following‍ can be anticipated in th​is case?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. No poisonous action

The image shows seeds of Strychnos nux-vomica. No poisonous action is anticipated.

If swallowed uncrushed, the seeds of nux vomica have no poisonous action, as they are not dissolved in the gastrointestinal tract and are passed entirely in the feces.

Strychnine is a competitive antagonist of glycine at the postganglionic receptors in the motor neurons of the anterior horn of the spinal cord. This leads to increased activity in the motor neurons. 

The fatal dose is 15-30 mg of strychnine or one crushed seed. When crushed seeds are ingested, the symptoms are delayed for an hour or more.

Convulsions are produced as the reflex centers of the spinal cord are directly affected. The convulsions are first clonic but eventually become tonic.  Risus sardonicus results from the contraction of the jaws and facial muscles in which the corners of the mouth are drawn back. The convulsions are most marked in anti-gravity muscles so that the body typically arches in hyperextension, the posture known as opisthotonos. If the spasm involves the abdominal muscles, the body bends forward (emprosthotonos), or to the side (pleurosthotonos). If death is preceded by a severe convulsion, as in strychnine poisoning, it causes an increase in the body temperature known as postmortem caloricity.

question.text: Which of the following dru‍gs should not be given al​ong with levodopa
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pyridoxine

Pyridoxine abolishes the therapeutic effect of levodopa (not combined with carbidopa) by enhancing its peripheral decarboxylation so that less of it remains available to cross to the brain.

Drug Interactions of Levodopa

  • Pyridoxine: Abolishes the therapeutic effect of levodopa 
  • Phenothiazines, butyrophenones, metoclopramide reverse the therapeutic effect of levodopa by blocking DA receptors
  • Nonselective MAO inhibitors along with levodopa may cause hypertensive crisis
  • Antihypertensive drugs accentuate the postural hypotension caused by levodopa
  • Antiparkinsonian anticholinergic drugs have additive therapeutic action with low doses of levodopa, but retard its absorption—more time is available for peripheral degradation—efficacy of levodopa may be reduced.

question.text: Which of the following dru​gs used in the treatment ​of diabetes is known to c​ause urinary tract infect​ions?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dapagliflozin

Dapagliflozin is known to cause urinary tract infections.

Dapagliflozin is a sodium-glucose transporter 2 (SGLT-2) inhibitor. It acts by inhibiting the SGLT-2 transporter which is present on the proximal segment of the renal tubule and is responsible for the reabsorption of 80-90% of filtered glucose. This results in glycosuria. Other SGLT-2 inhibitors include canagliflozin and empagliflozin.

Apart from their effect on lowering blood glucose levels, SGLT2 inhibitors can cause mild weight loss and reduction in blood pressure. They have also been shown to reduce the risk of hospitalization in patients with heart failure.

The common side effects include urinary tract infections and genital mycotic infections due to the high glucose content of the urine. There is a risk of the development of diabetic ketoacidosis.

Other options :

Option B - Sitagliptin is a dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor. Its use is associated with an increased risk of heart failure.

Option C - Pioglitazone is an activator of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ (PPARγ), which is involved in the regulation of genes related to glucose and lipid metabolism. Its adverse effects include increased incidence of heart failure, peripheral edema, weight gain, macular edema, and osteoporosis.

Option D - Glimepiride belongs to the class of sulfonylureas. It stimulates insulin release by inhibiting the activity of the β cell KATP channel complex. Its side effects include hypoglycemia and weight gain.

question.text: A drug having a half-life ‌of 8 hours is administere​d orally thrice daily. Ho​w much time will be taken​ for the plasma concentra​tion to reach a steady st‌ate?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 36 hours

The time taken to reach steady-state plasma concentration is 4-5 half-lives. As the half-life of the given drug is 8 hours, so it will take 32-40 hours to reach a steady state. Hence, 36 hours will be the most appropriate answer.

Steady-state: The amount of drug administered is equal to the amount of drug eliminated within one dosing interval resulting in a plateau or constant drug plasma concentration, with the plasma concentration fluctuating between a minimum and maximum.

The time taken to reach steady-state plasma concentration is 4-5 half-lives.

Drugs with a shorter half-life reach a steady state rapidly, whereas drugs with longer half-life take days to weeks to attain a steady state.

Steady-state concentration (Css) = F x Dosing rate/ CL

  • where dosing rate is the dose per time interval and is dose/T
  • F is the fractional bioavailability, CL is clearance.

In the case of intravenous infusion,

Steady-state concentration (Css) = Rate of infusion/ CL

Pharmacokinetics of repeated drug dosing:

Plasma concentration of the drug will increase, reach a maximum, and decline after the first dose. A second dose will be administered before the first dose is completely eliminated. Consequently, the plasma concentration resulting from the second dose will be higher than from the first dose.

This increase in plasma concentration of the drug will occur continuously on repeated dosing (drug accumulation occurs) until a steady state at which drug elimination is equal to drug administration is reached. This is known as the plateau principle of drug accumulation.

A graph is plotted between plasma drug concentration and time as shown below. The given graph depicts the plateau principle of drug accumulation on repeated oral dosing.

question.text: A physiologist studies a c​hemoreceptor that detects‍ elevated sodium levels a​nd decreases the glomerul‌ar filtration rate. In th​e given image of the juxt​aglomerular apparatus, wh​ich of the marked structu‍res represents this chemo​receptor?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1

The chemoreceptors that detect elevated sodium and decrease the glomerular filtration rate are the macula densa cells in the distal convoluted tubule. These are marked as '1' in the given illustration.

Macula densa cells are chemoreceptors that detect sodium and chloride concentrations of the tubular fluid. In response to elevated sodium and chloride, the macula densa cells trigger the contraction of the afferent arteriole, resulting in decreased flow of blood to the glomerulus and reduced glomerular filtration rate (GFR). This vasoconstriction is mediated via increased sodium-potassium ATPase activity leading to increased adenosine formation resulting in calcium release. 

The given illustration shows:

1- Macula densa: These are specialized cells at the start of the distal convoluted tubule form the macula densa. 

2- Granular cells/JG cells: These are modified smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole; these are mechanoreceptors that secrete renin in response to a fall in blood pressure, which in turn, increases the blood pressure. 

3- Lacis cells: These are extraglomerular mesangial cells situated between afferent and efferent arteriole. 

4- Proximal tubular cells: These are involved in sustaining glomerulotubular balance, a mechanism by which the percentage of the reabsorbed solutes is maintained at constant levels. This is achieved by increasing the reabsorption of the solutes and water in the proximal convoluted tubule in response to increased GFR.

question.text: Which of the following tes‌ts on live birth are base‌d on the changes in the m​iddle ear?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Wredin’s test

Wredin’s test is based on the changes in the middle ear.

Tests for live birth:

  • Wredin’s test – Before birth, the middle ear does not contain air. It only contains gelatinous embryonic connective tissue. With respiration, the eustachian tube opens and the gelatinous substance is replaced by air. For this, the middle ear must be opened underwater by removing tegmen tympani. If an air bubble comes out, the test is said to be positive. This is not at all reliable.
  • Fodere’s test – Based on the increase in the weight of the lung due to increased blood flow after birth. The weight of unrespired lung is 30–40g whereas the weight of respired lung is 60–66 g.
  • Ploucquet’s test – Based on the ratio of the weight of the lung to the weight of the body in unrespired and respired lungs.
    • Unrespired lungs: Weight of lungs: weight of body = 1:70
    • Respired lungs: Weight of lungs: weight of body = 1:35
  • Breslau’s second life test: Air enters the stomach and intestine during respiration in a live-born fetus. So if respiration has taken place, they float in water, otherwise, they sink.

question.text: Match the following substa‌nces with their Respirato​ry quotient 1. Carbohydra‍tes A. 0.8 2. Fats B. 1 3​. Proteins C. 0.85 4. Mix​ed diet D. 0.7

question.text: Which of the following dru‌gs is representative of t​he graph as given below?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Penicillin

The graph represents the time-dependent killing and is demonstrated by penicillin (Beta-lactam antibiotics) and macrolides. 

In antimicrobial pharmacodynamics, antibiotics are generally categorised based on how their antimicrobial action depends on time or concentration.  

1. Time-dependent killing: These antibiotics rely on the amount of time the drug concentration remains above the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) to exert their effect. Once the concentration is above the MIC, increasing the concentration further does not significantly increase the rate of bacterial killing. Instead, the duration of exposure is key to effective bacterial eradication. This type is typically seen in beta-lactam antibiotics. 

Penicillins, cephalosporins, and vancomycin are examples of medications that demonstrate time-dependent killing. For these drugs, multiple daily doses are preferred over single doses.

The image below shows time-dependent killing.

2. Concentration-dependent killing: These antibiotics rely on achieving high peak concentrations to maximize bacterial killing. The higher the peak concentration relative to the MIC, the more effective the drug is. This means that the maximum concentration (Cmax) is more critical for efficacy. This type is seen in aminoglycosides (e.g., amikacin, gentamicin) and fluoroquinolones (e.g., ciprofloxacin).  

The image below shows concentration-dependent killing

question.text: The autopsy of a 1-year-ol‌d child who died of conge​stive cardiac failure rev​ealed multiple tumours of‍ the heart located in the​ ventricles. The histopat‍hologic findings is shown​ in the image below. Whic​h of the following is the​ most probable diagnosis?‌
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rhabdomyoma

The given histological slide shows abundant spider cells which are characteristic of cardiac rhabdomyoma.

Microscopically, cardiac rhabdomyomas are composed of bizarre, markedly enlarged myocytes. Histologic processing of the sample usually removes the glycogen and artifactually reduces the cytoplasm to thin strands. These strands stretch from the nucleus to the surface membrane. This gives an appearance that resembles a spider and is hence referred to as spider cells.

Rhabdomyomas are mostly seen in the first year of life. They are discovered when there is an obstruction to a valvular orifice or cardiac chamber. Approximately half the cardiac rhabdomyomas are due to sporadic mutations. The other 50% of cases are associated with tuberous sclerosis. They are usually multiple and appear in ventricles preferentially. They often regress spontaneously and may, therefore, be considered as hamartomas and not true neoplasms.

The image below shows histopathological findings of cardiac rhabdomyoma with spider cells.

Myxomas are the most common primary tumour of the adult heart. Unlike rhabdomyomas, they are usually single and the common site of origin is the region of the fossa ovalis in the atrial septum. Histology reveals the presence of stellate or globular myxoma cells embedded within an abundant acid mucopolysaccharide ground substance. There are characteristic vessel-like or glandlike structures.

Papillary fibroelastomas are mainly present in the valves. It appears as a cluster of hairlike projections up to 1 cm in length.

question.text: A patient diagnosed with h​ypertriglyceridemia was s​tarted on a medication, f‍ollowing which, he develo‌ped flushing, hyperglycem​ia, and elevated liver en​zymes. Identify the drug ‌consumed by the patient.
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nicotinamide

The drug most likely responsible for causing flushing, hyperglycemia, and elevated liver enzymes in a patient being treated for hypertriglyceridemia is Nicotinamide (Niacin). 

Niacin (nicotinic acid), is commonly used to treat hypertriglyceridemia and hypercholesterolemia. However, it is associated with side effects such as flushing, which is due to prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation. Niacin can also lead to hyperglycemia by impairing insulin sensitivity and may cause elevated liver enzymes, indicating potential hepatotoxicity. 

Other options: 

Option B: Rosuvastatin is a statin, primarily used to lower LDL cholesterol, and while it may elevate liver enzymes, it is less commonly associated with flushing and hyperglycemia. It can cause myopathy in patients. 

Option C: Ezetimibe inhibits cholesterol absorption in the intestines and is not typically associated with these side effects.

Option D: Fenofibrate is used to lower triglycerides can elevate liver enzymes and can increase the risk of developing myopathy if used concomitantly with statins, but it does not commonly cause flushing or hyperglycemia.

question.text: A patient with heart disea‌se has breathlessness on ​going to the bathroom. Wh​at grade does he belong t‌o?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. NYHA 3

This patient with heart disease with dyspnea on going to the bathroom, which is an activity of daily living/ ordinary activity, may be classified as NYHA class 3.

The New York Heart Association (NYHA) has outlined criteria that may be used to classify patients with heart disease based on their functional disability.

The Modified Medical Research Council (mMRC) Dyspnea Scale is used to classify the severity of symptoms in respiratory diseases, specifically COPD.

question.text: Which of the following is ​not essential in the work‍up of a mosaic Turner syn‌drome?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anti-nuclear antibodies

Among the given options, anti-nuclear antibodies are not essential in the workup of a mosaic Turner syndrome.

Turner syndrome occurs when females have a deletion or non-functional X chromosome. Approximately 50% of individuals with Turner syndrome have a condition called monosomy X (45, XO), where they only have one X chromosome. The remaining 50% have a mosaic chromosomal component (45, X with mosaicism).

Mosaic Turner syndrome does not stem from inheritance. Instead, it is the outcome of a random occurrence during cell division in the early development of the fetus. This results in a combination of cells in the affected individual's body, where some cells possess the usual two sex chromosomes, while others have only one copy of the X chromosome.

The clinical features of Turner’s syndrome are mentioned in the image below:

 

Prenatal diagnosis of Turner syndrome can be conducted through procedures like chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis. If a prenatal ultrasound reveals fetal hydrops, cystic hygroma, or cardiac defects, it may raise suspicions of Turner syndrome. However, the definitive confirmation of the diagnosis is typically done after birth through karyotype testing.

After receiving a diagnosis of Turner syndrome, it is essential to manage the condition by assessing for any associated abnormalities such as cardiac anomalies, renal anomalies, and learning disabilities. Screening should be conducted as part of the initial evaluation, followed by regular periodic screenings.

During the initial diagnosis, patients should undergo renal ultrasonography and cardiovascular evaluation. Echocardiography is typically performed in infants and children, while MRI is recommended for older girls and women. Regular monitoring of hearing, including serial audiology evaluations, is recommended throughout life, with an audiology evaluation every 3 yrs in children and every five years in adults.

Several laboratory tests are recommended for screening purposes at specific ages:

For patients aged four years and above, screening involves checking serum TSH to detect autoimmune thyroiditis and conducting tissue transglutaminase testing with total IgA to screen for celiac disease.

For patients aged ten years and above, screening includes fasting blood glucose, glycated hemoglobin, ALT, AST, serum creatinine, and urinalysis. These tests are performed to screen for conditions such as diabetes mellitus, fatty liver, and kidney disease.

For evaluation of vitamin D deficiency, serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D should be measured between 9 to 11 years of age and every 2 to 3 years thereafter.

question.text: A 45-year-old male patient​ presented with a history​ of bilateral lower limb ​weakness which progressed‌ to his upper limbs in a ​year. On examination, he ​had weakness in both lowe‌r limbs and wasting in th‌e left upper limb. Babins​ki sign was positive and ‍the deep tendon reflexes ​were absent. He has no se​nsory loss or any autonom‌ic dysfunction. What is t‍he likely diagnosis?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. ALS

The given clinical scenario with both UMN (Babinski positive) and LMN (absent deep tendon reflexes, wasting) findings in the absence of sensory loss and autonomic dysfunction points towards a diagnosis of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).

ALS is a progressive motor neuron disease with mutations in the genes encoding:

  • protein C9orf72 (open reading frame 72 on chromosome 9)
  • cytosolic enzyme SOD1 (superoxide dismutase),
  • RNA binding proteins TDP43 (encoded by the TAR DNA binding protein gene), and fused in sarcoma/translocated in liposarcoma (FUS/TLS).

The pathologic hallmark of ALS is the death of lower motor neurons (anterior horn cells in the spinal cord and cranial nerves innervating bulbar muscles) and upper motor neurons (corticospinal neurons originating in layer five of the motor cortex). At onset, ALS may involve only upper or lower motor neurons, but ultimately causes progressive loss of both categories of motor neurons. Clinical features of ALS include:

  • LMN findings: fasciculations, muscle cramps, asymmetric distal weakness, atrophy, and bulbar palsy. 
  • UMN findings: spasticity, increased reflexes, flexor spasms, and pseudobulbar palsy. 
  • Pseudobulbar affect: degeneration of corticobulbar projections manifested as inappropriate laughing, crying, or yawning which is often mood incongruent or may be triggered by stimuli that would not have elicited such a response.
  • Even in the late stages, sensory, bowel and bladder, ocular motility, and cognitive functions are preserved.

Treatment:

  1. Riluzole (100mg/day) reduces excitotoxicity by diminishing glutamate release and improves survival.
  2. Edaravone (IV infusion) works in the central nervous system as a potent scavenger of oxygen radicals that has the capability of slowing down ALS progression and improving survival.
  3. Tofersen is a newer drug proven to be effective for ALS associated with SOD1 mutation. It is an antisense oligonucleotide that targets SOD1 mRNA to reduce the synthesis of SOD1 protein.

 

Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune demyelinating and inflammatory disease of the CNS characterized by gliosis and neuronal loss. It is caused by an autoimmune response directed against components of the myelin sheath. Genetic predisposition with HLA-DRB1, cigarette smoking, vitamin D deficiency, and exposure to Epstein Barr virus (EBV) are known risk factors. Clinical features of MS include:

  • Visual impairment due to the involvement of the optic nerve (optic neuritis).
  • Involvement of the brainstem causes cranial nerve signs such as ataxia, nystagmus, and internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO).
  • Weakness of limb (usually UMN type), facial weakness, spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski signs, sensory impairment of the trunk and limbs, and loss of bladder control.

Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) is an acute inflammatory demyelinating neuropathy causing rapidly evolving ascending paralysis.  It is associated with diminished reflexes (areflexia) and autonomic involvement with or without sensory impairment.

Tropical spastic paraparesis also known as HTLV-1 associated myelopathy is a slowly progressive spastic syndrome with variable sensory and bladder disturbance but no LMN involvement. Diagnosis is by demonstration of HTLV-1 specific antibody in serum by ELISA and confirmation is done using radioimmunoprecipitation or Western blot analysis.

question.text: In a patient with type 1 d​iabetes with 3rd stage be‍ta cell damage, which of ‍the following situations ‌is associated with the sa‌me?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Autoimmune positive with dysglycemia

In type 1 diabetes mellitus, autoimmune positivity with dysglycemia indicates Stage 3, where clinical diabetes has become evident. This advanced stage is characterized by significant beta cell destruction and insulin deficiency, resulting in symptomatic diabetes.

Individuals with a genetic predisposition are exposed to a trigger that initiates an autoimmune process, leading to the production of islet autoantibodies and a progressive decline in beta cell function.

Stages of type 1 diabetes mellitus are:

Stage 1: It is marked by the presence of two or more islet cell autoantibodies, such as antibodies against zinc transporter (ZnT-8 antibodies), islet cell antibodies (ICA), anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies (GAD) and insulin autoantibodies (IAA) while glucose levels remain normal.

Stage 2: It involves ongoing autoimmunity and the onset of dysglycemia, where glucose regulation becomes impaired but does not yet meet the criteria for diabetes. This stage reflects a decline in beta cell function but is not yet characterised by the full-blown clinical symptoms of diabetes.

Stage 3: It is defined by the development of hyperglycemia that exceeds the diagnostic criteria for diabetes, indicating significant beta cell destruction and the onset of symptomatic diabetes. At this stage, patients have both autoimmune markers and impaired glucose regulation, confirming advanced disease progression.

question.text: Which of the following cau‍ses maximum malnutrition?​
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Duodenal fistula

Among the given conditions, maximum malnutrition is caused by duodenal fistulas.

Enterocutaneous fistulas are classified according to their location and volume of daily output.

  • Proximal fistulas are associated with higher output, greater fluid and electrolyte loss, and greater loss of digestive capacity.
  • Distal fistulas tend to have lower output, making them easier to manage and more likely to close spontaneously.

Although both gastric and duodenal fistulas are proximal fistulas, duodenal fistulas receive an additional 1 to 2 liters of enzymes, electrolytes, and water from the pancreatic and bile ducts. Hence duodenal fistulas are at greater risk for more electrolyte imbalance than gastric fistulas.

The management of enterocutaneous fistula is based on well-established principles known as SNAP which include:

  • S - Sepsis elimination and skin protection
  • N - A period of parenteral nutrition may well be required
  • A - Anatomical assessment
  • P - Definitive planned surgery

question.text: A 30-year-old man underwen‌t elective cholecystectom‌y. The cut specimen is se​en below. The calculi obs​erved is not associated w​ith which of the followin​g conditions?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Rapid weight reduction

The given image shows pigmented gall stones and they are not associated with rapid weight reduction.

Pigment gallstones represent complex mixtures of insoluble and inorganic calcium salts with unconjugated bilirubin. Disorders with elevated levels of unconjugated bilirubin increase the risk of developing pigmented gallstones. The various conditions associated with increase risk of pigmented gallstones are:

  • Demography: Asians more than Westerners, rural more than urban
  • Chronic hemolytic syndromes
  • Biliary infection with E.coli, Ascaris lumbricoides, and C. sinensis
  • Ileal disease
  • Ileal resection or bypass
  • Cystic fibrosis with pancreatic insufficiency

Cholesterol gallstones are non-pigmented. Cholesterol is rendered soluble by bile by forming micelles with bile salts and lecithins. When cholesterol concentrations increase and surpass the solubilizing capacity of bile(supersaturation), it precipitates into solid cholesterol monohydrate crystals. The four mechanisms of cholesterol gallstone formation are:

  • Supersaturation of bile with cholesterol
  • Hypomobillity of the gallbladder
  • Accelerated cholesterol crystal nucleation
  • Hyper- secretion of mucus in the gallbladder

The conditions associated with an increased risk of development of cholesterol gallstones are:

  • Demography: Northern Europeans, North and South Americans, Native Americans, Mexican Americans
  • Advancing age
  • Female gender and sex hormones
  • Oral contraceptives
  • Pregnancy
  • Obesity and metabolic syndrome
  • Rapid weight reduction
  • Gallbladder stasis
  • Inborndisorders of bile acid metabolism
  • Hyperlipidemia syndromes

question.text: Which condition is associa‌ted with the pancake brai‍n sign on CT?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Holoprosencephaly

The pancake brain sign represents the appearance of the cerebral parenchyma in the case of alobar holoprosencephaly.

Holoprosencephaly is a developmental disorder of the brain caused by the defective formation of the prosencephalon and impaired induction of forebrain structures. It is commonly associated with trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome), with alobar holoprosencephaly representing the most severe form. Features of holoprosencephaly include a single ventricular cavity (boomerang-shaped/horseshoe ventricle), fusion of frontal lobes, corpus callosum dysgenesis and other abnormalities.

Option C: Schizencephaly is the presence of unilateral or bilateral clefts within the cerebral hemispheres due to an abnormality of morphogenesis. The image given below shows schizencephaly:

question.text: A 60-year-old patient comp‌lains of decreased distan​t vision but now he does ​not use spectacles for ne​ar vision. The image of h​is ocular examination is ​given below. What is this‌ type of refractive error‌ called?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Index myopia

The most likely diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario and the image is index myopia seen in nuclear senile cataracts.

Index myopia occurs due to an increase in the refractive index of the crystalline lens due to nuclear sclerosis. Nuclear sclerosis is an ageing process in which the lens becomes hard and inelastic resulting in an increase in the refractive index, causing progressive myopia (decreased distant vision). A patient with presbyopia may be able to read again, without the aid of spectacles. This improvement in vision is termed second sight.

Other options:

Option B: Axial myopia is the most common type of myopia resulting due to an increase in the anteroposterior length of the eyeball. 

Option C: Curvatural myopia results due to increased curvature of the cornea, lens, or both.

Option D: Positional myopia results due to anterior placement of the crystalline lens in the eye.

question.text: What is the drug used for ‌estrogen dependant breast​ cancer?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tamoxifen

Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) that is mainly used for estrogen receptor-positive breast cancers in pre-menopausal women.

It exhibits selective agonistic and antagonistic activity for ER receptors (ERα and ERβ):

  • Agonist activity at the uterus, bone, liver, and pituitary
  • Antagonist activity in breast and blood vessels

Uses: 

  • Part of the primary treatment regimen for estrogen receptor-positive (ER+) breast cancers in pre-menopausal women
  • Adjuvant therapy after breast conservative surgery to prevent a recurrence
  • Tamoxifen also is effective (a 40%–50% reduction in tumor incidence) in preventing ER+ breast cancer in women at increased risk.

Adverse effects: 

  • Vasomotor symptoms (hot flashes) and sweating
  • Endometrial cancer
  • Increased risk of thromboembolic events
  • Fatty liver disease

question.text: Patients with sickle cell ‌disease are particularly ​susceptible to osteomyeli​tis caused by which of th​e following?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Salmonella enteritidis

Salmonella enteritidis is commonly implicated in osteomyelitis in patients with sickle cell anemia.

The common causative organisms include:
  • Staphylococcus aureus - the most common cause overall
  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa - most common cause in IV drug abusers
  • Salmonella - most common in patients of sickle cell anemia
  • Haemophilus influenzae - was a common causative organism in children, less common now due to vaccination
  • Streptococcus pyogenes - neonates
  • Escherichia coli, Klebsiella- most common cause in patients with genitourinary tract infections

question.text: A 25-year-old woman, who w​as admitted with accident​al rodenticide ingestion,​ was started on atropine.‌ All of the following sym​ptoms would improve in re​sponse to therapy except:​
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Muscle cramps

Atropinization in organophosphate (rodenticide) poisoning does not cause regression of nicotinic symptoms like muscle cramps. Hence, oximes are used for the reversal of nicotinic symptoms.

Atropine is effective against muscarinic receptors. It can be used to treat muscarinic symptoms like bradycardia, urinary incontinence, and hypotension.

question.text: A 37-week primigravid moth‌er presents to you in act‌ive labor. Her serology d‍one 2 weeks before reveal​ed the following findings​. What is the best step i‍n the management of the n‌ewborn? HBsAg positive HB​eAg positive Anti-HBc IgG‌ positive HBIG- Hepatitis‌ B immune globulin

options.text: Single-dose HBIG and vacci‌nation after 1 week
options.label: D

question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Single-dose HBIG and routine vaccination

The best step for an infant born to a hepatitis B carrier mother is single-dose HBIG and routine vaccination.

This pregnant woman having HBeAg and HBsAg positive with anti-HBc-IgG positive has a chronic hepatitis B viral (HBV) infection or is in a chronic carrier state. Both of the above scenarios put the infant at risk of HBV transmission. The recommended management is to give a single dose of hepatitis B immune globulin immediately and the first dose or routine vaccination within 12 hours of birth. HBIG confers passive immunity and is also given to persons exposed to HBV percutaneously or by contamination of mucosal surfaces along with the HBV vaccine. HBIG does not interfere with the antibody response to the hepatitis B vaccine. This combined procedure is ideal both for postexposure prophylaxis of persons accidentally exposed to blood known to contain hepatitis B virus and for the prevention of the carrier state in the newborn babies of carrier mothers.

Interferon alfa, entecavir, and tenofovir are first-line treatments indicated for patients with chronic active hepatitis to prevent the progression of liver fibrosis. It is not indicated as prophylaxis for babies born to seropositive mothers.

question.text: A newborn infant develops ‌respiratory distress 2 da‌ys after birth. On examin​ation, she is mottled and‌ has weak upper extremity​ pulses and absent femora​l pulses. Investigations ​reveal the coarctation of‌ the aorta. Which of the ​following drugs can you u‌se to keep the ductus ope​n medically before surgic​al repair?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Alprostadil

Alprostadil, a prostaglandin E1 (PGE1) analogue, can be used to keep the ductus open medically in the coarctation of the aorta.

The ductus arteriosus (the fetal connection between the pulmonary artery and the descending aorta) is functionally closed at 10-15hrs after birth and anatomically closed at 10-21 days after birth.

Survival of newborns with certain heart lesions such as coarctation of the aorta, hypoplastic left heart syndrome and transposition of great vessels depends on the patency of ductus arteriosus. Closure of PDA in such conditions can lead to hypoperfusion, severe hypoxia and cyanosis.

PGE1 is a potent and specific relaxant of ductal smooth muscle. PGE1 analogues like alprostadil, misoprost and rioprostil can be used to keep the ductus open and support systemic blood supply.

In patent ductus arteriosus, the ductus is closed medically by NSAIDS (which inhibit prostaglandin synthesis) like ibuprofen trometamol/ ibuprofen lysine and indomethacin. Morphine can be used to manage respiratory distress  but rarely preferred in a neonate.

question.text: A young man presented with‌ chronic cough and evenin‌g rise in body temperatur​e. He has a history of de​creased appetite and weig​ht loss. On examination, ​a mass is found in the ri​ght iliac fossa. A barium‍ meal follow-through imag​e of the patient is given‌ below. Which of the foll‌owing radiological findin​gs is not seen in this co‌ndition?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Apple-core sign

The clinical scenario and the barium meal follow-through study showing conical caecum, narrowing of the terminal ileum, and proximal ileal dilation are suggestive of ileocaecal tuberculosis. The radiological finding not seen in ileocecal tuberculosis is the apple-core sign. Apple-core or napkin-ring sign is typically seen in carcinoma colon as seen in the image below. It appears as short irregular stenosis with sharp shoulders at either end (yellow arrows).

 

Intestinal tuberculosis is an infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Patients typically present with cough, evening rise in temperature, weight loss, malaise, abdominal pain with distension, and intermittent diarrhea. On palpation, the abdomen feels doughy and a mass may be palpated in the right iliac fossa. The ileocaecal junction is the most common site of tuberculosis in the gastrointestinal tract. Other sites involved in the abdomen are the proximal colon and peritoneum.

Barium meal follow-through study findings in ileocaecal tuberculosis include:

  • Fleischner sign- narrow ileum with the thickened ileocecal valve
  • The ileocaecal angle becomes obtuse
  • Caecum appears pulled up and hepatic flexure is pulled down
  • Contracted conical caecum
  • Gooseneck deformity - due to contracted, and pulled-up cecum as well as straightening of the terminal ileum
  • String sign - due to persistently narrowed intestinal segment due to inflammation

The image below shows the findings seen in ileocaecal tuberculosis:

  • Yellow arrow- shrunken conical caecum
  • Red arrow- strictures narrowing of the terminal ileum and ileocaecal junction
  • Blue arrow- proximal ileal dilation

question.text: Which of the following dru‌gs does not represent the​ action of the graph labe‌lled as '4'?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Varenicline

Graph 4 represents an inverse agonist. Among the given options, varenicline is not an inverse agonist. It is a partial agonist.

Inverse agonist (graph 4): An agent that activates a receptor to produce an effect in the opposite direction of the agonist.
Examples:

  • Pimavanserin is an inverse agonist at 5HT2A 
  • β-Carboline is an inverse agonist at the benzodiazepine site of the GABA-A receptor.
  • Rimonabant is an inverse agonist at cannabinoid receptor.  
Graph 1 represents the agonist: An agonist is an agent that initiates the normal physiological response when combined with a receptor. Eg: Salbutamol is a beta-2 receptor agonist.
 
Graph 2 represents a partial agonist: An agent that produces a submaximal or partial effect when combined with a receptor. Eg: Buprenorphine and butorphanol are partial agonists at opioid receptors.
 
Graph 3 represents the competitive antagonist: An agent which blocks or reduces the action of an agonist on a receptor, but does not have any effect of its own. Eg: Naltrexone and naloxone are antagonists at opioid receptors

question.text: A 65-year-old man presente​d with anorexia, weight l‍oss, and anemia. Endoscop​y revealed a gastric ulce‍r. Which of the following​ barium study finding in ​this patient is suggestiv‌e of a malignant gastric ​ulcer?

options.text: Folds around the ulcer are​ smooth and even
options.label: B

question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Carman meniscus sign

The Carman meniscus sign is suggestive of a malignant gastric ulcer.

It is seen in the setting of a large, flat, malignant ulcer with healed-up edges. These edges trap the barium, which gives a convex formation towards the lumen of the stomach. In benign ulcers, it forms a concave shape towards the lumen of the stomach.

The Kirklin complex is a combination of the Carman meniscus sign associated with a radiolucent semi-circular zone surrounding the elevated ridge of the ulcer. This complex is seen in cases of gastric adenocarcinoma in barium studies.

Differences between benign and malignant gastric ulcers:

Folds Smooth, even Irregular, nodular, may fuse
Carman meniscus Absent Present
Ulcer shape Round, oval, linear Irregular

question.text: A child presents with irri‌tation and redness of the​ left eye at a primary he‌alth center. There are no​ previous immunization re‍cords. Examination showed‍ a greyish-white membrane​ over the bulbar and palp‌ebral conjunctiva which b‌led on peeling. What is t‌he likely etiology?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Corynebacterium diphtheriae

The of a child with irritation and redness of the eye with no previous vaccination records is suggestive of a case of membranous conjunctivitis and among the given options, Corynebacterium diphtheriae is the most likely etiological agent.

Membranous conjunctivitis presents with irritation and redness of the eye and is characterized by the formation of a greyish-white membrane that bleeds on peeling. Vaccines are routinely used to prevent diphtheria infection and hence, unvaccinated status increases his susceptibility to the bacteria. Moreover, the bacteria thrive in crowded populations and poor hygienic surroundings, hence a background of low socioeconomic context, such as an orphanage, acts as a risk factor in this case.

This condition is associated with the formation of fibrinous exudates on the surface and into the substance of the conjunctival epithelium. The causes include beta-hemolytic streptococci, Streptococcus pneumonia, Haemophilus aegyptius, Corynebacterium diphtheria, and Neisseria gonorrhea

The image given below shows the eye of a patient with pseudomembranous conjunctivitis. It differs from membranous conjunctivitis in that the membrane can be easily peeled off in this condition leaving an intact underlying epithelium.

question.text: Arrange the following in t​he sequence of auditory p​athway: Cochlear nucleus ‌Spiral ganglion Superior ​olivary nucleus Inferior ​colliculus Medial genicul‍ate body
question.explanation:

The correct sequence of the auditory pathway is spiral ganglion (2) - cochlear nucleus (1) - superior olivary nucleus (3) - inferior colliculus (4) - medial geniculate body (5). 

The spiral ganglion contains bipolar cells whose dendrites form the afferent supply for inner and outer hair cells of the organ of Corti and whose axons form the cochlear division of CN VIII that end in the cochlear nuclei.
