question.text: A 42-year-old teacher visi​ted the OPD for an annual‌ checkup. On examination,‍ prominent tortuous, dila‌ted subcutaneous veins ar‌e present on the medial s‌ide of her lower leg with‌ the CEAP classification ‌C2a Ep As Pn. She is awar​e of her varicose veins a‌nd is asymptomatic. She i​s wondering if treatment ​is required at this stage‌. What is the next step i​n management? CEAP - Clin‍ical - Etiology - Anatomy‌ - Pathophysiology classi​fication of varicose vein​s
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Compression stockings

The above clinical scenario is suggestive of mild asymptomatic varicose veins according to the CEAP classification. Therefore, the next step in management is compression stockings.

In addition, she has no venous complications like pigmentation, eczema, or venous ulcers. Thus, she can be initially managed with compression stockings. 

Compression stockings provide external pressure to the limb which compresses the veins and improves venous return. There are two lengths available - knee or thigh length. However, knee-length stockings are commonly prescribed as they have better compliance. 

They are useful for the initial management of varicose veins as they relieve symptoms and are a conservative approach. If the varicose veins become symptomatic or become visually distressing then non-conservative approaches described below can be considered. 

Other options: 

Option A: Radiofrequency ablation uses electromagnetic currents to destroy the vein without damaging the other structures. It can only treat junctional and truncal incompetence and not varicosities. 

Option B: Saphenopopliteal ligation is a surgical procedure where the saphenopopliteal junction is dissected with flush ligation. Alternatively, the small saphenous vein can also be ligated as proximally as possible. Sural nerve neuropraxia and common peroneal nerve injury are possible complications. 

Option C: Saphenofemoral ligation is a surgical procedure made where the great saphenous vein is ligated and stripped. There are complications associated with this procedure such as saphenous nerve injury and neovascularization due to trauma leading to reoccurrence.

question.text: An autopsy of a 38-year-ol​d male patient who died o​f cardiac failure showed ​the following histopathol‌ogical image of the endoc​ardium. Which of the foll‍owing best describes the ‌form of vegetation found ‌in this condition?

options.text: Small, warty vegetations a​long the line of closure ​of the valve leaflets
options.label: A
B
options.text: Large, irregular masses on​ valve cusps and chordae

options.label: C
options.text: Small, bland vegetations o​n the line of closure

options.label: D
options.text: Small to medium sized vege​tations on either sides o​f the valve

question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Small, warty vegetations along the line of closure of the valve leaflets

The clinical vignette with histopathology showing Anitschkow cells and Aschoff bodies are pathognomic of the rheumatic fever (RF) phase of rheumatic heart disease (RHD). It is associated with small, warty vegetations along the lines of closure of the valve leaflets.

RF is an acute, immunologically mediated, multisystem inflammatory disease classically occurring a few weeks after group A streptococcal pharyngitis. RHD is principally characterized by deforming fibrotic valvular disease, particularly the mitral valve.

Important pathological findings in rheumatic fever are:

  • Inflammation in the three layers of the heart can result in endocarditis, myocarditis, pericarditis, or pancarditis.
  • Inflammation of the endocardium and the left side valves can lead to fibrinoid necrosis. Over these areas of necrosis, small vegetations can be seen along the lines of closure, called verrucae.
  • In the subendocardium, irregular thickenings called MacCallum plaques can be present.
  • Aschoff bodies are collections of lymphocytes (primarily T cells), scattered plasma cells, and plump-activated macrophages (called Anitschkow cells). The Anitschkow cells have abundant cytoplasm and nuclei with chromatin that is centrally condensed into a slender, wavy ribbon. Hence they are also called caterpillar cells.
  • Mitral valve in chronic RHD shows leaflet thickening, commissural fusion and shortening, and thickening and fusion of the tendinous cords.This leads to narrowing of the mitral orifice, giving it a fish mouth appearance.

Image: Histology of a rheumatic fever patient showing Aschoff bodies and Anitschkow cells.

We mainly test for hepatitis A, B, and C. Tests for hepatitis D and E are not used routinely.

Hepatitis D only occurs concurrently with Hepatitis B, either as a co-infection (when it is clinically indistinguishable from HBV infection) or superimposed on chronic HBV infection. In the latter scenario, it presents as a sudden worsening of the patient’s condition. IgM anti-HDV, IgG anti-HDV, and HDV RNA assays are useful for diagnosis when hepatitis D is suspected.

Hepatitis E is not tested as the majority of patients who acquire hepatitis E virus (HEV) infection spontaneously clear the virus. Acute hepatic failure is more likely in those who are pregnant and in those who are malnourished or have preexisting liver disease. Chronic HEV has been described almost exclusively in immunocompromised hosts (e.g., organ transplantation). The diagnosis of acute HEV is typically based upon the detection of IgM antibodies to HEV. Both false positives and negatives are common with available assays and are thus, not very reliable. Thus, additional serologic testing or HEV RNA testing should be performed to confirm the diagnosis and not be useful as a screening test. [Please note the difference between anti-HBe and anti-HEV]

question.text: A patient is brought to th‌e casualty following a ro‍ad traffic accident. On e‍xamination, the patient i‌s conscious, BP is 90/60 ​mm Hg, respiratory rate i​s 40 breaths per minute, ‌and pulse rate is 120 bpm‌. The X-ray is shown belo​w. What is the next best ‌step in management?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chest tube insertion

The given X-ray features showing a well-demarcated area devoid of lung markings on the left side with tracheal deviation and the mediastinal shift to the right side, along with the clinical scenario is suggestive of tension pneumothorax. The next best step in the management is chest tube insertion.

Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis, and treatment should never be delayed while waiting for radiological confirmation. Imaging modalities used are ultrasound–extended focused assessment with sonar for trauma (eFAST), chest x-ray, and spiral CT.

A tension pneumothorax develops when there is a tear either in the parietal or visceral pleura. This tear acts as a one-way valve i.e., air enters from the lung or chest wall through it during inspiration but has no way to escape during expiration. This ultimately leads to the collapse of the affected lung.

It usually occurs following penetrating or blunt chest trauma, iatrogenic lung injury, or mechanical positive pressure ventilation.

It is characterized by:

  • Chest pain
  • Tachypnea and acute dyspnea
  • Sudden onset hemodynamic compromise (tachycardia, hypotension, low O2 saturation, loss of consciousness)
  • Neck vein distention
  • Tracheal deviation away from the side of the injury 
  • Decreased chest movements on the affected side
  • Hyper-resonance on percussion on the affected side
  • Absence or decreased breath sounds on the affected side

The X-ray below shows a left-sided tension pneumothorax. There is a large, well-demarcated area devoid of lung markings on the left side. The yellow arrows are pointing to the tracheal deviation and the mediastinal shift to the right side.

Management of tension pneumothorax:

  • Immediate management- needle decompression or needle thoracostomy i.e. insertion of a wide-bore needle in the 5th ICS anterior to the midaxillary line
  • Definitive management- tube thoracostomy or chest tube insertion in the 5th ICS in the triangle of safety, identified as a triangle that lies anterior to the midaxillary line above the nipple, below, and lateral to the pectoralis major muscle.

The images below show the triangle of safety and technique of chest drain insertion.

Other options:

  • Pericardiocentesis is done in cases of cardiac tamponade which is characterized by the presence of hypotension, distended jugular veins, and muffled heart sounds (Beck's triad). The breath sounds are absent in tension pneumothorax while they are present in cardiac tamponade.
  • Surgery for pneumothorax can be performed by video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) or as an open procedure (thoracotomy) in cases of spontaneous pneumothorax failing to settle despite chest drainage. Pleural adhesion is achieved by chemical pleurodesis where talc is used and is insufflated into the chest cavity.

question.text: Least frequency of slow waves is seen in:
question.explanation:
Among the given options, the least frequency of slow waves is seen in the stomach (4/min).

The Basal electrical rhythm (BER), also called slow-wave, is a rhythmic fluctuation of membrane potential in the gastrointestinal smooth muscle. It is initiated by the interstitial cells of Cajal. The membrane potential fluctuates between -65mV and -45mV.

The BER is seen in all sites of gastrointestinal smooth muscle except in the esophagus and proximal stomach.

The rate of BER in various sites is as follows:
  • Stomach: 4/min
  • Duodenum: 12/min
  • Distal ileum: 8/min
  • Cecum: 2/min
  • Sigmoid colon: 6/min
The BER does not cause contraction of the smooth muscle. However, when the BER is superimposed by the spike potentials, it increases muscle tension.

Acetylcholine causes an increase in the number of spike potentials and muscle tension. Epinephrine causes a decrease in the number of spike potentials and muscle tension.

Muscle contraction can occur only when the motor stimulus is provided during the depolarisation part of the BER.

Thus, BER does not cause muscle contraction by itself, but controls the rate and organization sites of the muscle contractions, as in coordination of the peristaltic activity and setting the rhythm of segmentation.

question.text: Valley fever or desert rhe​umatism refers to which o‍f the following diseases?‍
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Coccidioidomycosis

  • Coccidioidomycosis commonly known as Valley fever or desert rheumatism is a mammalian fungal disease caused by Coccidioides immitis or Coccidioides posadasii.
  • C. posadasii and C. immitis are morphologically identical, but genetically and epidemiologically distinct.
  • Infections usually occur due to inhalation of the arthroconidial spores after soil disruption.

Sins & Symptoms:

  • The primary infection is most often respiratory, with symptoms resembling bronchitis or pneumonia that resolve over a matter of a few weeks.
  • The classic triad of coccidioidomycosis known as "desert rheumatism" includes the combination of fever, joint pains, and erythema nodosum.
  • Chronic fibro cavitary disease is manifested by cough, sputum, fevers, night sweats and weight loss.
  • Osteomyelitis, including involvement of the spine, and meningitis which may occur months to years after initial infection.

Coccidioidomycosis may be divided into the following types:

  1. Acute coccidioidomycosis, sometimes described in literature as primary pulmonary coccidioidomycosis
  2. Chronic coccidioidomycosis
  3. Disseminated coccidioidomycosis, which includes primary cutaneous coccidioidomycosis

Treatment:

  • Fluconazole and intravenous amphotericin B are used in progressive or disseminated disease, or in immunocompromised individuals.
  • Itraconazole or ketoconazole may be used for milder disease.
  • Fluconazole is the preferred medication for coccidioidal meningitis, due to its penetration into CSF.
  • Intrathecal or intraventricular amphotericin B therapy is used if infection persists after fluconazole treatment.
  • The antifungal medications posaconazole and voriconazole have also been used to treat coccidioidomycosis.

question.text: Enterogastric inhibitory reflexes are stimulated by all of the following except:
question.explanation:
Enterogastric inhibitory reflexes are stimulated by acidic contents, not alkaline.

The duodenal factors that can initiate enterogastric inhibitory reflexes (enterogastric reflexes) are:
  • Distention of the duodenum
  • Presence of any irritation of the duodenal mucosa
  • Acidity of the duodenal chyme
  • Osmolality of the chyme - either hypotonic or hypertonic fluid initiate enterogastric inhibitory reflexes. Thus, the flow of non-isotonic fluids into the small intestine is regulated. This prevents rapid changes in electrolyte concentrations in the extracellular fluid during the absorption of the intestinal contents.
  • Presence of certain breakdown products in the chyme, especially proteins and to a lesser extent, of fats

question.text: The inclusion body rickett‌sial morula is found in n​eutrophils during infecti‍on caused by:

Correct answer: C. Anaplasma phagocytophilum

The inclusion body rickettsial morula is found in granulocytes (neutrophils) during infection caused by Anaplasma phagocytophilum. 

Anaplasma causes human granulocyte anaplasmosis. It is transmitted by ticks. Clinical features are fever, headache, confusion, vomiting and myalgia. Inclusions in granulocytes are seen. The image below shows a morula of Anaplasma in a neutrophil:

Ehrlichia chaffeensis is a gram-negative, obligate intracellular bacterium that is transmitted by hard ticks such as the lone star tick. Clinical presentation of Ehrlichia chaffeensis infection is similar to that of Anaplasma infection. Severe human monocytic ehrlichiosis is characterized by meningoencephalitis, renal failure, respiratory failure, and shock. The treatment of choice for human monocytic ehrlichiosis is doxycycline. 

The image below shows a morula of Ehrlichia in a monocyte:

Note: Infection by both Anaplasma and Ehrlichia can lead to the formation of rickettsial morulas in leukocytes. However, Anaplasma leads to the formation of morulas predominantly in the granulocytes, whereas Ehrlichia predominantly affects the monocytes.

Other options:

Option A: Rickettsia rickettsii causes rocky mountain spotted fever. It is transmitted by ticks. Patients present with fever, headache, and rash.

Option B: Rickettsia conorii causes Mediterranean spotted fever. The parasite is transmitted by ticks, and the patients present with fever, headache, rash, and eschar (tache noire).

question.text: A child presents with ment‌al retardation, bone pain‍, and inability to walk. ​On funduscopy examination‌, a cherry red spot is se‌en. There is no organomeg​aly. What is the most lik​ely diagnosis?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tay-Sachs disease

The given clinical scenario, along with the fundoscopy image showing a macular cherry-red spot, indicates that the most likely diagnosis is Tay-Sachs disease. 

Tay-Sachs disease is a lysosomal storage disease caused by the deficiency of β-hexosaminidase. It can present during infancy with macrocephaly, increased startle reaction, gradual loss of motor skills, and a macular cherry-red spot. Affected children usually die by the age of 10–15 years. 

It is of two types—juvenile-onset and adult-onset. The symptoms of the juvenile-onset form include ataxia and dementia. Dysarthria, lower motor neuron signs, and psychiatric disorders are common in the adult-onset type. 

Other options:

Options B - Niemann-Pick disease is an autosomal recessive inborn error of lipid metabolism. It results due to the deficiency of the sphingomyelinase enzyme. This results in the accumulation of sphingomyelin in the brain, lungs, liver, and spleen. The clinical features include a combination of hepatosplenomegaly, developmental delay, failure to thrive, severe psychomotor regression, interstitial lung disease, and a cherry-red spot in the macula. 

Option C - Hurler syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis I) is an autosomal recessive condition that affects multiple organs. Presentation is usually at 6–24 months with corneal clouding, coarse facial features, joint stiffness, and skeletal dysplasia. Glaucoma, retinal degeneration, and nasal discharge are the other features. The condition is generally fatal.

Option D - Gaucher disease is a glycolipid storage disorder that can present with hepatosplenomegaly, mental retardation, and erosion of long bones. It is caused by the deficiency of β-glucosidase. The Gaucher cell has a wrinkled-paper appearance due to intracytoplasmic inclusions, which is a characteristic feature.

Bisphosphonates are given for periods of more than one year (Option B is false). In this case, as the patient is having a history of osteoporotic fracture, teriparatide can be given before bisphosphonates.

Pharmacologic management of osteoporosis:

Bisphosphonates: These are pyrophosphate analogs that act by directly inhibiting bone resorption. The antiresorptive action is mainly due to its direct inhibitory effect on osteoclasts. It causes osteoclast apoptosis as well as the prevention of hydroxyapatite dissolution. Long-term bisphosphonates therapy is given for durations of 3-5 years, depending on the fracture risk of the patient. Since they are associated with osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical femur fractures, a drug holiday may be advised after long-term management.

Teriparatide is a recombinant PTH analog that has an anabolic effect on bone homeostasis by increasing osteoblastic activity. It increases bone mineral density and decreases the risk of fractures in postmenopausal women. Indications of teriparatide therapy include the history of osteoporotic fracture, multiple risk factors for fracture, intolerance, or failure of previous osteoporosis therapy. It is only approved for 2 years of use. Clinical trials that used teriparatide prior to bisphosphonate have been proven effective.

Denosumab is a human monoclonal antibody with a mechanism of action similar to that of osteoprotegerin (OPG). It binds to RANK Ligand (RANKL), thereby inhibiting its binding to the RANK receptor of the surface of osteoclasts. This prevents RANK receptor activation and subsequent bone resorption.

Selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs) - Estrogen has a protective effect that prevents accelerated bone loss. This is carried out by reducing the bone resorption effects of parathyroid hormone (PTH). Keeping in line with these effects, osteoporosis prevention in postmenopausal women has been attributed to the use of SERMs such as raloxifene. It acts as an estrogen agonist on the bone and liver.

Calcium and Vitamin D supplementation: Calcium supplementation in the elderly suppresses bone turnover and improves bone mineral density. 1200mg of calcium is daily required in adults of more than 50 years of age. Vitamin D supplementation with 400-800IU/day improves intestinal calcium absorption, suppresses bone remodeling, and improves bone mineral density.

question.text: Arrange the following even‌ts in the sequence in whi​ch they occur, after 'p w​ave' in ECG: a wave in JV​P First heart sound Rapid​ filling of ventricles T ‍wave in ECG
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1-2-4-3

The correct sequence of events that occur after the p-wave is 1-2-4-3, ie:-

a wave in JVP → First heart sound  → T wave in ECG  → Rapid filling of ventricles.

The sequence of the events in this question can be better understood with the following diagram:

  • The p wave in the ECG represents atrial depolarization, which causes contraction of the atria, represented by the 'a' wave in the JVP. Atrial contraction causes final filling of the ventricles (fourth phase of ventricular diastole) 
  • Atrial contraction is followed by the closure of the mitral valve, which causes the first-heart sound.
  • This is followed by the isovolumetric contraction of the ventricle, which causes c wave in JVP, due to bulging of the tricuspid valve. This is followed by the rapid ejection phase of the ventricle.
  • The T wave of ECG occurs during ventricular repolarization, which is followed by the opening of the mitral valve, followed by rapid filling phase of the ventricle (second  phase of ventricular diastole).

Note: Passive rapid filling occurs as the mitral valve opens just before atrial contraction occurs.

question.text: You are conducting an expe​riment on mitochondrial r​espiration. You add malat‍e/pyruvate and respiratio​n is normal. You add succ​inate and respiration is ​normal. When you add anot‌her substance in the pres‍ence of pyruvate/succinat‌e and malate, respiration‌ is blocked. Which of the​ following substances is ‌most likely added?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Oligomycin

In the experiment conducted on mitochondrial respiration, respiration will be blocked by the addition of oligomycin, an antibiotic, when added in the presence of pyruvate/ succinate and malate. Oligomycin inhibits oxidative phosphorylation in the mitochondria and hence blocks respiration.

Electron transport chain (ETC)/respiratory chain is the final pathway by which all the electrons derived from the oxidation of carbohydrates, fatty acids, and amino acids are directed towards the final reaction with oxygen, to form water and adenosine triphosphate (ATP).

The chemiosmotic theory states that the flow of electrons through the respiratory chain generates a proton motive force. This force drives the formation of ATP by the process of oxidative phosphorylation.

Complexes of ETC     Inhibitors
Complex I: NADH-CoQ oxidoreductase Piericidin, amobarbital, rotenone
Complex II: Succinate-CoQ reductase TTFA (thenoyltrifluoroacetone), carboxin, malonate
Complex III: CoQH2-cytochrome c oxidoreductase BAL(British anti-lewisite), antimycin A
Complex IV: cytochrome oxidase Hydrogen sulfide, carbon monoxide, cyanide
Complex V (informally): ATP Synthase Atractyloside, oligomycin


In the given experiment, malate and pyruvate are electron donors (NADH) at complex I of the ETC, and succinate is the electron donor (FADH2) at complex II. Normal respiration is observed on the addition of substances at both complexes I and II i.e., both oxygen consumption and ATP synthesis from ADP (adenosine diphosphate) take place.

Oligomycin is a competitive inhibitor of the Fo (oligomycin-sensitive) complex of ATP synthase (complex V) and blocks oxidation and phosphorylation by stopping the flow of protons through the ATP synthase enzyme complex. Hence the addition of oligomycin will inhibit complex V and stop respiration.


Other options:

Options A and B: Rotenone (option A) if added, will inhibit complex I. Electron transfer before complex I will be blocked but not after. Hence, normal respiration will occur. Similarly, antimycin A (option B) inhibits complex III, and electron transfer prior to complex III will be blocked and not after. Hence, respiration will not be completely hindered.

Option C: 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP) is an uncoupler that dissociates oxidation in the respiratory chain from phosphorylation. Hence, respiration continues without ATP synthesis.

question.text: The glucose transporter re‌sponsible for insulin-med‌iated glucose uptake into​ adipocytes is ______.
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. GLUT 4

The glucose transporter responsible for insulin-mediated glucose uptake into adipocytes is GLUT-4.

Glucose transporters, also referred to as GLUTs, are transport proteins in the cell membrane responsible for the transfer of glucose into the cells by facilitative diffusion. Facilitative diffusion involves the passage of molecules or ions through the cell membrane by them binding chemically to a carrier/ transport protein that is responsible for their movement across the cell membrane.

GLUT-4 is a transport protein present in adipocytes. When there is a rise in blood glucose level, insulin secreted by the pancreatic beta cells binds to its receptors on the plasma membrane of adipocytes. Upon binding of insulin to its receptor, activation of the receptor's tyrosine-kinase domain occurs. This activation starts a protein activation cascade leading to the translocation of GLUT4 to the plasma membrane.

Once translocation occurs and GLUT4 is inserted into the plasma membrane, facilitated diffusion of glucose down its concentration gradient into the cell occurs.

Additionally, GLUT-4 is also present in skeletal muscle cells and cardiomyocytes.

Other options:

Option B: GLUT-2 is found in the liver, pancreatic β cell, small intestine, and kidney. Its function is the rapid uptake or release of glucose.

Option C: GLUT-5 is present in the small intestine and is involved in the absorption of fructose.

Option D: SGLT-1 is a sodium dependent unidirectional transporter present in the small intestine and kidney that is involved in the active uptake of glucose against a concentration gradient.

options.text: Pain on attempt of hyperex​tension of fingers
options.label: A

question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Abscess of midpalmar space

The above image classically shows Infectious Tenosynovitis.

Tenosynovitis

  • Infection of the flexor tendon sheath.
  • Puncture wounds on flexor creases
  • May involve ulnar and radial bursa
  • Kanavel’s sign
    • 4 cardinal signs are
    • Tenderness over involved sheath
    • Finger in flexion deformity

  • Note:

    Extensor and flexor tendon sheaths have two surfaces: an inner visceral layer (visceral paratenon) adherent to the tendon and an outer parietal layer (parietal paratenon) abutting adjacent structures such as adjacent muscles and retinacular structures. Normally, the visceral and parietal layers abut one another. In the setting of tenosynovitis, the potential space between these two layers may fill with inflammatory or purulent fluid.

    The visceral and parietal layers of most tendons coalesce at the proximal and distal ends to produce a closed tendon sheath compartment. The thumb flexor sheath is contiguous with the radial bursa, and the small finger flexor sheath is contiguous with the ulnar bursa; these two bursae extend proximally into the carpal tunnel. The radial and ulnar bursae communicate at the wrist in 50 to 80 percent of patients . Therefore, infection in the thumb tendon sheath can spread to the small finger sheath via the ulnar bursa (or vice versa), creating a "horseshoe abscess."

question.text: What is the frequency of t​etanic stimulation used i​n neuromuscular monitorin​g?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 50 Hz

The commonly used frequency of tetanic stimulation in neuromuscular monitoring is 50 Hz.

Tetanic stimulation is a method to evaluate residual neuromuscular blockade.

Tetanic stimulation consists of a series of extremely rapid electrical stimuli typically applied over 5 seconds. The most commonly used frequency is 50 Hz stimulation given for 5 seconds.

  • During a depolarizing block, the muscle response to 50 Hz tetanic stimulation for 5 seconds is sustained.
  • In contrast, during a phase II block after the injection of succinylcholine, the response following tetanic stimulation is not sustained i.e., a fade occurs. 

Disadvantages of tetanic stimulation are:

  • This method has only 70% sensitivity to detect residual paralysis and its specificity is only about 50%. Hence, this test is of limited value for assessing neuromuscular recovery.
  • This method is very painful, which makes it difficult to use in unanesthetized patients.
  • During the late phase of neuromuscular recovery, tetanic stimulation can produce lasting antagonism of neuromuscular block in the stimulated muscle. This may change the response of the tested site such that it may no longer be representative of other muscle groups.

Note:

Other patterns of nerve stimulations, which are used to assess the patients for residual blockade are

  • Train of four stimulation: Here four supramaximal stimuli (2 Hz) are delivered every 0.5 seconds.
  • Double-burst stimulation: Here two short bursts of 50 Hz tetanic stimuli is delivered, which are separated by 750 ms.

question.text: A 5-year-old with gradually progressive hoarseness of voice over three months and respiratory distress for 2 weeks. What is the most likely diagnosis?
question.explanation:
The given clinical scenario of a child presenting with chronic hoarseness (3 months) of voice and respiratory distress for 2 weeks suggests the diagnosis of respiratory papillomatosis (juvenile papillomatosis).

Croup (Option A) and acute epiglottitis (Option D), which cause acute upper respiratory tract obstruction, are ruled out due to the chronic nature of the symptoms. In croup, the upper airway obstruction becomes apparent after 1 to 3 days of low-grade fever, rhinorrhea, and pharyngitis. On the other hand, in epiglottitis, a child experiences respiratory distress within hours of developing a fever.

Vocal nodules (Option C) are not typically associated with respiratory distress.

Respiratory papillomatosis is the most common respiratory tract neoplasm in children. They are simple warts (benign tumors) caused by human papillomavirus types 6 and 11 commonly seen in children aged 3 to 5 years.

The course involves remissions and exacerbations of recurrent papillomas, mostly affecting the glottic area (vocal cords), and supraglottis. The patient presents with progressively worsening hoarseness, sleep-disordered breathing, dyspnea, stridor, and severe airway obstruction if left untreated.

Diagnosis confirmed by direct laryngoscopy, which shows grape-like projections (shown below), and biopsy. Treatment consists of micro laryngoscopy and CO2 laser excision. Antivirals like interferon alpha2a, ribavirin, cidofovir, and acyclovir are used as adjunct therapies.

Other options:
  • Option A: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) is caused by the parainfluenza virus. The patient initially presents with an upper respiratory tract infection (rhinorrhea, pharyngitis, cough, low-grade fever) followed by a characteristic barking cough, hoarseness, and inspiratory stridor.
  • Option C: Vocal nodule (singer’s or screamer's nodule) occurs as a result of chronic vocal abuse. They appear symmetrically at the junction of the anterior one-third and posterior two third of the vocal cord. The patient presents with chronic hoarseness and voice fatigue.
  • Option D: Acute epiglottitis is caused by streptococcus pyogenes, pneumococci, Hemophilus influenzae, and staphylococcus aureus. It is characterized by an acute rapidly progressive course of high-grade fever, dyspnea, and stridor.

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of left superior gluteal nerve injury.

The patient shows characteristic lurching gait/ Trendelenburg's gait (positive Trendelenburg's sign), which is seen in paralysis of gluteus medius and gluteus minimus muscles. These muscles are supplied by the superior gluteal nerve.

When the leg on one side is lifted off the ground, the gluteus medius and minimus muscles, on the opposite supported side, exert traction on the hip bone by acting from the femur. This action results in the slight raising of the pelvis on the unsupported side, which helps maintain the trunk in the upright position.

When the gluteus medius and minimus are paralyzed, the pelvis sinks down on the unsupported (normal) side, when the patient tries to stand on the affected limb.

In the given case, when the patient lifts up his right leg and tries to stand on the left leg, his right pelvis tilts down. This shows that the left side abduction mechanism is paralyzed and the right side is normal. Hence, the left superior gluteal nerve injury is present in this case.

The image given below shows the Trendelenberg test.

Note: Inferior gluteal nerve supplies the gluteus maximus muscle.

question.text: Which of the following is the most common etiological agent associated with epiglottitis in children, overall in the world?
question.explanation:
The most common etiological agent, overall in the world, of acute epiglottitis in the pediatric age group, now is Streptococcus.

In the past, Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) used to be the most commonly identified cause of acute epiglottitis. But, since the widespread use of the H. influenzae type b vaccine, invasive disease caused by H. influenzae type b in pediatric patients has been reduced by 99%.

Therefore, other organisms, such as Streptococcus pyogenes (GAS), Streptococcus pneumoniae, non-typeable H. influenzae, and Staphylococcus aureus, have become the common causes of acute epiglottitis in pediatric age group, overall in the world.

Lateral X-ray of the neck shows the thumb sign in acute epiglottitis.

question.text: Which part of the spine is most commonly affected in patients with rheumatoid arthritis?
question.explanation:
The atlantoaxial joint (C1 & C2) is the most commonly affected part of the spine in patients with rheumatoid arthritis.

The joints in rheumatoid arthritis are bilaterally and symmetrically involved. The commonly affected joints are:
  • Metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints
  • Wrists
  • Proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints

question.text: The presence of which of t‌he following indicates th‌at CPR is of high quality​? Chest compression at a ​rate of 100-120/minute Br‍eathing rate of 20-25/min‍ute Depth of compression ‍should be 5-6 cm Allow ch​est recoil
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 3, 4 only

Chest compressions at a rate of 100-120/minute, depth of compression 5-6 cm, and allowing complete chest recoil indicate high-quality CPR. The compression-to-ventilation ratio in the absence of an advanced airway should be 30:2 (30 compressions to be followed by 2 breaths). If an advanced airway (endotracheal tube or supraglottic airway device) is present, 10 breaths/minute should be given.

question.text: A 19-year-old male patient‌ comes to your office wit​h a 3-month history of no‌n-bloody diarrhea, abdomi‌nal pain, and weight loss​. Laboratory tests reveal‍ anemia, increased inflam​matory markers, and incre​ased ASCA (Anti-Saccharom​yces cerevisiae antibodie‌s). A barium small bowel ‍follow-through reveals an‌ early finding of the sus​pected pathology, shown i​n the image below. Identi‍fy the finding.
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Aphthous ulcer

The barium follow-through shows an aphthous ulcer, seen in Crohn's disease.

Aphthous ulcers are one of the earliest radiological features of Crohn’s disease in the small bowel. They are shallow ulcers of the gastrointestinal mucosa which are separated by normal intervening mucosa.

CT or MR enterography has a higher sensitivity for the diagnosis of Crohn’s disease. They may reveal additional features such as a fat halo sign due to submucosal fat deposition and a comb sign due to engorgement of the vasa recta.

Other radiological features of Crohn's disease in the small bowel include:-

Option B: Progressive disease results in longitudinal ulcerations on the mesenteric bowel surface with pseudosacculation formation on the anti-mesenteric surface as shown below.

Option C: Cobblestone appearance is due to longitudinal and transverse ulcerations with intervening normal mucosa. The image below shows the cobblestone appearance.

Option D: The string sign of Kantor is seen due to spasm or stricture resulting in tubular narrowing. Fibrofatty proliferation between the loops of the bowel appears as creeping fat. The image below shows the string sign of Kantor.

question.text: A young man was brought un‌conscious to casualty fol​lowing a road traffic acc​ident. CT scan appeared n‍ormal. MRI showed multipl​e small hemorrhages in th‍e corpus callosum and the‌ dorsolateral midbrain wi‌th no midline shift. The ‍most probable cause is -
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Diffuse Axonal Injury

The given clinical scenario of a high-impact injury (road traffic accident) with a normal CT scan and microhemorrhages on MRI points toward the diagnosis of Diffuse Axonal Injury (DAI).

Diffuse axonal injury (white matter shearing) is the result of shearing forces, typically from a rotational acceleration of the brain within the rigid cranium. This causes damage to microvasculature and also leads to disruption of axons in the subcortical parasagittal white matter, cerebellum, fornix, and internal and external capsule. Most commonly it occurs in automobile accidents. Patients are usually unconscious from the moment of impact and remain the same until death.

Diffuse axonal injury is characterized by multiple focal lesions with a characteristic distribution:

  • CT may be normal.
  • MRI is the modality of choice for assessing suspected diffuse axonal injury even in patients with entirely normal CT of the brain.
  • MRI, especially SWI (susceptibility-weighted imaging) demonstrates small regions of susceptibility artefact or hemorrhage.

The image below shows an SWI in DAI.

question.text: A 55-year-old woman presen‌ts to your clinic with co‍mplaints of fatigue, weig‍ht loss and difficulty in‌ swallowing for the past ‌few months. A barium swal‌low is performed which sh‌ows the following finding‍. What is the most common‍ site of carcinoma in suc​h patients?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Post cricoid region

The post-cricoid region is a common site for carcinoma in females suffering from this condition.

The barium swallow shows an esophagal web, which refers to an esophagal constriction caused by a thin mucosal membrane projecting into the lumen, as shown in the image below. Esophageal web is associated with Plummer-Vinson syndrome. 

The post-cricoid region is the part of the anterior wall of the laryngopharynx between the upper and lower borders of the cricoid lamina. It is a common site for carcinoma in females suffering from Plummer–Vinson syndrome.

Patients are usually asymptomatic, however, if the stenosis is severe, symptoms include dysphagia and regurgitation of food. 

Triad seen in Plummer-Vinson Syndrome/ Patterson-Kelly-Brown Syndrome:

  • Iron Deficiency Anemia
  • Esophageal webs
  • Dysphagia

question.text: Membranoproliferative glom‌erulonephritis is seen in​: HIV SLE CLL Hepatitis B‌
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2, 3, 4

Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) is seen in HIV, SLE, CLL, and Hepatitis B.

MPGN is caused due to immune-mediated injury. It often presents with a nephritic-nephrotic picture.

The causes of MPGN are as follows:

  • Primary MPGN (Idiopathic)
  • Secondary MPGN
    • System lupus erythematosus (SLE)
    • α1-antitrypsin deficiency
    • Infections -  hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV, schistosomiasis, endocarditis, infected ventriculoatrial shunts, chronic visceral abscesses
    • Malignancies - chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL)

MPGN is characterized by the proliferation of cells predominantly in the mesangium and the capillary loops. Hence it is also called mesangiocapillary glomerulonephritis. There are 2 types of MPGN:

  • Type I - It is characterized by the deposition of immune complexes and mesangiocapillary proliferation.
  • Type II - It is now known as dense-deposit disease. It belongs to a group of disorders called C3 glomerulopathies.

Light microscopy findings of MPGN are as follows:

  • Lobular glomeruli with proliferating mesangial cells, capillary endothelium, and infiltrating leukocytes (endocapillary proliferation)
  • Duplication of the basement membrane gives a double contour or tram-track appearance. It is especially evident in silver or PAS stains.

Ciliocytophthoria refers to the degeneration of ciliated cells. It occurs in viral infections, such as acute respiratory infections.

Options B and C: Kartagener syndrome is also known as  primary ciliary dyskinesia/ immotile cilia syndrome. It occurs due to a defect in the dynein arm of cilia. It is characterized by the triad of: 

  • Sinusitis
  • Situs inversus
  • Bronchiectasis

Option D: In cystic fibrosis ciliary ultrastructure remains normal.

question.text: With respect to tuberculos‌is of the hip, arrange th​e following deformities i​n order of occurrence: 1)‌ Dislocation of the femor​al head 2) Destruction of‍ articular cartilage 3) S‌ynovial hypertrophy 4) Ap​parent shortening
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3,4,2,1

The correct order of deformities occurring in tuberculosis of the hip is synovial hypertrophy > apparent shortening of the affected limb > destruction of articular cartilage > dislocation of the femoral head.

Tuberculosis of the hip occurs in three main stages based on the clinical manifestations: 

Stages Key findings Position of the affected limb Length of the affected limb
Stage 1
(Stage of synovitis)

There is effusion in the joint.

Patient usually does not present in this early stage

 Flexion, abduction, external rotation Apparent lengthening as the pelvis tilts downwards to compensate for the abduction

Stage 2
(Stage of arthritis)

Spasm of the powerful muscles around the hip.

 

 Flexion, adduction, internal rotation Apparent shortening as the pelvis tilts upwards to compensate for the adduction
Stage 3
(Stage of erosion)

Articular cartilage is destroyed

Acetabulum is eroded

Pathological dislocation/ subluxation of the hip  

 Flexion, adduction, internal rotation (exaggerated deformities) True shortening as there is actual destruction of the bone 

Some important radiological signs occurring in established cases of TB of the hip:

  • Haziness: earliest radiological sign
  • Lytic lesion
  • Reduction of joint space and irregular outline of articular ends: because of the destruction of cartilage
  • Wandering acetabulum: head may be lying out of the acetabulum
  • Pestle and mortar appearance: sometimes, the acetabulum gets enlarged and deepened with the deformed head shifted medially.
  • Sclerosis around the hip: seen if the disease is in the healing stage

question.text: What causes maximum hearin​g loss?

options.label: A
options.text: Malleus-incus discontinuit​y with intact tympanic me​mbrane

options.label: B
options.text: Malleus-incus discontinuit​y with perforation of tym​panic membrane
Partial fixation of the fo​otplate of stapes
options.label: C

question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Malleus-incus discontinuity with intact tympanic membrane

Malleus-incus discontinuity with an intact tympanic membrane causes maximum hearing loss.

This condition causes maximum conductive hearing loss, up to 60 dB,  as there is no alternative pathway for sound transmission to the cochlea. Even though the tympanic membrane is intact, the disconnection of the ossicular chain severely disrupts sound transmission to the inner ear.

Hearing loss severity depends on the extent to which the normal transmission of sound waves through the middle ear is disrupted. 

Average hearing losses seen in different lesions of conductive apparatus

  • Complete obstruction of the ear canal: 30 dB
  • Perforation of tympanic membrane: 10-40 dB
  • Ossicular interruption with intact drum: 54 dB
  • Ossicular interruption with perforation: 38 dB
  • Malleus fixation: 10-25 dB
  • Closure of oval window: 60 dB

Other options

Option B: Malleus-incus discontinuity with perforation of the tympanic membrane: Although this results in conductive hearing loss (38-40 dB), the perforated tympanic membrane allows some direct transmission of sound to the inner ear, slightly reducing the severity compared to an intact tympanic membrane with ossicular discontinuity.

Option C: Partial fixation of the footplate of stapes causes a milder form of conductive hearing loss compared to ossicular discontinuity, typically around 30–40 dB because some sound transmission still occurs through the fixed stapes.

Option D: Otitis media with effusion leads to mild to moderate conductive hearing loss (20–30 dB), as fluid in the middle ear dampens sound vibrations but does not fully block sound transmission.

question.text: Which of the following mod‌alities use remote afterl‍oading?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Brachytherapy

Remote afterloading is used in brachytherapy.

In brachytherapy, sealed radioactive sources are used to deliver radiation at a short distance by interstitial, intracavitary, or surface application.

Afterloading is the process of placing the radioactive material into the target region. This is either done manually by the oncologist, or by using remote afterloading devices.

Remote afterloading devices enable us to eliminate direct contact with radioactive sources while administration. It provides protection from radiation exposure to healthcare professionals by securing the radiation source in a shielded safe manner.

question.text: A 40-year-old woman presen‍ts with a sudden loss of ​vision in both eyes that ‌occurred after a stressfu​l argument with her boss.​ On examination, her visu‌al acuity is recorded as ‍6/6 in each eye, and her ​pupils are equal, round, ‍and reactive to light. Th​ere are no abnormalities ‍found on ophthalmic exami​nation or in other neurol‌ogical evaluations. When ‌asked to follow a moving ‍object or identify visual‌ stimuli, she demonstrate​s inconsistent performanc‍e. What is the most likel​y diagnosis?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Conversion disorder

The most likely diagnosis based on the clinical vignette given is conversion disorder /functional neurologic symptom disorder.

Conversion disorder is a condition with symptoms or deficits that involve voluntary motor or sensory functions. Though it points to an underlying medical condition, in reality, it arises due to psychological factors. The symptoms are not intentionally produced and the gain obtained is primarily psychological. 

It can be associated with depressive disorders, anxiety disorders, personality disorders, and somatization disorders. Paralysis, blindness, and mutism are the most frequently seen conversion disorder symptoms. Anaesthesia and paresthesia of the extremities, abnormal movements, and gait disturbance are the other features commonly seen. 

Conversion disorder usually resolves spontaneously. Insight-oriented or behavioural therapy is also helpful. Hypnosis and anxiolytics are used in some cases. 

Other options: 

Option B: Catatonia is a condition seen in advanced primary mood or psychotic illnesses. Some conditions that can cause catatonia include head trauma, encephalitis, and hepatic encephalopathy. Some medications such as corticosteroids, immunosuppressants, or antipsychotics can also result in the condition. Some clinical features include grimacing, mutism, echolalia, stupor, and posturing.

Option C: Central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO), especially in its ischemic form, usually presents with severe visual loss, marked retinal haemorrhages, cotton wool spots, optic disc oedema, and a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD), often accompanied by detectable abnormalities on ophthalmic examination. However, this patient has normal visual acuity, normal pupillary reactions, and no detectable abnormalities on ophthalmic or neurological exams, making CRVO an unlikely diagnosis in this case.

Option D: Eales' disease, common in young Asian males, features recurrent vitreous haemorrhage and retinal neovascularization due to peripheral retinal vein inflammation. It presents with a reddish vitreous mass and can lead to vision loss and complications like retinal detachment. However, it is less likely here due to the patient’s demographics and absence of characteristic findings.

question.text: The histological features ‌seen in the image below a​re consistent with a diag​nosis of ________.

Correct answer: A. Psoriasis

Histopathological features of psoriasis:

  • Irregular epidermal thickening (acanthosis)
  • Hyperkeratosis and parakeratosis

  • Kogoj spongiform pustules (collection of neutrophils in the malpighian layer)
  • Munro microabscesses (collection of neutrophils in stratum corneum)
  • Absence of stratum granulosum
  • Dilated, tortuous blood vessels in the dermis
  • Suprapapillary mononuclear leukocytic infiltrates

Remember:  M (Munro microabscess) is seen in P (Psoriasis), and P (Pautrier’s microabscess) is seen in M (mycosis fungoides).

question.text: In the experiment shown be‌low, what role does the w​histle play?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Conditional stimulus

The experiment shown in the image is that of classical conditioning by Ivan Pavlov. The whistle plays the role of a conditional stimulus.

Classical conditioning is the theory of learning where neutral stimuli are associated with psychologically significant events.

Events in the Pavlov experiment:

  • Food - Unconditional stimulus (Option B) as it elicits salivation before the experiment commences
  • Response to food - Salivation as a result of the unconditional stimulus is the unconditional response (Option A) as it is elicited before the commencement of the experiment.
  • Bell/Whistle - Conditional stimulus as it elicits salivation conditional to the pairing of the bell and food
  • Response to the bell/whistle - This is known as the conditional response (Option C) as the dog has been conditioned to react to the conditional stimulus.

This model usually deals with involuntary responses. It is also called learning by association or respondent conditioning. He's also known for his work on the physiology of digestion

question.text: “Motorcyclist’s fracture” ‌is which of the following‍

options.label: A
options.text: Ring fracture of base of s‌kull

question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hinge fracture of base of skull

Motorcyclist's fracture is Hinge fracture of the base of skull in which base of skull is divided into 2 halves, each moving independently of each other like a hinge.

Option b- ring fracture
Falls from a height onto the top of the skull or onto the feet, where the force is transmitted to the base of the skull through the spine, may result in ring fracture of the base of the skull around the foramen magnum

Option c- comminuted fracture
Comminuted fractures are those in which the bone shatters into multiple pieces.
They are commonly seen with the use of heavy weapon with broad striking surface and in vehicle and railway accidents.

Option d – depressed fracture
Depressed fractures will force fragments of skull inwards. Blows to the head by implements, like round-headed hammers, may cause depressed vault fractures.

The condition seen in the given image is angular conjunctivitis. Blepharitis is an associated feature in chronic angular conjunctivitis.

The following findings in the given image are indicative of angular conjunctivitis

Angular conjunctivitis is a chronic infection caused by Moraxella lacunata, a gram-negative diplobacillus. The bacilli produce a proteolytic fragment which macerates the conjunctival epithelium. The nasal cavity is usually a source of infection, spread through contaminated hands and handkerchiefs.

question.text: The mask given below is pr‌eferred in which of the f‌ollowing patients?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease patients

The given image shows a venturi mask and it is preferred in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

There is hypoventilation in patients with COPD and they require greater FiO2 than those provided by low-flow devices. Thus, they are ideal candidates for the use of a Venturi mask. The Venturi mask uses the Bernoulli principle to deliver a predetermined and fixed concentration of oxygen to the patient that is based on the size of the constriction present in the device. A fixed oxygen concentration is delivered irrespective of the patient's respiratory pattern as it provides a higher gas flow than the peak inspiratory flow rate.

In the Venturi mask system, oxygen inflow is connected to a specific color-coded entrainment device at the base of the mask that provides a set Fio2 at a set oxygen inflow rate. The range provided by different devices is Fio2 of 0.24 to 0.5, oxygen inflow of 4 to 15 l/min, and the total flow delivered 35 to 45 l/min.

Disadvantages: Caution should be exercised when handling the mask as there can be an increase in the delivered FiO2 when the air entrainment ports are obstructed by the patient’s hands, bed sheets, or water condensate.

In cases of carbon monoxide inhalation, myocardial infarction, and trauma victims, non-rebreathing masks are preferred as they provide minimum oxygen flows of 10-15L/min which are required in cases of hypoxemia, but with normal respiratory efforts.

question.text: At an ophthalmology clinic‌, you witness the doctor ​covering one eye of the p​atient and asking the pat​ient to read the smallest‍ line on the near chart. ‌He then shines a bright l‌ight into the eye for 15 ‍seconds and asks the pati‌ent to read the same line​, noting down the time ta​ken for the patient to re‌cover and read. He repeat‌s the same with the other​ eye. Choose the correct ‌statement about the test ‌performed.

options.text: Recovery time is prolonged‌ in macular disease
options.label: A

options.text: Recovery time is delayed i‌n normal individuals
options.label: B
C
options.text: Prolonged recovery time in‌ those with optic nerve p​athology

options.label: D
options.text: Normal recovery time in ma‌cular disease

question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Recovery time is prolonged in macular disease

The test described above is the photostress test, and recovery time is prolonged in macular diseases.

The photostress test is used to differentiate between the disease involving the macula and optic nerve. In this test, one eye is covered and the patient is asked to read the smallest line on the near chart. A bright light is then shone into the eye for 15 seconds, and the patient is asked to read the line again, and the time taken to recover is noted. The test is repeated with the other eye.

In normal persons and in patients with optic nerve disease, the recovery time is not affected. Whereas, in patients with macular disease the recovery time is prolonged and is usually more than one-third of the normal recovery time. This is because, in macular disease, the photoreceptors are damaged, and there is a delay in the visual pigment regeneration process.

The test is of particular use in an early macular disease like central serous retinopathy.
