Diagnostic criteria for the tuberous sclerosis complex:

 
Major features  
  • Facial angiofibromas or forehead plaque
  • Non‐traumatic ungual or periungual fibroma
  • Hypomelanotic macules (more than three)
  • Shagreen patch (connective tissue naevus)
  • Multiple retinal nodular hamartomas
  • Cortical tuber
  • Subependymal nodule
  • Subependymal giant cell astrocytoma
  • Cardiac rhabdomyoma, single or multiple
  • Lymphangiomyomatosis
  • Renal angiomyolipoma
Minor features 
  • Multiple randomly distributed pits in dental enamel
  • Hamartomatous rectal polyps
  • Bone cysts
  • Cerebral white matter migration lines
  • Gingival fibromas
  • Non‐renal hamartoma
  • Retinal achromic patch
  • Confetti’ skin lesions
  • Multiple renal cysts 
Diagnosis

Definite TSC: either two major features or one major feature with two minor features

Probable TSC: one major feature and one minor feature.

Possible TSC: either one major feature or two or more minor features

question.text: When will a psychiatrist b‌e more concerned about a ‍patient committing suicid​e?

options.label: A
options.text: When he is in mania rather‌ than depression

options.label: C
options.text: Soon after he starts antid‌epressant medication

options.label: D
options.text: At the peak of a depressiv‌e episode

question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Soon after he starts antidepressant medication

Patients are more likely to commit suicide soon after they are started on antidepressant medication. 

Somatic symptoms of depression improve faster than psychological symptoms when a patient is started on antidepressant medication and hence patients have the energy to act on their thoughts of deliberate self-harm and suicide (paradoxical suicide).

Option A: For bipolar disorder, the suicidal risk is higher in the depressive phase than the manic phase.

Option B: The highest risk of suicide is within a period of 6 months after discharge from a psychiatric facility than when admitted.

Option D: During the peak of the depressive episode though the desire to die is intense, the energy level is low to execute the plan. The risk of suicide is higher at the onset and the end of the depressive episode.

question.text: Which of the following rul‌es of law are associated ​with insanity? Durham's r​ule Curren's rule Ashley'​s rule Murphy's rule
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2 only

Durham's rule and Curren's rule are laws associated with insanity.

Durhams's rule states that an accused person is not criminally responsible if his unlawful act is the product of mental disease or mental defect.

Curren’s rule states that an accused person is not criminally responsible if, at the time of committing the act, he did not have the capacity to regulate his conduct to the requirements of the law as a result of mental disease or defect.

In India, the law of Criminal responsibility is under BNS Section 22 (Section 84 IPC) It states that "Nothing is an offense which is done by a person who, at the time of doing it, by reason of unsoundness of mind, is incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or what he is doing is either wrong or contrary to the law”. This is slightly different from McNaghten's rule followed in Britain.

M'Naghten's rule states that every man is to be presumed to be sane, and possesses a sufficient degree of reason to be responsible for his crimes until the contrary is proved.

Other rules to assess the criminal responsibility of insane persons:

  • The Irresistible Impulse
  • Federal rule or American Law Institute test (ALT)
  • The Brawner rule

Note: Ashley's rule is used to differentiate males and females based on the combined length of the manubrium and sternum. It is considered to be a male sternum when the combined length is >149 mm, while if the combined length is <149 mm, then it is considered female.

question.text: Buttonhole sign is can be ‌seen all the following co‌nditions, except?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Bullous pemphigoid

Buttonhole sign is not seen in bullous pemphigoid.  

In Von-Recklinghausen's disease (type 1 neurofibromatosis), neurofibromas can be invaginated with the tip of index finger back into the subcutis and again reappear after the release of pressure. (Buttonhole sign).

Other conditions where one can find this sign are anetoderma and dermatofibroma.

question.text: A 52-year-old male present‌ed to you during your rur‍al posting as a part of a​ routine checkup camp to ‍show the lesions as below​. The red papular lesions‍ do not cause him any dis‌comfort and have been pre‌sent for 6 months. His sp‌ot blood sugar is 300mg/d​l. What could be the poss​ible diagnosis?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diabetic dermopathy

The given maculopapular lesions on the shins along with uncontrolled blood sugar point towards a diagnosis of diabetic dermopathy.

Diabetic dermopathy:

  • It presents as asymptomatic, oval, dull‐red papules 0.5–1 cm in diameter that evolve slowly on the shins, forearms, thighs, and over bony prominences, producing a superficial scale and, ultimately, atrophic brown scars.
  • Binkley's spots or diabetic shin spots is another name for diabetic dermopathy. The phrase diabetic dermopathy was coined by Binkley in 1965.
  • Pathologically, there is hyperpigmentation of the epidermal basal layer, deposition of haemosiderin and melanin in the dermis, and arteriolar basement membrane thickening.
  • Diabetic dermopathy is common and is a marker for complications of diabetes such as retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropathy.

Other Options:

Option A: Necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum is a rare chronic and granulomatous skin disorder that is seen in diabetic patients. The most likely etiology is microangiopathy. Most rashes are located on the legs, especially above the tibiae. The patches are initially brown and later may progress to yellow atrophic plaques.

Option C: Granuloma annulare is most commonly found in children and females <30 years. It manifests as groups of 1-2mm papules that range from skin-colored to violaceous, in an annular arrangement over distal extremities. There is no confirmed association with diabetes.

Below image shows granuloma annulare:

Option D: Furuncle/ boil is caused by Staphylococcus. It is painful and usually situated in the neck area. It is pustular and later becomes necrotic and forms a scar.

question.text: The MRI of a patient who p‌resented with seizures is‍ shown below. What is the‌ likely diagnosis?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sturge-Weber syndrome

The given clinical presentation of seizures, characteristic port-wine stain on the face(capillary malformation), along with the above MRI findings of leptomeningeal enhancement and cortical atrophy, indicate a diagnosis of Sturge-Weber syndrome. These findings are because of plial angiomatosis best visualized in contrast-enhanced MRI.

It occurs due to leptomeningeal hemangioma, resulting in a vascular steal affecting the subjacent cortex and white matter producing localized ischemia and calcification.

The CT brain below, also shows tram-track cortical calcifications, a characteristic feature of Sturge-Weber syndrome.

question.text: A woman complains that her‌ 5-year old child has bec‍ome very indifferent towa​rds her. He attempts to s‌queeze his genitals and i​s always stuffing his mou‍th with food and objects ​like knives and toys. Whi‌ch of these syndromes cou‍ld her child be suffering​ from?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Kluver Bucy syndrome

The given clinical scenario of a 5-year boy who mouths non-food items (hyperorality/hyperphagia), constantly squeezes genitals (hypersexuality), indifferent to parents is suggestive of Kluver-Bucy syndrome.

Kluver Bucy syndrome is characterized by hyperorality, hyperphagia, hypersexuality, hypermetamorphosis (constantly shifting attention). It is due to damage to the temporal lobe and amygdala, which leads to an inability to access memory and emotional connections.

Option A: In medial hypothalamic disease, there is an increase in eating behavior, marked by a lack of satiety and resultant obesity.

Option B: Kleine–Levin syndrome, also known as sleeping beauty syndrome, is a rare sleep disorder characterized by persistent episodic hypersomnia, hyperphagia, and hypersexuality with cognitive or mood changes.

Option D: Charcot Willbrand disease leads to loss of visual imagery with occipitotemporal damage.

question.text: Which of the following tum‌ors are wrongly matched w‍ith their response to rad​iotherapy? RCC-Renal cell‌ carcinoma
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dysgerminoma - Radioresistant

Dysgerminoma is highly radiosensitive. All other options are correctly matched.

Dysgerminoma is the counterpart of testicular seminoma. It may occur in childhood, but 75% occur in the second and third decades. 80 to 90% of tumors are unilateral. Some appear in patients with gonadal dysgenesis, including pseudohermaphroditism. 

Mostly dysgerminomas are malignant with variable degrees of histologic atypia and one-third of lesions are aggressive. 

Radiotherapy is not preferred despite the fact that they are radiosensitive due to the risk of radiation injury to the bowel. These neoplasms are responsive to chemotherapy, which is preferred over radiotherapy.

Other options:

Option B: Seminomas are radiosensitive tumors and adjuvant radiotherapy was the mainstay of treatment in Stage 1 tumors previously.

Option C: Spinal metastasis from renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is radioresistant. Spinal metastasis from gastrointestinal adenocarcinoma, metastatic melanoma, and thyroid are also radioresistant. Lymphoma, lung, breast, and prostate metastasis are radiosensitive.

Option D: Ewing sarcoma is a radiosensitive tumor.

question.text: A 30-year-old woman who is​ in her 12th week of gest​ation was referred to you​ by an obstetrician for s​onographic evaluation. Yo‍u notice the following si​gn on USG. Identify the s‌ign and the type of twin ​gestation it indicates.
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lambda sign, dichorionic diamniotic

The image shows the lambda sign or twin peak sign seen in dichorionic diamniotic pregnancy.

Chorionicity of the placenta is best diagnosed by ultrasound at 10–13 weeks of gestation. In dichorionic twins, there is a thick septum between the two gestational sacs.

A triangular projection is seen at the base of the membrane. This is known as lambda or twin peak sign. The presence of lambda or twin peak sign indicates a dichorionic placenta.

The "T sign" seen in sonographic images signifies a monochorionic twin pregnancy, where there is a lack of chorion extending between the layers of the intertwin membrane.

question.text: Identify the defect shown ‌in the image:
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Herbert pits

The image shows tiny lesions at the limbus, indicating Hebert's pits. This finding is seen in trachoma, which is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, more specifically the trachoma inclusion conjunctivitis (TRIC) serovars A, B, Ba, C. 

Trachoma is a form of chronic infective conjunctivitis and is one of the leading causes of blindness. It has an ‘active’ inflammatory stage and a ‘cicatricial’ chronic stage.

The active inflammatory stage is more prevalent in children and presents with nonspecific symptoms of ocular irritation, foreign body sensation, and discharge (often mild symptoms). Examination findings at this stage show: 

  • Conjunctival follicles contain Leber cells (multinucleated lymphocytes)
  • corneal Herbert's follicles (similar to conjunctival follicles)

Cicatricial chronic stage is seen in middle age. And when the chronic infection with sequelae sets in, the patient complains of pain, lacrimation, photophobia, and later blurring, and finally loss of vision. Conjunctiva shows concretions (whitish deposits of inspissated mucus in depressions called glands of Henle). Corneal signs include: 

  • Herbert pits (pitted scars in the limbal which are remnants of healed Herbert follicles)
  • corneal opacity is seen in later stages.

There can be associated trichiasis ( when at least one eyelash rubs the eyeball) and entropion.

At present WHO grading with 'FISTO' is in use.

Trachoma is treated according to the WHO classification using the SAFE strategy (Surgery, Antibiotics, Facial hygiene, and Environmental improvement). Azithromycin is the antibiotic of choice, and surgery involves the correction of trichiasis and entropion. In case of significant corneal scarring, penetrating keratoplasty is done.

Other options:

Option B: Horner–Trantas dots (image below) are distinct white, chalky, gelatinous nodules made up of eosinophils and epithelial debris that appear at the limbus, and they are characteristic of limbal vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC).

Option C: In giant papillary conjunctivitis (GPC), gelatinous papillae initially appear as small, elevated nodules on the conjunctiva. These papillae eventually grow larger, forming macropapillae and giant papillae, and may be accompanied by Trantas dots at the limbus.

The image below shows giant papillae in the conjunctiva:

Option D: Progressive pannus in trachoma involves the infiltration of the cornea with new blood vessels developing in the upper part, lying between the epithelium and Bowman's membrane. As the condition advances, these superficial vessels contribute to the destruction of Bowman's membrane, with corneal infiltration occurring before significant vascularization.

question.text: A 30-year-old male patient‌ presented to the dermato‍logy department with lesi​ons over the skin as show‍n below. On examination, ​the lesions were dry, sca‍ly, and slightly shiny, w‌ith moderately diminished‌ sensation. Which type of‌ leprosy do these lesions​ indicate?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Borderline type

The given clinical scenario with dry scaly lesions and moderately diminished sensation, with the image showing moderately hypo-esthetic annular plaques which are punched-out, is suggestive of the borderline type of leprosy.

Borderline (BB) leprosy is the most immunologically unstable type. The characteristic lesions of BB leprosy are annular plaques with well-demarcated, punched-out inner margins and sloping outer margins. They appear as large plaques with islands of clinically normal skin within the center, giving rise to a Swiss cheese appearance.


Other options:

Option A: Pure neuritic leprosy (PNL) is a rare variant of leprosy. It is characterized by the isolated involvement of peripheral nerve trunks in the absence of skin lesions.

question.text: What is the most common ro‍ute of the spread of reti​noblastoma?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Direct invasion

Direct invasion is the most common mode of spread of retinoblastoma.

Retinoblastoma arises from the neurosensory retina. It is a proliferation of neural cells that have failed to evolve normally. Retinoblastoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in children.  Tumours are composed of small basophilic cells (retinoblasts), with large hyperchromatic nuclei and scanty cytoplasm.

It is of 4 types:

  1. Endophytic (into the vitreous)with seeding of tumor cells throughout the eye
  2. Exophytic (into the subretinal space) leading to retinal detachment
  3. Mixed type
  4. Retinocytoma: retina may be diffusely infiltrated

question.text: A young boy developed mass‌eter spasm and tachycardi​a after being administere​d succinylcholine for RSI​. Which of the following ‌is the best site for moni​toring core body temperat‌ure in this patient?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Esophagus

The clinical features are suggestive of malignant hyperthermia in this patient and the distal oesophagus is the best site for core temperature monitoring in this condition.    

Pulmonary artery is the most accurate site for temperature measurement but it is not used routinely due to a higher incidence of complications. It is useful in patients already on Swan-Ganz catheter.

Option A: Oral cavity (sublingual) readings can be influenced by mouth breathing, tachypnea, and ambient temperature.

Option C: Axilla readings are influenced by contact with probe, skin perfusion, environment, etc.

Option D: Rectum readings are higher than central sites due to heat-producing flora in feces.

Other sites for core thermal monitoring:

  • Tympanic membrane
  • Nasopharynx
  • Trachea
  • Skin

question.text: A 35-year-old male patient‌ presents with headache. ​He also has a family hist​ory of glaucoma. On exami​nation, intraocular press‍ure was 23 and 24 mmHg in‌ the right and left eye r‌espectively. Iridocorneal‍ angles were normal on go‌nioscopy. There was no vi​sual field defects. Which​ of the following stateme‌nts is false regarding th‌e condition of the patien​t? (POAG- Primary open-an‌gle glaucoma)

options.label: A
options.text: Thin cornea is a risk fact‌or for POAG development

options.label: B
options.text: Reducing IOP is effective ‌in delaying the onset of ​POAG

options.label: C
options.text: Increased cup disc ratio i‌s a risk factor for POAG ​development

options.label: D
options.text: Younger people are more at‌ risk for progression to ​POAG than older people

question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Younger people are more at risk for progression to POAG than older people

The given clinical scenario of the patient points towards ocular hypertension. Older people are more at risk of progression than younger people.

Ocular hypertension (OHT) is characterized only by raised intraocular pressure (IOP). The optic disc and visual fields are normal, with no evidence of angle closure.

Significant risk factors for the progression of ocular hypertension to primary open-angle glaucoma include the following:

  • Increased IOP
  • Increasing age
  • Increased cup-disc ratio
  • Thin cornea 
  • African-American race
  • Male gender
  • Associated heart disease

question.text: Which of the following con‌ditions is a cause of pse​udoptosis?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Brow ptosis

Brow ptosis is a type of pseudoptosis, not ptosis.

Ptosis is abnormal drooping of the upper eyelid to a level that covers more than 2mm of the superior cornea. 

Types of ptosis:

  • Mechanical ptosis - Can be due to lid tumors, multiple/big chalazions, and conjunctival scarring
  • Aponeurotic ptosis - Due to dehiscence of the aponeurosis and in postoperative patients
  • Involutional ptosis seen in old age
  • Neurogenic ptosis due to a 3rd nerve palsy, Horner syndrome and synkinetic ptosis/Marcus–Gunn jaw-winking ptosis
  • Myogenic ptosis
    • Congenital: most common myogenic ptosis
      • Simple
      • Blepharophimosis syndrome
      • Congenital synkinetic ptosis
    • Acquired
      • Myasthenia gravis
      • Lambert–Eaton syndrome
      • Ocular myopathy

Causes of pseudoptosis (apparent ptosis):

  • Lack of support of the lids by the globe e.g. artificial eye, microphthalmos, phthisis bulbi, or enophthalmos.
  • Contralateral lid retraction
  • Ipsilateral hypotropia
  • Brow ptosis occurs due to excessive skin on the brow, or seventh nerve palsy, which is diagnosed by manually elevating the
    eyebrow 
  • Dermatochalasis

question.text: Under McNaughten's rule, w‌hich of the following cri​teria is not valid to cle​ar a mentally unsound per​son of all responsibility‌?

options.text: Inability to understand th‌at the act is wrong
options.label: D

question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Presence of uncontrollable impulse

The criterion of the presence of uncontrollable impulse is not included in McNaughten's rule. Therefore, it is not a valid criterion to clear a mentally unsound person of all criminal responsibility.

McNaughten's rule is followed by the British Courts of law to examine the liability of a mentally unsound person who has committed a crime. BNS 22 is the Indian adaptation of this rule. 

McNaughten's rule forms the basis of the legal test of insanity/the 'right or wrong' test. It states that a mentally unsound person is cleared of all criminal responsibility for the crime committed if the following criteria are met:

  • Presence of evidence of psychiatric illness.
  • Existence of psychiatric illness at the time of the commission of the crime.
  • Psychiatric illness is of such a degree that the person does not have the ability to understand the wrongness of the act, i.e., impaired intellectual ability. 

McNaughten's rule decide a person's soundness of mind based on the presence or absence of intellectual ability. However, it fails to consider any impairments in the person's emotional state or the presence of any uncontrollable/ irresistible impulses while committing the act.

question.text: Which of the following are​ direct gonioscopes? Gold​mann Richardson Zeis Koep​pe
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2, 4

Richardson and Koeppe are direct gonioscopes. 

A gonioscope is used for the measurement of the angle of the anterior chamber. The types of gonioscopes include:

  • Indirect gonioprism: Provides a mirror image of the opposite angle. Indirect goniolenses include Goldmann, Zeiss, and Posner.
  • Direct gonioprism: Provides a direct view of the angle. Direct goniolenses include the Koeppe, Richardson, Medical Workshop, Barkan, and Swan–Jacob.

Applications:

  • To view the angle of the anterior chamber. The structures visualized in order from front to back are:
    • Schwalbe’s line
    • Trabecular meshwork
    • Scleral spur
    • Ciliary body band
    • Root of iris
  • The localization of foreign bodies, abnormal blood vessels or tumors in the angle.
  • Demonstration of the extent of peripheral anterior synechiae. 
  • During goniotomy, a surgical procedure for the treatment of congenital glaucoma.

The below instrument is an indirect gonioscope of four-mirror type, which is used to visualize the angle of the anterior chamber.

question.text: A patient with Parkinson's‌ disease is brought by hi​s wife because of recent ‍changes in behaviour. A n‌ew medication was started‌ 4 weeks ago. He has been​ spending money irrespons‌ibly over the last two we‌eks and recently bought a​ boat when they don't liv‌e near a beach. Which of ‍the following explains hi‍s symptoms?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Therapy with a D2 agonist

Therapy with a D2 agonist explains his symptoms.

This patient with Parkinson's disease(PD) is now presenting with impulsivity and behavioural changes 2 weeks after he was started on a new medication, making medication-induced adverse effects the likely aetiology. Ropinirole is a selective D2/D3 receptor agonist. It is used for the treatment of PD in early disease as a monotherapy and as an add-on for Levodopa-Carbidopa. 

Ropinirole can cause multiple behavioral-related adverse effects, including gambling, impulsive shopping, and sexual proclivity. It can also cause increased daytime sleepiness and hallucinations, so these medications should be avoided in the elderly. 

Other Options:

Option A: Adjustment disorder is a diagnosis of exclusion made when symptoms are not explained by any other cause. This patient's symptoms are consistent with D2 agonist side effects.

Option B: Mania is diagnosed when patients have at least 4 of the DIGFAST criteria(Distractibility, Irresponsibility, Grandiosity, Flight of thoughts, Increased Activity, Sleeplessness, Talkativeness) for at least 1 week. He doesn't meet the criteria for a manic episode. 

Option D: Parkinson-induced psychosis can cause hallucinations and delusions, which is not seen in this patient.

question.text: Which of the following is ‌the site of lesion in int‍ernuclear ophthalmoplegia‍?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Medial Longitudinal Fasciculus

In internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) the lesion is at the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF).

In INO, there is impaired adduction on the ipsilateral side of the lesion, and nystagmus on abduction on the contralateral side. When the gaze is initiated in the motor cortex, the horizontal gaze center or the paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF) generates the eye movements.

The PPRF has two outputs. The first is to the ipsilateral 6th cranial nerve nucleus which causes abduction of the ipsilateral eye. The second output is to the contralateral MLF which sends an impulse to the contralateral 3rd cranial nerve nucleus causing contralateral adduction. These two outputs from PPRF lead to conjugate movement of the eyes to the same side. 

Therefore, a lesion in the right MLF leads to failure of the right eye adduction. The left eye, however, abducts normally. This is called internuclear ophthalmoplegia.

The following image shows the pathway for horizontal eye movements as described above.

question.text: A young man is brought to ​the casualty with pinpoin​t pupils. Which of the fo‍llowing is the most likel‍y substance he would have​ consumed?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Opium

Pinpoint pupils can be observed in the overdose of opium.

Causes of Miosis Causes of Mydriasis
Carbolic acid poisoning Datura poisoning
Morphine poisoning Cyanides
Organophosphorous poisoning Cocaine
Pontine haemorrhage Ether
Barbiturate poisoning Pethidine
  Nux vomica
  Viper venom
  Amphetamine

Opioid overdose symptoms:

  • Triad of coma, respiratory depression, and pinpoint pupils (miosis)
  • Hypotension, bradycardia
  • Shallow breathing
  • Hypothermia

Naloxone is also used for reversing neonatal asphyxia due to opioid usage in labour. Naloxone is a pure opioid antagonist which reverses all effects except sedation.

Note: Naloxone is contraindicated in infants born to mothers with opiate addiction as it may precipitate acute neonatal withdrawal with seizures.

question.text: A young woman comes with s‌udden onset ocular pain, ​tearing, and photophobia ​in the left eye. You susp‌ect a bacterial corneal u​lcer. What concentration ‌of cephazolin drops would​ you prescribe for this p​atient?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 5%

The concentration of fortified cephazolin used to treat uncomplicated bacterial keratitis is 5% ( 50 mg/mL)

Treatment of uncomplicated bacterial keratitis:

  • Antibiotic eyedrops (broad-spectrum)
  • If not responding, fortified antibiotic eye drops are used
    • Fortified cephazolin (5%)
    • Fortified tobramycin (1.3%)
    • Fortified vancomycin (5%)
  • Cycloplegic drugs- Preferably 1% atropine eye ointment or drops to prevent pain due to ciliary spasm. Also, it prevents the development of posterior synechiae.
  • Oral vitamin A and vitamin C help in the healing of the epithelium
  • Systemic analgesics and anti-inflammatory drugs

Management of non-healing ulcers:

  • Debridement
  • Chemical cauterization- 10–20% trichloroacetic acid, carbolic acid
  • Conjunctival flapping

Management of impending perforation:

  • Decrease intraocular pressure (IOP) by antiglaucoma drugs
  • Tissue adhesive glue such as cyanoacrylate
  • Bandage contact lens
  • No strain

question.text: Which Section of the IPC/B​NS deals with the punishm​ent of perjury?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 193/ BNS 229

The punishment of perjury is dealt with under IPC 193, has now been updated to BNS 229. 

Perjury is defined as the offence of wilfully telling an untruth or making a misrepresentation under oath.

question.text: Identify the postmortem ch‌ange given in the image.
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Marbling

The postmortem change shown above is marbling, which is an external sign of putrefaction.

In marbling, the superficial veins of roots of the limb, thighs, sides of the abdomen, and shoulders are stained greenish-brown or purplish-red, in a linear branching pattern. It is usually prominent 36–48 hours after death occurs due to the formation of sulfhemoglobin subsequent to hemolysis of red blood cells.

In putrefaction, bacteria from the gut enter into and multiply in the surrounding tissues, eventually spreading through the blood vessels to other parts of the body. The bacterium Clostridium welchii is largely responsible for the putrefactive changes spreading through the body, due to its production of the enzyme lecithinase. The first external sign of putrefaction in a body lying outside in the air is a greenish discoloration of the skin over the region of the cecum.

Other options:

Option B: Tattooing around the entry wound of a bullet is due to the deposition of unburnt powder particles. These are difficult to remove. They are also called stippling or peppering. This is seen up to 50 cm of firing

Option C: Postmortem hypostasis/Postmortem staining/Postmortem lividity/Livor mortis/Suggilation refers to bluish-purple or reddish-purple discoloration of the superficial layers of the dermis. It is an early postmortem change that occurs due to the stagnation of blood in the vessels of the dependent parts due to the effect of gravity. 

Option D: Filigree burns also known as Lichtenberg's flowers are superficial, thin, irregular, and tortuous markings on the skin indicative of a lightning strike. They resemble the branches of a tree and are usually found over the skin of the shoulders or the flanks.

question.text: The injury shown in the im​age results from:
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Moist heat

The injury shown in the image is suggestive of a scald burn, which results due to the application of moist heat commonly involving only superficial layers of the skin.

Moist heat includes

  • Hot water or oil or any liquid at or near boiling point
  • Superheated industrial steam

Degree of Scalding:

  1. Erythema
  2. Vesication
  3. Necrosis of the dermis

Note:

Traits Burn (Dry heat) Scald (Moist heat)
Cause Flame, hot metal Boiling water, milk, oil, etc
Site At or above the site of contact At or below the site of contact
Singeing of hair Present Absent
Depth Deep (upto skin or more) Depth is less
Healing Delayed Comparatively early
Scar Thick Thin
Contracture Common Not common

question.text: A female patient presents ‍with sudden onset palpita​tions, sweating, breathle‌ssness, and a feeling lik​e she is being choked. Ph​ysical examination and ro‌utine investigations were‍ within normal limits. Wh​ich of the following is f‍alse about this condition​?

options.label: D
options.text: Occurs only in the presenc‍e of a trigger

question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Occurs only in the presence of a trigger

This clinical vignette describes a classic panic attack, which can occur even in the absence of an identifiable trigger.

A panic attack is a sudden surge of intense fear or discomfort that may last from minutes to hours. Recurrent panic attacks can point to a panic disorder.

Panic attacks can also be seen in other disorders such as specific phobias, social phobias, and post-traumatic stress disorder. Unexpected panic attacks occur at any time and are not associated with any identifiable situational trigger. Attacks in patients with social and specific pho­bias are usually expected in response to a specific stimulus.

Some panic attacks are neither unexpected nor expected attacks and are known as situationally predisposed panic attacks. They may or may not occur on exposure to a specific trigger, or may occur immediately after exposure or after a considerable period of time.

Four or more of the following should be present to label it a panic attack:

  • Palpitations, pounding heart, or tachycardia
  • Perspiration
  • Trembling 
  • Breathlessness or a sensation of smothering
  • Feelings of choking
  • Chest pain or discomfort
  • Nausea or abdominal distress
  • Dizziness, unsteadiness, light-headedness, or fainting 
  • Chills or heat sensations
  • Paresthesias
  • Derealization (feelings of unreality) or depersonalization (feeling detached from oneself)
  • Fear of losing control 
  • Fear of death

Alprazolam and paroxetine can be used for the medical management of panic disorders. Cognitive and behavior therapies can also prove effective.

question.text: Gas from which of the foll‌owing cylinders can be us​ed in patients with acute​ exacerbation of bronchia‍l asthma along with oxyge​n?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Brown

The gas in the cylinder with a brown shoulder and body is helium. Helium along with oxygen, together known as heliox can be used in the treatment of acute exacerbation of bronchial asthma as they decrease the work of breathing. Heliox can be used to deliver inhaled 𝛃2 agonists in patients with severe critical asthma.

Principle:

  • When the flow across the bronchus is laminar, the flow rate increases as the gas viscosity decreases.
  • In airway obstructing conditions, where there is turbulent flow, the flow rate decreases as the gas density increases. Hence helium, having low density is added with oxygen to increase the flow rate. It decreases the resistance in the airways and improves ventilation and gas exchange.

The other options represent general anaesthetics and are not useful in treating bronchial asthma.

  • Blue: N2O
  • Orange: Cyclopropane

question.text: A 40-year-old smoker who i‌s a known case of hyperte​nsion was on enalapril an​d hydrochlorothiazide. He‌ had an episode of hemopt​ysis and on evaluation he‍ was found to have bronch‍ogenic carcinoma with bra​in metastasis. His lab va‌lues were Na -124 mg/dl, ​creatinine – 2.8 mg%, blo‍od sugar 112 mg/dl, blood​ urea - 24 mg/dl, serum o‌smolality – 255mosm, urin‌e osmolality-350mosm, 24 ‍hour urinary sodium 110 a‍nd BP-150/90 mmHg. Which ​of the following is the m‍ost probable diagnosis of‌ the low sodium values in‍ him
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. SIADH

The clinical scenario of patient who is a known hypertensive, smoker and bronchogenic carcinoma with brain metastasis having low sodium, low serum osmolality and high urine osmolality, the most probable diagnosis is of SIADH (Syndrome of Inappropriate secretion of ADH).

From the given information, reduced serum osmolality rules out pseudohyponatremia(Option D) as such patients should be isotonic or have normal serum osmolality. The BP of the patient indicates there is no hypotension and patient is euvolemic, hence ruling out Cerebral Salt Wasting Syndrome(Option C) in which patient is hypovolemic and volume depleted.  In thiazide induced SIADH(Option B), patients will be dehydrated and not euvolemic.  

In this patient, lung cancer and thiazides may cause SIADH. 

Bartter and Schwartz diagnostic criteria of SIADH

  • Hyponatremia
  • Clinically Euvolemic
  • Serum osmolality less than 275 mOsm/Kg
  • Urine Osmolality more than 100mOsm/Kg
  • Urine sodium more than 40 mmol/L
  • No use of diuretics

In SIADH, if the hyponatremia is mild and asymptomatic, restrict total water intake to 30 mL/kg/day less than urine output until the syndrome resolves spontaneously. If the hyponatremia is severe and symptomatic, the goal is to partially correct it by intravenous infusion of hypertonic (3%) saline or administration of an AVP antagonist such as tolvaptan or conivaptan. With hypertonic saline or vaptans, plasma osmolarity and sodium should be checked every 1–2 h, and water intake should be adjusted to keep osmolarity 270 mosm/L, at which point the treatment should be discontinued.

question.text: A lady underwent cholecyst‌ectomy and now she presen​ts with abdominal pain, o​ne month later. An erect ​abdomen x-ray was taken, ‌and the image is given be​low. The following offens​e comes under _______.
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Res ipsa loquitur

The x-ray shows a pair of surgical scissors left behind in the abdomen after surgery. The offense comes under res ipsa loquitur. It is obvious evidence of the negligent act committed.

"Res ipsa loquitur" means "the thing or fact speaks for itself." The negligent act is so obvious that the patient need not prove the negligence. He has to merely state what according to him was the negligent act.

This doctrine applies to both civil and criminal negligence. All of the following conditions should be fulfilled for this doctrine:

  • In the absence of negligence, there would not have been any injury usually
  • The doctor had complete control over the injury-producing instrument or treatment.
  • The patient was not a part of contributory negligence.

Other options:

Option A: Novus actus interveniens: A person is responsible not only for his actions but also for the logical consequences of those actions. This principle applies to cases of assault and accidental injury.

Option C: Res judicata (Section 337, BNSS) -If a question of negligence against a doctor has already been decided by a court in a dispute between the doctor and his patient, the patient will not be allowed to contest the same in another legal proceeding, based on the same set of facts. Multiple appeals cannot be made. 

Option D: The principle of respondeat superior is used to explain vicarious liability, which explains that the employer is responsible for his employees’ negligence if such an act occurs in the course of the employment and within its scope.

question.text: Cyclosporine-induced chole‌stasis is due to which re​ceptor?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. MDR 1

Cyclosporine induced cholestasis is due to MDR1 transporter.

ABC transporters such as MRP2, MDR1, BCRP, BSEP, and MDR3 in the bile canalicular membrane of hepatocytes mediate the efflux (excretion) of drugs and their metabolites, bile salts, and phospholipids against a steep concentration gradient from liver to bile. This primary active transport is driven by ATP hydrolysis.

Cyclosporine, an MDR1 substrate can cause cholestatic liver injury through the following mechanisms:

  • Competitive inhibition of ATP dependent transporters.
  • Inhibition of intrahepatic vesicle transport and targeting of ATP dependent transporters to the canalicular membrane.
  • Impairment of bile secretion partly by increasing canalicular membrane fluidity without affecting the expression of canalicular transporters. 

Cyclosporine is an immunomodulatory drug that inhibits calcineurin activity by forming a complex with cyclophilin, a cytoplasmic-receptor protein present in target cells, to form a cyclosporine-cyclophilin complex.Calcineurin is a calcium/calmodulin-dependent phosphatase required for the induction of T cell lymphokine production and proliferation.

This drug-receptor complex specifically and competitively binds to and inhibits calcineurin, a calcium and calmodulin-dependent phosphatase. This, in turn, inhibits the translocation of a family of transcription factors (NF-AT), leading to reduced transcriptional activation of cytokine genes for interleukin (IL)-2, tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-alpha, IL-3, IL-4, CD40L, granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor, and interferon-gamma. Ultimately, the proliferation of T lymphocytes is reduced, resulting in immunomodulation.

Its uses are as follows:

  • In solid organ transplantation, to prevent organ rejection in kidney, liver, and heart allogeneic transplants
  • In patients with rheumatoid arthritis, when the disease has not adequately responded to methotrexate
  • Cyclosporine reportedly is effective in Behçet’s disease, acute ocular syndrome, endogenous uveitis, atopic dermatitis, inflammatory bowel disease, and nephrotic syndrome.

Adverse effects of cyclosporine include a decrease in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and metabolic disturbances like hypomagnesemia, hyperkalemia, dyslipidemia, gynecomastia, hypertrichosis; neurotoxicity in the form of convulsions. There is an increased risk of developing skin and lymphoproliferative malignancies in cyclosporine-treated psoriasis patients.

Symptoms include cough, evening rise in temperature, weight loss, malaise, abdominal pain with distension, and intermittent diarrhea. question.text: During intravenous pyelography of a patient, the left kidney could not be visualized. What condition is this suggestive of?
question.explanation:
Non-visualization of the kidney on IVP is seen in the case of multicystic dysplastic kidney (MCDK).

MCDK is a form of renal dysplasia characterized by multiple, non-communicating cysts of varying sizes, separated by dysplastic parenchyma, with the absence of a normal pelvicalyceal system. It results from a developmental abnormality due to failure of the renal mesenchyme to unite with the ureteric bud. This condition is associated with ureteral or ureteropelvic atresia, and the affected kidney is non-functional.

Most cases of MCDK are detected antenatally through ultrasonography. In some cases, the cysts identified prenatally may regress in utero, resulting in the affected kidney being undetectable on imaging at birth. Renal ultrasonography is the initial investigation of choice. It reveals a soap bubble appearance. Bilateral MCDK can lead to pulmonary hypoplasia and Potter syndrome.

The following image shows a non-visualized right kidney (red arrow).

Other options:

  • Option A: In the duplicated collecting system, the drooping lily sign is seen. It refers to the inferolateral displacement of the opacified lower pole moiety due to an obstructed (and un-opacified) upper pole moiety.
  • Option B: In polycystic kidney disease, a streaky appearance is seen due to ectatic collecting ducts.
  • Option D: In renal hypoplasia, there is a congenitally small kidney with smaller calyces, lobules, and papillae but essentially normal residual parenchyma. On imaging, a hypoplastic kidney is small but otherwise normal.

question.text: A 54-year-old man presents with abdominal pain, anorexia, and weight loss. A barium study was performed and is as shown. What is the probable diagnosis?
question.explanation:
The given clinical scenario along with the barium study showing an enlarged duodenal loop with ‘reversed 3 sign' of Frostberg is suggestive of carcinoma head of the pancreas.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas arise most commonly in the head of the gland. Pancreatic carcinoma presents with varied symptoms, commonly including weight loss and anorexia, which may or may not be accompanied by abdominal pain. Tumours in the pancreatic head often cause early bile duct obstruction, leading to jaundice.

Frostberg's inverted 3 sign is a sign seen on a barium examination. There is effacement and distortion of the mucosal pattern on the medial wall of the second part of the duodenum due to focal mass and local edema. It is associated with carcinoma of the head of the pancreas, duodenal carcinoma and pancreatitis (widening of the C loop of the duodenum).

Antral pad sign may also be seen in barium studies in patients with carcinoma head of the pancreas. Percutaneous transhepatic cholangiogram shows a characteristic 'gloved finger' obstruction of the intrapancreatic common bile duct, which is pathognomonic for carcinoma of the pancreatic head.

question.text: What is the investigation of choice to assess the prognosis of patients with acute pancreatitis?
question.explanation:
The investigation of choice to assess prognosis in patients with acute pancreatitis is CECT. It is used to calculate the modified CT severity index.

Plain erect chest x-ray and abdominal radiographs are not diagnostic of acute pancreatitis and can only be used to rule out certain differentials. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) is the imaging investigation of choice, but may not always be needed. Various scoring systems are used to grade the severity of acute pancreatitis based on blood investigations and radiographic findings.

The optimal time for the performance of contrast-enhanced CT imaging in cases of acute pancreatitis is more than 72 hours from the onset of symptoms. In the first 72 hours, CT may underestimate the extent of necrosis. CT scan in pancreatitis is indicated in patients with severe acute pancreatitis, organ failure, sepsis, and patients with clinical deterioration despite the treatment.

question.text: Which among the following ‌is not an indication for ​the use of electroconvuls‍ive therapy (ECT)?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Panic disorder

Indications of ECT:

Diagnostic indications - 

  • Major depression (Bipolar and unipolar)
  • Psychotic depression (Option A)
  • Mania
  • Acute exacerbation of schizophrenia
  • Catatonic schizophrenia
  • Schizoaffective disorder (Option D)
  • Parkinson's disease (Option C)
  • Neuroleptic malignant disorder

Panic disorder is not an indication of the use of electroconvulsive therapy. 

Clinical indications - 

  • Primary - 
    • When rapid response is required
    • When the risk of other treatment modalities outweighs the benefits
    • Poor response to previous antipsychotic therapy
    • Good response to previous ECT therapy
    • Preference of patient
  • Secondary - 
    • Poor response or failure to respond to pharmacotherapy in the current episode
    • Rapid definitive response necessitated by the deterioration of the patient's condition

Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is not effective in somatization disorder (unless accompanied by depression), personality disorders, and anxiety disorders such as panic disorder.

question.text: Which of the following is the best investigation that can be done in a patient with suspected solitary pulmonary nodule?
question.explanation:
Plain CT is the standard investigation of choice for solitary pulmonary nodule.

Solitary pulmonary nodule (SPN) is defined as a relatively well-defined, round or oval, pulmonary parenchymal lesion that is equal to or smaller than 30 mm in diameter. It is surrounded by pulmonary parenchyma and/or visceral pleura and is not associated with lymphadenopathy, atelectasis, or pneumonia.

Features favouring malignancy in an SPN:
  • Spiculated margin
  • Lobulated margin
  • Umbilication
  • Cavitation
  • Fine peripheral calcification
  • Double its volume in 1 to 6 months
The gold standard investigation is CT-guided biopsy. PET scan is helpful in detecting malignancy in patients with inconclusive high-resolution CT findings.

question.text: The CT abdomen of a patient presenting with abdominal pain and vomiting is shown below. What is the probable diagnosis?
question.explanation:
A patient presenting with abdominal pain and vomiting, with CT showing a Mercedes-Benz sign, is characteristic of cholelithiasis.

Mercedes-Benz sign (triradiate sign), is seen when a gallstone contains central radiolucent gas.

The fissures may be tri-radiate or bi-radiate (seagull sign). These fissures appear dark on CT or radiographs, giving the sign its characteristic appearance.

Gallbladder stones or cholelithiasis are the most common condition affecting the gallbladder.

They are often discovered incidentally and typically remain asymptomatic. However, they become symptomatic when the stones obstruct the cystic duct. In such cases, patients may experience dull or colicky right upper quadrant or epigastric pain radiating to the back, along with symptoms like nausea and vomiting.

Only about 10% of gallstones are radiopaque. Ultrasonography (USG) is the most accurate initial imaging modality of choice for the diagnosis of gallbladder stones. These stones appear as echogenic foci producing acoustic shadows. The sensitivity of USG for gallstones is > 95%.

question.text: Formation of which of the following indicates the beginning of gastrulation?
question.explanation:
The formation of the primitive streak from the epiblast is an indicator of the beginning of gastrulation.

By the 15th day of development, some epiblast cells lying along the central axis, near the tail end of the embryonic disc, begin to proliferate. These proliferated cells form an elevation called primitive streak that bulges into the amniotic cavity.

Gastrulation is the process that forms all the 3 germ layers namely, ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm in the embryo. It occurs during the 3rd week of gestation.

The image given below shows the formation of the primitive streak.

question.text: The neuropore facilitates communication between the neural tube and
question.explanation:
The neuropores facilitate communication between the neural tube and the amniotic cavity.

The neural plate first becomes tubular in the middle. The cranial and caudal ends of the neural tube remain open and are called the anterior and posterior neuropores, respectively.

The neuropores facilitate communication between the neural tube and the amniotic cavity. Amniotic fluid provides nutrition to the developing neuroectodermal cells before the circulatory system is established.

question.text: Which of the following neural tube defects is characterized by gaps in the vertebral arches?
question.explanation:
Spina bifida is characterized by gaps in the vertebral arches.

Spina bifida is a general term used for neural tube defects affecting the spinal region and associated with splitting of the vertebral arches. It may or may not involve the underlying neural tissue.

Rachischisis is the most severe type of neural tube defect, where the entire neural tube fails to close. Rachischisis can occur in the spinal cord or brain regions of the neural tube. The exposed neural tissues often become necrotic.

question.text: A neonate was shifted to the NICU due to respiratory distress and periodic seizures. CT scan revealed cystic dilatation of the fourth ventricle due to blockage of the median and lateral apertures. What is the likely diagnosis?
question.explanation:
Blockage of the medial and the lateral apertures of the 4th ventricle is seen in Dandy-Walker syndrome (DWS).

DWS is congenital hydrocephalus associated with atresia of the median aperture (foramen of Magendie) and lateral aperture (foramen of Luschka) of the 4th ventricle. This causes enlargement of the 4th ventricle and hydrocephalus.

The other associated defects seen in DWS include:
  • Agenesis of the cerebellar vermis
  • Agenesis of the splenium of corpus callosum

question.text: Which of the following gives rise to the hypophysis cerebri?
question.explanation:
The hypophysis cerebri or pituitary gland develops from two sources, i.e., surface ectoderm and neuroectoderm.

The adenohypophysis or anterior pituitary, develops from the surface ectoderm. An ectodermal diverticulum, called Rathke's pouch, grows upward from the roof of the stomatodeum (primitive mouth). This becomes the anterior lobe of the pituitary (pars distalis).

The neurohypophysis or posterior pituitary, develops from the neuroectoderm. A downward extension of the diencephalon, called infundibular process, grows down from the floor of the 3rd ventricle, during the 6th week. It gives rise to the stalk and the posterior lobe of pituitary (pars nervosa).

The anterior lobe of pituitary gives rise to a small extension called the pars tuberalis. It grows along the stalk of the infundibulum and eventually surrounds it.

The posterior wall of the Rathke's pouch develops into the pars intermedia.

The image given below shows the development of the pituitary gland.

question.text: Where are the cells of the adrenal cortex and medulla respectively derived from?
question.explanation:
The cells of the adrenal cortex and medulla are respectively derived from the mesoderm and neural crest cells.

The adrenal glands consist of a superficial cortex and deeper medulla:
  • Adrenal cortex - formed by proliferation of the coelomic epithelium (mesodermal origin).
  • Adrenal medulla - formed by the invading neural crest cells from somite levels 18-24.

question.text: Which of the following zones of the adrenal cortex are present at birth?

options.text: Zona glomerulosa, Zona fasciculata, and Zona reticularis
options.label: D

question.explanation:
The zona glomerulosa and zona fasciculata of the adult cortex are present at birth.

The differentiation of the cortical zones of the adrenal gland begins during the late fetal period:
  • Zona glomerulosa and zona fasciculata of the adult cortex are present at birth.
  • Zona reticularis is formed during the 3rd year of life.

question.text: What is the adult representation of the location of anterior neuropore?
question.explanation:
The location of the anterior neuropore is represented in adults as lamina terminalis.

The anterior neuropore closes around the 25th day of intrauterine life. Its location in adults is represented by the lamina terminalis. The lamina terminalis forms the anterior boundary of the third ventricle.

The posterior neuropore closes around the 28th day of intrauterine life. Its location in adults is represented by the terminal ventricle. The terminal ventricle is present in the proximal 5 to 6 mm of filum terminale.

question.text: 1-year-old baby with loss of pharyngeal reflex was diagnosed to have infantile progressive bulbar palsy. Which of the following gives rise to the affected structure?
question.explanation:
In infantile progressive bulbar palsy, the affected structure is the medulla oblongata. It arises from the rhombencephalon (hindbrain).

The rhombencephalon is further subdivided into a cranial part (metencephalon) and a caudal part (myelencephalon):
  • Metencephalon - forms the pons and cerebellum
  • Myelencephalon - forms the medulla oblongata

question.text: What is the flexure between the metencephalon and the myelencephalon called?
question.explanation:
The flexure between the metencephalon and the myelencephalon is called the pontine flexure.

The prosencephalon, mesencephalon, and rhombencephalon are initially arranged craniocaudally. Due to differential growth of different regions of the brain, various flexures form between them:
  • Telencephalic flexure
  • Cephalic flexure
  • Pontine flexure
  • Cervical flexure

Note: A deep furrow called the rhombencephalic isthmus separates the mesencephalon from the metencephalon.

question.text: Which of the following is the first commissure to develop?
question.explanation:
The first commissure to develop is the anterior commissure.

Commissures are fiber bundles that cross the midline and connect the right and left brain hemispheres. Many important fiber bundles cross at the lamina terminalis.

Commissures at lamina terminalis:
  • Anterior commissure - first commissure to appear. These fibers connect the olfactory bulb and related brain areas to the corresponding structures in the contralateral hemisphere.
  • Hippocampal commissure (fornix commissure) - develops second. The fibers emerge from the hippocampus and reach the lamina terminalis. From here, they arch outside the choroid fissure to the mamillary body and the hypothalamus.
  • Corpus callosum - appears by the 10th week. It connects the non-olfactory areas of the right and the left cerebral cortices.
Commissures at other areas are:
  • Posterior commissure
  • Habenular commissure
  • Optic chiasma
The image given below shows the anterior commissure:

question.text: The septum pellucidum extends between:
question.explanation:
The septum pellucidum extends between the corpus callosum and the fornix.

The septum pellucidum is a membrane separating the anterior horns of the left and right lateral ventricles of the brain. It extends from the corpus callosum to the fornix.

It develops from the lamina terminalis. The part of the lamina terminalis that stretches between the corpus callosum and fornix persists as septum pellucidum.

The image given below shows the septum pellucidum.

question.text: A man presented with frequent urination and increased thirst. MRI revealed the absence of the posterior pituitary bright spot. He was initiated on desmopressin which improved his symptoms. The affected structure is derived from:
question.explanation:
The given clinical scenario of polyuria and polydipsia along with the investigation findings is suggestive of central diabetes insipidus. It involves the diencephalon, a structure that is derived from the prosencephalon.

The diencephalon forms the thalamus, epithalamus, subthalamus, and hypothalamus.

The MRI given below shows the posterior pituitary bright spot. The arrow points at the posterior pituitary and the arrowhead at the anterior pituitary.

question.text: What structure is not a part of the epithalamus?
question.explanation:
Tuber cinereum is not a part of the epithalamus. It is a part of the hypothalamus.

The epithalamus consists of:
  • Anterior and posterior paraventricular nuclei
  • Medial and lateral habenular nuclei
  • Stria medullaris thalami
  • Posterior commissure
  • Pineal gland

question.text: An image showing a section of the brain is provided, with a structure marked 'X'. Which of the following is true about the marked structure?

options.label: A
options.text: The external medullary lamina is a sheet of grey matter on the lateral surface of thalamus.

options.label: B
options.text: The intralaminar nuclei lie outside the internal medullary lamina.

options.label: C
options.text: The internal medullary lamina divides the thalamus into three parts.
The internal medullary lamina divides the thalamus into two parts.
options.label: D

question.explanation:
The marked structure 'X' is the thalamus. The internal medullary lamina is a Y-shaped sheet of white matter dividing the thalamus into three parts:
  • Anterior nuclear groups
  • Medial nuclear groups
  • Lateral nuclear groups
The external medullary lamina is a sheet of white matter on the lateral surface of the thalamus that separates the thalamus from the reticular nucleus.

The intralaminar nuclei lie embedded within the internal medullary lamina, and the midline nuclei lie close to the lateral walls of the third ventricle.

The thalamus plays an important role in sensory and motor integration.

Input and output of the thalamus:
  • Pre-cortical input: All sensory systems (except olfactory system).
  • Cerebral cortex input: Largest input (from modified pyramidal cells of layer VI).
  • Projection fibers to other areas: Cerebral cortex (most fibers), Basal nuclei and hypothalamus (few fibers).

question.text: Which of the following is false about the anterior thalamic nuclei?

options.text: Largest subdivison is the anteromedial nucleus
options.label: A
B
options.text: Receives fibers from the mamillary body
Lesion on this nuclei can cause amnesia
options.label: C
D
options.text: Involved in regulation of alertness and attention

question.explanation:
The largest subdivision of anterior thalamic nuclei is the anteroventral nucleus (and not the anteromedial nucleus).

The anterior thalamic nuclei have three subdivisions:
  • Anteroventral nucleus
  • Anteromedial nucleus
  • Anterodorsal nucleus
Major input: Mamillothalamic tract from the mammillary nuclei of the hypothalamus.

Major cortical output: Anterior limbic area, cingulate, and the parahippocampal gyrus.

Major functions:
  • Regulation of alertness and attention.
  • Acquisition of memory.

question.text: The medial nucleus of the thalamus predominantly receives input from the ___ and sends output to the ___.
question.explanation:
The medial nucleus of the thalamus predominantly receives input from the hypothalamus and sends output to the prefrontal cortex.

The medial thalamic nuclei contain the large dorsomedial nucleus and several smaller nuclei:
  • Internally, the dorsomedial nucleus is connected to all other thalamic nuclei.
  • Externally, it has two major connections: the prefrontal cortex and the hypothalamus.
Its functions include integration of somatic, visceral, and olfactory sensory information, as well as the relation of this sensory information to emotional feelings and subjective states.

testTitle: 19 Hyperbilirubinemias and Tests of Liver Function
subject: Medicine

question.text: Which among the following is the most specific indicator of liver cell injury?
question.explanation:
Among the given options, alanine aminotransferase is the most specific indicator of liver cell injury.

Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) are indicators of liver cell injury. This is because ALT is found primarily in the liver, whereas, AST is found in the liver, cardiac muscle, skeletal muscle, kidneys, brain, pancreas, etc.

GGT and ALP are enzymes that primarily reflect cholestasis.

testTitle: 19 Hyperbilirubinemias and Tests of Liver Function
subject: Medicine

question.text: Liver function tests of a patient show isolated elevation of gamma-glutamyltransferase with other liver enzymes within normal limits. All of the following drugs could be responsible for this finding except:
question.explanation:
Among the given options, penicillin does not lead to elevated gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) levels.

GGT is a microsomal enzyme. Hence, drugs that are microsomal enzyme inducers can lead to an increase in GGT levels. However, other liver enzyme levels will be normal. Therefore, an isolated rise in GGT level does not indicate cholestatic liver disease.

Drugs that increase levels of GGT are:
  • Barbiturates
  • Carbamazepine
  • Ethanol
  • Griseofulvin
  • Rifampicin
  • Phenytoin

testTitle: 19 Hyperbilirubinemias and Tests of Liver Function
subject: Medicine

question.text: Which of the following statements regarding prothrombin time is false?

options.text: Indicates prognosis in acute liver disease
options.label: A

options.text: Indicates prognosis in chronic liver disease
options.label: B

options.text: Measures factors II, V, VIII, X
options.label: C

options.text: Measures factors II, V, VII, X
options.label: D

question.explanation:
Prothrombin time (PT) can help in estimating the levels of factors II, V, VII, and X.

PT evaluates the extrinsic and the common pathway of coagulation. Factor VII is required in the extrinsic pathway and factors II, V, X are required in the common pathway.

Coagulation factors are produced by the liver (except factor VIII) and they have a short half-life. Hence, they indicate the synthetic function of the liver and are very useful in assessing acute hepatic dysfunction. Factor VIII is produced by vascular endothelial cells.

Prolonged PT that is not corrected by vitamin K administration indicates poor prognosis in both acute and chronic liver disease.

testTitle: 19 Hyperbilirubinemias and Tests of Liver Function
subject: Medicine

question.text: Which among the following is a marker of chronic liver disease?
question.explanation:
Serum albumin is a marker of chronic liver disease because it is synthesized by the hepatocytes and has a long half-life of 18-20 days. Serum albumin is not a good indicator of acute or mild hepatic dysfunction.

Hypoalbuminemia is more common in chronic liver disorders such as cirrhosis and usually reflects severe liver damage. In hepatitis, albumin levels < 3 g/dL should raise the possibility of chronic liver disease.

Prothrombin time is used to assess acute parenchymal liver disease. 5' nucleosidase is elevated in cholestasis. Elevation of ALP (< 3 fold) is not specific to liver diseases.

testTitle: 19 Hyperbilirubinemias and Tests of Liver Function
subject: Medicine

question.text: Which of the following can be seen in a patient with chronic liver disease?
question.explanation:
Chronic liver disease is associated with hypergammaglobulinemia. Chronic liver diseases with hypergammaglobulinemia include autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cirrhosis, and alcoholic liver disease.

The liver produces all globulins except gamma globulin which are produced by B cells. In chronic liver diseases like liver cirrhosis, there is impaired reticuloendothelial function in hepatic sinusoids. Hence the liver fails to clear the bacterial antigens. This causes an increased production of gamma globulin.

testTitle: 19 Hyperbilirubinemias and Tests of Liver Function
subject: Medicine

question.text: Which of the following is not a marker for liver fibrosis?
question.explanation:
Telopeptide is not a marker for liver fibrosis. It is a marker for bone resorption.

Various non-invasive markers to detect hepatic fibrosis are given below:
  • Fibrotest/FibroSure: α2-macroglobulin, Haptoglobin, Apolipoprotein A-1, GGT, Total bilirubin
  • Enhanced Liver Fibrosis (ELF) assay: Hyaluronic acid, Procollagen peptide III (PIIINP), Tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase (TIMP)
  • Transient elastography (FibroScan): Ultrasound waves are used to measure liver stiffness
  • Fibrospect II: Hyaluronic acid, Alpha 2 macroglobulin, Tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase 1 (TIMP 1)

testTitle: 19 Hyperbilirubinemias and Tests of Liver Function
subject: Medicine

question.text: In which of the following patients planned for a liver biopsy, would you not be required to use the transjugular approach?
question.explanation:
Liver biopsy can be performed in a patient with splenomegaly via the percutaneous approach.

When the percutaneous approach is not advisable, liver biopsy can be performed via the transjugular approach. In this approach, a cannula is inserted via the jugular vein which is then passed into hepatic veins through which the biopsy sample is taken. Therefore, any bleeding resulting from the procedure will drain into the hepatic veins.

Indications of transjugular liver biopsy:
  • Percutaneous approach contraindicated
  • Significant ascites
  • Prolonged INR
  • Coagulopathies
  • Difficulty in accessing the liver via the percutaneous route
  • Morbid obesity

testTitle: 19 Hyperbilirubinemias and Tests of Liver Function
subject: Medicine

question.text: A 24-year-old woman presents with jaundice. She had been on OCPs for the past month. Her LFT and liver biopsy findings are given below. What is the probable diagnosis?
question.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Dubin Johnson syndrome (DJS). The LFT describes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with normal liver enzyme levels. The given image of microscopic examination of liver biopsy shows an accumulation of dark melanin-like pigment in the hepatocytes which is seen in this condition.

DJS is an autosomal recessive condition causing defective expression of MRP2 protein which is important for the biliary excretion of conjugated bilirubin. The patient has icterus but is otherwise asymptomatic.

DJS also impairs biliary excretion of various compounds like epinephrine metabolites. The dark melanin-like pigment is derived from these metabolites causing the liver to appear black.

Rotor syndrome is also an autosomal recessive condition causing conjugated hyperbilirubinemia but it does not present with pigmentation of the liver.

Gilbert and Crigler-Najjar syndromes are characterized by unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

question.text: All are true about the types of celiac disease except :

options.label: A
options.text: Latent type is associated with HLA DQ 2,8

options.label: B
options.text: Atypical type has a negative serology

options.label: C
options.text: Silent type has a positive serology

options.label: D
options.text: Classic type presents with diarrhea and steatorrhea

question.explanation:
Atypical celiac disease has a positive serology with atypical symptoms.

Serology in celiac disease refers to either anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies (anti-tTG) or anti-endomysial antibodies.

Note: Tropical sprue and celiac disease have similar clinical, endoscopic and histologic findings. A diagnosis of tropical sprue must be considered with a negative celiac serology.

Atypical celiac disease presents with:
  • Iron deficiency anemia
  • Osteopenia
  • Ataxia
  • Peripheral neuropathy
  • Infertility

question.text: A patient who presented with severe malabsorption is found to be positive for IgA tissue trans-glutaminase antibodies. What will be the next best step?
question.explanation:
In this patient with positive serology, a biopsy should be done next, to confirm the diagnosis of celiac disease.

Tissue transglutaminase Ab (tTG-IgA) is the best screening test. IgA endomysial antibodies (EMA) are most specific.

But a small-intestinal biopsy is required to establish a diagnosis of celiac disease, before starting treatment.

question.text: A 30-year-old man presented with chronic diarrhea, steatorrhea, and weight loss. IgA tissue trans-glutaminase antibodies were found to be positive. Duodenal biopsy revealed the following. Which of the following complications would you not expect in this patient?
question.explanation:
The above scenario along with the presence of IgA tissue trans-glutaminase antibodies and biopsy showing villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, lamina propria infiltrates indicate a case of celiac disease. Pancreatic insufficiency is not a complication of celiac disease.

The complications of celiac disease are:
  • Intestinal lymphomas
  • Intestinal ulcers (also known as ulcerative jejunoileitis)
  • Collagenous sprue (development of a subepithelial collagen layer)

question.text:
Match the following malabsorption disorders with their most commonly involved sites in the small intestine:

DisorderSite of Involvement
1. Whipple's diseasei. Whole small intestine (panintestinal involvement)
2. Tropical sprueii. Proximal > distal small intestine
3. Celiac diseaseiii.Proximal small intestine predominance
question.explanation:
The sites involved in the given malabsorption syndromes are as follows:

  • Whipple's disease: Predominantly proximal small intestine more than distal involvement.
  • Tropical sprue: Diffuse involvement of the whole small intestine (panintestinal).

question.text: What is the most common CNS manifestation associated with Whipple’s disease?
question.explanation:
The most common CNS manifestation associated with Whipple’s disease is progressive dementia.

Other important CNS manifestations in Whipple's disease are:
  • Personality and mood changes
  • Progressive supranuclear ophthalmoplegia
  • Focal neurologic presentations
  • Oculomasticatory myorrhythmia - an unusual combination of rhythmic eye and jaw movements which is pathognomonic of Whipple's disease.

Whipple's disease associated with CNS symptoms has a poor prognosis.

Note: Opsoclonus myoclonus syndrome is a paraneoplastic syndrome associated with neuroblastoma.

question.text: What is the most common cardiovascular presentation seen in patients with Whipple's disease?
question.explanation:
The most common cardiovascular presentation in Whipple's disease is culture-negative endocarditis.

Other cardiovascular findings include:
  • Congestive heart failure
  • Pericarditis
  • Myocarditis

question.text: A 38-year-old man presented with chronic diarrhea, weight loss, and joint pains. A duodenal biopsy was done. Which of the following drug is used in the maintenance phase of treatment of this condition?
question.explanation:
The above image shows PAS-positive foamy macrophages present in the lamina propria. This along with the given features suggests Whipple's disease. Cotrimoxazole is used in the maintenance phase of the treatment of Whipple's disease.

Treatment of Whipple's disease:
  • Induction phase: ceftriaxone or meropenem or penicillin G + streptomycin - 2 weeks
  • Maintenance phase: trimethoprim / sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX) for 1 year. It has high CNS penetration so it is used in maintenance to prevent relapse.

question.text: What is the most common cause of short bowel syndrome in adults?
question.explanation:
The most common cause of short bowel syndrome in adults is mesenteric vascular occlusion.

Short bowel syndrome (SBS) is a malabsorption disorder caused by a lack of functional small intestine. In adults, the common causes are:
  • Mesenteric vascular disease (e.g., mesenteric vascular occlusion)
  • Primary mucosal and submucosal disease (e.g., Crohn’s disease)
  • Operations without any preexisting small-intestinal disease (e.g., after trauma)

In children, necrotizing enterocolitis is the most common cause.

question.text: Patients with which of the following conditions are unlikely to have protein malabsorption?
question.explanation:
Homocystinuria is not a protein malabsorption disorder. It is a disorder of methionine metabolism that leads to increased homocysteine levels.

Proteins are broken down by pancreatic enzymes and are absorbed as amino acids and peptides.

So, protein malabsorption usually occurs only in pancreatic insufficiency. Additionally, there are three rare genetic disorders that lead to protein malabsorption. They are:
  • Enterokinase deficiency
    Defective conversion of the proenzyme trypsinogen to trypsin. It is characterised by:
    • Diarrhoea
    • Growth retardation
    • Hypoproteinemia
  • Hartnup disease
    Defective transport of tryptophan and other neutral amino acids. It is characterised by:
    • Pellagra-like rash
    • Neuropsychiatric symptoms
  • Cystinuria
    Defective transport of cystine and other dibasic amino acids. It is characterised by:
    • Renal calculi
    • Chronic pancreatitis

question.text: The image shows a peripheral smear. Which of the following conditions is characterized by defective chylomicron formation, retinitis pigmentosa, and acanthocytes?
question.explanation:
The image showing retinitis pigmentosa and presence of acanthocytes along with the given clinical features is suggestive of abetalipoproteinemia.

Abetalipoproteinemia is a rare genetic disorder in which there is defective chylomicron formation.

Chylomicrons are required for the absorption and transport of fats and fat-soluble vitamins.

It presents in early childhood with steatorrhoea and diarrhea, hypolipidemia, failure to thrive, ataxia, sensory and motor neuropathies.

question.text: Which of the following is not a part of the vulva?
question.explanation:
Cervix is not a part of the vulva.

The vulva includes:
  • Mons veneris
  • Labia majora
  • Labia minora
  • Clitoris
  • Vestibule
  • Vestibular bulb
  • Greater vestibular glands
The vulva is posteriorly related to the perineum.

The triangular space bounded by clitoris, labia minora and fourchette is the vestibule. It is present between the labia minora anteriorly and the introitus posteriorly. The posterior part of the vestibule between the fourchette and the vaginal introitus is called fossa navicularis. The vestibule has 4 openings:
  • Urethral opening
  • Vaginal orifice opening
  • Bartholin’s duct on either side
  • Ducts of paraurethral glands

question.text: What is the cavity of the uterus lined by?

options.text: Single layer of ciliated columnar epithelium
options.label: A

options.text: Double layer of ciliated columnar epithelium
options.label: B

options.text: Single layer of ciliated cuboidal epithelium
options.label: C

options.text: Double layer of ciliated cuboidal epithelium
options.label: D

question.explanation:
The uterine cavity is lined by a single layer of ciliated columnar epithelium.

The wall of the uterus consists of 3 layers:
  • Perimetrium: is the serous coat adherent to the underlying muscle.
  • Myometrium: it consists of thick bundles of muscles that form 3 distinct layers during pregnancy:
    • Outer longitudinal
    • Inner circular
    • Middle interlacing called living ligature
  • Endometrium: It is the mucous lining of the cavity. It consists of lamina propria and surface epithelium which is a single layer of ciliated columnar epithelium.

question.text: A woman with regular menstrual cycles is undergoing an ultrasound on the 14th day of her cycle. What will the endometrial thickness be?
question.explanation:
During ovulation, the thickness of the endometrium is around 11 mm.

  • Immediately after menstruation / Early proliferative phase: 1-2 mm
  • Postmenopausal - abnormal, requires biopsy: >4 mm

question.text: Which of the following is false about the contents of the broad ligament?

options.text: Ovarian vessels in its infundibulopelvic part
options.label: A

options.text: Ureter is present the lower portion
options.label: C
D
options.text: Ovarian ligament in its anterior fold

question.explanation:
The ovarian ligaments are contained in the posterior fold of the broad ligament.

The broad ligament contains the following parts:
  • Mesosalpinx: it lies between the fallopian tube and ovarian ligament. It contains the pelvic vessels - anastomoses between uterine and ovarian arteries. The ovary is attached via ovarian ligament through the posterior folds to the mesovarium.
  • Mesometrium: it contains the ovarian vessels within the infundibulopelvic ligament.
The ureter is present in the inferomedial part of the broad ligament. It is related to the uterine artery here and may be damaged during hysterectomy.

Note: Broad ligament is not a support of the uterus.

question.text: Where are Peg cells seen?
question.explanation:
Peg cells are seen in the fallopian tubes.

A peg cell is a non-ciliated epithelial cell within the fallopian tube. These cells are also known as intercalated or intercalary cells whose function is not yet known.

The image below shows pale ciliated cells (arrows) and narrow, dark, non-ciliated peg cells (arrowheads).

question.text: What is the longest part of the fallopian tube?
question.explanation: The longest and widest part of the fallopian tube is the ampulla (5 cm).

question.text: Where is the tunica albuginea of the adult ovary derived from?

options.text: The sub epithelial connective tissue layer
options.label: B

question.explanation:
Tunica albuginea of the adult ovary is derived from the sub-epithelial connective tissue layer.

Structure of the ovary:
  • Surface epithelium: a single layer of cuboidal cells is present, which later gives rise to the surface epithelium of the adult ovary. It is morphologically continuous with the mesothelium of the peritoneum.
  • The subepithelial connective tissue layer: gives rise to the tunica albuginea of the adult ovary and the basement membrane beneath the surface epithelium.
  • The parenchymatous zone: becomes the cortex and contains the egg nests and ovarian follicles.
  • Zona vasculosa: becomes the medulla and contains the blood vessels. Hilar cells present here are homologous to interstitial cells of testes. They can rarely produce hilar cell tumors of the ovary.

question.text: A patient with stress incontinence required surgical management. While performing a Burch colposuspension, the surgeon approached the space of Retzius. What is this space also known as?
question.explanation:
The space of Retzius is the other name for prevesical or retropubic space.

Burch colposuspension is a procedure done to relieve stress urinary incontinence. If an extraperitoneal approach is selected, the retropubic space is entered by perforating the transversalis fascia layer of the anterior abdominal wall.

Once the retropubic space is dissected, the bladder neck and the vaginal fascia underneath are identified. The bladder is mobilized to the opposite side. At each side of the bladder neck, two to four, preferably nonabsorbable sutures are placed in the space of Retzius.

Note: The presacral space is a retroperitoneal space that lies between the peritoneum of the posterior abdominal wall and the sacrum. It contains the superior and inferior hypogastric plexuses. The sacral sympathetic trunk lies against the sacrum’s ventral surface.

question.text: When does the ovary contain the maximum number of oogonia?
question.explanation:
The ovary contains the maximum number of oogonia at the 5th month of intrauterine life. The number of oogonia is estimated to be 7 million.

Oogenesis is the process wherein oogonia differentiate into mature oocytes. It begins before birth.

At birth, there are approximately 2 million primordial follicles. At the initiation of puberty, the follicle count is less than 400,000, of which less than 500 are destined to ovulate. Every month, 15-20 follicles are released, out of which one matures to form the ovum.

question.text: What do the Langhans cells form?
question.explanation:
Langhans cells form the cytotrophoblast.
