The cells of the blastocyst differentiate into an outer trophectoderm and an inner cell mass.

The trophectoderm is further differentiated into:
  • An inner mononuclear cellular layer called cytotrophoblast or Langhans layer made of Langhans cells.
  • An outer layer of multinucleated syncytium called syncytiotrophoblast.
The blastomere further divides to form the morula.

question.text: A man with oligospermia has completed his course of hormonal treatment. After how many days will you test his sperm count?
question.explanation:
The sperm count is tested 80-90 days after hormonal treatment, as the average time taken for spermatogenesis is 74 days, and approximately 14 days to reach the ejaculatory ducts.

The effect of hormonal therapy on the early phase of spermatogenesis is reflected in the ejaculated sperm concentration after three months.

Spermatogenesis is the process of the formation of sperms from spermatogonia. Approximately 100 million sperms are produced daily.

In patients diagnosed with oligospermia, hormonal treatment is carried out using FSH, hCG, or testosterone. Improvements in sperm count can take a few months, hence the course is usually for 3-6 months. Normal spermatogenesis occurs after this time period.

Spermiogenesis refers to the series of changes that occur in the formation of spermatozoa from spermatids. These are:
  • Acrosome formation
  • Condensation of the nucleus
  • Formation of the neck, middle piece, and tail
  • Shedding of cytoplasm as residual bodies
Complete motility is obtained in the epididymis.

question.text: What is the time taken for capacitation of the sperm?
question.explanation:
The time taken for the capacitation of sperms is 6-8 hours (approximately 7 hours).

Sperms have to undergo two changes in the female reproductive tract to be able to fertilise the ovum:
  • 1) Capacitation
    • It is the functional maturation of the spermatozoa.
    • It occurs in the fallopian tube and involves epithelial interactions between the sperm and the mucosal surface of the tube.
    • The glycoprotein coat and seminal plasma proteins are removed.
    • Only capacitated sperms can pass through the corona cells and undergo the acrosomal reaction.
  • 2) Acrosomal reaction
    • It occurs after binding to zona pellucida, induced by zona proteins.
    • Enzymes such as acrosin and trypsin-like protein are released to penetrate the zona pellucida.
    • Ca2+ plays an important role.

question.text: In which of the following steps does reductional division occur?
question.explanation:
Meiosis I or reductional division occurs in the transition from primary spermatocyte to secondary spermatocyte.

Meiosis takes place in germ cells to generate male and female gametes. Meiosis involves two stages of cell division, namely, meiosis I and II.

Meiosis I produces two haploid cells. Because the ploidy is reduced from diploid to haploid, meiosis I is referred to as a reductional division. Meiosis II is an equational division analogous to mitosis, resulting in the creation of four haploid daughter cells.

question.text: You are performing intrauterine insemination during the ovulatory period in a patient with infertility. When will you expect implantation to occur?
question.explanation:
The fertilized ovum implants by 6–10 days in the uterine cavity.

Implantation involves:
  • Apposition: Initial contact of the blastocyst to the uterine wall
  • Adhesion: Increased physical contact between the blastocyst and uterine epithelium
  • Invasion: Penetration and invasion of syncytiotrophoblast and cytotrophoblasts into the endometrium
A successful implantation requires receptive endometrium primed with estrogen and progesterone released by the corpus luteum.

question.text: The following figure shows the transverse section of the uterus with an implanted zygote. Identify structure A.
question.explanation:
In the given image, the decidua basalis is marked as A. This part of the decidua forms the placenta.

Implantation occurs 6 to 7 days after fertilization. After implantation, the endometrium is called the decidua. It is of the following types:
  • Decidua basalis - present over chorion frondosum. Decidua basalis and chorion frondosum form the placenta.
  • Decidua capsularis - present over abembryonic pole.
  • Decidua parietalis - present on the opposite side of the uterus.
The villi cover the entire surface of the chorion during the early weeks. As the fetus grows, the villi on the embryonic pole continue to grow, giving rise to the chorion frondosum. At the abembryonic pole, the villi degenerate. By the third month, this side of the chorion becomes smooth, and is called the chorion laeve.

As the fetus grows, the chorion laeve comes into contact with the decidua parietalis on the opposite side of the uterus, and fusion occurs. Thus, the uterine lumen is obliterated. The amnion and chorion fuse, to form the amniochorionic membrane. Rupture of the amniochorionic membrane during labor is called 'breaking of waters'.

Note: Superfetation can theoretically occur till the time the uterine lumen is not obliterated.

question.text: The anatomical classification of the pelvis based on shape was given by .
question.explanation:
The anatomical classification of the pelvis based on shape was given by Caldwell and Moloy.

The greatest transverse diameter of the pelvic inlet divides the pelvis into anterior and posterior segments. The shapes of these segments help classify the pelvis as follows:
  • Gynecoid
  • Anthropoid
  • Android
  • Platypelloid
The various differences between these types are summarised below:

Gynecoid Pelvis:
  • Shape: Round
  • Sacral angle: >90°
  • Side walls: Straight or slightly divergent
  • Ischial spines: Not prominent
  • Subpubic angle: Wide (85°)
  • Fetal Position: Occipitolateral/Oblique occipitoanterior
  • Engaging diameter: Transverse / oblique
  • Delivery: No difficulty

Anthropoid Pelvis:
  • Shape: Anteroposteriorly oval
  • Sacral angle: >90°
  • Side walls: Straight or divergent
  • Ischial spines: Not prominent
  • Subpubic angle: Slightly narrow
  • Fetal Position: Direct occipitoanterior/Occipitoposterior
  • Engaging diameter: Anteroposterior
  • Delivery: Face-to-pubis - most common.

Android Pelvis:
  • Shape: Triangular/Heart-shaped
  • Sacral angle: <90°
  • Side walls: Convergent
  • Ischial spines: Prominent
  • Subpubic angle: Narrow
  • Fetal Position: Occipitolateral/Oblique occipitoposterior
  • Engaging diameter: Transverse / oblique
  • Delivery: Deep transverse arrest is common. Difficult delivery with an increased chance of perineal injuries.

Platypelloid Pelvis:
  • Shape: Transversely oval / Flat
  • Sacral angle: >90°
  • Side walls: Divergent
  • Ischial spines: Not prominent
  • Subpubic angle: Very wide (>90°)
  • Fetal Position: Occipitolateral
  • Engaging diameter: Transverse
  • Delivery: No difficulty

Caldwell-Moloy classification of the types of the pelvis.

Option B: McAfee and Johnson's regimen is for the conservative management of placenta previa.
Option C: Page's and Sher's classification system is used to grade abruptio placentae.
Option D: Burns and Marshall maneuver is used in breech delivery.

question.text: Which of the following statements is true regarding amenorrhoea?

options.text: MRKH syndrome is associated with secondary amenorrhoea
options.label: A

options.text: Primary amenorrhoea is seen in Turner syndrome
options.label: B
C
options.text: Primary amenorrhea is absence of menarche by 13 years
Secondary amenorrhea is absence of menses for 6 months
options.label: D

question.explanation:
Primary amenorrhoea is seen in Turner syndrome.

Amenorrhoea is a symptom and not a disease entity. It refers to the absence of menstruation that can be physiological or pathological.

Primary amenorrhea is defined as an absence of menstruation by the age of 15 years. At age 13 years, if no menses have occurred and there is a complete absence of secondary sexual characteristics such as breast development, evaluation for primary amenorrhea should begin. Mullerian agenesis (MRKH syndrome), androgen insensitivity syndrome, and Turner syndrome present with primary amenorrhea. In Turner's syndrome, gonadal dysgenesis causes primary ovarian failure, resulting in hypogonadism and amenorrhea.

Secondary amenorrhea is defined as the absence of menses for 3 or more months or fewer than 9 cycles per year after the establishment of regular menstrual cycles. Polycystic ovarian syndrome and hypothyroidism are associated with secondary amenorrhea. Pregnancy is the most common physiological cause of secondary amenorrhea.

question.text: A young girl with McCune-Albright syndrome is noted to have precocious menstruation. This condition is defined as the occurrence of menstruation at what age?
question.explanation:
Precocious menstruation refers to the occurrence of menstruation before the age of 10 years.

Precocious puberty in a girl is the appearance of any of the secondary sexual characteristics before the age of 8 years or the occurrence of menarche before the age of 10 years.

McCune Albright syndrome is associated with cafe-au-lait spots, precocious puberty (and precocious menstruation), and polyostotic fibrous dysplasia leading to recurrent fractures. The image given below shows cafe-au-lait spots.

question.text: A 45-year-old woman presents with profuse, painless vaginal bleeding. She has a history of 6-8 weeks of amenorrhea and her UPT is negative. On ultrasound, endometrial thickness is 21mm. What is the likely diagnosis?
question.explanation:
The given case scenario is suggestive of metropathia hemorrhagica.

Metropathia hemorrhagica is a form of anovulatory abnormal uterine bleeding. It is characterized by continuous painless vaginal bleeding at the onset of menses or preceded by a 6-8 week period of amenorrhea. It is usually seen in the age group of 40-45 years. A history of menorrhagia may be present.

On examination, the uterus is bulky and uniformly enlarged. Histopathological findings are:
  • Myohyperplasia of the uterine wall - up to 2.5 cm.
  • Thick endometrium with cystic glandular hyperplasia appearing as swiss cheese pattern.
  • Absence of secretory endometrium i.e. absence of corkscrew glands.
  • Thin, slender endometrial polyps project into the uterine cavity.
  • Corpus luteum is absent.
  • One or both ovaries may contain a cyst.
Option A: Senile endometritis occurs after menopause when the endometrium is thin and atrophic. It may be associated with accumulation of pus in the uterine cavity.

Option B: Halban's disease is irregular shedding and is due to persistent corpus luteum. Regular cycles with prolonged bleeding and normal flow is present.

Option D: Endometriosis usually presents in the reproductive age group, with symptoms of menorrhagia, dysmenorrhea and chronic pelvic pain.

question.text: A 28-year-old P1L1 woman presented with heavy menstrual bleeding and occasional spotting between cycles. What is the first investigation to be done for her?
question.explanation:
The first investigation to be done in a case of abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) in the reproductive age group is urine B-hCG estimation. This is done to rule out pregnancy.

In the reproductive age group, anovulatory uterine bleeding is encountered less often. Therefore, pregnancy must be excluded. Pregnancy complications such as miscarriage, ectopic pregnancies, and molar pregnancies may present with AUB, hence these need to be ruled out by urine B-hCG levels. This is done for all women in the reproductive age group.

Other investigations to be done for AUB are:
  • Pap smear - to rule out cervical cancer and preinvasive lesions (CIN).
  • Transabdominal ultrasound - to visualize the pelvic organs and lesions such as endometrial hyperplasia, polyps, fibroids, etc.
  • Transvaginal ultrasound - to visualize the pelvic organs. It is done after evaluating B-hCG. This is more comfortable for a patient compared to a transabdominal ultrasound as it doesn't require a full bladder.

question.text: A woman with AUB-E, who was unresponsive to medical management, underwent a hysteroscopic ablation. Which of the following is false about this procedure?
question.explanation:
Fertility is not preserved with ablative procedures, because the endometrium and superficial myometrium are destroyed.

In ablative procedures, the uterus is preserved, and hysterectomy is avoided. The endometrium along with 2-3mm of superficial myometrium is destroyed.

Various methods of endometrial ablation include:
  • Hysteroscopic endometrial ablation
  • Transcervical endometrial resection (TCRE) - now replaced by bipolar electrode called Versapoint
  • Radiofrequency induced thermal ablation (RITEA)
  • Microwave ablation
  • NovaSure - impedance-controlled endometrial ablation
  • Bilateral uterine artery embolization
  • Uterine tamponade

question.text: When is dilatation and curettage contraindicated?
question.explanation:
Dilatation and curettage (D&C) is contraindicated in pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) as it increases the risk of ascending genital infection.

D&C is a minor gynecological procedure of dilating the cervix and curetting the endometrial tissue from the uterine cavity. Diagnostic indications of D&C include AUB, secondary amenorrhea to detect tubercular endometritis, postmenopausal bleeding to rule out endometrial cancer or hyperplasia, and infertility due to genital TB.

Therapeutic indications of D&C include missed abortion, incomplete abortion, retained products of conception, and endometrial polypectomy.

Absolute contraindication of D&C includes suspected/desired pregnancy and lower genital tract infection. However, D&C is performed in some cases with genital infections like septic abortion (where retained pieces of placenta act as a nidus and need to be removed) and pyometra (as there is cervical obstruction with superinfection of menstrual blood and cellular debris, D&C is appropriate to remove the obstruction as well as the source of infection).

Complications of D&C include ascending infection, cervical tear with bleeding, incompetent os, uterine perforation, and Asherman syndrome.

question.text: An increase in which of the following is spasmodic pain during dysmenorrhoea attributed to?
question.explanation:
Spasmodic pain is attributed to myometrial contractions occurring due to increased PGF2α. This is secreted under the effect of progesterone.

Progesterone is secreted after ovulation by the corpus luteum. Hence, in anovulatory cycles, menstruation is not accompanied by spasmodic pain.

question.text: A patient with uterine fibroids complains of frequent menstruation with an average cycle duration of 19-21 days. What is this menstrual irregularity called?
question.explanation:
The given case scenario is suggestive of polymenorrhoea, also known as epimenorrhea. It refers to frequent episodes of menstruation, usually occurring at intervals of 21 days or less.

The definitions of various menstrual cycle irregularities are:
  • Amenorrhoea refers to the absence of menstruation.
  • Intermenstrual bleeding refers to occasional episodes of bleeding (usually not excessive) that occur between otherwise normal menstrual cycles.
  • Hypomenorrhoea refers to regularly timed cycles, but having scanty episodes of bleeding.
  • Menorrhagia refers to regularly timed menstrual cycles with excessive bleeding (> 80 mL in amount) and/or increased duration of flow (> 8 days).
  • Metrorrhagia refers to normal cyclical bleeding with superimposed irregularly timed episodes of bleeding.
  • Menometrorrhagia refers to excessive, prolonged bleeding that occurs at irregularly timed and frequent intervals.
  • Oligomenorrhea refers to infrequent, irregularly timed cycles with intervals of more than 38 days.
  • Precocious menstruation refers to the occurrence of menstruation before the age of 10 years.

question.text: Which of the following is not a feature of menometrorrhagia?
question.explanation:
Menometrorrhagia refers to menstrual bleeding at frequent intervals.

Menometrorrhagia means excessive, prolonged bleeding that occurs at irregularly timed and frequent intervals. It can be caused by cervical cancer and granulosa cell tumors.

question.text: A patient who had undergone a dilatation and curettage procedure comes to the clinic 6 months later for a follow-up visit. She informs you that since the procedure, she has had scanty blood loss during menses which only lasts for 1-2 days. What is this pattern of bleeding called?
question.explanation:
In the given clinical scenario, the pattern of bleeding is called hypomenorrhea. Hypomenorrhea along with a prior history of dilatation and curettage are suggestive of partial Asherman's syndrome.

Hypomenorrhoea refers to regularly timed but scanty episodes of bleeding. It can be seen in:
  • Partial Asherman's syndrome - uterine synechiae, causing scarring.
  • Oral contraceptive use.
  • Perimenopausal age group.

question.text: Which of the following types of genitourinary fistulas has not been reported?
question.explanation:
Uterourethral type of fistula has not been reported.

A genitourinary fistula is defined as an abnormal communication between the urinary system (ureter, bladder, urethra) and the genital systems (vagina, cervix, uterus).

Most genitourinary fistulas are acquired. In developing countries, the most common cause is obstetric trauma. In developed countries, iatrogenic injury during pelvic surgery is responsible for 90% of the vesicovaginal fistulas.

Congenital genitourinary fistulas are rare. If present, they are commonly associated with other renal or urogenital abnormalities.

question.text: You are performing an abdominal hysterectomy and need to identify the ureter to avoid iatrogenic injury. Which of the following sets of features is most characteristic of the ureter in the intraoperative field?

options.label: A
options.text: Pulsatile on palpation, pale appearance, and located lateral to the ovarian vessels.

options.label: B
options.text: Glistening appearance, vermicular peristalsis upon stimulation, and crossed superiorly by the uterine artery
Non-distensible cord-like structure, crossed anteriorly by the internal iliac artery, and shows no movement on stimulation.
options.label: C
D
options.text: Dark tubular appearance, passes anterior to the uterine artery, and located medial to the uterosacral ligament.

question.explanation:
The ureter is identified intraoperatively by the following features:
  • Appearance: It has a characteristic pale, whitish, and glistening appearance.
  • Peristalsis: It exhibits vermicular (worm-like) contraction when gently pinched or stimulated with forceps.
  • Palpation: It is cord-like on palpation and is non-pulsatile.
  • Anatomical Relationships:
    • Ovarian artery crosses anterior to it at the pelvic brim.
    • Uterine artery crosses superior to it (the 'water under the bridge' relationship) approximately 2 cm lateral to the cervix.

Note: If you are unsure if a structure is the ureter or a vessel, look for peristalsis; while arteries pulsate, only the ureter will 'crawl' when stimulated.

question.text: Which of the following does not cause genitourinary fistulas?
question.explanation:
Hysteroscopy is not an etiology for genitourinary fistulae. It can occur following hysterectomy.

Most genitourinary fistulas are acquired. Its causes are enumerated below:
  • Prolonged obstructed labor - major cause in developing countries
  • Difficult instrumental or manipulative deliveries
  • Injury to bladder or ureter during hysterectomy - major cause in developed countries
  • Congenital (rare)
  • Other causes include:
    • Radiation
    • Malignancy
    • Trauma
    • Infections - PID, tuberculosis etc.

question.text: A 40-year-old woman came for a follow-up visit one week following a vaginal hysterectomy. You note she has developed a large vesicovaginal fistula. What is the best time for fistula repair in this case?
question.explanation:
In the given scenario, the best time to perform fistula repair is 6 weeks after the inciting surgery.

In uncomplicated fistulas, early surgical intervention is preferred within the first 24 to 48 hours following the inciting surgery. This avoids the brisk postoperative inflammatory response.

However, if extensive and severe inflammation is present, repair of fistula can be delayed to 6 weeks after the surgery. This is usually done in a patient who has undergone major surgery. During this delay it is ensured that all the tissue inflammation has subsided, tissue vascularisation has improved and local infection has cleared. Estrogen therapy should be instituted in postmenopausal women in this time period.

In case the fistula repair fails, a second attempt is made only after 3 months.

question.text: A 34-year-old woman presents to the OPD with complaints of blood in her urine. She informs you that this happens every month for 1 week and stops on its own. She underwent a C-section 1 year ago and has no history of incontinence. During clinical examination, a catheter is inserted into the bladder, and the following finding is seen. What is the likely diagnosis?
question.explanation:
The given image shows the catheter emerging from the cervical os. This, along with the history of cyclical hematuria, is suggestive of Youssef syndrome seen in a case of vesicouterine fistula.

Vesicouterine fistulas can develop after cesarean section, uterine rupture, and placenta accreta.

Most cases present weeks to years later.

Vesicouterine fistulas can present with cyclical hematuria, urinary incontinence or complete continence, menstrual abnormalities, and urinary tract infections. Youssef syndrome is seen in cases of vesicouterine fistulas, and it is associated with a classic triad:
  • Amenorrhea
  • Cyclical hematuria - also called menouria: Menstrual blood trickles into the bladder through the fistula, causing hematuria
  • Urinary continence (there is no vaginal leakage of urine)
Hysteroscopy and cystoscopy are gold-standard investigations.

Vesicouterine fistulas are treated as follows:
  • Prolonged bladder catheterization - leads to spontaneous closure
  • Surgical repair via abdominal route

question.text: At what age would a child attain full visual acuity?
question.explanation:
Full visual acuity is attained by the age of 6 years.

Important milestones in visual development are:
  • At birth, there is no central fixation, and the eyes move randomly.
  • By the first month of life, the fixation reflex starts developing and becomes established by 6 months.
  • By 3 months, binocular vision is established.
  • By 6 months, macular stereopsis and accommodation reflex are fully developed.
  • By 6 years of age, full visual acuity (6/6) is attained.

question.text: The optic foramen is situated between the:

options.label: A
options.text: Lesser and greater wings of the sphenoid

options.label: B
options.text: Lesser wing and body of the sphenoid
Greater wing and body of the sphenoid
options.label: C
D
options.text: Two roots of the lesser wing of the sphenoid

question.explanation:
The optic foramen is situated between the two roots of the lesser wing of the sphenoid.

The optic foramen leads into the optic canal, which is formed medially by the body and laterally by the lesser wing of the sphenoid bone, connecting the orbit's apex to the middle cranial fossa.

The optic canal transmits the optic nerve with its meningeal coverings; the ophthalmic artery, which is below the nerve, is embedded in its dural sheath, and a few twigs from the sympathetic plexus accompanying the artery.

question.text: The posterior chamber in the eyeball is filled with .
question.explanation:
The posterior chamber of the eyeball is filled with aqueous humor.

The eyeball is divided into anterior and posterior segments. The anterior segment includes the lens and the structures anterior to it, such as the cornea, iris and two aqueous humor-filled spaces:
  • Anterior chamber: Located between cornea and iris, contains aqueous humor and communicates with the posterior chamber through the pupil.
  • Posterior chamber: Triangular-shaped space, also contains aqueous humor, bounded anteriorly by the posterior surface of the iris, laterally by the ciliary body, and posteriorly by the lens.
The posterior segment includes all structures located posterior to the lens, comprising of the vitreous humor, retina, choroid and optic disc.

question.text: Which of the following structures is attached to Whitnall’s tubercle?

options.label: A
options.text: Check ligament of the medial rectus
Check ligament of the lateral rectus
options.label: C

question.explanation:
Check ligament of the lateral rectus is attached to Whitnall’s tubercle.

Lateral orbital tubercle or Whitnall's tubercle is a small elevation on the orbital surface of the zygomatic bone, just within the lateral orbital margin. It is about 11 mm below the fronto-zygomatic suture.

Four structures are attached to it:
  • Check ligament of the lateral rectus
  • Lockwood’s ligament (Suspensory ligament of the eyeball)
  • Lateral palpebral ligament
  • Lateral horn of the levator aponeurosis
The Whitnall's ligament or the superior transverse ligament of the eye, is attached to the superior tarsal plate and the orbital bone.

question.text: Which of the following statements is false regarding the tarsal plates?

options.label: B
options.text: They give structural support to the eyelid.

options.label: C
options.text: LPS aponeurosis is attached to the superior border of the upper tarsal plate.

options.label: D
options.text: Their medial and lateral ends form the medial and lateral palpebral ligaments, respectively.

question.explanation:
The tarsal plates are not cartilaginous structures but firm, dense connective tissue (fibrous tissue) plates.

The tarsal plates serve as the structural support of the eyelids. The height of the upper tarsal plate is about 10 mm, and that of the lower tarsal plate is 4 mm. Both plates have a thickness of about 1 mm. The ends form the medial and lateral palpebral ligaments (medial and lateral canthal tendons). The levator palpebrae superioris (LPS) aponeurosis is attached to the superior border of the upper tarsal plate.

The meibomian glands are located within the tarsus. These are holocrine-secreting sebaceous glands that are not associated with lash follicles.

question.text: 55-year-old man is being evaluated for herpes zoster ophthalmicus. On eliciting corneal reflex, there is no response. Which of the following nerves forms the afferent limb of this reflex?
question.explanation:
The sensory supply of the cornea comes from the long ciliary nerve (branch of the nasociliary nerve). It forms the afferent limb of the corneal reflex.

The sensory nerve supply of the eye is by the ophthalmic nerve:
  • Lacrimal nerve: lacrimal gland, conjunctiva, lateral eyelid.
  • Frontal nerve: conjunctiva, eyelid, part of the forehead.
  • Nasociliary nerve:
    • Long ciliary nerve: cornea, ciliary body, iris.
    • Infra-trochlear nerve: conjunctiva, lacrimal sac, caruncle, medial part of the eyelids.
Corneal sensation is reduced in leprosy and diabetes mellitus (neuropathy).

question.text: What is the thinnest part of the retina?
question.explanation:
The retina is the thinnest (0.080 mm) at the ora serrata, and thickest, at the foveal rim (0.23, 0.320 mm).

The ora serrata is the serrated junction between the retina and ciliary body.

question.text: By how many weeks of embryonic development does the optic groove appear?
question.explanation: The optic groove appears by 3 weeks. By approximately day 22, 2 small grooves appear on either side of the developing forebrain in the neural folds; these are called optic grooves. As the neural tube closes, these grooves develop outpouchings called optic vesicles. These optic vesicles extend from the forebrain to the surface ectoderm.

question.text: Embryonic development of ciliary muscles is from .
question.explanation: Embryonic development of ciliary muscles is from the neural crest.

question.text: What is the anteroposterior diameter of the adult eyeball?
question.explanation:
The anteroposterior (AP) diameter of the adult eye is 24 mm/2.4 cm.

At birth, the average axial length of the eyeball is 16.5 mm. By 3 years, it grows rapidly to approximately 23 mm. From 3 to 14 years of age, the axial length gradually increases by a further 1 mm, bringing it to the adult size of 24 mm. This overall adjustment in the eye size, including the refractive power, is called emmetropization.

question.text: 34-year-old lady comes to the clinic complaining of problems in her vision. On perimetry, a visual field defect as shown below is obtained. Which of the following vessels does not supply the anatomical location of the lesion?
question.explanation:
The image shows bitemporal hemianopia, a defect caused by optic chiasmal lesions. The middle cerebral artery does not supply the optic chiasma.

Blood supply of optic chiasma:
  • Anterior cerebral artery - dorsal chiasma
  • Anterior communicating artery - ventral chiasma
  • Internal carotid artery - ventral chiasma
  • Superior hypophyseal artery - ventral (branch of internal carotid artery).

question.text: A college student comes to the OPD for refractive error testing. Her eyes are dilated using tropicamide. Which of the following statements is false about the structure this drug acts on?

options.text: It is triangular in cross section.
options.label: A
B
options.text: There are around 30-40 processes in pars plana and pars plicata.
Its epithelium is derived from the anterior edge of the optic cup.
options.label: C

options.text: The pars plana is approximately 4.5 mm from the limbus.
options.label: D

question.explanation:
Tropicamide is a cycloplegic drug that acts on the ciliary body to cause mydriasis for refractory error testing. The ciliary body is a triangular structure that contains 60-70 ciliary processes in each eye, present on the pars plicata.

The pars plana is 4.5 mm from the limbus while the distance between the equator and the limbus is 14mm.

The ciliary epithelium is derived from the optic cup (neuroectoderm) by the continued growth of the outer lip's anterior edge.

question.text: What is the innermost layer of the sclera?
question.explanation:
Lamina fusca is the innermost layer of the sclera.

Lamina fusca faces the choroid. It is the transition zone between the sclera and the choroid. It consists of a delicate meshwork of elastic fibres, fibrocytes and melanocytes, traversed by long posterior ciliary nerves and vessels.

Layers of the sclera from outside to inside include episclera, sclera proper, and lamina fusca, in that order.

question.text: The sclera is the thinnest at which of the following locations?

options.text: Anterior to attachment of the superior rectus
options.label: C
D
options.text: Posterior to attachment of the superior rectus

question.explanation:
The sclera is the thinnest posterior to the insertion of the rectus muscles.

The sclera is 1mm thick posteriorly, with maximum thickness around the optic nerve, 0.66 mm at the insertions of the rectus muscles and 0.33 mm beneath the rectus muscles and thinnest behind their insertions.

question.text: An intern comes across a 7-year-old girl with the following features. All the following are components of her condition except:
question.explanation:
The given scenario of a young girl with facial asymmetry, deviation of angle of the mouth, flat nasal bridge, preauricular tags and limbal dermoid (lenticular yellow tumour at the limbus) of the eye is suggestive of Goldenhar syndrome. Lung hypoplasia is not a component of this syndrome.

Goldenhar syndrome or oculoauriculovertebral spectrum is a congenital developmental anomaly affecting structures derived from the first branchial arch. It has the following features:
  • Systemic:
    • Hypoplasia of the malar, maxillary, and mandibular regions
    • Macrostomia and microtia
    • Preauricular and facial skin tags
    • Hemivertebrae (usually cervical)
    • Mental handicap
    • Cardiac, renal, and central nervous system (CNS) anomalies.
  • Ocular:
    • Dermoid
    • Upper lid notching or coloboma
    • Microphthalmos
    • Disc coloboma

question.text: A patient sustained a severe blow to the right eye from the lateral side during a fistfight. The eyeball is soft to touch and a rupture of the sclera is suspected. What is the least likely site of rupture?
question.explanation:
The lateral limbus is the least likely site to be involved in a traumatic scleral rupture.

Traumatic scleral rupture, or globe rupture, occurs after blunt-force trauma. It usually occurs due to the compression force of the trauma. It therefore likely occurs at the insertion of rectus muscles, at the equator, or in an area parallel to the limbus opposite from the site of the impact.

Rupture at the site of trauma, in this case lateral limbus, is rare.

The major signs of scleral rupture are:
  • conjunctival edema and subconjunctival hemorrhage
  • hyphema
  • ocular hypotony
  • impairment or dislocation of the lens
  • vitreous hemorrhage
  • retinal detachment

question.text: A patient with glaucoma presents with a bulging cornea. What is the most likely diagnosis?
question.explanation:
High intraocular pressure leads to the thinning of the outer tunics of the eyeball such as cornea and sclera, thereby resulting in their ectasia (bulging) which is known as staphyloma. Ciliary and equatorial staphylomas are most commonly associated with glaucoma.

Staphyloma is an abnormal protrusion of the uveal tissue through a weak and thin portion of the cornea or sclera. So, staphyloma is lined internally by uveal tissue and externally by weak cornea or sclera.

Types of Staphyloma:
  • Anterior staphyloma: Due to bulging of the pseudo cornea, internally lined by the iris & externally by the newly formed epithelium. Associated with sloughing corneal ulcer.
  • Intercalary staphyloma: Due to bulging of weakened limbal tissue at the limbus, internally lined by the root of iris & the anterior most part of the ciliary body. Associated with developmental glaucoma, secondary angle closure glaucoma, healing of perforating injury, peripheral corneal ulcer.
  • Ciliary staphyloma: Due to bulging of the weakened sclera, internally lined by the ciliary body, can extend up to 8mm behind the limbus. Associated with scleritis, end stage glaucoma, perforating injuries.
  • Equatorial staphyloma: Due to bulging of sclera with a choroidal lining, seen around 14 mm behind the limbus, in the equatorial region. Associated with scleritis, chronic uncontrolled glaucoma, scleral degeneration in pathological myopia.
  • Posterior staphyloma: Due to bulging of sclera lined by the choroid, seen behind the equator. Associated with posterior scleritis, pathological myopia, perforating injuries.

Keratoconus (Option A) is a progressive bilateral corneal ectatic disorder due to defective synthesis of mucopolysaccharide and collagen tissue. It usually starts at puberty and progresses slowly, not associated with risk factors like glaucoma. Therefore, we can rule out keratoconus in this patient.

question.text: The most common type of scleritis is
question.explanation:
Non-necrotizing anterior scleritis is the most common type of scleritis.

Scleritis can be classified into anterior and posterior scleritis. Anterior scleritis affects the sclera in front of the equator, while posterior scleritis affects the sclera behind the equator of the eye.

Anterior scleritis is further classified into the following types:
  • Non-necrotizing:
    • Diffuse: The most common variety.
    • Nodular: Scleral nodules are present. Annular scleritis is a variant in which the scleral nodules are arranged in a ring around the limbus.
  • Necrotizing:
    • With inflammation
    • Without inflammation: Also known as scleromalacia perforans. It is seen in elderly females with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis.

The image below shows anterior nodular scleritis.

question.text: Which of the following statements regarding the clinical sequelae expected in a patient with orbital blowout fracture is false?

options.label: A
options.text: Anesthesia of the cheek is very common.
Emphysema of eyelids is more common with medial wall fracture.
options.label: B
C
options.text: Enophthalmos develops about 10 days after the injury.
Severe ocular damage is seen in most cases.
options.label: D

question.explanation:
Severe ocular damage associated with a "blowout" fracture is rare.

This is because a "blowout fracture" is nature’s way of protecting the globe from injury.

Clinical features of blowout fracture are as follows:
  • Periorbital edema
  • Paresthesia and anesthesia in the distribution of the infraorbital nerve (lower lid, cheek, side of the nose, upper lip, and upper teeth)
  • Emphysema of the eyelids—more frequent with medial wall fractures
  • Proptosis—seen initially due to orbital edema and hemorrhage.
  • After about 10 days, as the edema decreases, the eyeball sinks backward and somewhat inferiorly, resulting in enophthalmos and mechanical ptosis.
  • Double diplopia—diplopia in upward as well as downward gaze

question.text: All of the following are characteristic clinical findings that are associated with a history of blunt trauma to the eye, except:
question.explanation:
Vossius ring, not Soemmering’s, is seen after blunt trauma to the eye.

Soemmering’s ring refers to a thick ring of after cataract, also known as "secondary cataract." It is the opacity that persists or develops after extracapsular lens extraction.

Blunt trauma to the eye produces:
  • Vossius ring - It is a circular ring of brown pigment seen on the anterior capsule. It occurs due to the striking of the contracted pupillary margin against the crystalline lens.
  • Rosette cataract - It is the most typical form of concussion cataract.
  • Commotio retinae (Berlin’s edema) - It manifests as milky white cloudiness involving a considerable area of the posterior pole with a "cherry-red spot" at foveola.

question.text: Which of the following is not included in the WHO definition of health?
question.explanation:
According to the WHO, health is “a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity”.

In recent years, the definition has been modified to also include the ability to lead a “socially and economically productive life.”

question.text: Which of the following is not a socio-economic determinant of health?
question.explanation:
Lifestyle is a behavioural and socio-cultural determinant of health. It is not a socio-economic determinant.

Socio-economic determinants of health are the following:
  • Economic status (per capita GNP)
  • Education
  • Occupation
  • Political system

Lifestyle is simply the way people live. It reflects our social values, attitudes, and activities. It is composed of:
  • Cultural patterns (daily nutrition, superstitions)
  • Behavioral patterns (personal hygiene, sedentary life)
  • Lifelong personal habits (e.g. smoking, alcoholism)

Lifestyle is learned by social interaction with parents, siblings, friends, school, and mass media.

Our political system determines our health. It can help shape community health services with regards to resource allocation, manpower policy, choice of technology, and the degree to which these services are made available & accessible to all segments of the society.

The percentage of GDP spent on health is an indicator of political commitment. WHO recommends at least 5% of GDP to be spent on health care. India spends about 2.1% of its GDP on health (budget 2022-23).

question.text: Which of the following is not a socio-economic indicator of health?
question.explanation:
Annual family income is not a socioeconomic indicator of health.

Socio-economic indicators of health (mnemonic: H — FLAGGED):
  • Housing (number of persons per room)
  • Family size
  • Literacy rate (especially female literacy rate)
  • Availability of per capita calorie
  • GNP per capita
  • Growth rate of population
  • UnEmployment level
  • Dependency ratio

question.text: Which of the following statements is false regarding positive health in today’s world?

options.text: It is dependent on social, economic, and cultural determinants
options.label: A

options.text: It is a mirage because of changing environment
options.label: B
C
options.text: It means that the body and mind are at peace
It includes provision of free health camps by the government
options.label: D

question.explanation:
The provision of free health camps by the government is a concept of state medicine.

Health does not merely mean the absence of disease or provision of diagnostic, curative, and preventive services. It is a state of physical, mental, and social well-being.

The state of positive health is based on the idea of perfect functioning of the body and mind.

According to this concept, health is:
  • Biologically a state in which every cell and organ in the body is functioning at optimum capacity
  • Psychologically a state in which the individual feels a sense of perfect well-being and mastery over his environment
  • Socially a state in which the individual's capacities for participation in the social system are optimal

This concept is too idealistic and can never become a reality. Humans can never be so perfectly adapted to the environment because everything in our life is subject to change.

As the goal of positive health is unattainable, a broader concept of improving the quality of life has emerged. This highlights that positive health depends on medical action and also on economic, cultural, and social factors in the community.

question.text: As per the WHO, which of the following is not included in the standard of living?
question.explanation:
Social security is a component of the level of living as per the United Nations and not standard of living.

According to the WHO, the standard of living includes:
  • Income and occupation
  • Standards of housing, sanitation, and nutrition
  • Level of provision of health, educational, and recreational services

It depends on per capita GNP.

question.text: What are the minimum and maximum values established for the calculation of the life expectancy index in HDI?
question.explanation:
The minimum value established for the calculation of the life expectancy index in HDI is 20 years and the maximum is 85 years.

These minimum and maximum values are used to calculate the dimension indices in HDI and are called goalposts.

Each dimension index is calculated using the formula: Dimension Index = (Actual Value - Minimum Value) / (Maximum Value - Minimum Value).

question.text: Which of the following is not true regarding the education index used for calculating the HDI?

options.label: A
options.text: It includes expected years of schooling
Adult literacy rate is not considered
options.label: C

options.text: Minimum and maximum values are based on global data
options.label: D

question.explanation:
The gross enrollment ratio is no longer used in obtaining the education index in HDI. It was used as an indicator earlier.

The education index is calculated by taking into account the mean years of schooling and expected years of schooling. Maximum and minimum values are based on global data.

Adult literacy rate and gross enrollment ratio were used as indicators before 2009.

question.text: Which of the following is a mortality indicator?
question.explanation:
Life expectancy is a positive mortality indicator.

A set of values that measure the rate of mortality or death is known as mortality indicators.

Disability-adjusted life years (DALY), health adjusted life expectancy (HALE), and Sullivan’s Index are disability rates.

question.text: Which of the following indices measures the deprivation in basic dimensions of the country in human development?
question.explanation:
Human poverty index (HPI) measures deprivation in basic dimensions of human development.

HPI-1 is used for developing countries and HPI-2 is used for developed countries. It is based upon the following indicators:
  • A long and healthy life:
    • HPI-1: Probability at birth of not surviving to age 40
    • HPI-2: Probability at birth of not surviving to age 60
  • Knowledge:
    • HPI-1: Adult illiteracy rate
    • HPI-2: Percentage of adults lacking functional literacy skills
  • A decent standard of living:
    • HPI-1: Percentage of the population not using an improved water source, Percentage of children underweight for age
    • HPI-2: Percentage of people living below the poverty line, Long term unemployment rate

The range of HPI is from 0 to 100. The term HPI has now been replaced with multidimensional poverty index (MPI).

question.text: Which of the following is not included in the Ottawa charter for health promotion?
question.explanation:
Building social security is not included in the Ottawa charter for health promotion.

The first international conference for health promotion was held in Ottawa on 21st Nov 1986. It produced a charter known as the Ottawa charter.

The charter identified five key action areas as given below:
  • Build healthy public policy
  • Create supportive environment for health
  • Strengthen community action for health
  • Develop personal skills
  • Reorient health services

question.text: An epidemiologist is tasked with measuring the overall health status of a community using a morbidity indicator. Which of the following indicators will she not use?

options.label: C
options.text: Number of days of restricted activity

question.explanation:
Number of days of restricted activity is a disability indicator.

Morbidity is defined as public health outcomes focusing on diseases, traumas, or injury. Morbidity indicators can be used to measure the overall health and extent of healthcare utilisation in a given population.

Disability is defined as public health outcomes related to health conditions that include limitations in personal activities and societal participation. There are two types of disability indicators as follows:
  • Event type indicators:
    • Number of days of restricted activity
    • Bed disability days
    • Work loss days (or school loss days) within a specified period
  • Person type indicators:
    • Limitation of mobility: e.g. confined to bed
    • Limitation of activity: e.g. limitation to perform the basic activities of daily living such as eating and going to the toilet

question.text: Which of the following indicators can be used to estimate the number of years a newborn would be expected to live in full health based on the current rates of ill health and mortality?
question.explanation:
HALE (Health Adjusted Life Expectancy) is an indicator that can be used to estimate the number of years a newborn is expected to live in full health based on the current rates of ill health and mortality.

HALE is calculated using the life expectancy at birth with an adjustment for time spent in poor health. It captures both fatal and non-fatal health outcomes of average levels of population health.

It is also sensitive to changes over time or differences between countries in the distribution of health states.

Sullivan's index is also known as disability-free life expectancy (DFLE) or active life expectancy. It is the average number of years an individual is expected to live free of disability if the current patterns of mortality and disability continue to apply. It doesn’t take into account premature death. As HALE includes not just disability but the larger definition of poor health, it is a better option with respect to the question.

question.text: Which of the following is the best indicator of availability, utilization, and effectiveness of health services?
question.explanation:
Infant mortality rate (IMR) is the best indicator of the availability, utilization, and effectiveness of health care. It is a very sensitive indicator.

Infant mortality rate (IMR) = Number of deaths in the first year of life / Number of live births x 1000. It is also one of the best indicators of state failure. It is the most universally accepted health status indicator of the whole population and of the socio-economic status in which they live.

Note: The best indicator of socio-economic development is the under-5 mortality rate.

question.text: What is the analysis of routine measurements aimed at detecting changes in the health status of a population called?
question.explanation:
The analysis of routine measurements aimed at detecting changes in the health status or environment of a population is called monitoring.

Surveillance is the continuous scrutiny of factors that determine the occurrence and distribution of disease and ill health.

Sentinel surveillance is a method of identifying the missing cases and thereby supplementing the notified cases.

Systematic reviews involve a detailed plan with the goal of reducing bias by identifying, appraising, and synthesizing all relevant studies on a particular topic.

question.text: Which of the following is included under primordial prevention of coronary artery disease?
question.explanation:
Adoption of a healthy lifestyle from childhood would fall under the category of primordial prevention of coronary artery disease.

Primordial prevention is preventing the emergence of risk factors among population groups in which these risk factors have not yet appeared. Most adult health problems (obesity, hypertension) have their early origins in childhood. It is in childhood that lifestyles are formed i.e., eating patterns, physical exercise, smoking, etc.

In primordial prevention, efforts are made to discourage children from adopting harmful lifestyles.

These lifestyle changes when made by adults are known as primary prevention.

question.text: What form of prevention is prospective screening?
question.explanation:
Prospective screening is a type of primary prevention.

Prospective screening is done on healthy individuals to screen for disease. It is done prior to the onset of the disease. E.g., screening donated blood for HIV before it is transfused. This type of prevention reduces the incidence of disease.

Note: Prescriptive screening is done for case detection. People are screened for their own benefits. It is an early diagnosis of diseases existing in them. This is a form of secondary prevention. E.g., neonatal screening for hypothyroidism, Pap smear for detection of cervical cancer.

question.text: Which of the following diseases shows the iceberg phenomenon?
question.explanation:
Rubella shows the iceberg phenomenon of disease.

The iceberg phenomenon of diseases is not shown by diseases such as tetanus, rabies, and measles.

Iceberg phenomenon is shown by:
  • Polio
  • Influenza
  • Rubella
  • Mumps
  • Japanese Encephalitis
  • Diphtheria
  • Hepatitis A and B
  • Tuberculosis
  • Diabetes
  • Malnutrition
  • Hypertension
Note: If a disease has more number of subclinical infections, it shows the iceberg phenomenon of disease depicted in the image below.

question.text: What is the term used to describe the interruption in the transmission of a disease?
question.explanation:
Interruption in the transmission of a disease is called elimination. It is a step towards eradication.

Elimination is a reduction in the number of new cases of an infectious disease to zero (or a very low defined target rate) in a defined geographical area as a result of deliberate efforts. Continued measures to prevent re-establishment of transmission are required.

Eradication is a complete and permanent worldwide reduction to zero new cases of an infectious disease through deliberate efforts. No further control measures are required.

Surveillance is the continuous scrutiny of factors that determine the occurrence and distribution of disease and ill health.

Control aims at decreasing the incidence, duration and transmission of the disease. It also aims at decreasing the physical and psychological complications of a disease.

question.text: Among the following, which measurement can be used as a yardstick for the assessment of standards of therapy?
question.explanation:
The survival rate can be used as a yardstick for the assessment of standards of therapy.

It is used as a method of describing prognosis and is widely employed in cancer studies.

The survival rate is given by the following formula:
Survival Rate = (Total number of cases alive at 5 years / Total number of cases diagnosed) x 100

question.text:
Which of the following statements about incidence are true?
1. Incidence is affected by the duration of the disease.
2. Analysis of incidence rates may provide useful insights into the effectiveness of the health services provided.
3. Incidence is the number of new cases occurring in a defined population during a period of time.
4. Prevalence is more than incidence as it is the product of incidence and duration.
5. Incidence is a type of rate and not a proportion.
question.explanation:
• Incidence is not affected by the duration of the disease.
  • Analysis of incidence rates may provide useful insights into the effectiveness of the health services provided.
  • Incidence is the number of new cases occurring in a defined population during a period of time.
  • Prevalence is more than incidence as it is the product of incidence and duration.
  • Incidence is a type of rate and not a proportion.

question.text: An HIV positive patient was suffering from multi-drug resistant tuberculosis. He died of respiratory failure due to lobar pneumonia. Which of the following options is the most appropriate for the line I (a) of the death certificate?
question.explanation:
Lobar pneumonia is appropriate for line I (a) of the death certificate. Line I (a) consists of the immediate cause of death such as the disease/condition. Immediate cause is the immediate/terminal event leading to death.

In this patient:
  • I(a) - Disease directly leading to death: Lobar pneumonia
  • I(b) - Antecedent cause: MDR tuberculosis.
  • II - Other significant conditions: HIV
Respiratory failure is a mode of dying in this patient. It is not the cause of death.

Terminal events like circulatory failure and respiratory failure, are modes of dying. They should not be written as the immediate cause of death in the death certificate because they are just signs of death.

Simply put, respiratory failure is 'how he died' whereas lobar pneumonia is 'why he died'.

Therefore, lobar pneumonia (why he died) is the cause of the death.

question.text: Which of the following is a good indicator of efficacy of health programs?
question.explanation: Incidence is a good indicator of the efficacy of health services and programs.

question.text: In a village having a population of 5000, a diagnostic test for a particular disease showed the following results. What is the prevalence of the disease?
question.explanation: No explanation available

question.text: Case fatality rate is:

options.label: B
options.text: Killing power of a disease in time

options.label: D
options.text: Killing power of a disease with no time interval

question.explanation: Case fatality rate reflects the killing power of a disease with no specific time interval.

question.text: A researcher is planning to study the etiology of certain painful idiopathic peripheral neuropathies. Which of the following study methods shall he choose?
question.explanation: Diseases of unknown etiology or new diseases can be studied with descriptive epidemiology.

question.text: How often did the cyclical trends of measles occur in the pre-vaccination era?
question.explanation: In the pre-vaccination era, the cyclical trends of measles occurred every 2-3 years, while that of rubella occurred every 6-9 years.

question.text: Which of the following cannot be depicted by the image given below?

options.label: B
options.text: Rural - urban distributions of a disease

question.explanation:
The given image is of a spot map. Spot maps are not used to depict rural-urban distributions of a disease. They help to understand the local distributions of a disease.

They are also called shaded maps. This method was used by John Snow to investigate the epidemic of cholera in London in 1854. They depict areas of high or low frequency, the boundaries, and patterns of disease distribution.

question.text: The National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases is planning to study the natural history of COVID-19. Which of the following studies can be used?
question.explanation:
Longitudinal studies are useful to study the natural history of a disease.

It is also used to identify risk factors, and to find the incidence rate. In longitudinal studies, observations are repeated in the same population over a prolonged period of time by follow-up examinations. Their disadvantage is that they are difficult to organize and take a very long time.

question.text: An outbreak of viral hepatitis A was reported from a town between June and September of a particular year. The peak of the outbreak occurred in July. What is this an example of?
question.explanation:
This outbreak of viral hepatitis A is an example of a common source, multiple exposure type of epidemic.

The incubation period of hepatitis A is approximately 28 days (range 15 to 50 days). In this scenario, the cases of viral hepatitis A have occurred over a period from June to September (120 days) which is more than one incubation period of the disease. This is suggestive of multiple exposures from a common source.

If the period of the outbreak falls within one incubation period, then the type of epidemic is common source, single exposure or point source epidemic.

Propagated epidemic results from person to person transmission of the infectious agent over a prolonged duration of time. For example, Polio epidemic, COVID-19.

Note: Hepatitis A epidemic is generally an example of a propagated epidemic. However, it does not always follow this pattern. In the given scenario, since the outbreak lasts for a short duration of 3 months (about 3 incubation periods for hepatitis A), it is considered to be a point source, multiple exposure outbreak.

Difference between single exposure and multiple exposure epidemics:
  • Single, brief exposure:
    • Nature of epidemic: Explosive with clustering of cases within a short interval of time.
    • Duration of epidemic: Falls <1 incubation period of a particular disease.
    • Example: An epidemic of food poisoning.
  • Multiple, continuous or intermittent exposures for a prolonged time:
    • Nature of epidemic: Less chance of clustering of cases within short interval of time.
    • Duration of epidemic: Extends >1 incubation period of a particular disease.
    • Example: Outbreak of cholera.

question.text: A researcher is planning to conduct a study to investigate the relationship between oral contraceptives and breast cancer. He wants to remove age as a confounding factor. Which of the following methods will not help him reduce this bias?
question.explanation:
Deletion is not a method to reduce confounding.

Methods to reduce confounding are:
At the time of designing the study:
  • Randomization
  • Matching
  • Restriction
At the time of analysis:
  • Stratification
  • Statistical modelings like regression analysis, multivariate analysis, and the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel method.

question.text: An epidemiologist determines to evaluate the strength of association between asbestos exposure and mesothelioma in a case-control study. Which of the following variables would he use for it?
question.explanation:
Odds ratio (OR), also known as cross-product ratio, is used to measure the strength of association between risk factor (asbestos exposure) and outcome (mesothelioma) in case-control studies.

A case-control study yields only odds ratio and not incidence or relative risk.

question.text: While testing the deleterious health hazards on a group of people after giving a new drug and placebo, the following results were obtained as tabulated. Based on these results, which of the following is true?

options.label: A
options.text: Absolute risk reduction (ARR) is 1% and relative risk reduction (RRR) is 0.1

options.label: B
options.text: Absolute risk reduction (ARR) is 10% and relative risk reduction (RRR) is 0.9
Absolute risk reduction (ARR) is 1% and relative risk reduction (RRR) is 10
options.label: C

options.text: Absolute risk reduction (ARR) is 10% and relative risk reduction (RRR) is 9
options.label: D

question.explanation:
In the given scenario, absolute risk reduction (ARR) is 1% and relative risk reduction (RRR) is 0.1.

Let us reconstruct the design table in the following way:
GroupEventNo EventTotal
New Drug1603 (a)13622 (b)15225 (a+b)
Placebo1804 (c)13421 (d)15225 (c+d)

Incidence of a disease is the absolute risk of contracting it.
Absolute risk rate of the group using new drug = a / (a+b) = 1603 / 15225 = 0.1053 or 10.53%.
Absolute risk rate of the group using placebo = c / (c+d) = 1804 / 15225 = 0.1185 or 11.85%.

Absolute risk reduction (ARR) is the difference in the absolute risk rates between the placebo and the drug. In this scenario, ARR = 11.85% - 10.53% = 1.32% ≈ 1%.

Relative risk (RR) = Incidence (New Drug) / Incidence (Placebo) = 0.1053 / 0.1185 = 0.8886 ≈ 0.90.
Relative risk reduction (RRR) = 1 - Relative risk. In this scenario, RRR = 1 - 0.90 = 0.10 or 10%.

question.text: A study found that the incidence of bladder carcinoma is 5 times higher in smokers than in non-smokers. Calculate the attributable risk.
question.explanation:
In the given scenario, the attributable risk (AR) is 80%.

Formula for Attributable Risk (AR):
AR = [(Incidence of disease rate among exposed - Incidence of disease rate among non-exposed) / Incidence of disease rate among exposed] * 100

Taking the incidence of disease in non-exposed as x, the incidence of disease in exposed would be 5x.

Attributable risk (AR) would be given as [(5x - x) / 5x] * 100 = [4x / 5x] * 100 = (4/5) * 100 = 80%.

question.text: In a population of 9000 people, 2100 are alcoholics. 70 alcoholics and 23 non-alcoholics developed cirrhosis. What is the attributable risk?
question.explanation:
In the given scenario, the attributable risk (AR) is 90%.

Number of people exposed (to alcohol) = 2100
Number of people not exposed (to alcohol) = 9000 - 2100 = 6900

Incidence of cirrhosis among exposed (IExposed) = 70 / 2100 = 1/30
Incidence of cirrhosis among non-exposed (INon-exposed) = 23 / 6900 = 1/300

Attributable risk (AR) = [ (IExposed - INon-exposed) / IExposed ] * 100
= [ (1/30 - 1/300) / (1/30) ] * 100
= [ (10/300 - 1/300) / (1/30) ] * 100
= [ (9/300) / (1/30) ] * 100
= [ (9/300) * (30/1) ] * 100
= [ 270 / 300 ] * 100
= [ 9 / 10 ] * 100 = 90%

Thus, the attributable risk (AR) is 90%.

question.text: A case-control study was conducted to see if symptoms of upper gastrointestinal dysfunction occurred more frequently in patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Which of the following cannot be used as controls in this study?
question.explanation:
Siblings cannot be used as controls while studying genetic conditions because the outcome would be distorted due to their similarities.

Controls in a case-control study:
  • Usually disease-free
  • Can be up to 4 times the number of cases in small studies
  • In large studies, a 1:1 ratio of cases and controls can be sought
  • Sources: general population, hospitals, relatives (spouses and siblings), neighbors, or colleagues
  • Although, siblings cannot be used as controls for studies on genetic conditions

question.text: Which of the following is not true about random errors?

options.label: D
options.text: Systematic errors are different from random errors

question.explanation:
Random errors are not causes of bias.

Random error arises when a value of the sample measurement diverges, due to chance alone, from that of the true population value. They can never be completely eliminated.

Sources of random errors are individual biological variations, sampling errors, and measurement errors.

Systematic errors are also called biases. They are different from random errors.

question.text: Which of the following study designs is the best to prove causation?
question.explanation:
Randomized controlled trials (RCT) are the strongest and best study design to prove causation. They are the gold standard of clinical research.

Case-control and cohort studies have a moderate ability to provide evidence for causality. Ecological studies or correlational studies are considered as the weakest study design in this aspect.

The difference between analytical studies and randomised controlled trials is that in the former there is no randomisation because it requires the participants to be divided into diseased and non-diseased. This can lead to a number of biases that are avoided in RCTs.

question.text: What does evidence-based medicine refer to?

options.label: A
options.text: Use of experiments to prove the cause of a disease
Use of clinical trials to prove safety of drugs
options.label: B

options.text: Use of research findings for taking decisions about patient care
options.label: C
D
options.text: Use of behavioral modification to prevent disease

question.explanation:
Evidence-based medicine (EBM) refers to the use of modern research findings to guide decision-making about the treatment of individual patients.

EBM integrates clinical experience and patient values with the best available research information. Research and studies are given high importance in EBM, while opinions and conventional wisdom of experts are not taken into consideration in the practice of EBM.

question.text: In the hierarchy of evidence, which of the following rankings is correct?
question.explanation:
The correct order of ranking of the hierarchy of evidence is:

Meta-analysis and systemic review > Randomised control trial > Cohort study > Case-control study > Case reports.

question.text: Which of the following is not an example of a randomised controlled trial?
question.explanation:
Before and after comparison studies are a type of non-randomized trials.

These are community trials and centre around comparing the incidence of disease before and after the introduction of a preventive measure. They are of two distinct types:
  • Before and after comparison studies without control.
  • Before and after comparison studies with control.
Non-randomized trials include:
  • Before and after comparison studies.
  • Uncontrolled trials.
  • Natural experiments.

question.text: In a community, there are usually 40-50 reported cases of dengue every week. This week, there were 48 reported cases. This would classify as:
question.explanation:
The given scenario is an example of an endemic disease.

Endemic diseases are those that have a constant presence and/or usual prevalence of a disease or infectious agent in a population within a geographic area.

Epidemic refers to an increase, often sudden, in the number of cases of a disease above what is normally expected in that population in that area.

Outbreak carries the same definition of an epidemic, but is often used for a more limited geographic area.

Sporadic diseases occur in a haphazard and irregular manner from time to time.
