question.text: In which of the following states will the host not shed the infectious organism?
question.explanation:
The host does not shed the infectious organism in case of a latent infection. This is defined as a state in which the host does not show signs and symptoms of the disease and does not shed the organism.

It can be seen in conditions like herpes simplex, ancylostomiasis, infections due to slow viruses, Brill-Zinsser disease, etc.

Subclinical infection is a state where the host harbours the infectious agent without developing signs and symptoms but sheds the infectious agent. This state is seen in conditions like hepatitis A, rubella, mumps, etc.

Healthy carriers are those who had subclinical infections and later developed a carrier state without suffering from the overt disease. This state is seen in: (mnemonic: CM - DPT)
  • Cholera
  • Meningitis
  • Diphtheria
  • Polio
  • Typhoid
Convalescent carriers are those which shed the infectious agent during the convalescent phase/recovery phase. Such carriers are seen in diphtheria, typhoid, cholera, pertussis, etc.

question.text: Which of the following is not communicable during the later part of the period marked '3' in the image provided?
question.explanation:
The period marked 3 in the figure is the incubation period while the later part of the period represents subclinical infection. Rabies is not communicable during its incubation period as it is transmitted from the saliva of a rabid animal through bite or scratch.

An incubatory carrier state is one in which carriers shed the organism during the incubation period of the disease, especially during the later parts of it.

Examples of diseases showing incubatory carrier state are:
  • Measles
  • Polio
  • Mumps
  • Whooping cough
  • Diphtheria
  • Influenza
  • Hepatitis A
Carriers of a disease are classified by the following:
  • Type: Incubatory, convalescent or healthy.
  • Duration: Temporary or chronic.
  • Portal of exit: Urinary, respiratory, intestinal or others.

question.text: A patient with chronic lymphedema was found to have a positive DEC provocation test. Which type of biological transmission does the pathogen implicated here undergo?
question.explanation:
In the given scenario, the patient most likely has lymphatic filariasis. The causative organism of this disease (Wuchereria bancrofti) undergoes cyclo-developmental transmission.

Cyclo-developmental transmission is a transmission where the agent undergoes only developmental changes and not multiplication within the vector.

DEC provocation test: In this test, a small dose of DEC is given 20-50 minutes before sample collection so that the microfilaria appears in the blood even during the daytime.

question.text: You are a rural medical health officer investigating an epidemic. What is the correct sequence of steps you must follow?
question.explanation:
Steps for the investigation of an epidemic are:
  • Verification of diagnosis
  • Confirmation of the existence of an epidemic
  • Defining the population at risk
  • Obtaining a map of the area
  • Counting the population
  • Rapid search for all the cases
  • Medical survey
  • Epidemiological case sheets
  • Searching for more cases
  • Data analysis on the basis of time, place and person
  • Formulation of hypothesis
  • Testing of hypothesis
  • Evaluation of ecological factors
  • Further investigation of the population at risk
  • Writing the report

question.text: You have been asked to write the final report following the investigation of a cholera epidemic. Which of the following will you not include in this report?

options.label: B
options.text: Usual number of cases that existed before the epidemic

question.explanation:
The final report of an epidemic does not include the incubation period of the disease.

The final report following the investigation of an epidemic should include:
  • Background information - Geography, climate, demography, socio-economic groups, health service organization, surveillance data and normal disease prevalence.
  • Historical data - Previous occurrences of the epidemic, the occurrence of any related diseases and discovery of the primary case in the present outbreak.
  • Methodology of investigations - Case definition, epidemiological questionnaires, collection and laboratory techniques.
  • Analysis of data - Clinical and epidemiological data, modes of transmission, laboratory data and all their interpretations.
  • Control measures - Strategy definitions, methodology of implementation, evaluation methods and preventive measures.

question.text: You have been sent to an area to study the ongoing typhoid epidemic. When will you declare the area to be free of the epidemic?
question.explanation:
The area will be declared free of the typhoid epidemic when no new cases are reported for 28 days.

An area is declared free of an epidemic when there are no cases reported for twice the incubation period of the disease since the last case.

The incubation period of typhoid is 14 days. So, in the given scenario, the area will be declared free of the epidemic when no new cases are reported for twice the incubation period i.e., 14 x 2 = 28 days.

question.text: The probability that infection will occur among susceptible persons following contact with an infectious person within the incubation period is known as the secondary attack rate.
question.explanation:
The probability that infection will occur among susceptible persons following contact with an infectious person within the incubation period is called secondary attack rate.

It is calculated by the following formula:
Secondary attack rate (SAR) = (Number of exposed or susceptible persons developing the disease within the incubation period x 100)/(Total number of close or exposed contacts that are susceptible)

Primary cases are usually excluded from the numerator and denominator.

Secondary attack rate measures the communicability of the disease.

question.text: Following an outbreak of a disease, you are asked to calculate the secondary attack rate (SAR). What is the denominator you would use?

options.label: A
options.text: All people having history of contact with a case
All people susceptible in the entire area
options.label: B
C
options.text: All the people in contact with the primary case

options.label: D
options.text: All the close or exposed contacts those are susceptible

question.explanation:
The denominator used for calculating SAR is all the close or exposed contacts that are susceptible.

The secondary attack rate is defined as the probability that infection will occur among susceptible persons following contact with an infectious person within the incubation period.

It is calculated by the formula:
Secondary attack rate (SAR) = (Number of exposed or susceptible persons developing the disease within the incubation period x 100)/(Total number of close or exposed contacts that are susceptible)

Primary cases are usually excluded from the numerator and denominator.

Secondary attack rate measures the communicability of the disease.

question.text: A village has 100 children under the age of 5. The coverage of measles vaccination is 60%. Following a case of measles, 26 children developed measles. What is the secondary attack rate?
question.explanation:
The secondary attack rate for the given scenario is 66%.

The secondary attack rate (SAR) is given by:
(Number of exposed or susceptible persons developing the disease within the incubation period x 100)/(Total number of close or exposed contacts that are susceptible)

Here, number who developed the disease after exposure = 26
Susceptible population = 100 - 60 (vaccinated) - 1 (primary case) = 39
Therefore, SAR = 26 / 39 x 100 = 66%.

SAR is a measure of communicability.

question.text: Which of the following pairs of diseases and their periods of isolation is wrongly matched?

options.text: Rubella — 3 days after onset of rash
options.label: A

options.text: Chickenpox — 6 days after onset of rash
options.label: B
C
options.text: Herpes zoster — 6 days after onset of rash

options.label: D
options.text: Measles — Up to 5 days after onset of rash

question.explanation:
Patients with rubella should be isolated for 7 days after they develop the rash.

Isolation is defined as separation, for the period of communicability of infected persons from others to prevent or limit transmission of the infectious agent.

In settings where women who are in their 1st trimester or sexually active or non-immune without contraception usage may be exposed, outbreak control measures should begin as soon as rubella is suspected and should not be postponed until laboratory confirmation of cases.

Note: Multiple sources have confirmed the period of infectivity of measles which is from 4 days before the onset of rash to 5 days after the onset of rash.

question.text: Which of the following diseases does not show vertical transmission?
question.explanation:
Tetanus does not show vertical or transplacental transmission.

Transmission of diseases or non-infectious agents transplacentally is called vertical transmission.

Diseases that show this type of transmission include:
  • Herpes
  • HIV
  • Rubella
  • Varicella
Apart from diseases, non-infectious agents like lithium, thalidomide, stilbestrol, etc. can cross the placenta and lead to the development of congenital anomalies in a foetus.

Note: Neonatal tetanus occurs as a result of the failure to use aseptic techniques in managing the umbilical stump, unclean hands, and instruments or contamination by dirt, straw, or other nonsterile materials in the delivery field. Immunisation of pregnant women can prevent this disease via the transplacental transport of immunoglobulins.

question.text: Which among the following is false about droplet transmission?

options.text: All droplets can travel only as far as 3 feet
options.label: A

options.text: Droplets are usually larger than 5 microns
options.label: B
C
options.text: It is a type of direct transmission

options.label: D
options.text: Basic ventilation decreases the potential for this type of transmission

question.explanation:
Droplet nuclei can travel as far as 6 feet, whereas a droplet (particle > 5um) travels < 30-60cm, as recent studies have shown.

Droplets are a mode of direct transmission of infectious agents. They are formed from saliva and nasopharyngeal secretions released during coughing, sneezing, or speaking into the surrounding atmosphere. The expelled droplets may impinge directly upon the conjunctiva, oro-respiratory mucosa or skin of close contact. This mode of transmission is seen in common cold, diphtheria, etc.

Proper basic ventilation and prevention of overcrowding reduce the potential for this type of transmission.

question.text: Which of the following is not a method of direct transmission of communicable diseases?
question.explanation:
Airborne transmission by droplet nuclei is not a method of direct transmission of diseases.

It is a method of indirect transmission of diseases.

Droplet nuclei are tiny particles of size 1-5 microns range that may be formed either due to evaporation of droplets coughed or sneezed into the air or are formed from aerosols.

These droplet nuclei remain airborne for long periods of time and can transmit diseases like tuberculosis, influenza, chickenpox, measles, Q fever and other respiratory infections.

Droplet transmission, vertical transmission, and contact with soil are methods of direct transmission of diseases.

Differences between droplet and droplet nuclei are summarised below:
  • Droplet nuclei: It is the residue from evaporated droplets. No need for close contact for transmission. Diseases transmitted: chickenpox, measles etc.
  • Droplet: It is produced while coughing, sneezing, talking. Requires closeness and direct contact for transmission. Diseases transmitted: diphtheria, meningococcal meningitis etc.

question.text: An entomologist was studying a vector and the pathogen it transmits. He found that the pathogen underwent changes in number and morphology in the vector. What is this type of biological transmission called?
question.explanation:
This type of biological transmission where a pathogen undergoes a change in number and morphology in a vector is called cyclo-propagative transmission.

Malaria is a disease whose causative organism (Plasmodium sp.) undergoes cyclo-propagative transmission. In malaria, the parasite undergoes both developmental changes and multiplication in the Anopheles mosquito (vector).

question.text: Which of the following is false about herd immunity?

options.label: A
options.text: It refers to group protection beyond what is afforded by the protection of immunized individuals
Vaccination allows the possibility of 100% herd immunity against a disease
options.label: B

options.text: It is affected by presence and distribution of alternative animal hosts
options.label: C
D
options.text: It doesn’t protect the individual in the case of tetanus

question.explanation:
It is not possible to achieve 100% herd immunity against a certain disease but studies have shown this is not necessary for disease control.

Herd structure is never constant. It is subject to constant variation because of new births, deaths and population mobility. An ongoing immunization programme will keep up the herd immunity at a very high level.

question.text: Herd immunity threshold does not vary with which of the following?

options.label: B
options.text: Efficacy of the vaccine for the disease

options.label: C
options.text: Number of vaccines for the disease

question.explanation:
Herd immunity threshold does not vary with the number of vaccines for the disease. It varies only due to the following factors:
  • Virulence of the disease
  • Efficacy of the vaccine
  • Contact parameter for the population

question.text: What is the main drawback of polysaccharide-based vaccines?

options.label: A
options.text: They cause severe pain at the injection site

options.label: B
options.text: The immune responses elicited are serotype specific
It cannot be conjugated with proteins to enhance immunogenicity
options.label: C

options.text: The rate of adverse reactions is very high
options.label: D

question.explanation:
Polysaccharide-based vaccines stimulate an antibody response against the surface polysaccharide of the pathogenic-capsulated bacteria. The polysaccharide structure varies not only between bacteria of different species but also between different strains within a single species. Thus, a limitation of these vaccines is that the immune responses are serotype-specific.

If these vaccines are conjugated with proteins, they are given the capability of eliciting a stronger immune response. Multivalent formulations of both polysaccharide-based vaccines and conjugated vaccines are required to achieve protection against multiple serotypes.

question.text: Which of the following is a subunit vaccine?
question.explanation:
Hepatitis B vaccine is an example of a subunit vaccine made using HBsAg.

Subunit vaccines are produced from macromolecules derived from immunogenic components of organisms by recombinant DNA technology. For example, HPV vaccine (uses Li major capsid protein) and hepatitis B vaccine (uses HBsAg).

BCG is a live attenuated vaccine, IPV is an inactivated vaccine and DPT has diphtheria and tetanus toxoids and a killed pertussis component.

question.text: Which of the following side effects is most likely to develop in a newborn, following BCG vaccination?
question.explanation:
Ulceration is the most common side effect post BCG vaccination.

Following vaccination, the local tissue response begins in 2-3 weeks and results in scar formation and healing within 3 months. Side effects most commonly seen include ulceration at the vaccination site and regional lymphadenitis. Some vaccine strains may also rarely cause osteomyelitis.

In immunocompromised states, disseminated BCG infection can occur.

The image below shows the typical adverse effects seen following BCG vaccination:
  • Regional lymphadenopathy
  • Suppurative lymphadenopathy with fistula
  • Ulcer at injection site
  • Cold abscess at inject site

question.text: A complete blood count was obtained for a patient after they were administered vaccine X. Which of the following options is most likely to be vaccine X?
question.explanation: The lab report shows a low platelet count or thrombocytopenia. This is a possible adverse effect of the MMR vaccine.

question.text: Which of the following is false about normal human immunoglobulin (NHIG)?

options.text: All live vaccines can be given simultaneously with NHIG.
options.label: A
B
options.text: They are used against measles and hepatitis A.

options.label: C
options.text: There should be a low IgA concentration in NHIG preparations.

options.label: D
options.text: Each NHIG fraction is obtained from at least 1,000 donors.

question.explanation:
Live vaccines should generally be avoided for 12 weeks following an injection of normal human immunoglobulin (Ig). If a live vaccine has already been administered, the injection of normal human Ig should be delayed for 2 weeks.

NHIG is an antibody-rich fraction that is usually obtained from a pool of at least 1,000 donors.

An NHIG preparation must contain at least 90% intact IgG and minimal IgG aggregates with low IgA concentration. NHIG is commonly used to prevent measles and hepatitis A infections.

Specific human immunoglobulins are made from the plasma of patients who have recently recovered from an infection or are obtained from individuals who have been immunized against a specific infection. These preparations have a high antibody content against an individual infection and provide immediate protection.

question.text: A patient presents with complaints of severe aching pain and weakness in his left arm and shoulder. He mentions he had recently been administered a vaccine in his left arm, but he does not remember the name of the vaccine. Which of the following could be the most common cause of his symptoms?
question.explanation:
The given scenario is suggestive of brachial neuritis which is a known complication of the tetanus vaccine.

Brachial neuritis is a dysfunction of nerves supplying the arm and shoulder without the involvement of the rest of the nervous system. It presents with a deep, steady, severe aching pain in the shoulder and arm followed by weakness and wasting in arm and shoulder muscles. Sensory loss may also be present. It is treated symptomatically by analgesics.

question.text: A child has come to you for the administration of the IPV vaccine, as part of his routine immunisation schedule. Which of the following antibiotics may be found in this vaccine?
question.explanation:
IPV may contain trace amounts of streptomycin, neomycin or polymyxin B.



MMR contains small amounts of neomycin.



Antibiotics are used during vaccine manufacture to prevent bacterial contamination of tissue culture cells.

question.text: Which of the following are the most and least heat-sensitive vaccines respectively?

options.text: Sabin vaccine and hep B vaccine
options.label: A
C
options.text: Japanese encephalitis vaccine and pneumococcal vaccine
Salk vaccine and hep B vaccine
options.label: D

question.explanation: Oral polio (Sabin) vaccine is the most heat-sensitive vaccine. Hepatitis B vaccines are the least heat-sensitive alongside meningococcal A vaccine, freeze-dried Hib vaccine and pneumococcal vaccines.

question.text: What is the temperature maintained in the freezer compartment of the solar refrigerator battery drive?
question.explanation:
The freezer compartment of the solar refrigerator battery drive is maintained at -7 °C, and it is used to store mainly ice packs.



The vaccine storage compartment of this solar cold chain equipment is maintained at 2 to 8 °C. The other solar cold-chain equipment commonly used is the solar refrigerators direct drive, which uses the sun’s energy to freeze phase-change materials like water and then uses this formed ice bank to keep the refrigerator cold.

question.text: A 50-year-old man developed myocardial infarction 3 days ago and now presents with jaundice. Laboratory findings are suggestive of acute hepatocellular injury due to ischemia. Which region of the hepatic lobule is most likely affected in this condition?
question.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of acute hepatocellular injury due to ischemia. Zone 3 (centrilobular zone) of the liver is most susceptible for ischemia because this zone is the farthest from the blood supply.

On the basis of blood flow, liver parenchyma can be divided into three zones. Zone 1 is closest to the blood supply and zone 3 is the farthest. They are:
  • Zone 1 - Periportal (around portal triad)
  • Zone 2 - Midzonal parenchyma
  • Zone 3 - Centrilobular (around hepatic vein)
A schematic diagram showing the hepatic lobule indicating the direction of blood flow and the zones of decreasing oxygenation is given below.

Note: Zone most susceptible to toxin damage is zone 1.

question.text: Patients with which of the following conditions are least likely to develop centrilobular necrosis of liver?
question.explanation:
Centrilobular necrosis is not seen in yellow fever. In yellow fever, swelling and necrosis of hepatocytes are seen in the midzone of the liver lobule.

Conditions causing tissue injury in the different zones of liver:
  • Centrilobular (Zone 3)
    • Chronic venous congestion (cardiac failure)
    • Acetaminophen toxicity
    • Budd Chiari syndrome
    • Ischemia
    • Alcoholic hepatitis
  • Midzonal (Zone 2)
    • Yellow fever
  • Periportal (Zone 1)
    • Viral hepatitis
A schematic diagram showing the hepatic lobule indicating the direction of blood flow and the zones of decreasing oxygenation is given below.

question.text: In patients with non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, which of the following features is not seen on liver biopsy?
question.explanation:
The presence of lymphoid follicles is not a feature on liver biopsy in patients with non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH). It is a feature of chronic hepatitis C infection.

The histopathological features of NASH include:
  • Ballooning degeneration of hepatocytes
  • Steatosis
  • Perisinusoidal inflammation and fibrosis
  • Portal fibrosis
  • Mallory-Denk bodies
  • Mononuclear infiltrate
NASH and alcoholic liver disease (ALD) have almost similar histopathological features. They can be differentiated as follows:
  • Mallory-Denk bodies: More prominent in ALD, Less prominent in NASH
  • Fibrosis: Perivenular and perisinusoidal > portal in ALD, Portal fibrosis is more prominent in NASH
  • Inflammatory cells: Neutrophils > macrophages in ALD, Macrophages > neutrophils in NASH

question.text: A patient with a history of unprotected sexual intercourse turns out to be HBsAg positive. Which of the following is the best predictor for development of chronic disease?
question.explanation:
The age at the time of infection is the best predictor of chronicity. Younger the age at the time of hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, higher the probability of chronicity.

Other predictors in the development of chronic disease:
  • Comorbid conditions (including exposure to other infectious agents)
  • Host immunity
Presentations of hepatitis B infection:
  • Asymptomatic - 65%
  • Non-specific symptoms - 25%
  • Chronic disease - 5-10%
  • Acute fulminant liver disease - 0.1-0.5%

question.text: An IV drug abuser has been found to be seropositive for HBsAg, HBeAg, and anti-HBc IgM. Which of the following is least likely to be seen in the liver biopsy of such patients?
question.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of acute hepatitis B infection. Ground-glass hepatocytes are not seen in the liver biopsy of such patients.

Histopathological findings in acute hepatitis are:
  • Ballooning degeneration - due to inflammation
  • Portal or lobular inflammatory infiltration - lymphocytes, plasma cells, and eosinophils
  • Necrosis
    • Confluent necrosis - group of hepatocytes
    • Panlobular or panacinar necrosis - entire lobule
    • Bridging necrosis (in severe cases) - connecting vascular structures
Ground-glass appearance of hepatocytes is due to the endoplasmic reticulum which is swollen with HBsAg accumulation. It is a diagnostic hallmark of chronic hepatitis B infection.

The image given below shows ground glass hepatocytes in the liver biopsy.

question.text: A man with a history of intranasal cocaine abuse is at most risk for which of the following infections?
question.explanation:
Intranasal cocaine abuse is a risk factor for hepatitis C.

Contaminated implements (like straws used to inhale cocaine) inserted into the nasal cavity might come into contact with hepatitis C virus (HCV)-infected mucus or blood. This might then be transmitted to a susceptible individual while sharing the same implements.

Transmission of hepatitis C infection:
  • Intravenous drug abuse (54%) - Most common
  • Multiple sex partners
  • Needle-stick injury
  • Multiple contacts with a person with hepatitis C virus infection
  • Employment in medical or dental fields
  • Blood transfusion
  • Perinatal - major route of infection in children

question.text: In patients with liver failure, which of the following tests is not used to evaluate the synthetic function of hepatocytes?
question.explanation:
Serum alkaline phosphatase is used to evaluate biliary excretory function. It is not used to evaluate the synthetic function of hepatocytes.

Serum ammonia, activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), and serum albumin are used to evaluate hepatic synthetic function.

Prothrombin time (PT), aPTT and serum ammonia levels are increased in liver failure, whereas serum albumin level is decreased.

question.text: Which of the following is not seen in the histopathological examination of the liver in patients with malaria?
question.explanation:
Macronodular cirrhosis is not seen in the histopathological examination of patients with malaria.

Histopathological changes in the liver in cases of malaria include the following:
  • Kupffer cell hyperplasia
  • Hemozoin pigment deposition within Kupffer cells and macrophages
  • Focal necrosis
  • Mild mononuclear portal infiltrate
  • Fatty change and periportal inflammation

question.text: Identify the incorrect match.
question.explanation:
Councilman bodies are apoptotic hepatocytes seen in acute hepatitis and yellow fever.

Option A: Mallory–Denk bodies are eosinophilic materials made of keratin intermediate filaments. They are seen in alcoholic liver disease, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, Wilson's disease, and chronic biliary tract diseases.

Option C: Ground-glass hepatocytes are liver cells that have eosinophilic granular, glassy cytoplasm seen on light microscopy. The appearance is due to the swelling of the endoplasmic reticulum by HBsAg and is a diagnostic hallmark of chronic hepatitis B.

Option D: Circumferential onion skin fibrosis around a degenerating bile-duct lumen is seen in primary sclerosing cholangitis.

question.text: A patient with ascites, melena, and splenomegaly is diagnosed with portal hypertension. Which of the following is not an intrahepatic cause of this condition?
question.explanation:
Obstructive portal vein thrombosis is the prehepatic cause of portal hypertension.

Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, cirrhosis, and schistosomiasis are intrahepatic causes of portal hypertension. The most dominant cause is cirrhosis.

question.text: Which of the following is not a feature of liver histology in patients with non-cirrhotic portal fibrosis?

options.text: Thrombosis of the medium and small portal vein branches
options.label: B

question.explanation:
Bridging fibrosis is not seen in non-cirrhotic portal fibrosis. In this condition, there is periportal and perisinusoidal fibrosis. The fibrous septa end blindly in the lobule and do not bridge with other portal tracts, unlike those seen in cirrhosis.

Idiopathic non-cirrhotic portal hypertension (INCPH) is a rare disease characterized by intrahepatic portal hypertension in the absence of cirrhosis or other causes of liver disease and splanchnic venous thrombosis.

A liver biopsy is essential in making a diagnosis of INCPH. The features observed are as follows:
  • Luminal narrowing or obliteration of portal vein branches
  • Micronodular transformation
  • Sinusoidal dilatation with formation of mega sinusoids
  • Periportal and perisinusoidal fibrosis

question.text: Match the histopathological sections of liver with the correct conditions:
question.explanation:
In the given image, images marked 1 is normal liver, 2 is alcoholic steatosis, 3 is micronodular cirrhosis and 4 is alcoholic hepatitis.

Histopathological findings in the following conditions are:
  • Alcoholic steatosis:
    • A mix of small and large fat droplets
    • Ethanol inhibits fatty acid metabolism, leading to lipolysis and increased triglyceride. These triglycerides accumulate and cause steatosis. Liver enzymes are normal at this stage.
  • Micronodular cirrhosis:
    • The average nodule size is 3 mm in this close-up view, which is typical of the micronodular cirrhosis of alcoholic liver disease
  • Alcoholic hepatitis:
    • Mallory-Denk bodies - clumped, amorphous, eosinophilic material in ballooned hepatocytes.
    • These inclusions are characteristic, but not a specific feature of alcoholic liver disease.

question.text: Histopathological examination of liver biopsy reveals steatosis. Which of the following conditions is least likely to cause this change?
question.explanation:
Steatosis or fatty change of liver is not seen in hepatitis B infections.

Steatosis is the abnormal accumulation of triglycerides within a cell due to impaired lipid metabolism. In the liver, pathological steatosis is defined as fatty change involving > 5% of hepatocytes. In the histologic sections, they appear as empty vacuoles within the hepatocyte cytoplasm.

Hepatitis C genotype 3 is reported to cause periportal steatosis. It is due to its association with metabolic syndrome and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD).

In Wilson's disease, there is focal hepatocyte necrosis and steatosis due to toxic injury by the excess copper.

In protein malnutrition, fatty liver results from the reduced synthesis of the carrier protein component of lipoproteins.

question.text:
Match the following drugs with their characteristic liver histopathological findings:

Drugs:
1. Valproate
2. Allopurinol
3. Amiodarone
4. Isoniazid

Findings:
A. Fibrin ring granuloma
B. Microvesicular steatosis
C. Noncaseating epitheloid granulomas
D. Mallory-Denk bodies
question.explanation:
• Valproate: Microvesicular steatosis
  • Allopurinol: Fibrin ring granuloma
  • Amiodarone: Mallory-Denk bodies
  • Isoniazid: Noncaseating epitheloid granulomas

question.text: Histopathological examination of liver biopsy in a patient with jaundice shows the following finding. Which of the following conditions is least likely in this patient?
question.explanation:
The marked structure in the image is Mallory hyaline body which is not seen in primary sclerosing cholangitis. In this condition, onion skin fibrosis is seen.

Mallory hyaline bodies (Mallory–Denk bodies) are usually present as clumped, amorphous, eosinophilic material in ballooned hepatocytes. They are made up of cytokeratin 8 and cytokeratin 18. They have a twisted rope-like appearance. On trichrome stain, they appear green/dark brown. They are seen in:
  • Alcoholic liver disease
  • Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease
  • Wilson's disease
  • Hepatocellular carcinoma
  • Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
  • Primary biliary cholangitis (formerly called primary biliary cirrhosis)
  • Indian childhood cirrhosis
The image given below shows Mallory hyaline bodies.

question.text: Which of the following histopathological findings will be seen in patients with chronic alcoholism?
question.explanation:
Chicken-wire fence pattern of fibrosis is seen in the liver biopsy of patients with alcoholic steatohepatitis. This pattern is due to perisinusoidal fibrosis encircling small clusters of hepatocytes.

Trichrome staining of liver biopsy specimen showing perisinusoidal fibrosis (stained blue) in characteristic chicken-wire fence pattern is given below.

Note: Other conditions with chicken-wire pattern in histopathology:
  • Chicken wire calcification - chondroblastoma
  • Chicken wire vasculature - oligodendroglioma and myxoid liposarcoma

question.text: Which of the following conditions does not result in micronodular cirrhosis?
question.explanation:
Viral hepatitis is associated with macronodular cirrhosis.

Cirrhosis is comprised of regenerating parenchymal nodules surrounded by dense bands of the scar and variable degrees of vascular shunting. It is of two types:
  • Macronodular Cirrhosis
    • Irregular nodules with variation in size > 3 mm
    • Causes: Chronic viral hepatitis, Wilson's disease, Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, Drugs and toxins, Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, Cryptogenic cirrhosis
  • Micronodular Cirrhosis
    • Uniform nodules of size < 3 mm
    • Causes: Alcoholic cirrhosis, Primary biliary cirrhosis, Hepatic vein obstruction, Large bile duct obstruction, Hemochromatosis, Intestinal bypass, Cystic fibrosis, Indian childhood cirrhosis
The images given below show gross and histopathological micronodular alcoholic cirrhosis.

question.text: A 35-year-old male patient with emphysema was found to have elevated liver transaminases. His liver biopsy image is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
question.explanation:
In the given clinical scenario, the most likely diagnosis is alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. The liver biopsy image shows periodic acid—Schiff (PAS)-positive and diastase-resistant round-to-oval cytoplasmic globular inclusions in hepatocytes. These are characteristic of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

It is an autosomal-recessive disorder of protein misfolding that results in impaired secretion of α1 antitrypsin into the serum. α1AT deficiency results in excessive degradation of alveoli by neutrophil elastase causing panacinar emphysema. It also causes liver disease as a consequence of an abnormal accumulation of the misfolded protein within hepatocytes. Cutaneous necrotizing panniculitis also occurs in a minor subset of patients. Hepatocellular carcinoma develops in 2% to 3% of cases.

The image given is a photomicrograph of a liver biopsy from a patient with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. The PAS with diastase stain shows the diastase-resistant pink globules that are characteristic of this disease.

question.text: An 11-year-old girl with persistently elevated serum aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) has been diagnosed with autoimmune hepatitis. Which of the following pathological features would you not expect in this patient?
question.explanation:
Bile duct injury and granulomas are uncommon in autoimmune hepatitis except in case of overlap with primary biliary cirrhosis.

Autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) is characterised by extensive inflammation, fibrosis and ultimately cirrhosis. The pathologic features include:
  • Emperipolesis - Lymphocytes and plasma cells within the cytoplasm of hepatocytes.
  • Interface hepatitis or piecemeal necrosis.
  • Rosette formation due to necrosis of groups of hepatocytes and resultant regeneration.

The image given below shows autoimmune hepatitis with lymphoplasmacytic interface hepatitis.

question.text: Which of the following statements is false with regard to autoimmune hepatitis?

options.label: A
options.text: Type 2 autoimmune hepatitis shows antinuclear antibodies (ANA).

options.label: C
options.text: It can progress to liver failure.
Inflammatory infiltrate is predominantly composed of plasma cells.
options.label: D

question.explanation:
Type 2 autoimmune hepatitis shows anti-liver kidney microsomal autoantibodies (anti-LKM1) and anti—liver cytosol-1 (ACL-1) antibodies, not ANA.

Type 1 autoimmune hepatitis shows anti-nuclear (ANA), anti-smooth muscle antibodies (ASMA) and anti—soluble liver antigen / liver pancreas antigen (anti-SLA/LP) antibodies. It less commonly shows anti-mitochondrial (AMA) antibodies.

Autoimmune hepatitis is a chronic disorder characterized by continuing hepatocellular necrosis and inflammation. It can progress to cirrhosis and liver failure.

Histocompatibility haplotypes such as HLA-B1, HLA-B8, HLA-DR3, and HLA-DR4 are common in patients with autoimmune hepatitis.

Histopathological features include:
  • Plasma cell predominance in inflammatory infiltrates
  • Extensive interface hepatitis (piecemeal necrosis)
  • Hepatocyte rosettes
The image given below shows autoimmune hepatitis showing characteristic lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate and interface hepatitis.

question.text: Identify the incorrect match.
question.explanation: Chronic hepatitis D is associated with anti-LKM 3 antibodies.

question.text: Which of the following is not a feature of primary sclerosing cholangitis?
question.explanation:
Primary sclerosing cholangitis is characterized by inflammation and obliterative fibrosis of intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts. There is dilation of preserved segments.

On histopathologic examination, large ducts show acute neutrophilic inflammation of the epithelium. The inflamed areas develop strictures. Small ducts show onion-skin fibrosis around the atrophic duct lumen. There is an obliteration of ducts by a tombstone scar.

question.text: Primary biliary cholangitis is most commonly associated with which of the following conditions?
question.explanation:
Primary biliary cholangitis is most commonly associated with Sjogren's syndrome. Other associated conditions are:
  • Thyroiditis
  • Scleroderma
  • Rheumatoid arthritis
  • Raynaud phenomenon
  • Celiac disease
PBC is an autoimmune disease. It is characterized by nonsuppurative, inflammatory destruction of small and medium-sized intrahepatic bile ducts. Large intrahepatic ducts and the extrahepatic biliary tree are not involved. It is a disease of middle-aged women, with a female predominance of 9:1. Antimitochondrial antibodies are the most characteristic laboratory finding in PBC.

Histopathologic examination shows diagnostic florid duct lesions. These are lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates with or without granulomas centred around the bile duct. They also show Mallory—Denk bodies.

The image given below shows primary biliary cholangitis. Florid duct lesion showing lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate and granuloma.

question.text: Which of the following would you use to screen an asymptomatic sibling of a patient with Wilson's disease?
question.explanation:
Genetic testing for the ATP7B gene is used to screen asymptomatic 1st and 2nd-degree relatives of patients with Wilson's disease. This helps to differentiate the heterozygous from the homozygous individuals. This can be useful in the early initiation of treatment before the onset of symptoms.

Low serum ceruloplasmin, raised 24 hr urinary copper, and Kayser-Fleischer rings are diagnostically helpful.

Estimation of hepatic tissue copper is the gold standard for diagnosis. It is measured using neutron activation analysis / atomic absorption spectrometry.

question.text:
Which of the following statements are true regarding hemochromatosis?
  1. Neonatal hemochromatosis is not an inherited disease.
  2. Adult hemochromatosis is generally a milder disease than the juvenile form.
  3. Bantu siderosis or African iron overload is due to dietary iron overload.
  4. Skin pigmentation in hemochromatosis mostly results from increased melanin synthesis due to iron deposition.
  5. In severe hemochromatosis, total iron accumulation may exceed 50 gm.
question.explanation:
Neonatal hemochromatosis is not an inherited disorder in the classical genetic sense. It is now recognized as gestational alloimmune liver disease caused by maternal antibodies against fetal hepatocytes.

Adult (HFE-related) hemochromatosis is generally milder than the juvenile form, which presents earlier and is more severe due to mutations in HJV or HAMP genes.

Bantu siderosis (African iron overload) results from chronic dietary iron excess, historically due to consumption of iron-rich homemade beer stored in iron containers.

Skin pigmentation in hemochromatosis is primarily due to increased melanin synthesis stimulated by iron deposition, with some contribution from dermal hemosiderin deposition.

In severe untreated hemochromatosis, total body iron stores may exceed 50 g (normal adult total body iron: approximately 2–6 g).

question.text: Which of the following organs does not show hemosiderin deposits in hemochromatosis?
question.explanation:
The testes do not show hemosiderin deposits in hemochromatosis.

Hypogonadism in hemochromatosis is not due to the deposition of iron in the testis. It is due to a derangement in the hypothalamic-pituitary axis. This results in decreased gonadotrophins and testosterone levels. The testis will appear small and atrophic.

Deposition of hemosiderin is seen in the following organs in the decreasing order of severity:
  • Liver
  • Pancreas
  • Myocardium
  • Pituitary gland
  • Adrenal gland
  • Thyroid
  • Parathyroid gland
  • Joints
  • Skin

question.text: Which of the following is the most common benign tumor of the liver?
question.explanation:
Cavernous hemangioma is the most common benign tumor of the liver.

It appears as a red-blue, soft nodule, usually < 2 cm in diameter. It may be mistaken radiographically or intraoperatively for a metastatic tumor.

question.text: 30-year-old woman presents with a history of abdominal pain. She has been taking oral contraceptives for the past 7 years. CECT reveals an isodense lesion in the liver with homogenous enhancement in the arterial phase and washout in the portal venous phase. Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding this condition?

options.label: B
options.text: It can be associated with MODY-3
Serum amyloid A may be upregulated
options.label: C
D
options.text: B-catenin-activated adenoma has no risk of malignant transformation

question.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of hepatic adenoma. B-catenin-activated adenomas have a high risk of malignant transformation.

Hepatic adenomas are benign tumors of hepatocytes. Spontaneous rupture of the hepatic adenoma may cause intraabdominal bleeding, which is a surgical emergency.

Hepatic adenomas are classified into 3 subtypes:
  • HNF1-inactivated adenomas:
    • No risk of malignant transformation
    • Often associated with oral contraceptive pill use (OCP) and MODY-3
  • B-catenin-activated adenoma:
    • High risk of malignant transformation
    • Associated with oral contraceptive pills (OCP) and anabolic steroids usage
  • Inflammatory adenomas:
    • Associated with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)
    • Upregulation of C-reactive protein (CRP) and serum amyloid A
    • 10% may have concomitant β-catenin activating mutations
    • Moderate risk of malignant transformation
The gross specimen of hepatic adenoma is shown below.

question.text: Patients with which of the following conditions are not at risk for cholangiocarcinoma?
question.explanation:
Typhoid carriers are not at risk of developing cholangiocarcinoma.

Cholangiocarcinoma is the second most common primary malignant tumor of the liver after hepatocellular carcinoma. It is a malignancy of the biliary tree, arising from bile ducts within and outside of the liver.

The risk factors for cholangiocarcinoma include the following:
  • Infestation by liver flukes (particularly Opisthorchis and Clonorchis)
  • Primary sclerosing cholangitis, and other chronic inflammatory diseases of the large bile ducts
  • Chronic hepatitis B and C infections
  • Cirrhosis
  • Inflammatory bowel disease
  • Diabetes mellitus, obesity, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)
  • Alcohol and tobacco
  • Precursor lesions:
    • Biliary intraepithelial neoplasias
    • Mucinous cystic neoplasms
    • Intraductal papillary biliary neoplasia

question.text: What does Klatskin tumor refer to?
question.explanation:
Klatskin tumors are extrahepatic cholangiocarcinomas located in the perihilar region.

These tumors are located at the junction of the right and left hepatic ducts. Distal tumors arise in the common bile duct posterior to the duodenum. Regardless of the site, the prognosis is poor.

question.text: Patients with cirrhosis of the liver are at a higher risk of developing which of the following?
question.explanation:
Dysplastic nodules are associated with liver cirrhosis.

High grade dysplastic nodules may eventually develop into hepatocellular carcinoma in viral hepatitis and alcoholic liver disease.

question.text: Patients with all of the following are at a higher risk of developing hepatoblastoma except:

options.label: A
options.text: A 6-year-old child diagnosed with new-onset hypertension
A premature infant with low birth weight
options.label: B
C
options.text: A 5-year-old child diagnosed with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome

options.label: D
options.text: A 9-year-old child with a family history of familial adenatomatous polyposis

question.explanation:
Hypertension is not a risk factor for hepatoblastoma.

Risk factors for hepatoblastoma include:
  • Prematurity and low birth weight (LBW)
  • Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
  • Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP)

question.text: Which of the following parameters indicates a good prognosis in hepatoblastoma?
question.explanation:
Pure fetal histology hepatoblastoma is associated with a very good prognosis. They may be cured by surgical resection without adjuvant chemotherapy.

Prognostic factors in hepatoblastoma include:
Prematurity and low-birth weight (LBW) are associated with hepatoblastoma but do not affect its outcome.

Factors indicating good prognosis:
  • Low tumor stage
  • Pure fetal histology
  • Low AFP levels
Factors indicating poor prognosis:
  • High tumor stage
  • Small cell undifferentiated histology
  • Rhabdoid features
  • Vascular invasion

question.text: Which one of the following syndromes is associated with a higher incidence of hepatoblastoma?
question.explanation:
Gardner syndrome, a variant of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) syndrome, is associated with hepatoblastoma.

Activation of WNT signaling plays a major role in hepatoblastomas. This occurs by a variety of mechanisms including mutations in the APC gene. Hence, patients with FAP syndromes frequently develop hepatoblastomas.

The following syndromes are associated with hepatocellular carcinoma:
  • Hereditary tyrosinemia
  • Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
  • Familial hemochromatosis

question.text: Which of the following is the most common cause of hepatocellular carcinoma?
question.explanation:
The most common cause of hepatocellular carcinoma is chronic hepatitis B virus infection. More than 85% of cases of hepatocellular carcinoma occur in countries with high rates of chronic hepatitis B virus infection.

Risk factors for hepatocellular carcinoma are:
  • Hepatitis B virus
  • Hepatitis C virus
  • Alcohol
  • Aflatoxin
  • Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
  • Hemochromatosis
  • Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis
  • Tyrosinemia
  • Smoking
Activation of β-catenin and inactivation of p53 are the two most common early mutational events seen in hepatocellular carcinoma.
