question.text: 25-year-old woman presents with chronic abdominal discomfort. Imaging reveals a solitary well-encapsulated hepatic mass with a central fibrous scar and stellate calcification. Further investigations reveal elevated neurotensin levels and negative hepatitis B serology. Which of the following is incorrect regarding this condition?

options.text: Histology reveals oncocytic hepatocytes separated by collagen bundles
options.label: A
B
options.text: It is associated with a relatively good prognosis
Majority of these tumors are resectable
options.label: C
D
options.text: It is associated with liver cirrhosis

question.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of fibrolamellar carcinoma. It is usually not associated with liver cirrhosis.

Fibrolamellar carcinoma is a distinctive and rare variant of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). It usually occurs < 35 years of age. There is no gender predilection and no identifiable predisposing conditions. It has a good prognosis compared to the classical HCC. Majority (50-75%) of these tumors are resectable.

It usually presents as a single large, hard scirrhous tumor with fibrous bands coursing through it.

Microscopically, it is composed of oncocytes growing in nests or cords separated by parallel lamellae of dense collagen bundles.

The histological section of fibrolamellar carcinoma is given below. It shows malignant-appearing, oncocytic hepatocytes separated by dense bundles of collagen.

question.text: What is the most frequent site of ectopic gastric mucosa?
question.explanation:
The most frequent site of the ectopic gastric mucosa is the upper third of the esophagus, where it is referred to as an inlet patch.

It is congenital and mostly asymptomatic. Occasionally, it can release acid, which can result in dysphagia, esophagitis, Barrett esophagus, or, rarely, adenocarcinoma.

question.text: Which organism can cause esophageal infections in healthy individuals?
question.explanation:
Esophagitis in healthy individuals can be caused by the Herpes simplex virus. However, it is relatively uncommon.

In immunosuppressed individuals, infections can be caused by:
  • Herpes simplex virus
  • Cytomegalovirus
  • Candida

question.text: A 28-year-old patient with haematemesis is found to have the following finding on upper GI endoscopy. He has traveled to Zambia several times over the past 3 years. What could be the likely cause of this condition?
question.explanation:
This clinical scenario and image showing bleeding esophageal varices are suggestive of hepatic schistosomiasis. It is the second most common cause of varices worldwide.

Liver cirrhosis, mostly in association with alcoholic liver disease, is the most common cause of varices.

question.text: Which of the following statements is false?

options.text: The most common site of extranodal lymphoma in GIT is the esophagus
options.label: A

options.text: The most common benign tumour of esophagus is leimyoma
options.label: B
C
options.text: The most common esophageal cancer overall is squamous cell carcinoma
The most common esophageal cancer in Western countries is adenocarcinoma
options.label: D

question.explanation: The most common site of extranodal lymphoma in GIT is the stomach, not the esophagus.

question.text: A patient with recurrent gastritis has been diagnosed with Helicobacter pylori infection. Which of the following is true in this patient?

options.text: Increased risk of adenocarcinoma of esophagus
options.label: A
B
options.text: Decreased risk of adenocarcinoma of esophagus
Increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma of esophagus
options.label: C
D
options.text: Decreased risk of squamous cell carcinoma of esophagus

question.explanation:
Helicobacter pylori infection is associated with decreased risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma.

Long-standing H. pylori gastritis (chronic inflammation) causes multifocal gastric mucosal atrophy, which in turn leads to reduced parietal cell mass, acid secretion. This leads to reduced incidence of Barrett's esophagus and decreased risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma.

H. pylori infection, however, increases the risk of gastric adenocarcinoma.

question.text: All of the following may be seen in patients with Plummer-Vinson syndrome except:
question.explanation:
Paterson—Brown-Kelly or Plummer—Vinson syndrome is associated with non-progressive dysphagia, especially with incompletely chewed food.

This syndrome is common in women aged > 40 years. The other components of this syndrome are:
  • Post-cricoid webs in the upper esophagus
  • Iron-deficiency anemia
  • Glossitis
  • Cheilosis

Esophageal webs are idiopathic, semi-circumferential lesions composed of fibrovascular connective tissue and overlying epithelium. They are usually limited to the proximal esophagus and may cause obstruction. They are associated with:
  • Plummer—Vinson syndrome
  • Gastroesophageal reflux disease
  • Chronic graft-versus-host disease
  • Blistering skin diseases

The images below show endoscopic and barium swallow appearances of esophageal webs.

question.text: 45-year-old woman presented with complaints of difficulty in swallowing solid foods. An upper GI endoscopy revealed the following finding just above the gastroesophageal junction. What is the likely diagnosis?
question.explanation:
The given image shows an esophageal ring. Rings located above the gastroesophageal junction are classified as type A esophageal rings.

Esophageal rings are circumferential and thick. They include mucosa, submucosa, and occasionally, hypertrophic muscularis propria. There are 3 types:

Steakhouse syndrome refers to intermittent food impaction causing complete obstruction due to the presence of Schatzki rings.

Type A Ring:
  • Caused by normal physiological smooth muscle contraction
  • Rare findings on radiographic studies due to diaphragmatic crural pressure
  • Seen above the gastroesophageal junction (GEJ) in the distal esophagus
  • Covered by squamous mucosa

Type B Ring (Schatzki Ring):
  • Most common type
  • Associated with hiatus hernia
  • Located at the squamocolumnar junction
  • Covered by gastric cardia-type mucosa

Type C Ring:
  • Found in the most distal portion of the esophagus

question.text: Which of the following statements is true about the pathology of achalasia cardia?

options.text: Decreased release of NO and VIP in the distal part of esophagus
options.label: C

options.text: Decreased tone of the lower esophageal sphincter
options.label: D

question.explanation:
Achalasia cardia is characterized by decreased release of NO (nitric oxide) and VIP (vasoactive intestinal polypeptide) in the distal part of esophagus.

Normally, NO and VIP are secreted by the inhibitory neurons of the Auerbach's plexus in the distal esophagus. This leads to relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES). In achalasia cardia, these inhibitory neurons degenerate leading to decreased release of NO and VIP. This causes increased LES tone.

The triad of achalasia cardia is as follows:
  • Incomplete relaxation of LES
  • Increased tone of LES
  • Absent peristalsis (aperistalsis)

question.text: A mother brought her 8-year-old son to the OPD with complaints of refusal to eat and poor weight gain. The child complained that food often gets stuck in his throat. Endoscopy revealed the following finding. What is the likely diagnosis?
question.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and image showing multiple stacked esophageal rings are characteristic of eosinophilic esophagitis.

Differentiating features between eosinophilic esophagitis and GERD:
  • Dysphagia: Eosinophilic esophagitis
  • Heartburn and regurgitation: GERD

  • Male predominance: Eosinophilic esophagitis
  • Male = female: GERD

  • Children, young adults: Eosinophilic esophagitis
  • Middle age: GERD

Esophageal findings on endoscopy:
  • Eosinophilic esophagitis: Edema, Multiple stacked rings (feline esophagus), longitudinal furrows, Punctate exudates, Strictures and narrow-caliber esophagus, Crepe-paper esophagus, Normal findings in <10% patients
  • GERD: Erosions and ulcers, Strictures, Barrett's esophagus and adenocarcinoma, Normal findings on endoscopy in majority of patients

  • Eosinophils/hpf: ≥15 eosinophils/hpf (Eosinophilic esophagitis)
  • Eosinophils/hpf: <7 eosinophils/hpf (GERD)

  • Etiology (Eosinophilic esophagitis): Atopic or immune-mediated, acid reflux is not prominent
  • Etiology (GERD): Acid reflux

Primary treatment:
  • Eosinophilic esophagitis: Proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs), Steroids (topical), Elimination diet
  • GERD: Antacids, H2 receptor blockers, Proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs)

question.text: 47-year-old woman comes to you with progressive heartburn and difficulty in swallowing. She also describes episodes of painful blanching and bluish discoloration of her fingers and toes on exposure to cold. The following findings are noted on examination. Antibodies to which of the following are most likely to be seen in this patient?
question.explanation:
The symptoms of the patient in the above case scenario and the image showing calcinosis are the characteristic findings of the CREST syndrome or limited scleroderma. Patients with this condition characteristically have antibodies directed against centromeric proteins (anti-centromere antibodies).

CREST syndrome is characterized by the following:
  • Calcinosis
  • Raynaud phenomenon
  • Esophageal dysmotility
  • Sclerodactyly
  • Telangiectasia

In the esophagus, progressive atrophy and fibrous replacement of the muscularis propria leads to hypomotility and dysphagia. The lower 2/3 of the esophagus develops a rubber-hose-like inflexibility. The associated dysfunction of the lower esophageal sphincter gives rise to gastroesophageal reflux, Barrett metaplasia, and stricture.

question.text: 3-weeks-old baby presents with projectile non-bilious vomiting after every meal. Abdominal examination reveals prominent peristalsis in the epigastrium and an olive-sized mass is felt on deep palpation of the right upper abdomen. Which of the following drug exposures is associated with this condition?
question.explanation:
The given scenario is suggestive of congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. It is associated with exposure to azithromycin.

Risk factors for congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis:
  • Turner syndrome
  • Trisomy 18
  • Erythromycin or azithromycin exposure in the first 2 weeks of life either orally or via mother's milk.

Hyperplasia of the pyloric muscularis propria obstructs the gastric outflow tract. It is three to five times more common in males. Generally presents between 3rd and 6th weeks of life as new-onset regurgitation, projectile, non-bilious vomiting after feeding.

Physical examination reveals a firm, ovoid, 1 to 2 cm abdominal mass. In some cases, abnormal left to right hyperperistalsis is seen.

Treatment is the surgical splitting of the muscularis (Ramstedt pyloromyotomy).

question.text: Endoscopy of a patient with chronic upper gastrointestinal bleeding showed the following finding. What is the likely diagnosis?
question.explanation:
The endoscopy findings of the watermelon stomach are suggestive of gastric antral vascular ectasia (GAVE).

In GAVE, endoscopy reveals longitudinal stripes of edematous erythematous mucosa that alternate with less severely injured, paler mucosa giving the appearance of watermelon. GAVE is responsible for 4% of non-variceal upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

Dieulafoy lesion is a non-stress-related cause of GI bleeding. It is due to a submucosal artery that does not branch properly within the wall of the stomach. It is shown in the image below.

question.text: Fundic gland polyps are associated with which of the following conditions?
question.explanation:
Fundic gland polyps are associated with familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP).

Fundic gland polyps may also occur sporadically or with proton pump inhibitor use. They occur in the gastric body and fundus.

They may be asymptomatic or associated with nausea, vomiting, or epigastric pain.

Dysplasia and neoplasia may occur in FAP-associated fundic gland polyps. Another gastric polyp associated with FAP is gastric adenoma.

The below histological image of fundic gland polyp shows cystically dilated, irregular glands lined by flattened parietal and chief cells. Inflammation is typically absent or minimal.

question.text: All are predisposing factors for the development of gastric adenoma except:
question.explanation:
Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is not a predisposing factor for the development of gastric adenoma. It may predispose to carcinoid tumors.

Risk factors for gastric adenoma:
  • Chronic gastritis with atrophy
  • Intestinal metaplasia
  • Familial adenomatous polyposis

The risk of adenocarcinoma in gastric adenomas is particularly increased in lesions greater than 2 cm in diameter. Overall, carcinoma may be present in up to 30% of gastric adenomas.

question.text: Which germline loss-of-function mutation is strongly associated with patients diagnosed with familial gastric cancer?
question.explanation:
Familial gastric cancer (diffuse type) is strongly associated with germline loss-of-function mutations in the tumor suppressor gene CDH1. It encodes the cell adhesion protein, E-cadherin.

Half of the sporadic diffuse gastric cancer cases occur due to loss-of-function mutations in CDH1. In the remaining cases, E-cadherin expression is decreased, due to hypermethylation and silencing of the CDH1 promoter. Thus, the loss of E-cadherin is a key step in the development of diffuse gastric cancer.

Sporadic intestinal-type gastric cancers are strongly associated with increased signaling via the Wnt pathway (loss-of-function mutation of APC/gain-of-function mutation of β-catenin).

Mutation of TP53 is also found in the majority of sporadic gastric cancers of both types.

question.text: All are true about diffuse gastric cancer except:
question.explanation:
The diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma does not form bulky tumors. It grows in a diffuse infiltrating pattern that stiffens the gastric wall (linitis plastica). In contrast, the intestinal type tends to form bulky masses.

Loss of E-cadherin is the key step in the development of diffuse gastric cancer, resulting in discohesive cells. These single cells have large, intracytoplasmic mucin vacuoles that push the nucleus to the periphery, creating a signet-ring cell morphology. Mutation of TP53 is found in a majority of sporadic gastric cancers of both diffuse and intestinal types.

The below H&E-stained smear shows normal gastric mucosa (red arrow) and the characteristic signet cells (green arrows) in a patient with diffuse gastric adenocarcinoma.

Note: Loss of E-cadherin is also seen in lobular carcinoma of the breast.

question.text: 68-year-old woman with long-standing chronic gastritis undergoes an endoscopic biopsy. The biopsy showed dense lymphocytic infiltration with lymphoepithelial lesions in the gastric glands. The cells of this tumor are likely to express all of the following markers except:
question.explanation:
The given scenario is suggestive of gastric MALToma. The tumor cells express the B-cell markers CD19 and CD20. They do not express CD5 or CD10.

They are positive for CD43 in about 25% of cases, a T-cell marker that can be diagnostically helpful.

question.text: Which of the following is least likely to be secreted by gastrointestinal carcinoid tumors?
question.explanation:
Gastrointestinal carcinoid tumors can secrete all of the above-mentioned secretory products except noradrenaline.

Carcinoid products at different sites:
  • Stomach - Histamine, somatostatin, serotonin
  • Duodenum - Gastrin, somatostatin, cholecystokinin
  • Jejunum and ileum - Serotonin, substance P, polypeptide YY
  • Colon - Serotonin, polypeptide YY

question.text: 50-year-old woman presents with complaints of abdominal pain and diarrhea. On examination, her face appears flushed and her pulse is 120/min. Increased levels of 5-HIAA are observed in a 24-hour urinary sample. Which of the following is not a prognostic factor for this condition?
question.explanation:
The given scenario is suggestive of carcinoid tumors. The most important prognostic factors include the degree of histological differentiation, mitotic rate, and Ki-67 proliferative index.

The diagnosis of carcinoid tumor is made by increased levels of 5-hydroxy indole acetic acid (5-HIAA) in a 24-hour urine sample. It is positive in larger tumors or if metastases are present.

Note: The most important prognostic factor for esophageal carcinoma and stomach carcinoma is the depth of invasion.

question.text: The absence of the structure marked as A will present with all except:
question.explanation:
The eosinophilic appearing cells marked as A are the parietal cells, the absence of which is not associated with Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome. The cells marked as B are Chief cells.

Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome is caused by gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumors, which leads to parietal cell hyperplasia. Gastrinomas are almost always found in the small intestine or pancreas.

The most remarkable feature found in the stomach is an increase in oxyntic mucosal thickness due to massive parietal cell hyperplasia.

Other options:
  • Option A and C: Pernicious anemia is an autoimmune disease characterized by the presence of autoantibodies that impairs the production or activity of the intrinsic factor (IF) that is released from the parietal cells, which is required for the uptake of vitamin B12. There are three types of autoantibodies namely, type I, II, and III. The action of each of these include:
    • Autoantibody type I prevents the binding of vitamin B12 to the intrinsic factor (IF).
    • Autoantibody type II prevents the binding of vitamin B12-IF complex to the ileal receptors.
    • Autoantibody type III acts against the α and β subunits of the gastric proton pump, which impairs the production of intrinsic factor.
    These patients also develop chronic atrophic gastritis, characterized by loss of parietal cells, infiltration of lymphocytes and plasma cells, and megaloblastic changes in mucosal cells.
  • Option B: Gastric carcinoid tumors originate from gastric enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells. They are referred to as well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumors. The peak incidence of carcinoid tumors is in the 6th decade. These tumors occur throughout the GI tract, most commonly in the appendix, ileum, and rectum, in decreasing order of frequency.

    Gastric carcinoid tumors may be associated with endocrine cell hyperplasia, autoimmune chronic atrophic gastritis, MEN-I, and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. Ileal carcinoid may cause carcinoid syndrome which is characterized by cutaneous flushing, sweating, bronchospasm, colicky abdominal pain, diarrhea, and right-sided cardiac valvular fibrosis.

question.text: What is the most common cause of chronic gastritis?
question.explanation:
The most common cause of chronic gastritis is infection with the bacillus Helicobacter pylori.

Causes of chronic gastritis:
  • Helicobacter pylori - 1st most common
  • Autoimmune gastritis - 2nd most common
  • Radiation injury
  • Chronic bile reflux
  • Mechanical injury (e.g., an indwelling nasogastric tube)
  • Systemic diseases such as Crohn disease, amyloidosis
  • Graft-versus-host disease

Options B and C: Acid hypersecretion and alcohol ingestion are the causes of acute gastritis.

Note: Autoimmune gastritis is the most common cause of diffuse atrophic gastritis.

question.text: In patients with autoimmune gastritis, what part of the stomach is least likely to get involved?
question.explanation:
Autoimmune gastritis typically spares the antrum.

Autoimmune gastritis causes diffuse mucosal damage of the acid-producing mucosa, within the body and fundus. It accounts for less than 10% of cases of chronic gastritis. CD4+T cells directed against parietal cell components, including the H+/K+ ATPase, are considered to be the principal agents of injury in autoimmune gastritis.

Characteristic features of autoimmune gastritis:
  • Antibodies to parietal cells and intrinsic factor
  • Reduced serum pepsinogen I concentration
  • Hypergastrinemia
  • Endocrine cell hyperplasia leads to carcinoid tumors
  • Vitamin B12 deficiency (pernicious anemia)
  • Defective gastric acid secretion (achlorhydria)

question.text: What is the most common site of peptic ulcers?
question.explanation:
The most common site of peptic ulcer is the anterior wall of the proximal duodenum, within a few centimeters of the pyloric valve.

Gastric peptic ulcers are predominantly located along the lesser curvature near the interface of the body and antrum.

Locations of peptic ulcers (in decreasing order of frequency):
  • Duodenum (first part)
  • Stomach (lesser curvature near the junction of body and antrum)
  • Gastroesophageal junction in gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) or Barrett's esophagus
  • Margins of jejunostomy
  • Stomach, duodenum, and/or jejunum in patients with Zollinger-Ellison syndrome
  • Ileal Meckel's diverticulum containing ectopic gastric mucosa

The below image shows a peptic ulcer with a round to oval, sharply punched-out defect, and clean mucosal margin.

question.text: What is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children younger than 2 years of age?
question.explanation:
The most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children < 2 years of age is intussusception.

Intussusception occurs when a segment of the intestine, constricted by a wave of peristalsis, telescopes into the immediately distal segment. It is usually idiopathic at younger ages. However, it can be associated with viral infections and rotavirus vaccines, perhaps due to reactive hyperplasia of Peyer patches.

Untreated intussusception may progress to intestinal obstruction, compression of mesenteric vessels, and infarction.

Note: The most common form of congenital intestinal atresia is imperforate anus. It occurs due to failure of the cloacal diaphragm to involute.

question.text: 10 month old infant is brought to the OPD with complaints of intractable diarrhea. His past history is significant for autoimmune thyroiditis. On examination, eczematous rashes were seen on the chest and back. Sequencing of which of the following genes would help to arrive at a definitive diagnosis?
question.explanation:
The given scenario is suggestive of autoimmune enteropathy or IPEX syndrome. Definitive diagnosis requires gene sequencing to identify mutations in the FOXP3 gene.

FOXP3 is a transcription factor expressed in CD4+ regulatory T cells.

Autoimmune enteropathy is an X-linked disorder characterized by severe persistent diarrhea and autoimmune disease in young children. A particularly severe familial form is termed IPEX, an acronym denoting immune dysregulation, polyendocrinopathy, enteropathy, and X-linked inheritance.

The classic presentation of IPEX is a triad of:
  • Failure to thrive with severe chronic diarrhea due to an autoimmune enteropathy
  • Autoimmune endocrinopathy (neonatal type 1 diabetes or thyroiditis)
  • Dermatitis (usually eczematous)

question.text: 7-day-old infant was brought with complaints of profuse watery diarrhea and severe dehydration. On detailed evaluation, labs showed metabolic acidosis and electron microscopy of small bowel biopsy showed characteristic intracellular microvillus inclusions. Mutations in which of the following genes is associated with this condition?
question.explanation:
The given scenario is suggestive of microvillus inclusion disease (MVID) which is associated with MYO5B gene mutations.

Microvillus inclusion disease or Davidson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder due to mutations of the MYO5B gene. This gene encodes a motor protein that is required for the transport of normal nutrients, ions, water, and plasma membrane components. Hence, it leads to defective vesicular transport that causes deficient brush-border assembly.

Clinical features of MVID are:
  • Profuse watery, secretory diarrhea - before 3 months of age (often in the first few days of life)
  • Metabolic acidosis
  • Hypotonic dehydration
Diagnosis of MVID include:
  • Electron microscopy:
    • Inclusion containing microvilli in the apical cytoplasm of the intestinal cells.
    • Brush border microvilli are poorly developed with only a few/blunted microvilli
  • Immunostaining of villin (the brush border protein)
  • CD10 immunohistochemistry to detect microvillus inclusions
Treatment is total parenteral nutrition and small bowel transplantation.

The following electron microscopy image shows characteristic intracytoplasmic inclusions that are lined by intact microvilli along the absorptive surfaces of the intestinal cells.

question.text: Malabsorption is not due to intestinal mucosal defects in which of the following disorders?
question.explanation:
In cystic fibrosis, malabsorption occurs due to exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, not intestinal mucosal defects.

Cystic fibrosis is caused by pathogenic mutations in the CFTR gene on chromosome 7 that encodes the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) protein.

The absence of CFTR protein interferes with Na+, HCO3-, and water secretion resulting in defective luminal hydration. This causes the formation of pancreatic intraductal concretions and causes exocrine pancreatic insufficiency.

question.text: Which of the following phases is impaired in patients diagnosed with Whipple's disease?
question.explanation:
In Whipple's disease, the cause of malabsorption is impaired lymphatic transport.

In Whipple disease, clinical symptoms occur because organism-laden macrophages accumulate within the small intestinal lamina propria and mesenteric lymph nodes, causing lymphatic obstruction. These bacteria-laden macrophages also accumulate within mesenteric lymph nodes, synovial membranes of affected joints, cardiac valves, and brain.

The clinical presentation of Whipple disease is usually a triad of diarrhea, weight loss, and arthralgia.

question.text: 35-year-old HIV-positive man is referred for evaluation of malabsorption. A duodenal biopsy shows the following finding. Which special stain can be used further to confirm the diagnosis?
question.explanation:
This clinical scenario and image showing distended foamy macrophages inside the lamina propria are characteristic of Whipple's disease. The diagnosis can be confirmed by acid-fast staining.

Distended foamy macrophages inside the lamina propria of the duodenum can be seen in:
  • Whipple's disease
  • Intestinal tuberculosis, particularly in immunocompromised hosts
As both organisms are PAS-positive, PAS staining cannot differentiate between the two diseases.

On the other hand, acid-fast staining can be used to confirm the diagnosis, as only mycobacteria are acid fast, whereas Tropheryma whipplei is not.

question.text: A 2-year-old boy was brought by his parents with complaints of vomiting, watery diarrhea, and fever. A rapid ELISA test for rotavirus was positive. Which of the following viral proteins causes damage to the intestinal epithelium?
question.explanation:
Rotavirus damages the intestinal epithelium by a viral factor called non-structural protein 4 (NSP4), which can induce epithelial apoptosis.

Rotavirus is a common cause of severe childhood diarrhea and diarrheal mortality worldwide.

Rotavirus selectively infects and destroys mature enterocytes in the small intestine. This causes repopulation of the villus surface by immature secretory cells.

question.text: 55-year-old man who presented with diarrhea and flushing was found to have an ileal tumor. The histological image of the resected specimen is given below. Which of the following markers will these cells be positive for?
question.explanation:
The given history and histological image are diagnostic of ileal carcinoid. The tumor cells are typically positive for synaptophysin on immunohistochemistry.

Histology of carcinoid typically reveals islands and nests of uniform cells with scant, pink granular cytoplasm and salt and pepper chromatin. Electron microscopy reveals cytoplasmic dense-core neurosecretory granules.

Carcinoid tumors most commonly occur in the gastrointestinal tract. The most common sites in decreasing order of frequency are the appendix, ileum, and rectum. These tumors may cause carcinoid syndrome, which is characterized by cutaneous flushing, sweating, bronchospasm, colicky abdominal pain, diarrhea, and right-sided cardiac valvular fibrosis.

Immunohistochemical (IHC) markers for carcinoid tumors are:
  • Neuron-specific enolase
  • Synaptophysin
  • Chromogranin A
  • Leu 7

question.text:
Match the following conditions with their most commonly involved sites:

List I (Conditions) List II (Sites)
1. Meckel's diverticulum A. Colorectal region
2. Acquired (false) diverticulum B. Ileum
3. Crohn's disease C. Terminal ileum
4. Intestinal polyps D. Sigmoid colon
question.explanation:
The most common sites of the following conditions are:

  • Meckel's diverticulum: Most commonly occurs in the ileum. It is a true diverticulum, a blind outpouching of the alimentary tract that communicates with the lumen and includes all three layers of the bowel wall. It occurs as a result of the failed involution of the vitelline duct, which connects the lumen of the developing gut to the yolk sac.
  • Acquired diverticulum: Most commonly occurs in the sigmoid colon. False or acquired diverticula either lack the muscularis entirely or have an attenuated muscularis propria.
  • Crohn's disease: Most commonly occurs in the terminal ileum, though it may occur in any area of the GI tract.
  • Polyps: Most common in the colorectal region. They can be sessile (without stalk) or pedunculated (with stalk). Intestinal polyps can be classified as non-neoplastic or neoplastic in nature. The non-neoplastic polyps can be further classified as inflammatory, hamartomatous, or hyperplastic. The most common neoplastic polyp is an adenoma.


The following image shows a Meckel's diverticulum.

question.text: Which of the following is true about the pathogenesis of Hirschsprung disease?

options.label: A
options.text: Failure of migration of neural crest cells

question.explanation:
Hirschsprung disease occurs due to the failure of migration of the neural crest cells to the bowel wall.

During normal embryogenesis, the neural crest cells migrate from the caecum to the rectum. The enteric neuronal plexuses develop from these migrated neural crest cells. In Hirschsprung disease, there is an arrest in the migration of these cells, which leads to the development of a distal intestinal segment that is devoid of Meissner (submucosal) and the Auerbach (myenteric) plexus. Hence this segment is referred to as the aganglionic segment.

As a result, there is a lack of coordination in the peristaltic contractions and functional obstruction, which further leads to the dilation of the intestine proximal to the affected segment, leading to congenital megacolon. Diagnosis is confirmed by demonstrating the absence of ganglion cells in biopsy sections.

Some conditions may cause acquired megacolon. These include:
  • Chagas disease, due to the loss of ganglion cells
  • Visceral myopathy
  • Obstruction by neoplasm or inflammatory stricture
  • Toxic megacolon complicating ulcerative colitis
  • Functional psychosomatic disorders

question.text:
Microscopic colitis encompasses which of the following?

1. Collagenous colitis
2. Ulcerative colitis
3. Crohn's disease
4. Lymphocytic colitis
5. Ischemic colitis
question.explanation:
Microscopic colitis encompasses two types of disorders: collagenous colitis and lymphocytic colitis.

Lymphocytic colitis shows a strong association with celiac disease and autoimmune diseases, including Graves disease and rheumatoid arthritis.

These idiopathic diseases both present with chronic, non-bloody, watery diarrhea without weight loss.

Comparison of Collagenous Colitis and Lymphocytic Colitis:
FeatureCollagenous ColitisLymphocytic Colitis
Subepithelial collagen layerDense subepithelial collagen layerOf normal thickness
Intraepithelial lymphocytesIncreased numbers of intraepithelial lymphocytesHigher ratio of intraepithelial lymphocytes

question.text: A male infant, with a history of not passing meconium, presented with abdominal distension days after birth. Barium enema showed marked colonic dilation above a narrow segment in the sigmoid region. A biopsy specimen from the narrowed region demonstrated absence of ganglion cells. This disease may be associated with which of the following conditions?
question.explanation:
The given scenario is suggestive of Hirschsprung disease. It is associated with Down's syndrome.

Hirschsprung disease is also known as congenital aganglionic megacolon. 10% of all cases occur in children with Down's syndrome.

The premature arrest of normal migration of neural crest cells from the cecum to the rectum produces aganglionosis of the distal intestinal segment. This causes functional obstruction of the affected bowel and proximal dilation. The absence of ganglion cells in the affected segment in biopsy confirms the diagnosis.

Gastrointestinal abnormalities associated with Down's syndrome include:
  • Duodenal atresia
  • Annular pancreas
  • Hirschsprung disease
Gastrointestinal abnormalities associated with Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18) include:
  • Meckel's diverticulum
  • Malrotation
Gastrointestinal abnormalities associated with Patau syndrome (trisomy 13) include:
  • Omphalocele
  • Incomplete rotation of the colon
  • Meckel's diverticulum

question.text: What is the most common site of gastrointestinal ischemia?
question.explanation:
The most common site of gastrointestinal ischemia is the colon.

Intestinal segments at the end of their respective arterial supplies are particularly susceptible to ischemia. These are termed watershed zones. These include:
  • Splenic flexure - where the superior and inferior mesenteric arterial circulations terminate
  • Junction of sigmoid colon and rectum - where the inferior mesenteric, pudendal, and iliac arterial circulations end

question.text: Campylobacter infection can result in all of the following complications except:
question.explanation:
Aplastic crisis is associated with parvovirus infection, not Campylobacter infection.

Campylobacter infection can cause:
  • Reactive arthritis, primarily in patients with HLA-B27
  • Erythema nodosum
  • Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS)
Molecular mimicry has been implicated in the pathogenesis of GBS because serum antibodies to Campylobacter jejuni lipopolysaccharide cross-react with peripheral and central nervous system gangliosides.

question.text: A pathologist is examining the following histopathological specimen from a patient with watery diarrhea and abdominal pain. What is the most probable diagnosis?
question.explanation:
The given histopathological image shows superficially damaged crypts with a typical pattern of mucopurulent exudates (neutrophils) emanating from a crypt that resembles a volcanic eruption.

This is pathognomonic of Clostridium difficile colitis.

In this condition, disruption of the normal colonic microbiota by antibiotics allows C. difficile overgrowth.

Risk factors for Clostridium difficile colitis are:
  • Antibiotic use
  • Advanced age
  • Gastric suppression (PPIs, H2 receptor blockers)
  • Immunosuppression

question.text: A 30-year-old man presented with loose stools and right lower abdominal pain for the past 6 months. Endoscopy was done which showed skip lesions with a cobblestone appearance. Histopathological examination showed aphthoid ulcerations and focal crypt abscesses. Which of the following genes is associated with this condition?
question.explanation:
The given scenario is suggestive of Crohn's disease. It is strongly associated with mutations in the nucleotide oligomerization binding domain 2 (NOD2) gene.

Crohn's disease occurs due to the host response against microbes. NOD2 encodes an intracellular protein that binds to bacterial peptidoglycans and activates the NF-κB pathway. Antibodies against the bacterial protein flagellin may be seen in NOD2-associated disease.

Other Crohn's disease-related genes are autophagy-related 16-like (ATG16L1) and immunity-related GTPase M (IRGM), which are critical for cellular responses to intracellular bacteria.

Crohn's disease most commonly involves the terminal ileum but can affect all parts of the GIT.

The following microscopic changes may be seen:
  • Aphthoid ulcerations
  • Focal crypt abscesses
  • Non-caseating granulomas can be found in all layers of the bowel, lymph nodes, mesentery, peritoneum, liver, and pancreas.
Note: Ulcerative colitis-associated genes are ECM1 and HNFA.

question.text: An endoscopy was performed on a patient who presented with lower abdominal pain and severe diarrhea. Which of the following is not associated with this condition?
question.explanation:
The given scenario along with cobblestone appearance on endoscopy is suggestive of Crohn's disease. This condition is associated with primary sclerosing cholangitis, not primary biliary cirrhosis.

Extraintestinal manifestations of Crohn's disease include the following:
  • Uveitis
  • Migratory polyarthritis
  • Sacroiliitis
  • Ankylosing spondylitis
  • Erythema nodosum
  • Clubbing of the fingertips
  • Primary sclerosing cholangitis (less frequently than ulcerative colitis)
  • Cutaneous granulomas form nodules referred to as metastatic Crohn's disease (a misnomer since there is no cancer)

question.text: A 70-year-old man with hematochezia and weight loss is diagnosed with colorectal cancer. Which of the following is the most important prognostic factor for this condition?
question.explanation:
The two most important prognostic factors of colorectal cancer are the depth of invasion and the presence of lymph node metastases.

The liver is the most common site of metastasis from the colon due to its portal drainage.

question.text: A 52-year-old lady has just been diagnosed with endometrial carcinoma. On taking history, she revealed that both her mother and her elder sister had been diagnosed with synchronous colorectal and endometrial cancer in their forties. She should be tested for mutations in which of the following genes?
question.explanation:
The given scenario is suggestive of hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC) or Lynch syndrome. She should be tested for mutations in MSH genes.

It occurs due to defective DNA mismatch repair. It is caused by inherited mutations in genes that encode proteins responsible for the detection, excision, and repair of errors that occur during DNA replication. They include MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, and PMS2 or EPCAM genes.

It is the most common syndromic cause of colon cancer. It tends to occur at younger ages than sporadic colon cancers and often involves the right colon. Familial clustering of cancers occurs at several sites including:
  • Colorectum, small bowel, and stomach
  • Endometrium and ovary
  • Ureters
  • Brain
  • Hepatobiliary tract and pancreas
  • Skin

question.text: Which of the following is incorrect about tumors of the appendix?

options.label: A
options.text: The most common tumor is carcinoid

options.label: C
options.text: Goblet cell variant of carcinoid is more aggressive

options.label: D
options.text: Peritoneal dissemination can result in pseudomyxoma peritonei

question.explanation:
Primary adenocarcinoma of the appendix is usually of mucinous type.

Peritoneal dissemination of mucinous tumors can cause pseudomyxoma peritonei.

The most common tumor of the appendix is carcinoid tumor. This neoplasm, which is almost always benign, most frequently forms a solid bulbous swelling at the distal tip of the appendix.

Goblet cell variant of carcinoid tumor is more aggressive.

question.text: A 5-year-old child was admitted to the hospital with a history of prolapsing rectal mass and painless rectal bleeding. The histopathological image of the mass is as shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
question.explanation:
The clinical features and the histopathological image showing characteristic cystically dilated crypts and glands are suggestive of a juvenile polyp.

Juvenile polyps are malformations of epithelium and lamina propria commonly located in the rectum. It is seen in children < 5 years of age. The typical presentation is painless rectal bleeding. Sometimes there may be a proliferating rectal mass.

The disease may be sporadic or syndromic.
  • Sporadic juvenile polyp occurs as a single mass and is called retention polyp.
  • Juvenile polyposis syndrome is characterized by multiple hamartomatous polyps, which may be premalignant.
Morphologically, both of these types are indistinguishable.

  • Gross appearance: They appear as pedunculated, smooth reddish lesions, and with cystic spaces.
  • Microscopic appearance: The cysts appear as dilated glands filled with mucin and inflammatory debris.
Note: Complex glandular architecture and the presence of smooth muscle cutting through the lamina propria are seen in Peutz-Jeghers polyps.

question.text: Which of the following is incorrect about Peutz-Jeghers syndrome?

options.text: It has an autosomal recessive inheritance
options.label: A

options.text: Baseline colonoscopy must be done at 20 years of age
options.label: B
C
options.text: There is increased risk of ovarian and uterine cancer

options.label: D
options.text: It is associated with loss-of-function mutations in STK11

question.explanation:
Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is an autosomal dominant syndrome.

It is commonly associated with germline heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the gene STK11.

It is characterized by:
  • Multiple gastrointestinal hamartomatous polyps
  • Mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation
  • Increased risk of gastrointestinal and extraintestinal malignancies (including ovarian and uterine cancer)
Baseline colonoscopy and upper endoscopy for screening are done at 20 years of age, followed by annual flexible sigmoidoscopy thereafter.

question.text: The total microbial population was found to be susceptible to antimicrobials on testing but a subset of the same population was resistant which was undetected. What is this phenomenon called?
question.explanation:
Heteroresistance occurs when a subset of the total microbial population is resistant, despite the total microbial population being susceptible on testing. The resistant subpopulation is usually well below the assay-detection limits.

Heteroresistant Staphylococci and M. tuberculosis have led to therapeutic failures and mortality.

C. albicans and C. neoformans with heteroresistance to fluconazole have resulted in increased treatment failures.

Note: For viruses, the resistant viral species occurring due to the above phenomenon is termed as 'quasi-species'. Quasi-species resistant to antiretroviral agents have resulted in the failure of antiretroviral therapy.

question.text: Which part of the basal ganglia receives the afferent input?
question.explanation:
The striatum receives the afferent input.

Note:
There are two main inputs to the basal ganglia:
  • From the cerebral cortex (corticostriate pathway)
  • From the thalamus (thalamostriate pathway)
They are both excitatory (glutamate) and they both terminate in the striatum.

The two major outputs of the basal ganglia are from GPi and substantia nigra. Both are inhibitory (GABAergic) and both project to the thalamus.

From the thalamus, there is an excitatory (glutamatergic) projection to the prefrontal and premotor cortex. This completes the cortical-basal ganglia-thalamic-cortical loop.

question.text: A patient is found to have a hemorrhage in the basal ganglia region. Which of the following is least likely to be affected in this patient?
question.explanation:
This patient will have dysfunction of the basal ganglia. Maintenance of equilibrium is a function of the cerebellum and vestibular apparatus, hence will not be affected in this patient.

Functions of basal ganglia:
  • Planning of movements
  • Regulation of muscle tone
  • Control of reflex muscular activity & posture
  • Programming of movement - speed, direction, and intensity
  • Role in the cognitive process (especially caudate nucleus)

question.text: Glutamate is synthesized mainly in which part of basal ganglia?
question.explanation:
Glutamate is synthesized mainly in the subthalamic nuclei of basal ganglia.

Connections within the basal ganglia and the respective neurotransmitters:
  • Substantia nigra pars compacta to striatum (Nigrostriatal projection): Dopamine
  • Striatum to substantia nigra pars reticulata: GABA
  • Striatum to GPe and GPi: GABA
  • GPe to subthalamic nuclei: GABA
  • Subthalamic nuclei to GPe and GPi: Glutamate

question.text: A 56-year-old woman presents with abnormal movements of the limbs. A lesion of the globus pallidus is suspected. Which of the following did she most likely present with?
question.explanation:
This woman with a lesion at the globus pallidus most likely presented with athetosis: Slow, writhing movements of a hand/arm/the face.

DisorderLesion SiteDescription
ChoreaStriatumFlicking movements in the hands, face, and other parts of the body
AthetosisGlobus pallidusSpontaneous, continuous writhing movements of a hand, an arm, the neck, or the face
HemiballismusSubthalamic nucleusSudden flailing movements of an entire limb
ParkinsonismSubstantia nigraSevere rigidity, akinesia, and tremors

question.text: Which of the following are climbing fibers?
question.explanation:
Climbing fibers are olivocerebellar fibers. They originate from the inferior olivary nucleus.

Climbing fibers and mossy fibers are the two main excitatory inputs to the cerebellum.

Note: Mossy fibers provide direct input via the pontine nuclei.

Climbing Fibers:
  • Come from one single source via the inferior olivary nuclei.
  • End on single Purkinje cells.
  • Convey proprioceptive inputs from all over the body.
Mossy Fibers:
  • Come from many sources and the fibers synapse with granule cells to form glomeruli.
  • Axons of granule cells bifurcate and form parallel fibers which excite multiple Purkinje cells.

question.text: Which of the following is the most potent choleretic?
question.explanation:
Bile salts (chemical choleretic) are the most potent choleretics.


Any substance that increases bile secretion is called a choleretic. Bile secretion may be increased by chemical (bile salts), hormonal (Secretin), and neural (vagal stimulation) mechanisms.


Note: Cholagogues cause contraction of the gallbladder. E.g., CCK.

question.text: Which of the following does not belong to the secretin family?
question.explanation:
CCK (Cholecystokinin) belongs to the gastrin family, not the secretin family.


Classification of GI hormones based on structure and function:

  • Gastrin family - Gastrin, Cholecystokinin
  • Secretin family - Secretin, Glucagon, VIP, GIP
  • Others - Motilin, Ghrelin, Somatostatin, etc

question.text: A patient underwent resection of the gastric antrum. A few weeks later, endoscopy revealed atrophy of the gastric mucosa. Serum levels of gastrin were found to be decreased. Which of the following is true regarding this GI hormone?
question.explanation:
Gastrin is a peptide hormone.


It is secreted by the G cells of the gastric mucosa present in the antrum of the stomach, primarily during the gastric phase of gastric acid secretion.


It causes gastric secretion at 1000-1500 mL/day. Its primary stimulus is gastric distension.


Primary functions of Gastrin:

  • Gastric acid (HCl) secretion
  • Pepsin secretion
  • Trophic action on the gastric mucosa

Other functions:

  • Stimulates gastric motility
  • Prevents gastroesophageal reflux by contraction of LES

Conditions associated with increased gastrin secretions (Ex: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome), will cause an increase in H+ secretion and hypertrophy of the gastric mucosa.


Conditions associated with reduced gastrin secretion (Ex: Resection of the gastric antrum), will cause a decrease in H+ secretion and atrophy of the gastric mucosa.

question.text: A 40-year-old man presented with abdominal pain and diarrhea. On investigations, multiple ulcers were seen in the proximal and distal duodenum and in the jejunum. The gastric pH was found to be 1.2 with a serum gastrin concentration of 2000 pg/ml. Which of the following is the primary site for the production of GI hormone raised in this patient?
question.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. In this condition, serum gastrin concentration is raised to around > 1000 pg/ml. Gastrin is primarily secreted by G cells present in the antrum of the stomach.

question.text: Which of the following gland secretes lingual lipase?
question.explanation:
Lingual lipase is secreted by von Ebner’s gland.


von Ebner's gland is a serous salivary gland situated around circumvallate and foliate papillae in front of the terminal sulcus.


Lingual lipase hydrolyzes dietary lipid. The optimal pH is 3-6. Unlike pancreatic lipase, it is not inhibited by bile salts, medium-chain FA, and lecithin. Hence, it remains active through the stomach and into the intestine.

question.text: Which of the following fluids have the highest daily secretion of potassium?
question.explanation:
The highest daily secretion of K+ is into the saliva.


In the process of formation of saliva, Na+ and Cl- are reabsorbed from the saliva, and K+ and HCO3- are secreted into the saliva.


Note: The highest concentration of K+ is in the rectal fluid.

question.text: The secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland causing a patient to salivate, pass through which of the following ganglions?
question.explanation:
The secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland pass through the Otic ganglion.


Salivary secretion is almost entirely controlled by the parasympathetic nervous system. Volume is mainly mediated by parasympathetic stimulation while the composition of saliva (increased proteinaceous content) is slightly modified by sympathetic input.


The parasympathetic preganglionic fibers are delivered by the glossopharyngeal and facial nerves to otic and submandibular ganglion respectively.


Regulation of salivary secretion by the parasympathetic nervous system:

question.text: In the stomach, H+ ions are secreted in exchange for which of the following ions?
question.explanation:
H+ ions are secreted into the lumen of the stomach in exchange for K+ by the H+-K+ pump (H+, K+-ATPase).


Mechanism of HCl formation:

  • In the parietal cells, CO2 and H2O are converted to H+ and HCO3-, catalyzed by carbonic anhydrase.
  • H+ is secreted into the lumen of the stomach by the H+-K+ pump in exchange for K+.
  • HCO3- moves out of the cell into the bloodstream in exchange for Cl- (Cl--HCO3- exchange). This Cl- moves into the lumen of the stomach.
  • H+ and Cl- combine to form HCl.

As HCO3- is added to the venous blood, the pH of the blood increases. This is called alkaline tide. Eventually, this HCO3- will be secreted in the pancreatic secretions to neutralize H+ in the small intestine.


Proton pump inhibitors inhibit H+-K+ pump.

question.text: Salivary amylase is activated by which of the following ions?
question.explanation:
Salivary amylase is activated by Cl-.

Human salivary and pancreatic amylases are activated by chloride (Cl-). They have optimum activities near-neutral pH (7.4). They hydrolyze internal 1:40 linkages but spare 1:6 linkages and terminal 1:40 linkages in starch.

question.text: Which of the following is passively absorbed in the gut?
question.explanation:
Lipids are passively absorbed in the gut.

The products of lipid digestion (monoglycerides and free fatty acids) are incorporated into micelles that are formed by bile salts and diffuse across the intestinal epithelium. Short and medium-chain fatty acids can directly diffuse across the intestinal epithelium.

Note: Recent evidence suggests that specific carrier proteins (membrane transporters) may be involved in the transport of long-chain fatty acids.

question.text: Short-chain fatty acids produced by bacteria are maximally absorbed in which part of the intestine?
question.explanation:
Short-chain fatty acids produced by bacteria are absorbed maximally in the colon by secondary active transport.

  • Almost all the iron absorption occurs in the duodenum.
  • Vitamin B12 is absorbed in the ileum.
  • Folate is absorbed in the upper small intestine (duodenum and jejunum).
  • Maximum water absorption takes place in the jejunum.

question.text: Which of the following is not a function of short-chain fatty acids in the colon?

options.text: Trophic effect on the colonic epithelial cells
options.label: A

question.explanation:
Short-chain fatty acids (2-5-carbon) in the colon promote the absorption of Na+, not secretion.

Short-chain fatty acids (SCFA) in the colon are formed by the action of colonic bacteria on complex carbohydrates, resistant starches, and other components of the dietary fiber i.e., the material that escapes digestion in the upper gastrointestinal tract and enters the colon.

Functions:
  • Exert a trophic effect on the colonic epithelial cells
  • Combat inflammation
  • Helps in maintaining acid-base equilibrium

question.text: What is the amount of fluid absorbed in the intestine in a day?
question.explanation:
The amount of fluid absorbed in the intestine in a day is around 8L.

About 2L of ingested water and 7L of various secretions enter the gastrointestinal tract. Out of this, the majority (8800 mL) is absorbed in the small intestine and colon. The small remaining volume that is not absorbed (100-200 mL) is excreted in feces.

question.text: Which of the following is not absorbed in the colon?
question.explanation:
K+ is not absorbed in the colon. It is secreted in the rectal fluid.

Electrolytes (Na+, Cl-), short-chain fatty acids (acetate, propionate, butyrate), and water are absorbed in the colon.

question.text: Which of the following is false about vitamin absorption?

options.label: A
options.text: Fat-soluble vitamin digestion needs cholesterol esterase

options.label: B
options.text: Vitamin B12 is absorbed in ileum

options.label: C
options.text: Folate is absorbed by carriers that are Na+ cotransporters
Most vitamins are absorbed in upper small intestine
options.label: D

question.explanation:
Folate and vitamin B12 absorption is Na+-independent.

The remaining water-soluble vitamins—thiamin, riboflavin, niacin, pyridoxine, pantothenate, biotin, and ascorbic acid are absorbed by carriers that are Na+ cotransporters.

  • Option A: Fat-soluble vitamins are ingested in the form of esters. Digestion needs hydrolysis by cholesterol esterase and absorbed after incorporating into micelles.
  • Options B and D: Most vitamins are absorbed in the upper small intestine, but vitamin B12 is absorbed in the ileum. Vitamin B12 binds to intrinsic factor, a protein secreted by the parietal cells of the stomach. This complex is absorbed across the ileal mucosa.

question.text: Which of the following stimulates ferritin synthesis?
question.explanation:
Elemental iron stimulates ferritin synthesis.

It synthesizes ferritin by causing the release of a cytoplasmic protein that binds to a specific region in the ferritin mRNA. This disruption activates ferritin mRNA and results in its translation.

Hepcidin binds to ferroportin and triggers its internalization and degradation. This results in decreased iron absorption and decreased circulating iron levels which reduces ferritin synthesis.

Note: Ferritin sequesters Fe2+, a potentially toxic molecule.

question.text: What is the end product after the action of colonic bacteria on dietary fiber?
question.explanation:
The action of colonic bacteria on dietary fiber would give butyrate.

Colonic bacteria act on complex carbohydrates, resistant starches, and dietary fiber to form short-chain fatty acids such as acetate, propionate, and butyrate.

SCFAs are 2-5-carbon weak acids that have an average normal concentration of about 80 mmol/L in the lumen.

question.text: Where are the cell bodies of the orexinergic neurons present?
question.explanation:
Cell bodies of orexigenic neurons are present in the lateral hypothalamic area. Orexin stimulates food intake.

Role of hypothalamus in gastrointestinal and feeding regulation:
  • Hunger center - lateral hypothalamic area
  • Satiety center - ventromedial nuclei
  • Feeding reflexes such as licking the lips and swallowing - mammillary bodies.
Note: The arcuate nucleus contains at least two different types of neurons that when stimulated lead to either increased or decreased appetite.

question.text: Which of the following is not a dietary fiber?
question.explanation:
Gum is the best answer among the given options. Even though all of the given options are dietary fibers, the consumption of gums through diet is very low and hence, it is the best answer.

Dietary fibers consist of both soluble and insoluble forms and include lignin, pectin, inulin, cellulose, hemicellulose, etc.

Advantages of fibers:
  • Forms bulk of the stool and reduces stool transit time
  • Reduces incidence of carcinoma colon, DM, CAD, diverticulitis

question.text: Which of the following is the main enzyme involved in the hydrolysis of 1,60 linkage of starch?
question.explanation:
The main enzyme involved in the hydrolysis of 1,60 linkage of starch is isomaltase.

Both salivary and the pancreatic a-amylases hydrolyze internal 1:40 linkages but spare 1:60 linkages and terminal 1:40 linkages of starch.

question.text: Which of the following processes converts trypsinogen to trypsin?

options.text: Removal of a few amino acids
options.label: C

question.explanation:
Trypsinogen is converted to trypsin by the removal of a few amino acids.

All proenzymes are converted to their active form by selective proteolysis (removal of a few amino acids).

Enterokinase cleaves trypsinogen to yield active trypsin. It is located on the brush border of duodenal enterocytes.

question.text: Which of the following is not an endopeptidase?
question.explanation:
Carboxypeptidase is an exopeptidase, not endopeptidase.

Peptidases (proteases) are of two types:
  • Endopeptidases - they act at interior peptide bonds in the peptide molecules. Expepsin, trypsin, chymotrypsin, elastase.
  • Exopeptidases - they hydrolyze the amino acids at the carboxyl ends of the polypeptides, one at a time. Excarboxypeptidase, aminopeptidase.

question.text: Peptide transporter 1 is involved in the absorption of which of the following?
question.explanation:
Peptide transporter 1 (PepT1) is involved in the absorption of the dipeptide.

The dipeptides and tripeptides are transported along with H+ into enterocytes by a system known as peptide transporter 1 (PepT1).

These peptides undergo intracellular hydrolysis to release amino acids. These amino acids are absorbed into the circulation from the basolateral membrane via basolateral amino acid transporter. H+ moves out of the cell via Na+-H+ exchanger on the luminal side.

question.text: Gastric emptying is mainly regulated by which of the following mechanisms?
question.explanation:
Gastric emptying is mainly regulated by enteric reflexes.

Regulation of gastric emptying is mainly by the inhibitory feedback signals from the duodenum that includes enterogastric reflex and hormonal feedback by cholecystokinin.

Enterogastric reflex: When food enters the duodenum, multiple nervous reflexes are initiated from the duodenal wall. They strongly inhibit the pyloric pump propulsive contractions and increase the tone of the pyloric sphincter.

These reflexes are mediated by three routes:
  • Directly from the duodenum to the stomach through the enteric nervous system in the gut wall (major role)
  • Through inhibitory sympathetic nerve fibers to the stomach (minor role)
  • Vagus nerves to the brain stem where they inhibit the normal excitatory signals transmitted to the stomach (minor role)
Hormonal feedback: Cholecystokinin is released from the mucosa of the jejunum in response to fatty substances in the chyme. This hormone acts as an inhibitor to block increased stomach motility caused by gastrin.

question.text: Which among the following increases gastric emptying?
question.explanation:
The distension of the stomach increases gastric emptying.

Distension activates the mechanoreceptors that trigger long and short reflexes in the stomach.

This increases the force of antral contraction and gastric emptying.

question.text: Which of the following does not delay gastric emptying?
question.explanation:
Gastrin increases gastric emptying. It does not delay it.

Gastrin has mild to moderate stimulatory effects on motor functions in the body of the stomach.

Thus, gastrin likely promotes stomach emptying.

question.text: In which of the following reflexes, gastric emptying is delayed when acidic content enters the duodenum?
question.explanation:
In the enterogastric reflex, gastric emptying is delayed when acidic content enters the duodenum.

When the food enters the duodenum, multiple reflexes are initiated from the duodenal wall which passes back to the stomach. These reflexes slow or stop the stomach emptying if the volume of the chyme in the duodenum becomes too much. These reflexes are called enterogastric reflexes.

This reflex can be triggered due to the following reasons:
  • Presence of irritants and acids in duodenal chyme (most sensitive factor)
  • Distension of duodenum due to the presence of an excessive volume of chyme
  • Rapid entry of hypertonic or hypotonic fluids into the duodenum
  • Presence of breakdown products of protein digestion and sometimes fat

question.text: Enterogastric inhibitory reflexes are stimulated by all of the following except:
question.explanation:
Enterogastric inhibitory reflexes are stimulated by acidic contents, not alkaline.

The duodenal factors that can initiate enterogastric inhibitory reflexes (enterogastric reflexes) are:
  • Distention of the duodenum
  • Presence of any irritation of the duodenal mucosa
  • Acidity of the duodenal chyme
  • Osmolality of the chyme - either hypotonic or hypertonic fluid initiate enterogastric inhibitory reflexes. Thus, the flow of non-isotonic fluids into the small intestine is regulated. This prevents rapid changes in electrolyte concentrations in the extracellular fluid during the absorption of the intestinal contents.
  • Presence of certain breakdown products in the chyme, especially proteins and to a lesser extent, of fats

question.text: Which of the following does not increase small intestinal motility?
question.explanation:
Secretin inhibits small intestinal motility.

Factors that increase the peristaltic activity of the small intestine:
  • Hormonal - gastrin, CCK, insulin, motilin, and serotonin.
  • Neural - duodenal distension by chyme, gastroenteric reflexes, gastroileal reflexes, parasympathetic (Ach) stimulation.
Factors that decrease the peristaltic activity of the small intestine:
  • Hormonal - secretin and glucagon.
  • Neural - sympathetic stimulation.
Gastroileal reflex - On reaching the ileocecal valve, the chyme is sometimes blocked for several hours until the person eats another meal. At that time, a gastroileal reflex intensifies peristalsis in the ileum and forces the remaining chyme through the ileocecal valve into the cecum of the large intestine.

question.text: Which part of the GIT has the longest transit time?
question.explanation:
The longest transit time is seen in the colon.

Average transit time:
  • Esophagus: 2-3 seconds
  • Colon: (e.g., First third, Second third, Sigmoid colon can take up to 9 hours or more)

question.text: The maximum motility of the colon is seen in which of the following part?
question.explanation:
The maximum motility of the colon is seen in the sigmoid colon.

The rate of BER at sigmoid colon is 6/min.

question.text: A patient is undergoing sigmoidoscopy as a part of his routine colon cancer screening. While doing the procedure, the rectum is inflated with gas. Which part of the intestine would you likely see increased peristalsis in this patient?
question.explanation:
While doing sigmoidoscopy, if the rectum is inflated with gas, increased peristalsis is seen in the distal colon.

The distention of the rectal wall initiates afferent signals. These signals spread through the myenteric plexus to initiate peristaltic waves in the descending colon, sigmoid (distal colon), and rectum.

question.text: Which of the following is seen in a patient on parasympathetic stimulation?
question.explanation:
Parasympathetic stimulation results in increased peristalsis.

Generally, the stimulation of parasympathetic nerves (PNS) causes an increase in the activity of the entire enteric nervous system. This, in turn, enhances the activity of most gastrointestinal functions.

PNS stimulation causes:
  • Contraction of smooth muscle in the wall
  • Relaxation of sphincters
  • Increased Salivary secretion
  • Increased Gastric secretion
  • Increased Pancreatic secretion
SNS stimulation causes:
  • Relaxation of smooth muscle in the wall
  • Contraction of sphincters

question.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and histopathology report point to malignant cystosarcoma phyllodes, which metastasize via the bloodstream. Metastasis to lymph nodes is rare.

Phyllodes tumor, also known as sero-cystic disease of Brodie or cystosarcoma phyllodes, originates from hormonally responsive stromal cells of the breast. It is usually a benign condition and affects women > 40 years of age, but can be seen in younger women. Sometimes, it may develop malignant transformation.

Clinical features:
  • Large, sometimes massive, with an unevenly bosselated surface
  • Ulceration of overlying skin occurs because of pressure necrosis
  • Remains mobile on the chest wall
There is no role of FNAC in phyllodes tumor. Histopathology of the lump biopsy shows increased stromal cellularity, overgrowth, and typical leaflike architecture.

Tumors are treated by excision with margins of at least 2 cm to prevent local recurrence. Large or malignant phyllodes tumors may require a mastectomy. The axillary dissection is not recommended because axillary lymph nodes rarely get involved.

Note: Malignant phyllodes tumors contain liposarcomatous or rhabdomyosarcomatous elements rather than fibrosarcomatous elements.

Boundary

 Structures forming

  • Alveolar dead space: alveoli which are only ventilated but not perfused. It is 60-80 mL on standing and 0 mL on lying down (perfusion is equal in all parts of lung on lying down)
  • Physiological dead space = anatomical dead space + alveolar dead space

question.text: A 70 kg athlete was posted​ for surgery on her injur​ed rotator cuff. She was ‍administered a total of 6‌40mg of succinylcholine b‌y intermittent dosing. Du​ring recovery, she was un‍able to respire spontaneo​usly and move her limbs. ​What is the most likely r​eason for this?

options.label: B
options.text: Undiagnosed muscular dystr​ophy and muscular weaknes​s
Phase II blockade produced​ by succinyl choline
options.label: C
D
options.text: Pseudocholinesterase defic​iency increasing action o​f succinylcholine

question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Phase II blockade produced by succinyl choline

The most likely reason which led to this scenario is phase II blockade produced by succinylcholine.

Phase II block is clinically seen with the dose >5 mg/kg. It is seen with a single large dose, repeated doses, or a continuous infusion of Sch which can lead to desensitization of the receptors resulting in a prolonged neuromuscular blockade.

Causes of prolonged apnea include:

  • Atypical/pseudocholinesterase deficiency - can result in apnea even with a normal dose of succinylcholine
  • Altered response of endplate to depolarizing relaxant (myasthenia gravis)
  • Accumulation of succinylcholine leading to phase II blockade

Note: Although options A, B, and D can lead to prolonged apnea, in the above case scenario, the patient has received ~9 mg/kg of succinylcholine. Hence, the most probable diagnosis is phase II blockade leading to prolonged apnea.

question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Can be given intratracheally

Intravenous Adrenaline is the drug of choice for CPR. However, adrenaline can be given intratracheally also. The concentration required for intratracheal administration is 2-2.5 times more than required for the IV route.

Option B: Intracardiac injection is not recommended as it can cause myocardial damage. Recommended routes for adrenaline are intravenous, intraosseous (children), and intra-tracheal.

Option C: Adrenaline converts fine fibrillation to coarse fibrillation which then responds well to defibrillation.

Option D: Adrenaline is available as a 1 mL injection containing 1 mg of adrenaline in 1:1000 concentration. The dose used in cardiac arrest is 1mg of adrenaline every 3-5 minutes, usually given as 1ml in 1:1000 concentration or 10ml in 1:10,000 concentration (more preferred since in cardiac arrest peripheral circulation is absent; hence larger volume is required for the drug to reach the central circulation).

Respiratory effects of Halothane:

  • Halothane is considered a potent bronchodilator, as it often reverses asthma-induced bronchospasm.
  • This action is not inhibited by α-adrenergic blocking agents.
  • Halothane attenuates airway reflexes and relaxes bronchial smooth muscle by inhibiting intracellular calcium mobilization.
  • Halothane also depresses clearance of mucus from the respiratory tract (mucociliary function), promoting postoperative hypoxia and atelectasis.
  • Halothane limits the increase in minute ventilation that normally accompanies a rise in PaCo2.
  • Hypoxic drive is severely depressed by even low concentrations of Halothane (0.1 MAC).
  • Apnoeic threshold also rises.

Effects of inhalational agents:

  • All inhalational agents are bronchodilator maximum with the Halothane, hence inhalational agent of choice in bronchial asthma is Halothane.
  • Inhalational agent cause respiratory depression to some extent, maximum is seen with Enflurane.
  • Maximum inhibition of respiration in relation to the ventilator response to the hypercarbia and hypoxia is seen with the Halothane only.
  • All inhalational agents vaso-dilate the pulmonary vascular bed by blunting the Hypoxic Pulmonary Vasoconstriction Response (HPV Response) which is seen maximally with the Halothane.
  • Ketamine is the intravenous agent of choice in case of asthmatics.

question.text: What is the most common ca​use of cardiac arrest in ​children?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Asphyxia

In children, the more common cause of cardiac arrest is asphyxia rather than ventricular fibrillation.

Even though asphyxia is the more common cause, pediatric resuscitation starts with chest compressions rather than rescue breaths as in adults for simplicity in training. This is because the cycle of 30 chest compressions before rescue breathing delays ventilation for only 15 to 20 seconds.

During cardiopulmonary resuscitation of infants and children, the ratio of chest compression to rescue breaths is 30:2 for a single rescuer and 15:2 if 2 or more rescuers are present. In adults, the ratio is 30:2 irrespective of the number of rescuers.

In infants and children, the depth of compression should be at least one-third of the anteroposterior diameter of the chest which is about 5 cm in children and 4 cm in infants.

question.text: The blood report of a pati‌ent shows increased uric ‍acid levels. All of the f‍ollowing could be a possi‌ble underlying pathology ‍except?

Other options:

Option A: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency, known as von Gierke's disease or glycogen storage disease type I, is characterized by severe fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, and hepatomegaly. In this case, glycogen is present in the liver but cannot be broken down efficiently into glucose.

Option B: Hereditary fructose intolerance occurs due to deficiency of the enzyme aldolase B. It is characterized by profound hypoglycemia and vomiting after consumption of fructose. Fructose-induced hypoglycemia occurs despite the presence of high glycogen reserves because fructose-1-phosphate allosterically inhibits liver glycogen phosphorylase. The sequestration of inorganic phosphate leads to depletion of ATP and hyperuricemia.

Option C: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder due to a complete deficiency of the HGPRT enzyme. This deficiency results in an inability to salvage hypoxanthine or guanine resulting in increased levels of phospho-ribosyl pyrophosphate (PRPP) and decreased levels of inosine monophosphate (IMP) and guanosine monophosphate (GMP). This causes increased de novo purine synthesis and excessive amounts of uric acid. Patients present with self-mutilating behavior, delayed developmental milestones, positive family history, and hyperuricemia

Integrins

  • Integrins consist of an α and a β subunit linked noncovalently.
  • Each subunit contains extracellular, transmembrane, and intracellular segments.
  • The extracellular segments bind to various cell surface proteins that possess Arg-Gly-Asp sequences (eg, several components of the extracellular matrix).

Selectins

  • Leukocytes and endothelial cells contain cell surface lectins, called selectins, which participate in intercellular adhesion.
  • Selectins are single-chain Ca2+-binding transmembrane proteins; the amino terminals contain the lectin domain, which is involved in binding to specific carbohydrate ligands.
  • Interactions between selectins on the neutrophil cell surface and glycoproteins on the endothelial cell trap the neutrophils temporarily, so that they roll over the endothelial surface.

question.text: Which of the following is ​true about DNA replicatio​n?

options.text: Replication can occur only​ from a single stranded D​NA template
options.label: A
B
options.text: Replication can occur only​ from a double stranded D​NA template

options.label: C
options.text: Deoxynucleotide polymeriza​tion is catalyzed by heli​cases
Only DNA polymerase functi​ons at the replication fo​rk
options.label: D

question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Replication can occur only from a single stranded DNA template

In all cells, replication can occur only from a single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) template.

Steps of DNA replication:

  • Identification of the origins of replication
  • ATP hydrolysis-driven unwinding of dsDNA to provide an ssDNA template
  • Formation of the replication fork; synthesis of RNA primer
  • Initiation of DNA synthesis and elongation
  • Formation of replication bubbles with ligation of the newly synthesized DNA segments
  • Reconstitution of chromatin structure

The replication fork is formed when DNA helicase unwinds a short segment of the parent dsDNA. Primase initiates the synthesis of an RNA primer. DNA polymerase then initiates DNA synthesis (deoxynucleotide polymerisation) in the 3' to 5' direction. Hence, helicase, primase and polymerases act at the replication fork.
