question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Estimated average requirement +2 standard deviation

Recommended dietary allowance (RDA) is calculated by using the formula, RDA = EAR + 2SD.  

Estimated average requirement (EAR): The EAR is the average daily nutrient intake level estimated to meet the requirement of one-half of healthy individuals in a particular life stage and gender group.

Recommended dietary allowance (RDA): The RDA is the average daily dietary intake level that is sufficient to meet the nutrient requirements of nearly all individuals in a life stage and gender group. The RDA is calculated based on EAR and is set above the EAR to provide a margin of safety for most individuals. So, RDA is set 2SDs above the EAR.

question.text: A patient presented with s​ymptoms of delayed adapta​tion to vision in dark pl​aces, a gritty sensation ‌in the eyes, and dry eyes​. Examination shows soft ‍corneas. Which of the fol​lowing is deficient in hi‌s retina?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Retinal

This patient with difficult dark vision and gritty sensations in the eye with findings of soft corneas suggests vitamin A deficiency. In the retina, a form of vitamin A called retinal (11-cis retinaldehyde) plays an important role in Wald's visual cycle. Its deficiency leads to vision defects.

Rhodopsin, the visual pigment of the rod cells in the retina, consists of 11-cis retinal specifically bound to the protein opsin. When rhodopsin is exposed to light, a series of photochemical isomerizations occurs. This results in the bleaching of the visual pigment and release of all-trans-retinal and opsin. This process triggers a nerve impulse that is transmitted by the optic nerve to the brain.

The image given below shows Wald's visual cycle.

question.text: Glycosylation is known for​ its role in the followin​g processes except for __​______.

options.label: B
options.text: Anchoring trans-membrane p​roteins by increasing hyd​rophobicity

question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Anchoring trans-membrane proteins by increasing hydrophobicity

Glycosylation does not anchor trans-membrane proteins by increasing hydrophobicity.

Sugar chains:

  • increase the hydrophilicity of glycosylated proteins.
  • Change physicochemical properties of the protein such as solubility, viscosity, charge, conformation, and denaturation
  • Provide binding sites for various molecules
  • Provide cell surface recognition signals
  • Ensure correct folding of proteins and target incorrectly folded proteins for transport from the endoplasmic reticulum back to the cytosol for catabolism
  • Protect peptide hormones and other plasma proteins against clearance by the liver
  • Permit anchoring of extracellular proteins in the cell membrane, and of intracellular proteins inside subcellular organelles
  • Direct intracellular migration, sorting and secretion of proteins

question.text: During the routine follow-​up of a 9-month-old child​, you notice a peculiar b​oiled cabbage odor. What ‌is the most likely diagno​sis?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hypermethioninemia

Boiled cabbage odor in urine, sweat, and breath occurs in hypermethioninemia. Dimethylsulphide, a metabolite of methionine, causes the characteristic boiled cabbage smell.

People with a genetic deficiency of α/β-methionine adenosyltransferase present with hypermethioninemia and neural demyelination. However, they're usually asymptomatic until early adulthood.

Methionine adenosyltransferase converts methionine to S-adenosyl Methionine (SAM) - a principal methyl donor. Hence the enzyme deficincy causes excess accumulation of methionine and its broken down to metabolites.

question.text: Which of the following is ​false regarding the role ​of insulin on lipid metab​olism?

options.label: B
options.text: Increasing the transport o​f glucose into the cells

question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Inhibition of pyruvate dehydrogenase

Inhibition of pyruvate dehydrogenase is not an action of insulin. Insulin activates the pyruvate dehydrogenase enzyme.

Insulin stimulates lipogenesis by the following mechanisms:

  • Decreasing the level of intracellular cAMP. This favours dephosphorylation of acetyl-CoA carboxylase, resulting in its activation. 
  • Increasing acetyl-CoA carboxylase activity. This accelerates the rate-limiting step of fatty acid synthesis.
  • Increasing the transport of glucose into the cell and activation of pyruvate dehydrogenase in the adipose tissue. This yields more acetyl CoA for fatty acid synthesis.

question.text: Accumulation of which of t​he following substances i​s responsible for Farber’​s disease?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ceramide

Accumulation of ceramide is seen in Farber’s disease.

Farber's disease occurs due to deficiency of ceramidase, which catalyses the breakdown of ceramide to fatty acid and sphingosine. Affected children present with painful joint swelling and nodules, progressive joint deformity, hoarse cry and breathing difficulty, mental retardation and failure to thrive.

question.text: Which is the first interme​diate in the conversion o​f cholesterol to bile aci​ds?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 7-hydroxycholesterol

The first intermediate in the synthesis of bile acids is 7α-hydroxycholesterol

This reaction is catalyzed by the enzyme 7α-hydroxylase, a microsomal CYP450 enzyme, which requires NADPH, oxygen, and vitamin C as co-factors. It is the rate-limiting step in the synthesis of bile acids.

Regulation of bile acid synthesis occurs by feedback inhibition of 7α-hydroxylase via the Farnesoid X receptor. When the level of bile acids in the enterohepatic circulation increases, FXR is activated and transcription of the enzyme is suppressed.

Other options:

Option A: 7-dehydrocholesterol is an intermediate in the conversion of cholesterol to vitamin D.

Option C: Lanosterol is an intermediate in the synthesis of cholesterol.

Option D: Ergosterol is a sterol found in plants.

question.text: Which of the following enz​yme does not participate ​in a ping-pong reaction?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Aldolase

Aldolase does not participate in a ping-pong reaction. Ping pong reactions are a type of Bi-Bi reaction.

Bi-Bi reaction is a two substrate two product reaction. Most of the Bi-Bi reactions follow Michaelis-Menten kinetics. There are three types of Bi-Bi reactions:

  • Ordered Bi-Bi reaction: Example- NAD(P)H-dependant oxidoreductases.
  • Random Bi-Bi reaction: Example- Most kinases and dehydrogenases.
  • Ping pong reaction: Example- Serine proteases, aminotransferases and pyruvate carboxylase.

question.text: Which of the following is ​a component of cytochrome‌ oxidase?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cu2+

Cu2+ is a component of cytochrome oxidase. Cytochrome C oxidase is complex IV of the ETC.

Components include two heme groups a and a3, and copper (Cu). It is an irreversible complex.

It receives electrons from complex III (Q-cytochrome C oxidoreductase). Components are Cyt b, Cyt c1. 

The final electron acceptor from complex IV is oxygen and it is reduced to water.

question.text: ATP can also be hydrolyzed​ directly to AMP, with th‌e release of PPi by _____‌____.
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Acyl-CoA synthetase

ATP can also be hydrolyzed directly to AMP, with the release of PPi by Acyl-CoA synthetase enzyme.

This occurs in the activation of long-chain fatty acids. This reaction is accompanied by the loss of free energy as heat, which ensures that the activation reaction will go to the right. It is further aided by the hydrolytic splitting of PPi, catalyzed by inorganic pyrophosphatase, a reaction that itself has a large ΔG0′ of −19.2 kJ/mol.

question.text: Which of the following enz​ymes is not present in th‌e mitochondrial matrix?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. ATP synthase

ATP synthase is located on the inner mitochondrial membrane, not mitochondrial matrix.

Note: In contrast to the other enzymes of citric acid cycle, succinate dehydrogenase is bound to the inner surface of inner mitochondrial membrane. Succinate dehydrogenase functions as complex II of electron transport chain.

question.text: What is fructose 2,6 bisph​osphate?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Positive allosteric regulator of PFK1

Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate is the most potent positive allosteric activator of phosphofructokinase-1 and inhibitor of fructose 1, 6-bisphosphatase. It is not an intermediate of glycolysis.

Fructose 2, 6-bisphosphate is formed by phosphorylation of fructose-6-phosphate by phosphofructokinase-2. It acts as an intracellular signal, indicating that glucose is abundant and hence causes an increase in the rate of glycolysis during the well-fed state.

question.text: Which of the following is ​an allosteric activator o‌f muscle glycogen phospho‌rylase?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 5'AMP

5'AMP serves as the allosteric activator of muscle glycogen phosphorylase.

Glycogen phosphorylase catalyzes the rate-limiting step in glycogenolysis. It is regulated by allosteric mechanisms and covalent modification by reversible phosphorylation and dephosphorylation in response to hormone action.

In both liver and muscle, the glycogen phosphorylase is:

  • Activated by phosphorylation catalyzed by phosphorylase kinase (to yield phosphorylase a)
  • Inactivated by dephosphorylation catalyzed by protein phosphatase-1 (to yield phosphorylase b)

Muscle phosphorylase differs from the liver isoenzyme in having a binding site for 5′ AMP. It acts as an allosteric activator of the (inactive) dephosphorylated b-form of the enzyme.

  Allosteric Activator Allosteric Inhibitor
Liver  
  • ATP
  • Glucose-6-phosphate
  • Free glucose
Muscle 

    5' AMP
  • ATP
  • Glucose-6-phosphate

question.text: Tetrahydrobiopterin is a c​oenzyme for all of the fo‌llowing except:
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Homogentisate oxidase

Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) is a coenzyme for the following enzymes:

  • Phenylalanine hydroxylase
  • Tyrosine hydroxylase
  • Tryptophan hydroxylase
  • Nitric oxide synthase

Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) resembles folic acid, but it is not a vitamin. It is derived from GTP.

question.text: A 3-week-old baby presente‌d with 2 episodes of fits‌. On examination, repetit‍ive movements as if the b‌aby was boxing and bicycl​ing were noticed. His uri‌ne had a sweetish odor an‌d was positive for the di‍nitrophenylhydrazine test‍. Blood concentrations of​ which of the following a​mino acids is relatively ​higher in the baby?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Leucine

The above clinical scenario with a positive urine dinitrophenylhydrazine test is suggestive of maple syrup urine disease (MSUD). The levels of leucine are higher than the other three amino acids.

MSUD is an autosomal recessive disorder which occurs due to deficiency of branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complex. This impairs the metabolism of branched-chain amino acids valine, leucine, isoleucine and alloisoleucine. These amino acids, particularly leucine and its metabolite accumulate in the blood, causing toxic effects on the brain.

The affected child develops poor feeding and vomiting a few days after birth. There is a period of hypertonicity with a period of flaccidity in between. These appear as repetitive boxing and bicycling movements. The babies may also have hypoglycemia, but this is not corrected by the administration of glucose. The urine, sweat, and cerumen of the baby have a sweetish maple syrup-like odor.

Laboratory investigations will show increased levels of branched-chain amino acids in the plasma and urine. Leucine levels are usually higher than isoleucine, valine, and alloisoleucine. Since the patient excretes ketoacids in the urine, the urine will be positive for the dinitrophenylhydrazine test.

Treatment involves controlled intake of branched-chain amino acids using commercially available formulas and judicious supplementation of isoleucine and valine. Very high levels of leucine are removed by hemodialysis.

question.text: What does the term folate ‌trap refer to?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Accumulation of methyl tetrahydrofolate

The term folate trap refers to accumulation of methyl tetrahydrofolate with deficiency of tetrahydrofolate. It is seen in vitamin B12 deficiency.

Vitamin B12 acts as a cofactor of methionine synthase, an enzyme involved in the regeneration of tetrahydrofolate from methyl-tetrahydrofolate. Hence, vitamin B12 deficiency leads to folate deficiency.

Since vitamin B12 is also linked to regeneration of methionine from homocysteine, there is hyperhomocysteinemia as well. It increases the risk of atherosclerosis, hypertension and thrombosis.

question.text: An infant with abdominal d‌istension, fever, and jau‌ndice was brought to the ‍pediatric OPD. On further‌ evaluation, a diagnosis ​of an autosomal recessive‌ disorder due to a defect‌ in the enzyme fumarylace‍toacetate hydrolase was a‍rrived at. What is the li​kely disorder?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hepatorenal tyrosinemia

The autosomal recessive disorder due to a defect in the enzyme fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase in a child with abdominal distension, fever and jaundice is associated with Hepatorenal tyrosinemia (Type 1 tyrosinemia or tyrosinosis). It is the most common type of tyrosinemia. 

There are three types of tyrosinemias:

  • Type 1 (Hepatorenal tyrosinemia):
    • Defective enzyme: Fumaryl acetoacetate hydrolase 
    • Inherited as an autosomal recessive trait
    • Clinical features: Liver failure, hypoglycemia, boiled cabbage odour in the urine, and mental retardation. 
  • Type 2 (Oculocutaneous tyrosinemia/Richner-Hanhart syndrome):
    • Defective enzyme: Tyrosine transaminase 
    • Clinical features: Palmoplantar keratosis, painful corneal erosions, photophobia, mental retardation are seen. 
  • Type 3 (Neonatal tyrosinemia): 
    • Defective enzyme: 4-Hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase 
    • Clinical features: Normal liver function, developmental delay, seizures and intermittent ataxia are seen.
  • Hawkinsuria
    • Defective enzyme: 4-Hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase 
    • Inherited as an autosomal dominant trait
    • Clinical features: Transient failure to thrive and metabolic acidosis in infancy

question.text: An adolescent boy presents‌ with jaundice and tiredn‌ess. On investigation, hi‍s AST was 150 IU/L, ALT w‌as 175 IU/L and bilirubin​ was 4.5mg/dl. Serum ceru‌loplasmin levels were fou‌nd to be low. Which of th‍e following minerals is u‍sed in the treatment of t​his condition?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Zinc

An adolescent with jaundice, elevated AST, ALT and low serum ceruloplasmin likely has Wilson’s disease. Zinc is used in the treatment of this condition.

Wilson’s disease is an autosomonal recessive disorder. It is charactered by mutations of the ATP7B gene, resulting in decreased biliary copper excretion and ceruloplasmin formation. The accumulation of copper leads to liver disease, hemolysis, a movement disorder neurologic disease, and/or psychiatric illness.

Elemental zinc is commonly used as a maintenance therapy along with chelating agents. Zinc acts by blocking the intestinal absorption of copper. It can also be used as first-line therapy in pregnancy.

question.text: A 2-month-old infant is fo‌und to be hypotonic, with‌ a high forehead, large a‍nterior fontanelle, marke‌dly separated cranial sut​ures, and hepatomegaly. F‌urther investigations con‌firmed a diagnosis of the‍ cerebro-hepato-renal syn‍drome. Which of the follo​wing biochemical findings​ would not be seen in thi​s case?

options.label: A
options.text: Elevated levels of very lo‌ng chain fatty acids

question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Elevated plasmalogen content of phospholipids

In cerebro-hepato-renal syndrome or Zellweger syndrome, there is a decreased level of plasmalogens.

Zellweger syndrome is caused by mutations in the peroxins (PEX) family of genes. As a result of this, there is a defective transport of the proteins to the peroxisomes. It severely impairs the functions of peroxisomes, resulting in defective beta-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids (VLCFA), defective alpha oxidation, and impaired synthesis of bile acids and plasmalogens.

The child presents with

  • Dysmorphic facial features like wide anterior fontanelles markedly separated cranial sutures, epicanthal folds, broad nasal bridge, hypoplastic supraorbital ridges, etc.
  • Profound developmental delay, profound hypotonia with depressed deep tendon reflexes, neonatal seizures, and impaired hearing
  • Calcific stippling of the epiphyses
  • Renal cysts
  • Hepatomegaly

Biochemical findings will show:

  • Accumulation of very-long-chain fatty acids, phytanic acid, and pipecolic acids
  • Abnormalities of the synthesis of bile acids
  • Marked reduction of plasmalogens
  • Elevated levels of plasma phytanic acid

There is no appropriate treatment for Zellweger syndrome. It is very severe, and infants rarely survive beyond six months of age.

question.text: A 1-year-old child is brou‌ght to the pediatrician w‌ith complaints that the c‍hild does not crawl or si‌t, does not smile, and do​es not recognize the moth‌er. During the examinatio‌n, it is noted that the c‍hild has a very fair comp‍lexion, light color hair,​ smaller head circumferen​ce for age, growth, and d​evelopmental delay. The c‌hild has a mousey odor. W‌hich of the following are​ used in the management o​f this condition? Pegvali​ase Tyrosine restriction ​Large neutral amino acids​ Sapropterin dihydrochlor‌ide Taliglucerase alpha
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 3, and 4

The given clinical manifestations point to the diagnosis of phenylketonuria (PKU). Pegvaliase, large neutral amino acids, and sapropterin dihydrochloride are used in the management of this condition. Tyrosine supplementation is used, and not restriction.

Phenylketonuria commonly occurs due to a defect in the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase, PAH (classic phenylketonuria). Less commonly it can also occur due to a defect in the enzymes producing tetrahydrobiopterin. These defects result in the impaired conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine. The patient develops clinical features due to elevated levels of phenylalanine metabolites and decreased levels of tyrosine.

Clinical features 

  • Intellectual disability, developmental delay, microcephaly, and seizures- due to accumulation of phenylalanine metabolites and decreased tyrosine.
  • Fair hair, light skin color, and blue eyes- Tyrosine is needed for the synthesis of melanin. Reduced levels of tyrosine lead to the decreased melanin synthesis.
  • The babies have a mousey odor due to the accumulation of phenylacetic acid.

Laboratory investigations that are useful in the diagnosis are

  • Blood levels of phenylalanine
  • Ferric chloride test
  • Guthrie test
  • Tandem mass spectrometry

Management

A diet low in phenylalanine and supplementation of tyrosine can prevent the mental retardation of PKU. The blood levels of phenylalanine are maintained between 2 and 6 mg/dL.

Administration of large neutral amino acid supplementation are useful. Tyrosine, tryptophan, leucine, isoleucine, valine, methionine, histidine, and phenylalanine share the same transporter for transport through intestinal membrane and blood-brain barrier. Hence, these amino acids compete and prevent the transport of phenylalanine.

Sapropterin is a synthetic form of BH4, which acts as a cofactor in patients with residual PAH activity. 

Pegvaliase is a phenylalanine ammonia-lyase (PAL), that converts phenylalanine to ammonia and trans-cinnamic acid.

Eliglustat, taliglucerase alpha, velaglucerase alpha, imiglucarase, miglustat are approved by FDA for Gaucher's disease treatment.

question.text: A patient was advised to t‌ake green leafy vegetable‌s as a natural dietary so‍urce of vitamin K. Which ‌is the compound that acts​ as the source of vitamin‌ K in these vegetables?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Phylloquinone

The normal dietary source of vitamin K is phylloquinone or vitamin K1, found in green leafy vegetables.

Vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin and its deficiency leads to bleeding disorders.

Three compounds have the biological activity of vitamin K:

  • Phylloquinone (Vitamin K1) is the normal dietary source of Vitamin K that is found in green leafy vegetables.
  • Menaquinone (Vitamin K2) is synthesized by intestinal bacteria.
  • Menadione (Vitamin K3) and menadiol diacetate are synthetic compounds that are metabolized to phylloquinone.

question.text: Which of the following are​ enantiomers?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. D-mannose and L-mannose

D-mannose and L-mannose are enantiomers. Enantiomers are mirror images of each other.

The designation of a sugar isomer as the D- or L- form is determined by its spatial relationship to the parent compound of the carbohydrates, that is, the three-carbon sugar glyceraldehyde. The orientation of the —H and —OH groups around the penultimate carbon atom determines whether the sugar belongs to the D- or L- series. When the —OH group on the penultimate carbon atom of the sugar is on the right side, then the sugar is designated as a D- isomer. When the –OH group is on the left, it is an L-isomer.

Naturally occurring monosaccharides are D-sugars and naturally occurring amino acids are L-isomers. Racemase enzyme interconverts between D and L isomers.

Examples of enantiomers include D-glucose and L-glucose, D-fructose and L-fructose and D-mannose and L-mannose

question.text: Which of the following enz​ymes is involved in the p‌rocess of oxidative deami‌nation?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Glutamate dehydrogenase

Glutamate dehydrogenase is involved in the process of oxidative deamination.

In contrast to transamination (transfer amino groups), oxidative deamination by glutamate dehydrogenase results in the liberation of the amino group as free ammonia. Glutamate dehydrogenase can use NADH or NADPH during oxidative deamination.

question.text: Primary hyperoxaluria is d​ue to the defect in the m‌etabolism of _____.
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Glycine

Primary hyperoxaluria is a defect in the metabolism of glycine.

The main defect in primary hyperoxaluria type I is the deficiency of the alanine glyoxalate aminotransferase in liver peroxisomes causing failure to catabolize glyoxylate formed by the deamination of glycine. This leads to a gross overproduction of oxalate, leading to the formation of oxalate stones and subsequent kidney damage.

question.text: Rossman fold-associated NA​DH domain is found in ___‌__.
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lactate dehydrogenase

Rossmann fold-associated NADH domain is found in lactate dehydrogenase.

Rossmann fold is an N-terminal NAD(P)+ -binding domain. It is seen in:

  • Lactate dehydrogenase
  • Alcohol dehydrogenase
  • Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase
  • Malate dehydrogenase
  • D-glycerate dehydrogenase
  • 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase
  • Formate dehydrogenase

question.text: Which of the following enz​ymes is required for the ‌only energy-requiring ste‌p of fatty acid oxidation‍?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thiokinase

The only energy-requiring step in fatty acid oxidation is catalyzed by the thiokinase enzyme.

In the presence of ATP and coenzyme A, the enzyme acyl-CoA synthetase or thiokinase catalyses the conversion of a fatty acid to acyl-CoA, the active form of fatty acid for oxidation.

question.text: A 3-year-old child is bein​g evaluated for anosmia, ‌deafness, and unstable ga‌it. Further investigation‍ reveals retinitis pigmen​tosa on fundoscopy and ca‍rdiac rhythm abnormalitie‍s on ECG. A rare congenit​al disease affecting lipi​d metabolism is being sus‌pected. Deficiency of whi​ch of the following enzym​es is expected to be foun​d in this patient?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Phytanoyl CoA α-hydroxylase

The given clinical vignette is suggestive of Refsum’s disease, characterized by impaired alpha oxidation due to the deficiency of phytanoyl CoA α-hydroxylase (also known as phytanic acid alpha oxidase).

Refsum disease is a rare, autosomal recessive disorder caused by a deficiency of peroxisomal phytanoyl CoA α-hydroxylase, an enzyme involved in the alpha oxidation of phytanic acid (branched-chain fatty acid). This results in the accumulation of phytanic acid in the plasma and tissues.

The manifestation of classic adult Refsum disease includes

  • Retinitis pigmentosa
  • Peripheral neuropathy
  • Ataxia
  • Ichthyosis
  • Anosmia
  • Deafness
  • Occasionally cardiac arrhythmias

Treatment: Restriction of dietary phytanic acid (found in dairy products and green leafy vegetables).

question.text: A 6-month-old infant with ​progressive failure to th‌rive and milestone regres‌sion is being evaluated f‍or an inborn error of met​abolism. On examination, ‍hypotonia, apathy, deafne‍ss, hepatosplenomegaly, a​nd generalized lymphadeno​pathy are present. Fundus‌ examination is shown bel​ow. A liver biopsy shows ​foamy hepatocytes loaded ​with sphingomyelin. Elect​ron microscopy reveals ze​bra bodies. What is the l‌ikely diagnosis?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Niemann-Pick disease type A

Progressive failure to thrive, milestone regression, hypotonia, apathy, deafness, hepatosplenomegaly, and generalized lymphadenopathy with the cherry-red spot on fundus examination suggests a diagnosis of Niemann-Pick disease type A.

 Niemann-Pick disease is a lysosomal storage disorder due to an inherited deficiency of sphingomyelinase. This results in the accumulation of sphingomyelin in the monocyte-macrophage system. Type A disease is a severe infantile form. Infants present with extensive neurologic involvement (hypotonia, milestone regression, apathy), marked visceral accumulations of sphingomyelin (hepatosplenomegaly, foamy hepatocytes, zebra bodies on EM), progressive wasting and early death within the first 3 years of life.

In contrast, patients with Niemann-Pick disease type B have organomegaly but generally no CNS involvement.

question.text: Which of the following is ​an activator of the key e‌nzyme required in reverse‌ cholesterol transport?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Apo A-I

Apo A-I is the activator of Lecithin: cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT), the enzyme present in HDL facilitating reverse cholesterol transport.

Lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT) is activated by apo A-I which then converts free cholesterol(amphipathic) in HDL to cholesterol ester(hydrophobic). As a result the initial discoidal shape now becomes spherical.

This facilitates reverse cholesterol transport.

Clinical correlation: Familial LCAT deficiency will lead to failure of reverse cholesterol transport resulting in cholesterol deposition in specific peripheral tissues - the cornea, kidneys, and erythrocytes. Major complications include premature atherosclerosis, renal failure, anemia and corneal opacities. HDL cholesterol level is decreased.

question.text: What is the first step in ​synthesis of eicosanoids?‌
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Activation of hydrolase

The first step in the synthesis of eicosanoids involves the activation of hydrolase.

Eicosanoid synthesis is governed by the rate of release of arachidonic acid from membrane lipids in response to appropriate stimuli (Eg: Increased calcium). These stimuli activate hydrolases, including phospholipase A2, which releases arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids. The released arachidonic acid is then converted into:

  • Prostaglandins and thromboxanes by the cyclooxygenase (COX) pathway. PGH2 synthase is the first enzyme of this pathway. 
  • Leukotrienes and lipoxins by the lipooxygenase (LOX) pathway

question.text: What is the by-product of ​the ​reaction catalyzed b‌y cytosolic hydroxymethyl‌bilane synthase in heme s‍ynthesis?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. NH3

The by-product of the reaction catalyzed by cytosolic hydroxymethylbilane (HMB) synthase in heme synthesis is ammonia (NH3). 

HMB synthase is also known as porphobilinogen deaminase or uroporphyrinogen 1 synthase. It catalyses the condensation of 4 molecules of porphobilinogen to release hydroxymethylbilane and 4 molecules of NH3. 

4 Porphobilinogen + H2O -------> Hydroxymethylbilane + 4 NH3

question.text: Which of the following is ​the rate-limiting enzyme ‌in the hepatic biosynthes‌is of heme? (ALA - α- ami‍nolevulinate)
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. ALA Synthase

The rate-limiting enzyme in the hepatic biosynthesis of heme is mitochondrial ALA synthase. 

ALA synthase (ALAS) is a mitochondrial enzyme catalysing the conversion of succinyl CoA and glycine to ALA. There are two isozymes of ALA synthase. ALAS-1 is expressed throughout the body. It is induced by drugs whose metabolism requires cytochromes (hemoprotein). Heme, probably acting through an aporepressor molecule, acts as a negative regulator of the synthesis of ALAS-1 i.e. ALAS-1 synthesis decreases in the presence of heme. 

ALAS-2 is expressed in the erythrocyte precursor cells. It is neither induced by drugs nor is its feedback regulated by heme.

question.text: Which of the following is ​not a hepatic porphyria?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Erythropoietic protoporphyria

Erythropoietic protoporphyria is not a type of hepatic porphyria. 

Porphyrias are classified into erythropoietic and hepatic porphyrias, based on the location of accumulation of heme pathway intermediates:

  1. Erythropoietic porphyrias:
    1. The overproduction of heme pathway intermediates occurs primarily in bone marrow erythroid cells.
    2. They are characterized by cutaneous symptoms and appear in early childhood.
    3. Examples: Congenital erythropoietic porphyria, erythropoietic protoporphyria, X-linked protoporphyria
  2. Hepatic porphyrias:
    1. The overproduction of heme pathway intermediates occurs primarily in the liver.
    2. Acute hepatic porphyrias are characterised by neurologic symptoms and present acutely. Examples: Acute intermittent porphyria, hereditary coproporphyria, variegate porphyria, ALA dehydratase deficient porphyria
    3. Chronic hepatic porphyrias present in adulthood with photosensitivity. Example: Porphyria cutanea tarda

question.text: All of the following is tr​ue about isoenzymes excep‌t ________.

options.text: They have the same number ​of charged amino acids.
options.label: B

options.text: They can be separated by e​lectrophoresis.
options.label: C

question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. They have the same number of charged amino acids.

Isoenzymes do not have the same number of charged amino acids.

Isoenzymes are physically distinct forms of the same enzyme. They catalyze the same reaction but differ in the following:

  • Amino acid sequence and the number of charged amino acids
  • Subunit composition: CK-1 contains BB while CK-2 contains MB subunits
  • Electrophoretic mobility: CK-1 moves faster than CK-3
  • Tissue localization: CK-1 is present in the brain, CK-2 in the heart
  • Substrate affinity: Glucokinase has low affinity but hexokinase has high affinity.

question.text: Which bond is catalyzed by​ amylase enzyme?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. α(1 → 4) glycoside bonds

α(1 → 4) glycoside bonds are catalyzed by amylase enzymes.

Starch is a polymer of glucose that is linked by α(1 → 4) glycoside bonds, which is catalyzed by salivary and pancreatic amylases.

Hydrolysis of starch yields dextrin.

Then the hydrolysis of dextrin will yield a mixture of glucose, maltose, maltotriose, and small branched dextrins.

question.text: Specific dynamic action is​ maximum for ______
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Proteins

Specific dynamic action is maximum for proteins.

Specific dynamic action/diet-induced thermogenesis/ thermic effect of food is the extra energy needed by the body for digestion, absorption, and disposal of ingested nutrients.

Specific dynamic action magnitude depends on the composition of the food consumed:

  • Carbohydrates: 5 to 15% of the energy consumed
  • Fats: at most 5 to 15 %
  • Protein: 20 to 35% 

The energy generated by the metabolism of the macronutrients is used for three energy-requiring processes that occur in the body:

  • Resting metabolic rate
  • Thermic effect of food (formerly termed specific dynamic action)
  • Physical activity

question.text: A farmer presents with loo​se stools, depression, an‌d photosensitive dermatit‌is as shown in the image.‍ On examination, a red be​efy tongue is noted. Whic‍h of the following is not‍ associated with this pre​sentation?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Wernicke's encephalopathy

Loose stools, depression, beefy red tongue and Casal's necklace, as seen in the image, is suggestive of pellagra. Pellagra-like symptoms are not seen in Wernicke's encephalopathy.

Pellagra is caused by niacin deficiency, either due to dietary deficiency or deficient conversion of tryptophan to niacin. Hence, pellagra-like symptoms are seen in:

  • Hartnup disease: It is an autosomal recessive disease caused by mutations in the SLC6A19 gene leading to defective membrane transport of tryptophan across PCT (kidney) and enterocytes (intestine). This leads to malabsorption, and hence deficiency of tryptophan.
  • Carcinoid syndrome: Due to excess conversion of tryptophan to serotonin, there is a decreased level of tryptophan availavle for niacin synthesis
  • Pyridoxine deficiency: Pyridoxine is required as the co-factor of kynureninase, an enzyme in the pathway of niacin synthesis.
  • Maize/corn rich diet: In these grans, niacin is in bound form (niacytin form) and is not absorbed.
  • Jowar diet (Sorghum): The increased leucine content inhibits QPRTase enzyme, an enzyme in the pathway of niacin synthesis.

question.text: Which of the following met​hod is not used for the m‌easurement of body free r‌adical burden?

options.text: Measurement of pentane and​ methane in exhaled air
options.label: B

question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Direct assay of free radicals

Direct assay of free radicals is not used for the measurement of total body free radical burden.

This is because free radicals are extremely reactive and short-lived. Free radical activity is usually assessed by indirect methods. Thus, the total body free radical burden can be estimated by measuring the products of lipid peroxidation using the following methods:

  • FOX (Ferrous oxidation in xylenol orange) assay
  • Estimation of dialdehydes: The dialdehydes formed from lipid peroxides can be measured by reaction with thiobarbituric acid.
  • Measurement of pentane and methane in exhaled air

Note: Radical damage to unsaturated fatty acids in cell membranes and plasma lipoproteins leads to the formation of lipid peroxides.

question.text: Zinc is a cofactor of whic​h of the following enzyme‌s?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Carbonic anhydrase

Zinc acts as a cofactor for carbonic anhydrase.

Zinc is a component of many metalloenzymes including carbonic anhydrase II. Zinc also has antioxidant activity as extracellular superoxide dismutase is zinc-dependent.

Chronic zinc deficiency can cause stunted growth, hypogeusia (decreased taste sensation) hypogeusia, impaired immune function, hypogonadism and hypopigmented hair. Acrodermatitis enteropathica is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by abnormalities in zinc absorption.

question.text: Which of the following clo​ning vectors has linear D‌NA?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Phages

Phages have linear DNA into which foreign DNA can be inserted at several restriction enzyme sites.

Amplification of DNA (cloning) is done using cloning vectors - bacterial plasmids, phages, or cosmids.

Bacterial plasmids are small, circular, duplex DNA molecules whose natural function is to confer antibiotic resistance to the host cell. Cosmid is a plasmid into which the DNA sequences from bacteriophage lambda (λ cos sites) have been inserted. This enables the packaging of plasmid DNA in vitro. They have a small, circular, duplex DNA. (Options B and C)

question.text: Which of the following is ​a primer acting as an acc‌eptor of glucose residues‌ in the process of glycog‍en synthesis?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Protein

A protein named glycogenin is the primer acting as an acceptor of glucose residues in the process of glycogen synthesis.

The ensuing entity is glycosylated further by UDP-glucose. Glycogenin further catalyzes the transfer of seven glucose residues from UDP-Glucose, in 1 → 4 linkages, to form a glycogen primer. This in turn serves as the substrate for the enzyme, glycogen synthase, which is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycogen synthesis.

question.text: Identify the true statemen​t regarding the regulatio‌n of the rate-limiting en‌zyme in de novo purine sy‍nthesis. ATP - Adenosine ​triphosphate GMP - Guanos‍ine monophosphate
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Inhibited by GMP

The rate-limiting enzyme in de novo purine synthesis is phosphoribosylpyrophosphate (PRPP) glutamyl amidotransferase; it is inhibited by GMP which is one of the end products of the pathway & activated by the concentration of glutamine.

De novo purine synthesis involves the synthesis of purines from amphibolic intermediates. The first step of this reaction involves the transfer of two phosphoryl groups from ATP to ribose-5-phosphate form 5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate (PRPP), catalyzed by the enzyme PRPP synthase. PRPP is then converted to 5-phosphoribosylamine by the enzyme PRPP glutamyl amidotransferase, in the presence of glutamine and H2O; this undergoes a series of changes to form inosine monophosphate (IMP).

The IMP formed can then be used for the synthesis of both AMP and GMP by different pathways. Subsequently, one ATP is used for the conversion of AMP to ADP and GMP to GDP; this is followed by the synthesis of GTP from GDP using another phosphoryl group from ATP, while ADP can be converted to ATP by oxidative phosphorylation.

The rate of the reaction is determined by the intracellular concentration of PRPP, which in turn depends on the rate of PRPP synthesis and utilization. The rate of PRPP synthesis depends on the availability of ribose-5-phosphate and on the activity of PRPP synthase, an enzyme whose activity is feedback inhibited by AMP, ADP, GMP, and GDP. Additionally, the enzyme PRPP glutamyl amidotransferase is inhibited by AMP and GMP, the end products of the pathway.

The other compounds that block purine biosynthesis include azaserine, 6-mercaptopurine, methotrexate and mycophenolic acid.

question.text: In which of the following ​conditions would you expe‌ct to see Darier's sign?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Urticaria pigmentosa

Darier's sign is seen in urticaria pigmentosa. It refers to the development of urticaria and erythema around the lesions after mild trauma, including scratching or rubbing of the lesion.

Urticaria pigmentosa is the most common pattern of cutaneous mastocytosis, which occurs due to an increased number of mast cells in the skin. It presents with reddish-brown or pale maculopapules, plaques, nodules in symmetric distribution, sparing the palms and soles.

Darier's sign is not specific for mastocytosis as it is also rarely seen in juvenile xanthogranuloma and acute lymphoblastic leukemia.

Note: Pseudo-Darier sign is seen in soft tissue hamartoma, with piloerection and transient induration after stroking the lesions. Darier's disease is an autosomal dominant disorder, characterized by hyperkeratotic papules and plaques along with nail changes.

question.text: A medical student is visit​ing her grandmother, who ‌is recovering from heart ​surgery. She decides to c‌heer her up by painting h​er nails. She notices tha‍t her nails look odd as s‌een below. What is this f​inding called?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Beau’s lines

This image shows Beau’s lines which are generalized transverse grooves on the nail which may be full or partial thickness. They usually occur a few weeks after a precipitating systemic event like MI, measles, mumps, or pneumonia. 

Isolated transverse grooves in individual nails may occur due to trauma, inflammation, or neurological events.

Option B: Mees or Aldrich–Mees lines or Leukonychia striata are white lines that occur as a 1–2 mm wide transverse band is in the arcuate form of the lunula. They are associated with arsenic and lithium poisoning as well as renal failure.

Option C: Lindsay nails or half-and-half nails are a rare finding where the proximal portion of the nail is white and the distal half is pink, with a sharp line of demarcation between the two halves. They are specific for renal failure.

Option D: Trachyonychia is roughening of nails observed in alopecia areata.

question.text: Identify the most common c‌omplication of a celiac p‌lexus block.
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Postural hypotension

The most common complication of a celiac plexus block is postural hypotension.

This occurs due to the resultant blockade of the lumbar sympathetic chain and the dilation of capacitance vessels in the splanchnic area. Therefore, patients should be adequately hydrated intravenously prior to this procedure and precautions should be taken to minimize the risk of orthostatic lightheadedness or syncope.

The celiac ganglia are found at the level of the body of the L1 vertebra. They are located lateral to the aorta, and posterior to the vena cava and the pancreas.

It is preferred when patients have pain originating from the abdominal viscera, as seen in intra-abdominal cancers.

Due to its proximity to the vena cava, accidental intravascular injection into the vena cava can occur, which can produce a severe systemic reaction. Damage to the retroperitoneal lymph nodes can result in chylothorax. Blocking the sympathetic chain leads to increased gastrointestinal motility due to unopposed parasympathetic activity, resulting in diarrhea.

It may lead to other complications such as pneumothorax, injury to the kidneys or pancreas, hemorrhage, sexual dysfunction, paraplegia due to injury to the lumbar artery of Adamkiewicz, and back pain.

question.text: A woman at 20 weeks of ges‌tation has come for regul‌ar follow-up. Which cardi​ovascular changes listed ‍below should you expect t​o find in this woman?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lateral displacement of apical impulse

The cardiovascular change that would be found in this normal patient is lateral displacement of the apical impulse. 

Cardiac functional changes become apparent in the first eight weeks of gestation. Lateral displacement of the apical impulse occurs due to progressive elevation of the diaphragm. This leads to a larger cardiac shadow on radiographs.

At apical or pulmonary area, systolic murmur may be heard due to decreased blood viscosity and torsion of great vessels. Mammary murmur is a continuous hissing sound heard over the tricuspid area in the left second and third intercostal spaces.

Other options:

All the other options are pathological changes.

Option A: Mid-diastolic and late diastolic murmurs can be seen in conditions like mitral stenosis. 

Option B: Pansystolic murmur can be seen in conditions like chronic mitral regurgitation and ventricular septal defect. 

Option C: Bradycardia in pregnancy can be seen in conditions like maternal complete heart block and cardiac pacemaker users.

question.text: A 70-year-old male patient‌ complaints of fatigue an‌d recurrent infections. H​e also notes epistaxis, v‍isual disturbances and pe​ripheral neuropathy. Peri​pheral smear shows roulea‌ux formation and marrow b‍iopsy shows Dutcher bodie​s. Coomb's test is also p‍ositive. Which of the fol​lowing malignancies does ‍the patient most likely h‌ave?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia

The malignancy that the patient most likely has is Waldenström's macroglobulinemia.

Waldenström macroglobulinemia is a neoplasm of small lymphocytes and a variable number of IgM-secreting plasma cells. It occurs in older adults. It most commonly occurs in association with lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma. It can also be associated with viral infections.

It occurs due to MYD88 L265P somatic mutation. Diffuse marrow infiltration by plasma cells, plasmacytoid lymphocytes, and lymphocytes (all from the same clone) is observed. Normocytic normochromic anaemia is seen with rouleaux formation. Coomb's test is positive. Cells do not form tumor masses or produce lytic lesions. There is hyperviscocity of blood.

Clinical features include lymphadenopathy, hyperviscosity of blood, hepatosplenomegaly, epistaxis, transient paresis, visual disturbance and other non specific symptoms like headache, dizziness, and weakness.

Investigations typically reveal increased levels of IgM. Lymphocytes commonly contain Dutcher bodies (intranuclear inclusions). Bence–Jones proteins are found in 20–30%. Coomb's test is positive. M’ or monoclonal spike is seen. Treatment is usually required when the patient is symptomatic and the preferred drug is ibrutinib. Other first-line drugs include rituximab and bortezomib.

Other options:

Option A: Diffuse large B cell lymphoma is characterized by the presence of large B cells with vesicular chromatin and distinct nucleoli.

Option B: Burkitt's lymphoma is characterized by a starry sky appearance due to the spread of reactive macrophages around the tumor cells against the background of pale cytoplasm. 

Option C: Follicular lymphoma - This is characterized by nodules of varying size with a cleaved nucleus and is composed of lymphocytes.

question.text: The lipid profile of a 48-‌year-old hypertensive mal‌e patient is given below.​ Which of the following a‍ntihypertensives would ha​ve a beneficial effect on​ his lipid profile? Total‌ cholesterol - 320 mg/dL ‍Low-density lipoproteins ​- 220 mg/dL High-density ‍lipoproteins- 40 mg/dL Tr​iglycerides - 299 mg/dL
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Prazosin

The patient in the given scenario has a deranged lipid profile. Among the given drugs, prazosin would have a beneficial effect on the lipid profile of this patient as it decreases LDL and triglyceride levels as well as increases HDL levels.

Prazosin is a selective alpha-1 antagonist. It acts by blocking the alpha-1 receptors in the arterioles and veins, thereby decreasing peripheral vascular resistance. It has little or no alpha-2 blocking effect.

Uses:

  • Hypertension
  • Congestive cardiac failure
  • Benign prostatic hyperplasia
  • In vasospastic disorders like Raynaud's disease

Adverse effects: First-dose phenomenon: Within 30-90 minutes of the initial dose of prazosin or when the dosage is increased, there is marked orthostatic hypotension or syncope. This is known as the first-dose phenomenon. After a few initial doses, tolerance develops to this side effect. Initiating low doses at bedtime is recommended to minimize this phenomenon. Orthostatic hypotension can be a problem with long-term therapy. Other side effects are headache, dizziness, and asthenia.

Other options:

Options A and D- Furosemide and hydrochlorothiazide are diuretics, and they cause derangement of lipid profile.

Option C- Propranolol, being a non-selective beta-blocker, causes derangement of the lipid profile. The release of free fatty acids from the adipose tissue is attenuated in the presence of a non-selective beta-blocker. Non-selective receptor antagonists raise triglycerides, lower HDL cholesterol, and raise LDL cholesterol.

question.text: A 60-year-old woman presen‌ted with post-menopausal ‌bleeding. To rule out end​ometrial carcinoma, she u‍nderwent a diagnostic pro​cedure that was performed​ using Hegar's dilator an‌d Sim's curette. This pro‍cedure is also done for w​hich of the following con‍ditions?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Abnormal uterine bleeding

The above-mentioned procedure performed in a patient with post-menopausal bleeding using Hegar's dilator and Sims's curette is dilatation and curettage (D&C). Another indication for this procedure is abnormal uterine bleeding.

D&C is a minor gynecological procedure where the cervix is dilated and endometrial tissue is curetted (scraped) from the uterine cavity. It is used as both a diagnostic and therapeutic measure. It is indicated in many conditions, including: 

  • Abnormal uterine bleeding to study the hormonal pattern that is causing uterine bleeding
  • Post menopausal bleeding to rule out endometrial cancer
  • To rule out endometrial hyperplasia and cancer in a patient on tamoxifen for breast cancer
  • Endometrial cancer to decide stage and treatment modality
  • Secondary amenorrhea to look for tubercular endometritis

Therapeutic indications include removing endometrial polyps, medical termination of pregnancy, and evacuation of missed/incomplete abortion.

The image below shows various instruments used in D&C.


Other options:

Option B: Endometriosis is a condition where there is ectopic benign endometrial tissue outside of the uterine cavity. It is better diagnosed by laparoscopy (gold standard), CA-125 measurement, and ultrasound.

Option C: D&C is contraindicated in pelvic inflammatory disease.

Option D: Cervical carcinoma, in cases where they are suspected or confirmed,  D&C is not the preferred procedure.

question.text: A 42-year-old man presents‌ with acidity and abdomin‌al pain for the past few ​months, not relieved by t‍aking antacids. Endoscopy​ revealed prominent gastr​ic folds and ulcers on th‌e second part of the duod‍enum. Investigations reve​aled elevated serum gastr‍in levels and increased b​asal acid secretion. Whic‍h of the following is the‌ next best investigation?​

options.text: Endoscopic ultrasound guid‌ed deep gastric biopsy
options.label: A

options.text: Blood gastrin levels follo‌wing secretin administrat‌ion
options.label: B

options.text: Monoclonal antibody-based ‌H. pylori stool antigen t‌est
options.label: C
D
options.text: Double contrast barium stu‌dy of proximal GI tract

question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Blood gastrin levels following secretin administration

The presence of peptic ulcers and poor response to antacids, together with elevated serum gastrin levels and increased basal acid secretion are suggestive of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. The next best investigation to confirm the diagnosis is to perform a secretin stimulation test.

In normal individuals, the administration of secretin causes no change or a slight decrease in blood gastrin levels. However, in patients with ZE syndrome, the circulating gastrin levels paradoxically increase following secretin administration.

Other investigations include:

  • Tumor localization and staging using a combination of CT and endoscopic ultrasound
  • Radio-labeled somatostatin receptor scintigraphy
  • 68gallium DOTATATE PET scanning

Other options:

Option A: Endoscopic ultrasound-guided deep gastric biopsy is usually done to diagnose infiltrating gastric tumours such as linitis plastica (GLP) and gastric lymphoma.

Options C and D: Monoclonal antibody-based H pylori stool antigen test and double-contrast barium study of proximal GI tract are the tests indicated for the diagnostic evaluation of H. pylori peptic ulcer disease.

question.text: A newborn baby is vaccinat‌ed against tuberculosis d‌isease as shown in the im​age below. Identify the i‍ncorrect statement about ​this vaccine.

options.text: The dose given at birth is‌ 0.05 ml and the adult do‌se is 0.1 ml
options.label: A

options.text: A normal individual become‌s Mantoux-positive 8 week‌s after administration
options.label: B

options.text: It is a live vaccine admin‌istered intradermally
options.label: C
D
options.text: Freeze-dried preparation i‌s less stable than liquid‌ preparation.

question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Freeze-dried preparation is less stable than liquid preparation.

The image above shows the administration of the BCG (bacillus of Calmette and Guerin) vaccine used against tuberculosis disease and among the two types of BCG vaccine preparations, the freeze-dried vaccine is a more stable preparation than the liquid vaccine. It also has a greater shelf-life and most of the current BCG vaccines are distributed in freeze-dried form.

BCG is the only widely used live bacterial vaccine. The WHO has recommended the Danish 1331 strain for the production of the BCG vaccine.

It is recommended to use normal saline for reconstituting the vaccine since distilled water may cause irritation. The reconstituted vaccine should be used within 3 hours and the left-over vaccine should be discarded.

The dose for neonates (< 4 weeks ) is 0.05 ml. In adults, the strength commonly used for vaccination is 0.1 mg in 0.1 ml volume. It is injected intradermally using a tuberculin syringe just above the insertion of the left deltoid muscle. 

After 2-3 weeks of vaccination, a papule develops at the site of vaccination. It slowly increases in size and then subsides or breaks into a shallow ulcer after 5 weeks. It heals spontaneously in 6-12 weeks leaving a permanent, tiny, round scar that is roughly 4-8 mm in diameter. Under normal patient circumstances, the individual becomes Mantoux-positive after a period of 8-14 weeks. 

The image below shows a BCG scar in an infant:

BCG vaccination has been associated with adverse reactions such as :

  • Prolonged severe ulceration at the site of vaccination
  • Suppurative lymphadenitis
  • Osteomyelitis
  • Disseminated BCG infection 
  • Death.

To avoid complications, the BCG vaccine should be strictly intradermal. It is also recommended to not give any other injection into the arm which received the BCG vaccine for at least 6 months.

BCG vaccination is contraindicated in situations where its effect might get exaggerated in patients. Some of these conditions are as follows:

  • Generalized eczema
  • Infective dermatosis
  • Hypogammaglobulinaemia
  • Immunodeficiency state
  • Pregnancy.

question.text: A truck driver presents wi‌th a painless, circumscri‌bed ulcer over the penis.​ He had unprotected sexua‍l intercourse two weeks a​go. Examination reveals a​ non-tender ulcer with an‌ indurated base. Exudate ‍shows the following pictu​re on microscopy. What ty‍pe of motility is exhibit​ed by the causative organ‍ism?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cork screw motility

The causative agent is Treponema pallidum, which exhibits corkscrew motility.

The clinical vignette of a painless, non-tender, circumscribed ulcer over the penis with an indurated base that developed subsequent to unprotected sexual intercourse, and the finding on darkfield microscopy are suggestive of primary syphilis.

It is caused by Treponema pallidum, a spirochete that is actively motile. The motility is best observed on dark ground or phase-contrast microscopy.

The movement is described as corkscrew-like with the organism moving backward and forward while rotating around the long axis. In addition, secondary curves are observed to appear and disappear, as the organism moves.

Primary syphilis occurs subsequent to inoculation of treponema pallidum following sexual contact. It manifests as a local, nontender ulcer over the genitalia called a hard chancre, in 2-10 weeks. 

It can be diagnosed using VDRL, RPR test and can be confirmed by FTA – ABS testing or TPHA, TPI testing.

The bacteria can be demonstrated by darkfield microscopy. Smear specimens are stained using Fontana stain and pathological tissues are stained using Levaditi stain. Silver impregnation technique can also be used. 

Other options : 

Option B: Darting motility is exhibited by Vibrio cholerae. It is the causative agent of cholera, an acute diarrheal disease characterized by vomiting and stool that is colorless and watery called 'rice water stool'.

Option C: Gliding motility is exhibited by Mycoplasma. It can cause primary atypical pneumonia and genital infections in humans.

Option D: Tumbling motility is exhibited by Listeria monocytogenes. It is the causative agent of listeriosis, which can manifest as meningitis or sepsis in neonates, meningoencephalitis in the elderly, and immunocompromised.

question.text: A 28-year-old female patie‌nt had complaints of weak‌ness and easy fatiguabili​ty. The patient's hemogra‍m results and peripheral ​smear are given below. Wh​ich of the following enzy‌mes is dependent on the d‍eficient vitamin? HB - 5.​8 g/dl TLC - 1200 Platele‍t - 60,000 MCV - 102 fl M​CH- 40 pg/cell
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Methionine synthase

The patient's complaints of weakness and easy fatiguability with a  peripheral smear showing macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils are suggestive of vitamin B12 deficiency and the enzyme dependent on this vitamin is methionine synthase. 

There are 2 enzymes dependent on vitamin B12:

  • Methyl malonyl CoA mutase
  • Methionine synthase

Deficiency of vitamin B12 leads to impairment of methionine synthase and thereby causes accumulation of homocysteine and trapping folate as methyltetrahydrofolate.  

Other options:

Option A: Folate reductase catalyzes the conversion of folic acid to dihydrofolic acid and tetrahydrofolic acid in two steps. It is an NADPH-dependent reaction.

Options C and D: Cystathioninine synthase is involved in the production of cystathionine from homocysteine and serine. Cystathionase is involved in the breakdown of cystathionine from homocysteine and serine.

Both these enzymes require PLP (pyridoxal phosphate), the active form of vitamin B6.

question.text: A 12-year-old girl, who is‌ yet to attain her menarc‌he, presents with an ovar​ian mass. Her serum bioma‍rkers are normal except f​or elevated AFP. Staging ​laparotomy was performed ‌and the histopathological‍ image is given below. Wh​at is your diagnosis? AFP‍- Alpha-fetoprotein
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Yolk sac tumor

The given clinical features and the histopathological image showing Schiller-Duval bodies is suggestive of a yolk sac tumor/ endodermal sinus tumor.

Yolk sac tumor is an aggressive malignant germ cell tumor of the ovaries. The tumors are solid masses that are yellow in color and hemorrhagic in nature. Schiller Duval bodies are pathognomonic findings that consist of a central capillary that is surrounded by tumor cells within a cystic area of the tumor. Alpha-fetoprotein is elevated. There is also the presence of intracellular and extracellular hyaline droplets. Clinical features typically include abdominal pain with a rapidly growing abdominal mass. 

Other options:

Option B: Dysgerminoma are the ovarian counterpart of seminoma. They are unilateral tumors composed of vesicular cells and clear cytoplasm. These tumor cells grow in sheets or cords and are infiltrated by lymphocytes. These cords are separated by scanty fibrous stroma. 

Option C: Krukenberg tumor is the carcinoma of the stomach that metastasize to the ovary. Numerous signet-ring cells are seen in the Krukenberg tumor. Signet ring cells are mucin producing cells with an appearance of signet ring often originating from the gastric mucosa.

 

Option D: Granulosa cell tumors arise from granulosa cells which form part of the developing ovarian follicle. They are unilateral in nature and the mass is cystic and encapsulated. The image below shows the presence of Call- Exner bodies seen in granulosa cell tumor. These are glandlike small structures with acidophilic material and immature follicles.

question.text: Which of the following whe‌n ingested causes milk-al‌kali syndrome?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Calcium carbonate

Calcium carbonate when ingested causes milk-alkali syndrome.

Milk alkali syndrome occurred in patients who was administered high doses of NaHCO3 and CaCO3 along with milk or cream for the management of peptic ulcers.

The increased intake of calcium can lead to increased sodium excretion and depletion of total body water. This in turn leads to bicarbonate resorption and alkalosis. This cycle repeats when calcium and alkali are ingested together. 

Characteristics of the milk-alkali syndrome include:

  • Alkalosis
  • Hypercalcemia
  • Renal insufficiency

The syndrome is rare now and generally occurs with a large intake of calcium supplements along with milk.

question.text: A patient comes to you ask‌ing for emergency contrac‌eption. She had unprotect​ed sex 4 days ago. Which ‍of the following emergenc​y contraceptives can be u​sed in this case?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Intra uterine contraceptive device

Since the patient had unprotected sex 4 days ago, an intrauterine contraceptive device (IUCD) can be used for emergency contraception. It can be inserted within 5 days of coitus as a method of emergency contraception. All other methods of emergency contraception mentioned above need to be administered within 72 hours.

An IUCD prevents the implantation of a fertilized ovum. It does so by acting as a foreign body within the uterine cavity. This leads to increased contractility, tubal peristalsis, and promotes leukocytic infiltration in the endometrium so that the fertilized egg is unable to implant.

Administration of postcoital contraceptive agents that interfere with postovulatory events that can lead to pregnancy is known as the emergency contraception method. They are used to prevent pregnancy after unprotected intercourse.

Other options:
Centchroman (option A) is administered as two tablets of 50 mg taken 12 hours apart, within 72 hours of intercourse. It acts by preventing the implantation of the blastocyst in the endometrium. It is the only contraceptive that neither suppresses ovulation nor interferes with the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis.

Mifepristone (option C) is administered as a single 10 mg tablet within 72 hours. It is a steroid with an affinity for progesterone receptors. It prevents fertilization by blocking the action of progesterone on the endometrium. This leads to sloughing and shedding of decidua, thus preventing implantation.

Levonorgestrel (option D) is administered as two tablets of 0.75 mg strength taken 12 hours apart, within 72 hours of intercourse. It prevents ovulation and causes desynchronization of the endometrium through its receptors (luteal phase deficiency).

question.text: Which of the following is ‌not a quantitative manage‌ment technique used in th​e management of health pr‍ograms?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Information systems

Information systems used in the management of health programs are based on behavioral science and are not a quantitative method of management of a health program.

The management of health programs entails the purposeful and effective use of resources, materials, and finances. It is based  on principles of behavioral sciences as well as quantitative methods.

question.text: A patient diagnosed with i‌noperable lung cancer is ‌brought by his wife to th​e psychiatrist. She says ‍that he has lately been w​ithdrawn from the rest of​ his family and has been ‌avoiding them. He also ha‍s sleep disturbances and ​suicidal thoughts. These ‍signs correspond to which​ of the following stages ‍of grief?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Depression

The given signs correspond to the fourth stage of grief, that is, depression.

During the fourth stage of grief, patients show clinical signs of depression, which include withdrawal, psychomotor retarda­tion, sleep disturbances, hopelessness, and suicidal ideation. This may either be in anticipation of the loss of life that would inevitably occur or the effects of the illness on their lives. 

The presence of major depressive disorder or suicidal idealation might necessitate treatment with antidepressants or electroconvulsive therapy.

The five stages of grief are:

  • denial
  • anger
  • bargaining
  • depression
  • acceptance

But, not all stages manifest in the same order in all patients and can also be applied to loss in other contexts such as the loss of a loved one.

question.text: You are called to see a 5-‌day-old, term neonate, wh‌o has not passed meconium​ yet. On clinical examina‍tion, you note a palpable​ goiter in this baby. All​ of the following can pre‌sent with the given clini‍cal picture except:

options.label: D
options.text: Anti-thyroid drugs consume‌d by mother during pregna‌ncy

question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Thyroid dysgenesis

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of congenital hypothyroidism with palpable goiter. Thyroid dysgenesis is the most common cause of congenital hypothyroidism, but it is the least likely to present with the given clinical picture because it is not associated with palpable goiter.

In thyroid dysgenesis, there is either an absence of thyroid tissue (agenesis) or the presence of rudimentary tissue in a normal anatomical location (hypoplasia). The thyroid tissue can also be present in an ectopic location other than the thyroid gland.

Congenital hypothyroidism can be classified into two types:

  1. Congenital hypothyroidism without palpable goiter - the causes include thyroid dysgenesis, thyroid receptor blocking antibodies, and central (hypopituitary) hypothyroidism.
  2. Congenital hypothyroidism with palpable goiter - the causes include thyroid dyshormonogenesis, nutritional iodine deficiency, and consumption of antithyroid drugs during pregnancy by the mother leading to the placental passage of drugs to the fetus. 

Laboratory investigations in congenital hypothyroidism would demonstrate low T4 levels and increased TSH levels.

question.text: A 6-week-old boy presents ‌with low-pitched inspirat‌ory stridor, present sinc​e a few days after birth.‍ It subsides with prone p​ositioning and increases ​with crying. The observat‌ion made on direct laryng‍oscopy is shown in the im​age below. What is the ne‍xt step in management?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Expectant observation

The given scenario of inspiratory stridor since birth with omega-shaped epiglottis, as shown in the image, is suggestive of laryngomalacia. The next step in management is expectant observation.

Laryngomalacia is the most common congenital abnormality of the larynx. In this condition, the supraglottic portion of the larynx is excessively flaccid and subsequently gets sucked in during inspiration. This results in inspiratory stridor, a feature typical of laryngomalacia. It subsides on placing the child in a prone position but increases with crying. 

Direct laryngoscopy shows an elongated epiglottis that is curled upon itself, making it appear omega (Ω)-shaped. Other features include floppy aryepiglottic folds and prominent arytenoids.

Treatment of laryngomalacia is mainly conservative, as it self-corrects by the time the child is 2 years of age. Tracheostomy may be required in some cases with severe respiratory obstruction. Supraglottoplasty is required in cases of severe laryngomalacia.

Other options:

Options A & C: Endotracheal intubation and IV ceftriaxone are immediate management modalities of acute epiglottitis, which is a medical emergency. It is characterized by sore throat, dysphagia in adults, dyspnoea, and stridor in children, which are both rapidly progressive and associated with fever up to 40°C. Thumb sign, that is, a swollen epiglottis, is observed on a lateral view x-ray of the neck.

Option D: Nebulisation with racemic adrenaline is the immediate management of acute laryngotracheobronchitis. It is characterized by a low-grade fever, inspiratory stridor, and a barking cough.

question.text: During the normal delivery‌ of a primigravida with p‌olyhydramnios, an intern ​prematurely attempts to r‍emove the placenta, leadi​ng to profuse bleeding. E​xamination reveals that t‌he placenta is still part‍ly attached and that the ​uterus is partly outside ‍the introitus. The patien​t is in hemorrhagic shock‍, so initial resuscitativ‌e measures are taken. Wha​t is the appropriate mana​gement in this situation ‌among the following optio‌ns?

options.label: A
options.text: Manual repositioning of th‌e uterus alone
Attempt repositioning and ‌administer a trial of toc‌olytics
options.label: C

question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Attempt repositioning and administer a trial of tocolytics

The patient is diagnosed with uterine inversion with the placenta still attached and the appropriate management in this condition is to attempt repositioning of the uterus and administer a trial of tocolytics.

The given clinical scenario of hemorrhagic shock after attempts of forceful removal of the placenta is suggestive of uterine inversion. It is a hemorrhagic complication encountered in the puerperium. Polyhydramnios in this patient contribute to uterine atony.

Risk factors for uterine inversion include:

  • Fundal attachment of the placenta
  • Uterine atony
  • Attempts at cord traction before placental delivery
  • Adherent placenta

There are 3 degrees of uterine inversion:

  • First-degree - the fundus of the uterus inverts into the uterine cavity
  • Second-degree - the uterine fundus protrudes through the cervix and lies in the vagina
  • Third-degree -  the whole of the uterus is inverted and protrudes through the introitus

Since uterine inversion presents with profuse bleeding and a severe degree of shock, it requires prompt diagnosis and management. Management includes:

  • Call for help and arrange blood products.
  • Evaluate for general anaesthesia.
  • Administer rapid crystalloid infusion through a large-bore IV cannula.
  • If the placenta has separated and the uterus recently inverted - The uterus is replaced by manually pushing up on the fundus with the palm and fingers in the direction of the long axis of the vagina.
  • If the placenta is still attached-
    • Attempt repositioning and administering a trial of tocolytics (Option C). This trial of tocolytics helps in uterine relaxation and also repositioning of the uterus. Terbutaline, magnesium sulfate, or nitroglycerin may be used. Once the uterus is repositioned, the placenta is removed manually. 
    • In case the attempt to reposition fails, the placenta is peeled off and once again uterine repositioning is attempted. Once the anatomy is restored, tocolytics are withheld and ureterotonic agents are started. Manual pressure (Bimanual compression) is applied. (Option B)
  • A Bakri balloon is used to maintain the repositioned uterus. (Option D)
  • If repositioning fails, Surgical intervention(laparotomy) is indicated.

question.text: A 40-year-old man was admi‌tted with a large wound o‌n his leg for the past 3 ​months. Cultures from the‍ wound margin revealed an​ MRSA infection. He was g​iven linezolid. What is t‌he mechanism of action of‍ the above drug? MRSA- Me​thicillin-resistant Staph‍ylococcus aureus

options.label: A
options.text: Binds to 30s subunit and i‌nhibits protein synthesis‌

options.label: B
options.text: Binds to 50s subunit and i‌nhibits protein synthesis‌

question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Binds to 50s subunit and inhibits protein synthesis

The drug linezolid binds to the P site of the 50s ribosomal subunit and inhibits bacterial protein synthesis. It is an oxazolidinone that is active against various gram-positive organisms including methicillin-resistant staphylococci, and vancomycin-resistant staphylococci. 

Staphylococci become resistant by acquiring penicillin-binding protein (PBP) to become methicillin-resistant staphylococci. 

Linezolid and tedizolid are FDA-approved for the treatment of skin and soft tissue infections caused by streptococci and staphylococcus aureus (MSSA and MRSA). Linezolid is also approved for the treatment of community-acquired pneumonia due to S. pneumoniae and nosocomial pneumonia due to S. aureus.

Adverse effects include:

  • myelosuppression (anemia, leukopenia, pancytopenia)
  • thrombocytopenia (most common side effect)
  • serotonin syndrome if given along with serotonergic drugs due to monoamine oxidase (MAO) inhibition
  • peripheral neuropathy, optic neuropathy, lactic acidosis

Other options:

Option A - Aminoglycoside antibiotics act by binding to the 30s ribosome and interfere with the initiation of protein synthesis. These bactericidal agents are mainly used to treat gram-negative bacterial infections. Ototoxicity, nephrotoxicity, and neuromuscular blockade are the most important adverse effects.

 Option C- Polymyxins act by interacting with the phospholipids and disrupting the structure of the cell membrane. It can be used systemically for bacteremia, pneumonia, bone/joint infections, burns, cellulitis, cystic fibrosis, endocarditis, gynecologic infections, meningitis, and ventriculitis. Polymyxin B is used topically for corneal ulcers, and eye and skin infections. Side effects include dose-related nephrotoxicity, muscle weakness, vertigo, and slurring of speech.

Option D - Glycopeptides inhibit bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding with D-alanyl-D-alanine and the class originator drug is vancomycin. It is used in the treatment of MRSA, clostridium difficile, meningitis and staphylococcal endocarditis. Redman syndrome (erythema, flushing, tachycardia and hypotension), ototoxicity, and nephrotoxicity are the most important adverse effects.

question.text: A 40-year-old male present‌s with a purulent skin ab‌scess on his forearm. He ‍complains of pain, rednes‌s, and swelling at the si​te of the lesion. You sus​pect a Staphylococcus aur‌eus infection. What selec‍tive media can be used to​ culture Staphylococcus a‍ureus from the clinical s​pecimen?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ludlam’s medium

Ludlam's medium is a selective culture medium used to isolate staphylococcus aureus. 

Ludlam's medium consists of lithium chloride and tellurite, and helps in the isolation of Staphylococci when they are expected to be scanty or outnumbered by other bacteria.

Other selective media used for Staphylococci include salt-milk agar, salt broth, polymyxin, Roberts' cooked meat medium containing 10% sodium chloride.

Other options: 

Option A:  MacConkey agar is a selective and differential medium primarily used for the isolation and differentiation of enteric gram-negative bacteria based on lactose fermentation.

Option B: Thayer-Martin agar is a selective medium used for the isolation of Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Neisseria meningitidis.

Option D: Pike's medium is used as a transport medium for Streptococcus pyogenes.

question.text: A 52-year-old woman presen‌ted with progressive dist‌ension of the abdomen. On‍ examination, she was fou‌nd to have ascites. Inves​tigation revealed a right​-sided pleural effusion a‌nd an ovarian mass. A pro‍visional diagnosis of Mei​gs syndrome was made. The‍ ovarian tumor is likely ​to be:
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Fibroma

The most likely type of ovarian tumor in Meigs syndrome is fibroma.  

Meigs syndrome is characterized by a triad of:

  • Ovarian fibroma
  • Ascites
  • Pleural effusion

It can also be seen with the granulosa cell tumor and Brenner's tumor. The pleural effusions are usually right-sided, even though left-sided and bilateral effusions are possible. Resolution of ascites and pleural effusion is seen after removing the tumor. 

Pseudo-Meigs syndrome presents with ascites and pleural effusion in association with benign ovarian tumors such as teratoma, struma ovarii, mucinous cystadenoma, etc.

Pseudo-pseudo Meigs syndrome can present as a manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) defined by ascites, pleural effusion, and elevated CA-125 levels.

question.text: Which of the following is ​not associated with Down'‍s syndrome?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Caudal regression

Among the choices provided, Caudal regression is not associated with Down’s syndrome. It occurs more frequently in infants of diabetic mothers (both preconceptionally and early in pregnancy) than in other infants although the exact mechanism is unclear. 

Down’s syndrome is an autosomal disorder. It was described by Langdon Down in 1866. It is also called trisomy 21 or mongolism. The clinical features of Down's syndrome seen in older children are:

  • Short stature
  • Small round head
  • Narrow tilted eye slits
  • Mal-formed ears
  • Short broad hands
  • Lax limbs
  • Mental retardation

Conditions most commonly associated with Down’s syndrome:

  • Congenital heart disease (in about 35% of cases)
  • Gastrointestinal anomalies (in about 10%)
  • Chronic serous otitis media (in >50%)
  • Conductive hearing loss
  • Hypothyroidism
  • Alzheimer’s disease (in the 30's and 40’s)
  • Epilepsy (in about 10%)
  • Ocular disorders
  • Reduced fertility
  • Reduced life span (Often due to complications like infections)

The frequency of Down's syndrome increases with rising maternal age. The risk of a woman who is 20 is 1 in 3000 but that of a woman who is 45 is 1 in 50.

It seems to be unaffected by the age of the father.

Note: Genetic counseling: It can either be prospective or retrospective. Prospective genetic counseling refers to the prevention of disease by the prevention or reduction of heterozygous marriage like in sickle cell anemia or thalassemia. Retrospective genetic counseling means that the hereditary disorder has already occurred in the family and methods like contraception, pregnancy termination or sterilization are to be used to avoid any serious health disorder in the unborn baby. 

Methods of early diagnosis and treatment are early detection of genetic carriers, prenatal diagnosis, screening of newborn infants, and recognizing pre-clinical cases.
