question.text: The laboratory investigati​ons of a 65 year old woma​n revealed a hemoglobin l​evel of 5.4 g/dl, creatin​ine level of 6 mg/dl, cal​cium level of 12 mg/dl, p​otassium level of 4.4 mmo‌l/L. Her urine output in ​the last 24 hours was 50 ‌ml. Bone marrow aspiratio‌n revealed more than 60% ​of plasma cells. What wou‌ld be the next appropriat‌e line of management for ‍this patient?

options.label: D
options.text: Chemotherapy followed by a​utologous stem cell trans​plantation

question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dexamethasone + fluids

The clinical scenario shows a patient with a bone marrow finding of plasma cells >60% which points to a diagnosis of multiple myeloma. 

Anemia (Hb- 5.4 g/dl), hypercalcemia (serum calcium-12 mg/dl) and acute kidney injury (creatinine-6 mg/dl, reduced urine output) are myeloma-defining events suggesting end-organ damage.

The most appropriate next step in managing this patient would be to administer fluids to treat the acute kidney injury and hypercalcemia (hypercalcemia is the most common cause of renal failure in multiple myeloma), and prevent further renal impairment. Therefore, among the given options, dexamethasone and fuids would be the best answer.

Multiple myeloma is a malignant plasma cell dyscrasia and its diagnosis requires bone marrow biopsy finding of ≥ 10% clonal bone marrow plasma cells, a serum/urine M component, and at least one of the myeloma-defining events (hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia and bone lesions).

Dialysis (Option A) is indicated in the following conditions:

  • Pulmonary edema not responding to diuretics
  • Uremic pericarditis, uremic encephalopathy or uremic syndrome
  • Metabolic acidosis not responding to treatment
  • Hyperkalemia

Lenalidomide + Bortezomib + Dexamethasone (Option B) is the preferred treatment in multiple myeloma and can be initiated after initial management of acute kidney injury.

Chemotherapy followed by autologous stem cell transplantation (Option D) in transplant-eligible patients prolongs overall survival in multiple myeloma patients.

question.text: Which of the following are​ true regarding KF ring? ​Seen in all patients with​ neurological involvement​ Is seen only for Wilson'​s disease Resolves with d​esferrioxamine Seen in al‌l patients with hepatic i​nvolvement Seen in superi‌or and inferior pole of D‌escemet's membrane
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 and 5 only

Among the given options only statements 1 and 5 are true.

Kayser-Fleischer (KF) rings are seen in almost all patients of Wilson's disease with neurological involvement. It initially appears as a crescent in the superior pole of Descemet's membrane and gradually extends inferiorly, eventually becoming circumferential in shape.

KF rings occur due to copper deposition in the descemet's membrane. It is golden-brown to greenish-brown in color and can be best seen by slit-lamp examination.

The image below shows a KF ring : 

While it is a characteristic sign of Wilson’s disease (statement 2), it can also be seen in: 

  • Primary biliary cholangitis
  • Primary sclerosing cholangitis
  • Cholestasis

KF rings are present in almost 95% of patients of Wilson's disease with neurological/psychiatric symptoms compared to around 65% of those with hepatic presentations (statement 4).

They disappear on treatment with copper-chelating agents like d-penicillamine (while desferrioxamine is an iron chelating agent) and reappear with disease progression (statement 3).

question.text: A diabetic nephropathy pat​ient is an ideal candidat​e for renal graft transpl​ant. Which of the followi​ng statements is true?

options.label: A
options.text: The survival rate of graft​ is 95% in the first year​
The transplantation is cos​t effective after the sec​ond transplant year
options.label: B

options.text: The life expectancy is dou​bled in a diabetic patien​t with renal transplant
options.label: C

options.text: The treatment of chronic r​ejection has improved ove​r the last 10 years
options.label: D

question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. The transplantation is cost effective after the second transplant year

Transplantation becomes cost-effective after the second transplant year in a patient with diabetic nephropathy, provided there is no chronic rejection.

The cost of transplantation after the second year becomes lesser compared to thrice-weekly dialysis.

Other options:

Options A: Graft survival in the first year is not 95%. It is around 80% 

Option C: The life expectancy is not doubled in a patient with diabetic nephropathy post-transplantation

Option D: As chronic rejection is due to so many variables, the treatment is very difficult. Risk factors that predispose a recipient to long-term graft rejection include HLA-mismatching, acute episodes of graft rejection, mismatch in donor-recipient age, and smoking. Better treatment options are still under research.

question.text: A diabetic patient enters ​the OPD and greets you wi​th a namaste. As the doct​or, you notice a deformit​y in his hand which is sh​own in the image below. B​ased on your observation,‌ what is the likely cause​ of this deformity?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cheiroarthropathy

The image shows a positive namaste or prayer sign where the patient is unable to touch the palmar aspects of both hands and fingers together which is suggestive of diabetic cheiroarthropathy.

Diabetic cheiroarthropathy also known as diabetic stiff hand syndrome is a cutaneous condition characterized by waxy, thickened skin and limited joint mobility of the hands and fingers leading to flexion contractures (namaste or prayer sign). This occurs due to the non-enzymatic glycosylation of collagen. It is seen in both diabetes type 1 and type 2. Its prevalence increases with age and poor glycemic control.

Other options:

Option A: Flexor tenosynovitis refers to inflammation of the sheath surrounding the flexor tendons in the hand. Infectious flexor tenosynovitis is associated with the Kanavel’s signs which include:

  • Fusiform swelling along the affected finger
  • Tenderness with palpation along the tendon sheath
  • Flexed posture of the affected finger
  • Pain with passive extension

Option C: Dupuytren's contracture is a fibroproliferative disorder affecting the palmar aponeurosis of mainly the 4th and 5th fingers. Skin puckering proximal to the flexor crease is the earliest sign, followed by the development of nodules and cords in the palmar fascia, leading to flexion contractures at the MCP and PIP joints as the disease progresses.

Option D: Ankylosis refers to the fusion of a joint, resulting in limited or no movement. It can occur due to various causes such as rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, trauma, or infection.

question.text: Which of the following is ​false about mycoplasma pn​eumonia?

options.text: Can be cultured in a cell-​free medium
options.label: D

question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Responds well to amoxiclav

Mycoplasma does not respond to amoxicillin-clavulanate (amoxiclav).

Mycoplasma is a bacteria that lacks a cell wall. Since beta-lactam antibiotics (amoxiclav) act on the cell wall of the bacterium, they can not be used in the treatment of mycoplasma infection. 

The diagnosis of mycoplasma pneumonia (also known as walking pneumonia/ primary atypical pneumonia) can be established by:

  • PCR detection of M. pneumoniae in respiratory secretions
  • Serological tests for IgM and IgG antibodies to M.pneumoniae in paired serum samples
  • Culture: Mycoplasma can be cultured on PPLO agar, a cell-free medium, and shows a typical fried egg appearance

Chest X-ray usually shows B/L peribronchial and perivascular interstitial infiltrates

Treatment options for mycoplasma pneumonia  include:

  •  Macrolides (e.g. azithromycin)
  •  Tetracyclines (e.g. doxycycline)
  •  Respiratory fluoroquinolones. (e.g. levofloxacin)

Azithromycin is the drug of choice for the management of mycoplasma pneumonia.

question.text: You have been called to de‌clare the brain death of ‍a 12-year-old child in th​e ICU. Which of the follo‌wing is not seen in brain‍ death?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Decorticate and decerebrate posturing

Decerebrate or decorticate posturing is not seen in brain death as they are motor responses to noxious stimuli that originate from the midbrain and cortex. 

Brain death, also known as death by neurologic criteria refers to the irreversible and total cessation of all functions of the entire brain, including the brainstem.

The three components for diagnosing brain death are a demonstration of coexisting irreversible coma with a known cause, absence of brain stem reflexes, and apnea. Coma requires the patient to be unresponsive, even to noxious stimuli. The diagnosis of brain death can still be made despite positive spinal reflexes. (option B)

Brainstem reflexes (pupillary responses, oculocephalic reflex, oculovestibular responses, corneal reflex, jaw reflex, facial grimacing, pharyngeal gag reflex, coughing) are absent. Apnea is the absence of respiratory drive at PaCO2 of ≥60mmHg and > 20mmHg above baseline, which is consistent with brain death.

The following manifestations are occasionally seen and should not be misinterpreted as evidence of brainstem function: 

  • Normal systolic blood pressure - SBP >100 mmHg (option A)
  • Movements originating from the spinal cord or peripheral nerve may occur
  • Sweating, flushing, tachycardia (option C)
  • Deep tendon reflexes; superficial abdominal reflexes; triple flexion response
  • Babinski reflex
  • Spontaneous movements of limbs other than pathologic flexion or extension response
  • Respiratory-like movements (shoulder elevation and adduction, back-arching, intercostal expansion without significant tidal volumes)

question.text: A male child presented wit​h arthralgia and abdomina​l pain. On examination, t‌here was palpable purpura‌ over the lower limbs. Th‌ere is past history of up​per respiratory tract inf‌ection prior to the onset​ of presenting symptoms. ​Which of the following is‌ the treatment for this c​ondition?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Glucocorticoids

The clinical scenario is suggestive of Henoch Schonlein's purpura (HSP). Glucocorticoids are used to treat HSP.

Henoch-Schönlein purpura (HSP), also known as IgA vasculitis, is a common small vessel vasculitis in childhood. It is a type III hypersensitivity reaction characterized by the deposition of IgA in the small vessels of the skin, joints, gastrointestinal tract, and kidney, resulting in vasculitis.

The exact etiology of HSP remains unknown. But, it usually occurs following an upper respiratory tract infection caused by group A Streptococcus, Staphylococcus aureus, Mycoplasma, and Adenovirus.

Children usually present with the following features:

  • Palpable purpura is symmetric and occurs in the lower extremities, extensor aspect of the upper limbs, and buttocks.
  • Arthralgia and arthritis- commonly affecting hip, knee, or ankle joints.
  • Gastrointestinal manifestations like abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, and intussusception.
  • About 30% of the patients with HSP develop renal manifestations, presenting as microscopic hematuria, hypertension, and progressive glomerulonephritis.

Glucocorticoids such as prednisolone are used for the treatment of gastrointestinal manifestations in HSP. Nephritis due to IgA vasculitis should be treated with immunosuppressants like prednisolone and azathioprine.

 The image given below shows palpable purpura in the lower limbs seen in HSP.

The criteria for diagnosis of childhood HSP are:

Palpable purpura with at least one of the following-

  • Diffuse abdominal pain
  • Any biopsy showing predominant IgA deposition
  • Arthritis or arthralgia
  • Renal involvement (proteinuria >3 g/24 hr), hematuria, or red cell casts

Lab findings seen in HSP are nonspecific and include leukocytosis, mild anemia, and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP). The platelet count is normal in HSP. A skin biopsy specimen can be useful in confirming leukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA and C3 deposition by immunofluorescence.

The image given below shows IgA and C3 deposition in vessels seen on immunofluorescence of skin biopsy in HSP.

Other options:

Immunosuppressants like azathioprine, methotrexate and cyclosporine are used in a variety of rheumatologic disorders like vasculitis, arthritis, inflammatory bowel diseases like Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, autoimmune hepatitis, and lupus nephritis.

question.text: True regarding the differe‌nce between adult and ped‍iatric resuscitation.

options.label: A
options.text: Ventricular dysrhythmias a‌re common in children
The no flow phase precedes‌ the period of cardiac ar‍rest in children.
options.label: B

options.text: More ventilation to be giv‌en compared to chest comp‍ressions in children
options.label: C
D
options.text: Dysrhythmias are most ofte‌n due to respiratory insu‍fficiency in children

question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Dysrhythmias are most often due to respiratory insufficiency in children

Dysrhythmias in the pediatric age group are most often the result of respiratory insufficiency or hypoxia and not of primary cardiac causes, as in adults.
Hypoxia, hypercapnia, and acidosis lead to bradycardia, hypotension, and secondary cardiac arrest in children.

Other options: 

Option A: Supraventricular tachycardia is the most common tachydysrhythmia that necessitates treatment in pediatric patients. Ventricular dysrhythmia is an uncommon presenting rhythm in infants and children.

Option B: The pre-arrest phase is the period that precedes the period of cardiac arrest. 

Four phases of cardiac arrest have been described as follows:

  • The prearrest phase- a period that precedes the period of cardiac arrest.
  • The no-flow phase- reflects untreated cardiac arrest before it is recognized by a bystander in the community or by a medical provider in the hospital
  • The low-flow phase- begins with the onset of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR)
  • The post-resuscitation phase - The post-resuscitation phase begins with the return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC).

Option C: The chest compression to ventilation ratio should be 30:2 or 15:2. Excessive ventilation results in decreased venous return into the chest, decreased coronary and cerebral blood flow, diminished cardiac output, and ultimately a decreased likelihood of return of spontaneous circulation. 

Guidelines for pediatric basic life support:

Compression method Two fingers or two thumb Two fingers or two thumb The heel of one hand or two hands
Compression depth One-third of the chest One-third to one-half of the chest One-third to one-half of the chest
Compression rate 120/minute 100/minute 100/minute
Compression to ventilation ratio 3: 1 15: 2 (single rescuer - 30: 2) 15: 2 (single rescuer - 30: 2)

question.text: A 5-year-old child with 4+ proteinuria is unresponsive to corticosteroid therapy. There is no history of hematuria and hypertension. Renal biopsy shows segmental sclerosis and hyalinosis, predominantly involving the juxtamedullary glomeruli. What is the most likely diagnosis?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis

In this patient with 4+ proteinuria, unresponsiveness to corticosteroid therapy, no history of hematuria and hypertension, with renal biopsy showing segmental sclerosis and hyalinosis in glomeruli, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis(FSGS) is the likely diagnosis.

FSGS is defined by sclerosis affecting some (focal) glomeruli and only part (segmental) of each involved tuft. It usually presents with nephrotic syndrome or significant proteinuria, often accompanied by hypertension, microscopic hematuria, and reduced kidney function at diagnosis.

Compared with minimal change disease, FSGS shows more hematuria, lower GFR, more hypertension, nonselective proteinuria, poor steroid response, and higher progression to ESRD.

FSGS is classified as follows:

  • Primary
    • Idiopathic FSGS
  • Secondary
    • HIV associated
    • Heroin addiction
    • Sickle cell disease
    • Obesity
    • Hypertensive nephropathy
    • Renal conditions
      • Focal glomerulonephritis (e.g., IgA nephropathy)
      • Renal ablation
      • Unilateral renal agenesis or renal dysplasia
      • Reflux nephropathy
  • Inherited
    • Mutated proteins of the slit diaphragm - podocin, alpha-actinin 4, TRPC6

Pathogenesis centers on podocyte injury, characterized by degeneration and foot-process effacement due to circulating factors or genetic defects, with resulting protein leakage, hyalinosis, and sclerosis.  Genetic mutations disrupt slit diaphragm integrity, causing steroid-resistant or progressive disease.

Morphologically, sclerotic segments show collapsed capillaries, matrix expansion, hyalinosis, and lipid-laden macrophages. Electron microscopy shows segmental tuft scarring with capillary lumen obliteration. IgM and C3 often deposit in sclerotic regions. Disease progression leads to global sclerosis, tubular atrophy, and interstitial fibrosis.

Some patients progress rapidly to ESRD within two years, with risk influenced by proteinuria severity, renal function at diagnosis, and histologic variant (collapsing type is worst; tip variant is more favorable. Recurrence after kidney transplantation can be seen.

Treatment for FSGS generally includes renin–angiotensin system blockers and SGLT2 inhibitors. Primary FSGS with nephrotic-range proteinuria may be treated with steroids, but responses are slower and less frequent. Cyclosporine may help maintain remission in steroid-responsive patients. Management of secondary FSGS focuses on addressing the underlying cause and reducing proteinuria; steroids and immunosuppressants have no role in secondary or genetic forms. 

Other options:

Option A- IgA nephropathy, also termed as Berger's disease, features mesangial IgA deposition and typically presents with episodic hematuria 1–2 days after respiratory or GI infections. Severe cases may show heavy proteinuria, hypertension, and chronic renal failure. The image below is an immunofluorescence study of IgA nephropathy showing the characteristic IgA deposition in the mesangial regions:

Option B: Membranous nephropathy, a common adult cause of nephrotic syndrome (especially in men 30–50), features diffuse capillary wall thickening with subepithelial immune deposits. Most cases are primary, driven by anti-PLA2R autoantibodies. It presents with heavy proteinuria, edema, hyperlipidemia, and sometimes microscopic hematuria. Silver stains show blackened basement membranes with characteristic “spikes” between subepithelial deposits. These findings are shown below:

Option D- Minimal change disease usually presents with sudden, severe proteinuria in children and shows a good response to corticosteroids. It shows minimal changes on light microscopy, and there are no deposits seen on immunofluorescent studies as well. The only changes observed on biopsy are diffuse effacement of the foot processes of visceral epithelial cells/podocytes seen on electron microscopy. This is shown in the image below:

question.text: A 3-week neonate presents ‍with ambiguous genitalia ​with Na+ - 127; K+ - 6 me‍q/L with a BP of 50/22 mm‍ Hg. Along with IV fluids​, what specific managemen​t is done?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hydrocortisone

The given clinical case of a neonate presenting with ambiguous genitalia, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypotension points towards a diagnosis of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH). Hydrocortisone must be administered along with IV fluids for the management of this baby.

The most common enzyme deficiency in CAH is 21-hydroxylase deficiency. Babies with 21-hydroxylase deficiency typically present around 10-14 days of age with the subset of symptoms due to aldosterone deficiency, cortisol deficiency, and androgen excess.

Aldosterone deficiency leads to salt-wasting crises marked by hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypotension, and metabolic acidosis.

Cortisol deficiency causes manifestations like hypoglycemia, hyperpigmentation, weight loss, weakness, anorexia, vomiting, and shock.

Androgen excess in 21-hydroxylase deficiency results in virilization of females, leading to female pseudohermaphroditism, and precocious puberty in males. Virilization is usually apparent at birth in females and within 2 to 3 years of life in males.

Without treatment, shock, cardiac arrhythmias, and death may occur within days or weeks.

Diagnosis is confirmed by elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels or by genetic testing.

Glucocorticoid replacement therapy is the primary treatment for cortisol deficiency, aiming to suppress androgen production and prevent complications associated with androgen excess. Fludrocortisone is given to control mineralocorticoid deficiency. 

If the condition is diagnosed prenatally, dexamethasone may be administered to the mother.

question.text: A child is NS1 antigen positive and presents with fever and warning signs. Laboratory findings show a hematocrit (Hct) of 41% and a platelet count of 50,000/µL. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. RL 7 mL/kg

A child who is NS1 antigen-positive and presents with fever and warning signs, with laboratory findings including a hematocrit (Hct) of 41% and a platelet count of 50,000/µL, is suffering from dengue with warning signs. The next step in management is to start Ringer's lactate(RL) 7 mL/kg.

In dengue with warning signs, crystalloids like NS/RL can be given. If the patient has documented hypotension, NS/RL infusion is started at 10-20ml/kg/hour, while in case of no hypotension, NS/RL can be given at 7ml/kg/hour. As there is no mention of hypotension in this case, Ringer's lactate 7 mL/kg is the best answer.

Dengue fever is an acute illness presenting with fever, muscle and joint pain, and a rash. Severe dengue is characterized by issues with blood clotting and plasma leakage from capillaries.

Management of Dengue with risk factors is given below:

Dengue infection progresses through three distinct phases:

  • Febrile phase- It lasts 2-7 days, presents with a sudden onset of high-grade fever, often accompanied by facial flushing, skin erythema, body aches, myalgia, arthralgia, headache, anorexia, nausea, and vomiting.
  • Critical phase- It is characterized by bleeding and shock, marked by a drop in platelet count and an increase in hematocrit, indicative of capillary leak.
  • Recovery phase- After 24-48 hours in the critical phase, patients enter the recovery phase. During this period, general well-being improves, appetite returns, gastrointestinal symptoms subside, hemodynamic status stabilizes, and diuresis begins.

The following is the revised WHO Classification of dengue infections:

The clinical criteria of dengue haemorrhagic fever are dengue fever with hemorrhagic tendencies, evidenced by one or more of the following:

  • Positive tourniquet test 
  • Petechiae, ecchymoses, or purpura

question.text: The cerebrospinal fluid (C​SF) specimen of a patient‍ is shown below along wit​h the microscopy. The rep‌ort shows mononuclear cyt​osis, elevated proteins, ‌and low sugars. Which of ​the following is the like​ly etiology?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tuberculous meningitis

The given clinical scenario along with the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sample with cobweb-like clot and slide showing lymphocytic predominance points to a diagnosis of tubercular meningitis. 

Tuberculous meningitis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis is caused by the formation of tubercles in the brain parenchyma. This happens during the hematogenous spread of the bacilli during primary infection. It can also be due to the rupture of a subependymal tubercle into the subarachnoid space.

Tuberculous meningitis presents as a subacute infection and has a longer course than bacterial meningitis. Ocular nerve palsy is a common association as there is marked meningeal involvement at the base of the brain. The patient can also develop hydrocephalus.

The CSF sample shows a pellicle or cobweb-like clots. Acid-fast bacilli can be best isolated from these. There is usually lymphocytic leukocytosis, low glucose concentration, and elevated proteins. CSF culture remains the gold standard for diagnosis. 

The clinical triad of fever, headache, and nuchal rigidity is common to all types of meningitis. Nuchal rigidity is the resistance of the neck to passive flexion and is pathognomonic of meningeal irritation. Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs are other features of meningeal irritation. Raised intracranial pressure (ICP) is a complication that presents as papilledema, disorientation, or dilated poorly reactive pupils.

Other options:

Option B - Aseptic meningitis is commonly caused by enteroviruses such as coxsackieviruses, and varicella-zoster virus. It is more benign and usually self-limiting compared to pyogenic meningitis. Gram's staining of the CSF sample shows lymphocytosis but not the organism.

Option C - Bacterial meningitis is most commonly caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis. Blood culture can be used for diagnosis. CSF findings are described in the pearl below. Antibiotic prophylaxis is provided to the close contacts of persons with confirmed meningococcal disease.

Option D - Chemical meningitis is a common cause of chronic meningitis. It can arise due to the rupture of tumor contents from a cystic glioma, dermoid cyst, or craniopharyngioma into the CSF.

question.text: A 27-year-old man presents with fever, shortness of breath. A fungating mass is seen in the right lung. Histopathology from the mass with modified Grocott's silver methenamine is shown below. Identify the organism.

options.text: Right angled branching, septate hyphae, Mucormycosis
options.label: A
C
options.text: Acute angled branching, septate hyphae, Aspergillus
Acute angled branching, septate hyphae, Rhizopus
options.label: D

question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Acute angled branching, septate hyphae, Aspergillus

The given slide stained with modified Grocott's silver methenamine shows acute-angled (45o) uniform, branching septate hyphae, which is suggestive of Aspergillus species.

Aspergillus species grow rapidly, producing aerial hyphae that bear conidia in chains. Long aseptate conidiophores (specialised conidia-bearing hyphae) are seen with terminal vesicles. Phialides (vase-shaped cells producing conidia) with conidia are arranged in basipetal chains on the terminal vesicle. The following image shows the lactophenol cotton blue solution (LPCB) mount of Aspergillus fumigatus showing the long conidiophores with terminal vesicles.

Conditions caused by Aspergillus species include:

  • Aspergilloma, a fungal ball that grows within the lung and is confined to an existing lung cavity, such as those formed by old tuberculosis.
  • Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, which leads to hypersensitivity reactions (Type I in atopic individuals and Type III reactions).
  • Superficial infections of the external ear (otomycosis), eye (keratitis), and nasal sinuses.

Laboratory diagnosis of Aspergillus species includes serum galactomannan assay, wet mount preparations in exudates, isolation by culture using Sabouraud dextrose agar, and microscopic examination of isolated colonies. Detection of galactomannan (a cell wall component of Aspergillus) in serum or bronchoalveolar lavage fluid is a marker for invasive aspergillosis in adults and children. Serological tests include ELISA and PCR.

Option A: Mucor produces nonseptate, broad hyphae with aerial sporangiophores that end in a sporangium.

Option B: Chromoblastomycosis (chromomycosis) is a subcutaneous mycotic infection that is usually caused by traumatic inoculation. Histopathology shows sclerotic bodies or medlar bodies.

Option D: Rhizopus appears similar to Mucor, but it has rhizoids with sporangiophores arising in groups directly above the rhizoids.

Pearl: Classification of fungus based on morphology

Fungi are classified into 4 types based on their morphology:

  • Yeast
  • Yeast-like
  • Molds
  • Dimorphic fungi

Yeast:

  • Unicellular fungi
  • Reproduces by budding
  • Oval to round forms
  • Example: Cryptococcus, Saccharomyces.

 

Yeast like:

  • Unicellular fungi
  • Reproduces by budding or binary fission
  • Spherical or oval forms
  • Pseudohyphae may be seen.
  • Example: Candida, Malassezia furfur.

 

Molds/filamentous fungi:

  • Have hyphae which may be septate or aseptate
  • Aseptate or coenocytic hyphae – Rhizopus, mucor, Lichtheimia.
  • Septate hyphae – Penicillium, Dermatophytes, Aspergillus, fusarium.

 

Dimorphic fungi

  • Filamentous forms in the culture at 220C – 250C and in the environment.
  • Yeast form in the culture at 370C and in tissues.
  • Examples – Histoplasma capsulatum, Blastomyces dermatitidis, Coccidioides immitis, Paracoccidioides brasiliensis, Talaromyces marneffei, Sporothrix schenckii.

question.text: Which of the following is ‌not true about lupus neph‌ritis in pregnancy?

options.text: Immunosuppression can be c‌ontinued during pregnancy‌
options.label: A
B
options.text: Pregnancy to be planned on‌ce the disease has been q‌uiescent for at least 6 m‍onths and there is no evi‌dence of renal dysfunctio‍n

options.label: C
options.text: High dose corticosteroids ‌for lupus flare in pregna‌ncy is safe

options.label: D
options.text: Ecospirin, methotrexate, c‌yclophosphamide, corticos‌teroids, azathioprine are‍ safe in pregnancy

question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ecospirin, methotrexate, cyclophosphamide, corticosteroids, azathioprine are safe in pregnancy

Option D is not true about lupus nephritis in pregnancy. Methotrexate and cyclophosphamide are teratogenic and hence they are not safe during pregnancy. 

Systemic lupus erythematosus(SLE) is a chronic autoimmune disorder involving the multisystem. It affects young women of childbearing age. The renal involvement of the disease can manifest in the form of active lupus nephritis or flare-ups during pregnancy.

Clinical features include fever, weight loss, migratory joint pain, and myalgias. It can lead to preterm births, preeclampsia, and pregnancy loss while the infant can suffer from neonatal lupus and heart block. 

Antinuclear antibodies are useful for screening the disease. Double-stranded DNA (ds DNA) is highly specific in diagnosing. Other antibodies such as lupus anticoagulant, antiphospholipid antibodies, anti-Ro, and anti-La antibodies are useful in diagnosis.

Management is as follows

  • Preconceptional planning plays an important role. Conception during a period of quiescence for at least 6 months determines a successful outcome. Stable remission of renal disease for at least 6 months before conception is recommended.
  • Corticosteroids are useful during episodes of lupus flare and can be used safely in pregnancy. For patients on chronic corticosteroid therapy, intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg, three doses are given 8 hourly during labor or at the time of cesarean delivery.
  • Immunosuppressants such as azathioprine can be continued during pregnancy. It may be used in case of severe SLE
  • Hydroxychloroquine is found to be the best for maintenance and is safe in pregnancy. It can prevent the need for prolonged corticosteroid therapy.

question.text: A 6-month-old boy was brou​ght to the casualty with ‌seizures. The pediatricia‍n tries to do CSF samplin​g. What are the structure​s punctured by the pediat‌rician while piercing thr​ough the marked structure‍?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Scalp, dura, arachnoid

The given image shows the skull of an infant and the arrow points towards the anterior fontanelle. The procedure of collecting CSF from the anterior fontanelle is called ventricular tapping. The various structures pierced are the scalp, dura, and arachnoid.

Fontanelle tap/ Percutaneous ventricular puncture:

A fontanelle tap or percutaneous ventricular puncture is performed in infants without access to a VP shunt, who require urgent ventricular decompression and have an open anterior fontanelle. The infants’ open fontanelle is directly punctured with a butterfly needle to enter the lateral ventricle to collect CSF samples or release the pressure or place a drain/catheter. 

A 25-gauge butterfly needle is inserted through the anterolateral aspect of the anterior fontanelle (away from the midline, avoiding the superior sagittal sinus).

The image below shows the various fontanelles.

 

 

The scalp is a soft tissue that covers the calvaria of the skull. It consists of five layers (Mnemonic: SCALP). Below the scalp and the calvaria lie the meningeal layers, namely, pachymeninges [arachnoid + dura mater (P-AD)] and leptomeninges [arachnoid + pia mater (L-AP)]. One must reach the subarachnoid space below the arachnoid layer to collect or tap CSF. So, the layers pierced in the order are as follows:

  1. Skin
  2. Connective tissue (superficial fascia) with blood vessels and nerves
  3. Aponeurosis (galea aponeurotica) with occipitofrontalis muscle
  4. Loose areolar (subaponeurotic) tissue
  5. Pericranium
  6. Dura mater
  7. Arachnoid membrane

question.text: A couple presents with inf​ertility even after 2 yea‍rs of unprotected interco​urse. The seminal analysi‌s reveals a volume of 2 m‌L, concentration of 40 mi​llion/ml, progressive mot‍ility of 55%, and morphol​ogy of 45%. The wife's ho​rmone levels were normal ‌with bilateral spillage o​f dye from both fallopian​ tubes on HSG. What perce‌ntage of couples can be a​ttributed to unexplained ​infertility?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 25%

25% of couples can be attributed to unexplained infertility.

Unexplained infertility refers to cases where no clear cause of infertility can be identified after a thorough evaluation of both partners. In the scenario provided, the male partner has normal seminal parameters, and the female partner has normal hormonal levels and patent fallopian tubes, making this a case of unexplained infertility.

Some causes of unexplained infertility include:

  1. Ovulatory Dysfunction
  2. Impaired sperm function despite normal semen analysis
  3. Tubal or Uterine Factors
  4. Endometriosis
  5. Antisperm antibodies or autoimmune issues.
  6. Lifestyle and Environmental Factors: Stress, smoking, diet, or environmental toxins.

Unexplained infertility is diagnosed when standard evaluations yield normal results:

  • Semen analysis showing normal volume, concentration, motility, and morphology.
  • Normal hormonal tests, basal body temperature, or ovulation predictor kits.
  • Hysterosalpingography (HSG) or saline sonography shows no blockages.
  • Transvaginal ultrasound or hysteroscopy ruling out structural abnormalities.

If no cause is identified after these tests, the couple is categorized as having unexplained infertility.

Management includes:

1. Expectant Management

  • Suitable for younger couples (<35 years) with a short duration of infertility.
  • Lifestyle modifications (e.g., weight management, smoking cessation, stress reduction).

2. Medical : 

  • Ovulation Induction: Clomiphene citrate or Letrozole.
  • Gonadotropins: Injectable hormones (FSH, LH) for controlled ovarian stimulation.

3. Intrauterine Insemination (IUI)

4. Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART)

  • In Vitro Fertilization (IVF)
  • Intracytoplasmic Sperm Injection (ICSI)

question.text: Which classification of bi‌le duct injury takes into​ account both vascular as‌ well as the location of ‍the injury?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hannover

Hannover classification of bile duct injury takes into account both vascular as well as the location of the injury.

Hannover, bile duct injuries were divided into five types from A to E. Vascular injuries are included in Type C and Type D.

  • Type A is peripheral bile leakage.
  • Type B is stricture of CHD or CBD without injury.
  • Type C is lateral CHD or CBD injury.
  • Type D is the total transection of CHD.
  • Type E is bile duct stricture of the main bile duct without bile leakage at the postoperative state.

Other Options: 

Option A: The Strasberg classification of bile duct injury is a widely used system to anatomically define bile duct injuries.

Option C: The Bismuth–Corlette classification system provides an anatomic description of the tumor location and longitudinal extension in the biliary tree.

Option D: The McMahon classification separated the injuries by the width of bile duct injury

question.text: A 37-year-old chronic alcoholic was brought to the Emergency department 24 hours after his last drink. He complains that unknown people are discussing him and planning to harm him. He reports hearing voices continuously, even when no one is present. Which of the following findings would most strongly favour alcoholic hallucinosis over delirium tremens?

options.text: Onset after cessation of alcohol intake
options.label: A

question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Preserved orientation and clear consciousness

Auditory hallucinations occurring 24 hours after alcohol cessation in a patient with preserved orientation and clear sensorium are characteristic of alcoholic hallucinosis.

Alcoholic hallucinosis typically develops within 12–24 hours of alcohol cessation or marked reduction of alcohol intake. Patients experience acoustic verbal hallucinations, delusions and mood disturbances. Hallucinations are predominantly auditory, unlike delirium tremens, where visual hallucinations are more common. The condition may progress to a chronic form which mimics schizophrenia.

Alcoholic hallucinosis persists even after the withdrawal syndrome is over, and it typically occurs in clear consciousness. On the other hand, delirium tremens is characterised by clouding of consciousness with disorientation to time and place.

Management involves benzodiazepines for detoxification, thiamine supplementation before glucose administration and correction of fluid and electrolyte abnormalities. Short-term antipsychotics (e.g., haloperidol) can be given if hallucinations are severe or distressing. Long-term management focuses on alcohol de-addiction and relapse prevention.

Other options

Option A: Both alcoholic hallucinosis and delirium tremens are alcohol withdrawal symptoms that occur after alcohol withdrawal. Therefore, cessation of alcohol does not differentiate between the two conditions.

Option B: Tremors are a common manifestation of alcohol withdrawal and may be present in both alcoholic hallucinosis and delirium tremens.

Option C: Hallucinations can occur in both disorders. The distinguishing feature is the type of hallucination and the preserved orientation.

question.text: A 34-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B is found to have chronic hepatitis D co-infection. He has compensated liver disease and persistent HDV RNA positivity despite previous therapy. The recently approved first-in-class drug that prevents hepatitis D virus entry into hepatocytes is-
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bulevirtide

The recently approved first-in-class drug that prevents hepatitis D virus entry into hepatocytes is Bulevirtide.

The presence of chronic hepatitis D with persistent HDV replication despite prior therapy is an indication for Bulevirtide, the first-in-class entry inhibitor that blocks HDV entry into hepatocytes.

Bulevirtide is the first approved targeted therapy for chronic hepatitis D virus (HDV) infection. HDV is a defective RNA virus that requires the presence of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) for its replication and transmission.

To infect hepatocytes, both HBV and HDV utilise the sodium taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide (NTCP) receptor located on the hepatocyte surface. Bulevirtide is a synthetic lipopeptide that binds to NTCP and prevents viral entry into hepatocytes, thereby blocking the spread of infection to uninfected liver cells.

Chronic HDV infection represents the most severe form of chronic viral hepatitis and is associated with accelerated progression to cirrhosis, hepatic decompensation, and hepatocellular carcinoma. Historically, pegylated interferon-α was the only therapeutic option, with limited efficacy and poor tolerability. The advent of Bulevirtide therefore represents a major advance in HDV management because it directly targets a critical step in the viral life cycle.

Option B: Pegylated interferon lambda does not prevent the entry of the virus into the hepatocytes. Instead, it enhances the host's innate antiviral immune response and is currently under evaluation for the treatment of chronic viral hepatitis. 

Option C: Bepirovirsen is an antisense oligonucleotide targeting HBV messenger RNA and is being developed for chronic hepatitis B rather than HDV entry blockade.

Option D: Fostemsavir is an HIV attachment inhibitor that blocks viral binding to CD4 cells through interaction with gp120 and has no role in hepatitis D treatment.

question.text: Which of the following ligaments is a modification of the investing layer of deep cervical fascia?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Stylomandibular ligament

The stylomandibular ligament is a modification of the investing layer of deep cervical fascia.

The investing layer of deep cervical fascia (the superficial layer) is attached superiorly to the external occipital protuberance, the superior nuchal line, the mastoid process, the styloid process, the external acoustic meatus, the tympanic plate, and the base of the mandible. Inferiorly, it is attached to the spine of the scapula, acromion process, clavicle, and manubrium. Posteriorly, it is attached to the ligamentum nuchae and the spine of C7. Anteriorly, it is attached to the symphysis menti and the hyoid bone. 

Between the angle of the mandible and the mastoid process, it covers the parotid gland by splitting into 

  • Superficial lamina (parotid fascia): It is thick and dense, attached to the zygomatic arch
  • Deep lamina: It is thin, attached to the styloid process, tympanic plate, and mandible. The deep lamina is thick between the styloid process and the angle of the mandible, forming the stylomandibular ligament. This ligament separates the parotid gland and the submandibular gland. It is pierced by the external carotid artery. 

Structures enclosed by the investing layer of deep cervical fascia are the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid (muscles), parotid and submandibular (salivary glands), suprasternal and supraclavicular (spaces). 

Contents of the suprasternal space are the sternal heads of the right and left sternocleidomastoid muscles, the jugular venous arch, the lymph node, and the interclavicular ligament. Contents of the supraclavicular space, the external jugular vein, the supraclavicular nerves, and cutaneous vessels, including lymphatics. 

The investing layer forms the roof of the anterior and posterior triangles of the neck. It also forms the pulleys to bind the tendons of the digastric and omohyoid muscles.

Other options:

Option A: The sphenomandibular ligament is derived from Meckel’s cartilage (1st arch), not from deep cervical fascia.

Option C: The interclavicular ligament is a content of the suprasternal space, a space formed by the investing layer of deep cervical fascia. 

Option D: The temporomandibular ligament is an intrinsic ligament of the temporomandibular joint formed by thickening of the joint capsule.

question.text: Which of the following correctly explains the pharmacological basis for the lower risk of severe hyperkalemia with finerenone compared to spironolactone?

options.text: It directly activates epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) to enhance potassium excretion
options.label: A

options.text: It is eliminated exclusively through the biliary route
options.label: B

options.text: It has a balanced heart-kidney distribution and lacks long-lived active metabolites
options.label: C
D
options.text: It increases aldosterone secretion from the adrenal cortex

question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It has a balanced heart-kidney distribution and lacks long-lived active metabolites

The pharmacological basis for the lower risk of severe hyperkalemia with finerenone compared to spironolactone is that finerenone has a balanced heart-kidney distribution and lacks long-lived active metabolites.

Finerenone has a balanced distribution between the heart and kidneys, higher receptor selectivity, and lacks long-lived active metabolites, which explains the lower risk of hyperkalemia with finerenone as compared to spironolactone. This results in less sustained inhibition of distal nephron sodium-potassium exchange, reducing potassium retention while preserving cardiovascular and renal protective effects. Finerenone is a selective, non-steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist approved for patients with chronic kidney disease associated with type 2 diabetes mellitus.

Like spironolactone, it blocks aldosterone-mediated sodium reabsorption in the distal nephron and can thereby increase serum potassium levels. While all MRAs carry a risk of hyperkalemia, finerenone causes less severe, treatment-limiting hyperkalemia compared to older steroidal agents like spironolactone.

question.text: Nerve passing through which of the following foramina is involved in the secretomotor supply to the lacrimal gland?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1

The secretomotor pathway to the lacrimal gland passes through the maxillary nerve (V2), which passes through the foramen rotundum (1).

Parasympathetic secretomotor fibres to the lacrimal gland originate from the superior salivatory nucleus and travel in the facial nerve. These fibres leave as the greater petrosal nerve and join the deep petrosal nerve to form the nerve of the pterygoid canal (Vidian nerve), which passes through the pterygoid canal to reach the pterygopalatine ganglion. After synapsing, postganglionic fibres accompany the maxillary nerve (V2), which traverses the foramen rotundum (1), then pass through the zygomatic nerve. Then it joins the lacrimal nerve (V1) to supply the lacrimal gland. Thus, the superior orbital fissure (V1), pterygoid canal and foramen rotundum are essential components of the secretomotor pathway.

Lesions involving the greater petrosal nerve, the pterygopalatine ganglion, the maxillary nerve, or the zygomatic nerve can lead to reduced lacrimation and dry eye symptoms. Such patients may complain of ocular irritation, foreign-body sensation, and recurrent conjunctival dryness.

The pterygopalatine ganglion is the largest parasympathetic ganglion of the head and is suspended from the maxillary nerve in the pterygopalatine fossa. Although parasympathetic fibres synapse here, the postganglionic fibres ultimately reach the lacrimal gland through branches of both V2 and V1.

Other options:

Option B: 2 is the foramen ovale, which transmits V3 and has no role in the lacrimal secretomotor pathway.

Option C: 3 is the foramen spinosum; it does not transmit nerves carrying parasympathetic fibres destined for the lacrimal gland.

Option D: 4 is the jugular foramen, and it does not transmit any nerves that supply the lacrimal gland.

question.text: A 42-year-old woman admitted to the Intensive Care Unit with septic shock remains hypotensive with a blood pressure of  75/40 mmHg. Despite adequate fluid resuscitation, she develops marked tachypnea. Her arterial blood gas analysis reveals severe metabolic acidosis,  and her partial pressure of arterial oxygen (PaO₂) is within normal limits. She is intubated and started on mechanical ventilation. Which type of respiratory failure best explains this indication for mechanical ventilation?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Type 4 respiratory failure

The given clinical scenario of persistent hypotension (75/40 mmHg) and marked tachypnea despite adequate fluid resuscitation in a patient with septic shock, along with a normal partial pressure of arterial oxygen (PaO2), indicates type 4 respiratory failure.

Type 4 respiratory failure occurs exclusively in the setting of shock, caused by hypoperfusion of the respiratory muscles due to increased workload. Normally, the respiratory muscles consume only 5% of the cardiac output. Patients in shock often experience respiratory distress due to pulmonary edema, lactic acidosis and anaemia.

In this case, around 40% of cardiac output may be distributed to the respiratory muscles. Although her arterial oxygenation is preserved, the respiratory muscles consume a significant portion of the body's limited oxygen delivery. 

Intubation in this type of respiratory failure is instituted not primarily to correct hypoxemia or hypercapnia, but rather to reduce the metabolic cost of breathing, unload the respiratory muscles, and redistribute cardiac output and oxygen delivery to essential organs such as the brain, heart, and kidneys.

question.text: A 34-year-old man presents for follow-up 8 months after a severe head injury sustained in a road traffic accident. He had a complete right oculomotor (third cranial) nerve palsy, which has partially recovered. He now notices that whenever he attempts to look to the left, his right upper eyelid elevates involuntarily, despite persistent limitation of ocular movements. Which of the following clinical signs best explains this abnormal eyelid movement?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pseudo von Graefe sign

The clinical vignette of partial recovery from complete right oculomotor nerve palsy is suggestive of aberrant regeneration of the oculomotor nerve. The involuntary elevation of the upper eyelid on adduction is best explained by the pseudo von Graefe sign.

The history is of traumatic third cranial nerve palsy followed by partial recovery several months later. During recovery, the patient develops involuntary elevation of the upper eyelid when attempting an eye movement, indicating aberrant regeneration.

Regenerating third nerve fibres are misdirected to the levator palpebrae superioris, causing the eyelid to elevate during eye movements. This characteristic finding is called the pseudo-von Graefe sign. The pseudo-von Graefe sign is a classic sign of aberrant regeneration of the oculomotor (III cranial) nerve, most commonly following traumatic or compressive third-nerve palsy.

Aberrant regeneration, also called oculomotor synkinesis, is the misdirection of regenerating oculomotor nerve fibres following a traumatic or compressive third nerve palsy. Instead of reconnecting to their original muscles, the regenerating nerve fibres innervate the wrong extraocular muscles or the levator palpebrae superioris, resulting in abnormal associated movements.

It is common after trauma, aneurysms, and compressive lesions, but is rare after microvascular (ischemic) third nerve palsy (e.g., diabetes or hypertension), because the endoneural nerve sheath may be breached in traumatic and compressive lesions, whereas it is well preserved in ischemic third nerve palsy. Important signs of oculomotor synkinesis are as follows.

Signs Interpretation
 Pseudo–Von Graefe sign Elevation of upper eyelid on downgaze or adduction
 Adduction on vertical gaze Eye adducts during attempted upward or downward gaze
 Globe retraction Retraction of globe with limited elevation/depression on vertical movement
 Pseudo–Argyll Robertson pupil Pupil constricts more to near effort (convergence) than to light; may show gaze-evoked constriction

Other options:

Option A: Argyll-Robertson pupil is characterized by light-near dissociation, in which the pupils constrict during accommodation but not in response to light. It is classically associated with neurosyphilis and does not cause abnormal eyelid movements or occur due to third nerve regeneration.

Option C: Marcus Gunn jaw-winking syndrome is a congenital synkinesis in which the upper eyelid elevates with jaw movements such as chewing or opening the mouth. In this patient, the eyelid elevates during eye movement following traumatic third nerve palsy, making this diagnosis incorrect.

Option D: Adie syndrome presents with a tonic dilated pupil that reacts poorly to light but better to near effort, often due to damage to the postganglionic parasympathetic supply to the sphincter pupillae and the ciliary muscle. It affects pupillary function, not eyelid movement, and is unrelated to traumatic third nerve palsy or aberrant regeneration.

question.text: An obese male diagnosed with hypertension is on statin therapy. However, his recent cholesterol levels are elevated and an additional drug that increases bile acid excretion in the stools is initiated. Which of the following drugs is likely prescribed?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Colestipol

The drug that is likely prescribed to this patient, which acts by increasing bile acid excretion in the stools, is colestipol.

Colestipol is a bile acid sequestrant that decreases reabsorption of bile acids in the intestine, which are thus excreted in the stools. Loss of bile acids in stools leads to increased hepatic bile acid synthesis. Therefore, hepatic cholesterol content decreases, stimulating the production of LDL receptors, an effect similar to that of statins. The increase in hepatic LDL receptors increases LDL clearance and lowers LDL-cholesterol (LDL-C) levels.

But this effect is partially offset by the enhanced cholesterol synthesis caused by upregulation of HMG-CoA reductase. Therefore, concurrent statin therapy substantially increases the effectiveness of bile acid sequestrants. 

Another effect of increased hepatic bile acid synthesis is that it also causes an increase in hepatic triglyceride synthesis, which is of consequence in patients with significant hypertriglyceridemia. Therefore, initial monitoring of fasting triglyceride levels every 1-2 weeks is important while starting on these drugs.

Other options:

Option A: Ezetimibe inhibits Niemann-Pick C1-like 1 (NPC1L1) transport protein, which is a cholesterol transporter in the jejunal enterocytes and thereby decreases cholesterol absorption in the diet.

Option C: Gemfibrozil belongs to the fibrate group of drugs that bind to peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARα), which stimulate fatty acid oxidation and thereby reduce triglyceride levels mainly.

Option D: Bempedoic acid acts by competitively inhibiting ATP-citrate lyase(ACL), a cytoplasmic enzyme that converts citrate to oxaloacetate and acetyl-CoA. Thereby reducing acetyl-CoA levels, which is the starting substrate in the de novo synthesis of cholesterol.

question.text: A 42-year-old man is brought dead after consuming an unknown amount of alcohol at a local gathering. During the autopsy, the forensic surgeon suspects methanol poisoning and sends blood for toxicological analysis. Which of the following collection vials should be used to ensure reliable analysis?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3

The vial marked as 3 shows the grey-top vial containing sodium fluoride and potassium oxalate, the specimen container of choice for toxicological analysis in suspected methanol poisoning.

In cases of suspected methanol poisoning, blood samples intended for toxicological analysis should be collected in a grey-top vial containing sodium fluoride and potassium oxalate.

Sodium fluoride acts as a preservative by inhibiting glycolysis and preventing post-collection metabolism of alcohols by blood cells and microorganisms, while potassium oxalate functions as an anticoagulant. This combination helps maintain the original concentration of methanol and other volatile alcohols, ensuring accurate and reliable toxicological estimation.

Methanol poisoning is a medical and forensic emergency. Methanol itself is relatively non-toxic, but it is metabolized by alcohol dehydrogenase into formaldehyde and subsequently formic acid, which are responsible for severe metabolic acidosis, optic nerve toxicity, visual disturbances, and death.

Accurate blood methanol estimation is crucial both for clinical management and for establishing the cause of death during medicolegal investigations. In living patients, investigations typically reveal a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, an elevated osmolar gap, and elevated serum methanol levels. Fundoscopic examination may show hyperemia of the optic disc and retinal edema. 

Treatment includes Fomepizole or Ethanol to inhibit alcohol dehydrogenase, correction of acidosis with sodium bicarbonate, folinic acid supplementation, and hemodialysis in severe poisoning.

From a forensic perspective, preservation of blood samples is critical because ongoing cellular metabolism after collection can alter alcohol concentrations, potentially affecting toxicological interpretation. Hence, sodium fluoride-containing grey-top tubes are considered the standard collection containers for blood alcohol and toxicology testing.

Option B: Vial 2 shows a green vial that contains heparin and is commonly used for biochemical and blood gas analyses, but it is not the preferred vial for forensic alcohol estimation due to the lack of fluoride preservative.

question.text: A 48-year-old male school teacher with a 25-year history of smoking presents with progressively deepening of voice and persistent hoarseness for the last 2 years. question.text:
An elderly male underwent TURP for BPH. He is a known case of CCF and on regular medication. The consultant opts for a bipolar TURP instead of a conventional monopolar TURP. Which complication is minimized by this preference?

TURP - Transurethral Resection of the Prostate
BPH - Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia
CCF - Congestive Cardiac Failure
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Water intoxication

The complication minimized by using bipolar TURP over the monopolar version is that it reduces the incidence of water intoxication. 

During the TURP procedure, there is a high risk that irrigating fluid will be absorbed into the patient’s systemic circulation during prostatic tissue resection. Fluid absorption occurs when the hydrostatic pressure of the irrigating solution exceeds the pressure within the prostatic venous plexus, which is approximately 10 mmHg. The amount of absorption depends on the irrigation pressure, duration of resection, and the extent of venous sinus exposure.

The absorption of hypo-osmolar irrigating fluids during transurethral resection can lead to dilutional hyponatremia, which can precipitate congestive cardiac failure and require hemodialysis. Along with this, due to water intoxication, the patient might experience confusion and other cerebral events that present like a stroke.

Monopolar TURP removes tissue with a wire loop that carries electrical current in one direction, with the surgical site irrigated with a non-conducting, non-ionic fluid such as 1.5% glycine, as normal saline would dissipate the electrical current and reduce cutting efficacy. 

In contrast, bipolar TURP uses ionic solutions, such as normal saline, as the irrigant because the current is confined between the two electrodes. The incidence of water intoxication and subsequent hyponatremia has been reduced with the introduction of isotonic normal saline as irrigating fluids during resection, and even further with the use of bipolar TURP. 

The incidence of other complications such as retrograde ejaculation, urethral stricture and incontinence is similar in both monopolar and bipolar TURP (Options A, C and D).

question.text: A 65-year-old man with a history of chronic right-sided ear discharge for the last 1.5 months presented with complaints of deep-seated ear pain, severe retro-orbital pain, and diplopia. On examination, the following finding is seen on lateral gaze. What is the most likely diagnosis in this case?

Correct answer: D. Petrous apicitis

The given scenario of persistent ear discharge, deep-seated earache, retro-orbital pain, and diplopia is suggestive of Gradenigo syndrome, seen in petrous apicitis or petrositis. It is due to the spread of infection from the middle ear and mastoid to the petrous part of the temporal bone.

In this case, there is a failure of abduction of the right eye on lateral gaze, which indicates paralysis of the right lateral rectus due to right abducent (cranial nerve VI) nerve palsy. 

Gradenigo syndrome consists of a triad :

  • Persistent ear discharge
  • Deep-seated ear or retro-orbital pain
  • VI nerve palsy

 Infection from the mastoid air cells reaches the petrous apex via two pathways:

1. Postero-superior tract: starts at the mastoid and runs behind or above the bony labyrinth or through the arc of the superior semicircular canal to the petrous apex.

2. Antero-inferior tract: starts at the hypotympanum and goes around the cochlea to reach the petrous apex.

Dorello's canal is a dural sheath at the petrous apex, which gives space for the passage of the abducent nerve, and hence this nerve is compressed by the epidural abscess formed at the apex in petrositis. Retro-orbital pain is due to the involvement of the trigeminal ganglion.

question.text: A 40-year-old HIV patient who presented with dry, non-productive cough and dyspnea is diagnosed to have Pneumocystis jirovecii infection. Which of the following statements is false about this organism?

options.label: B
options.text: Cyst wall stains black with methenamine silver stain

options.label: C
options.text: It grows readily on Sabouraud agar

options.label: D
options.text: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is used for prophylaxis in HIV patients

question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It grows readily on Sabouraud agar

Pneumocystis jirovecii does not grow readily on Sabouraud agar.

P. jirovecii is an extracellular pathogen that primarily resides in the lung's surfactant layer, impairing oxygen exchange and leading to symptoms like cyanosis. Diagnosis involves examining specimens from bronchoalveolar lavage, lung biopsies, or induced sputum for trophozoites and cysts using specialized stains and fluorescent microscopy. P. jirovecii cannot be cultured routinely in vitro. Serological tests mainly determine infection prevalence rather than aiding clinical diagnosis. Detection of a specific surface glycoprotein in serum is indicative of acute infection.

P. jirovecii has three morphological forms:

  • Trophozoite - thin-walled, irregularly shaped
  • Precyst - an intermediate stage of the sexual phase
  • Cyst - thick-walled, spherical in shape. It contains intracystic bodies

Trophozoites can be demonstrated by Giemsa, toluidine blue, methenamine silver, and calcofluor white stains. The cyst wall stains black with methenamine silver stain.

P. jirovecii causes pneumonia primarily in immunocompromised patients. It is commonly found in animals like rats and mice without causing disease unless the host's immune system is weakened. In humans, it historically affected malnourished infants and those undergoing immunosuppressive therapies, becoming a major cause of mortality in AIDS patients before effective preventive treatments. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMZ) and pentamidine isothionate are the drugs of choice for the treatment of acute cases. TMP-SMZ is also used for prophylaxis in HIV patients.

question.text:
A middle-aged shepherd presents with a CT report that shows the following image. Serology is positive for a hydatid cyst. According to the WHO-IWGE classification, how is this lesion categorized, and what is its appropriate management?

WHO: IWGE classification - World Health Organization Informal Working Group on Echinococcosis classification
PAIR: Puncture, Aspiration, Injection, and Reaspiration
question.explanation:
Correct answer: D. CE 5, Observation

The CT image is suggestive of a calcified hydatid cyst. According to the WHO-IWGE classification, the lesion is best classified as CE5, and observation is the appropriate management.

The minimally invasive percutaneous PAIR (Puncture, Aspiration, Injection, and Reaspiration) technique is an interventional radiology procedure done under albendazole and praziquantel cover. Surgical options include radical total/partial pericystectomy or hepatic segmentectomy. An asymptomatic cyst that is inactive needs observation. 

Other options: 

Option A: CE1 is a simple unilocular cyst, and PAIR is the appropriate management. 

Option B: CE 2 is a honeycomb type of cyst, and pericystectomy is the appropriate management. 

Option C: CE 3 is a transitional cyst with daughter cysts, and PAIR/ surgical catheter drainage can be done.

question.text: The structures shown in the below image are found in which of the following conditions?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Meningioma

The above image shows psammoma bodies. They are found in meningioma.

Meningioma is a benign tumor arising from the meningothelial cells of the arachnoid layer and is an intradural tumor. Psammoma bodies are concentric, lamellated structures formed as a product of dystrophic calcification. 

Conditions associated with psammoma bodies include:

  • Papillary thyroid carcinoma
  • Papillary renal cell carcinoma
  • Meningioma

Other options:

Option A: Russell bodies are cytoplasmic globular inclusions that are seen in multiple myeloma.

Option C: Verocay bodies are spindle cells that are arranged to form central “nuclear-free zones” ramified by palisading nuclei and are seen in Schwannoma.

Option D: Call-Exner bodies are diagnostic gland-like immature follicles that are filled with an acidophilic material and are seen in granulosa cell tumors of the ovary.

question.text: Identify the knot shown in the video.
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Surgeon’s knot

The knot shown in the video is the surgeon’s knot.

The surgeon’s knot is a modification of the square (reef) knot that contains a double turn in the first throw. A “throw” is one complete twist of two strands. The first throw with a double wrap makes the knot less likely to slip while the second throw is being tied, so it is used when added security is required.

Other options:

Option B: Reef (square) knot is formed by two throws in the opposite direction; the standard surgical knot.

Option C: Granny knot is a slip knot with two throws in the same direction; used to achieve tension and then secured with a reef knot.

Option D: Half-hitch knot is a single throw; the basic component from which other knots are built.

question.text: A 10-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with a history of falling off his bicycle. He complains of severe pain around his ankle. Which of the following findings is seen in this CT scan?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thurston Holland sign

The finding seen in the CT scan is Thurston Holland sign or fragment. The given CT of the ankle lateral shows a Salter-Harris type 2 epiphyseal fracture, in which there is involvement of the growth plate (physis) and a triangle of metaphyseal bone, with sparing of the epiphysis. This triangle of metaphyseal bone is known as Thurston Holland sign. 

Salter-Harris classified epiphyseal injuries into 5 types. Type 2 epiphyseal fractures are the most common type of epiphyseal injury in patients over 10 years of age.

Other options:

Option A: Trethowan's sign is seen in slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE). It is when Klein's line does not intersect the lateral part of the superior femoral epiphysis on an AP radiograph of the pelvis but passes superior to it.

Option B: Terry Thomas sign is seen in patients with scapholunate instability, which denotes the increased gap between the scaphoid and the lunate.

Option D: The teardrop sign is seen in orbital floor fractures and is also known as a blow-out fracture due to the herniation of orbital contents into the maxillary antrum.

question.text: A patient presents to the OPD with a history of swelling over the anterior part of the neck, fatigue, and weight loss for two months. On examination, the mass moves with deglutition. A biopsy from the patient's thyroid gland is shown below. Investigations reveal elevated plasma metanephrines, serum calcium, PTH, and calcitonin. She also gives a history of her mother undergoing surgery for a lump in the neck many years before. Which of the following is likely to result in the above condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Gain of function mutation in RET

options.label: B
options.text: Loss of function mutation in RET

options.label: C
options.text: Gain of function mutation in K-RAS

options.label: D
options.text: Loss of function mutation in K-RAS

question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gain of function mutation in RET

The given clinical vignette describes the features of MEN 2A syndrome, which includes medullary thyroid carcinoma (the given histopathology picture shows the presence of amyloid-rich stroma and a family history of thyroid surgery), parathyroid adenoma (elevated serum calcium, PTH, and calcitonin) and pheochromocytoma (elevated plasma metanephrines). The gain-of-function mutations in the RET proto-oncogene occur in MEN 2A syndrome.

Multiple endocrine neoplasia is characterised by the presence of tumors in two or more endocrine glands. It can be MEN 1, MEN 2A, MEN 2B (MEN 3), or MEN 4. MEN 1 is associated mainly with parathyroid adenoma, pancreatic tumors, and pituitary tumors. 

MEN type 2 comprises groups of disorders caused by gain-of-function mutations of the RET proto-oncogene at chromosomal locus 10q11.2. There are three variants:

  • MEN 2A (most common type)- MEN 2A is also known as Sipple's syndrome. It is characterized by medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), pheochromocytomas, and parathyroid tumors.
  • MEN 2B, also known as MEN 3- MEN 2B is characterised by MTC, pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas, marfanoid habitus, medullated corneal nerve fibres, and megacolon.
  • Medullary thyroid carcinoma only

MEN 4 is associated with parathyroid adenoma, pituitary adenoma, and reproductive organ tumors.

Other options

Option B: Loss-of-function mutation of the RET gene leads to Hirschsprung disease, in which defective migration of neural crest-derived enteric ganglion cells results in aganglionosis of the distal bowel. 

Option C: K-RAS is another proto-oncogene, and activating mutations are common in several sporadic malignancies, including colorectal carcinoma, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, and lung adenocarcinoma.

Option D: Loss-of-function mutations in K-RAS are not a recognized cause of MEN2A or other hereditary endocrine tumor syndromes. Since it is a protoconcogene, only gain-of -function mutations are associated with malignancies.

question.text:
A 5-year-old girl is referred to the gynaecology OPD with recurrent painless vaginal bleeding and rapidly enlarging breasts over the past year. On examination, she has Tanner stage III breasts and a segmental café-au-lait macule with an irregular border on the back. Pelvic ultrasound shows a large unilateral autonomous ovarian cyst with an enlarged uterus. Basal LH is low and shows no significant rise on a GnRH stimulation test, while estradiol is markedly elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?

LH- leutenizing hormone, GnRH- gonadotropin-releasing hormone.
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. McCune-Albright syndrome

The given symptoms of precocious puberty, cafe au lait spots with irregular borders, and an ovarian cyst suggest the diagnosis of McCune-Albright syndrome(MAS). 

It is characterized by a triad of segmental cafe-au-lait spots, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, and multiple endocrinopathies like hyperthyroidism, acromegaly, etc. MAS results from a postzygotic activating mutation in GNAS (Gsα subunit), causing autonomous ovarian estrogen production independent of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis(HPG).

The high estradiol suppresses pituitary gonadotropin secretion. It is characterised by low basal LH, as seen in this scenario, which does not increase during a GnRH stimulation test. Fibrous dysplasia is the fibrous replacement of cancellous bone. It can result in bony pain, repeated fractures, and cranial nerve compression.

Other options:

Option B: Central precocious puberty is caused by the early activation of the HPG axis. The GnRH-stimulated LH response would be significant in this scenario. It doesn't characteristically present with café-au-lait macules or ovarian cysts.

Option C: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (STK11/LKB1 mutation) presents with mucocutaneous pigmentation of the lips, oral mucosa, and hamartomatous GI polyps. 

Option D: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia causes androgen excess (virilisation, ambiguous genitalia, hirsutism). Estrogen-induced breast development and vaginal bleeding are not seen.

question.text: A middle-aged male presented to the OPD with an MRI fistulogram report stating an intersphincteric fistulous tract without any secondary extensions. On examination, there is a single posterior fistula-in-ano. What is the most appropriate management?
question.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fistulotomy

The clinical vignette of a single posterior fistula-in-ano without any secondary tracts is suggestive of simple fistula-in-ano, for which fistulotomy is the most appropriate management.

A fistula-in-ano is a chronic abnormal communication extending from the anorectal lumen (internal opening) to the external opening in the skin on the perineum. They present with intermittent purulent discharge and discomfort.

As per the American Gastroenterology Association Classification, anal fistulas can be classified into simple or complex:

  • Simple fistulas are low (superficial or low inter- or low trans-sphincteric tract) and have a single external opening
  • Complex fistulas are high (high inter- or trans-sphincteric tract). They have an extra- or suprasphincteric tract with the presence of an abscess or collection. They include ano-vaginal fistula and anal stricture.

Intersphincteric fistulae don’t cross the external sphincter as they run directly from the internal to the external opening across the distal internal sphincter but may extend proximally in the intersphincteric plane and end blindly at a second internal opening.  Fistulotomy involves the division of all structures lying between the internal and the external openings. It is the surgery of choice in intersphincteric fistulae and trans-sphincteric fistulae.

Fistulotomy is done in the lithotomy position by identifying the internal opening, and a grooved fistula probe is passed from the external to the internal opening. The track is laid open over the probe. It is then curetted to remove the granulation tissue. The wound edges are trimmed, and the wound is marsupialised. This heals well, and faecal continence is preserved with very low recurrence rates.

Other surgical managements include fistulotomy, fistulectomy, ligation of the intersphincteric fistula tract (LIFT), setons, or advancement flaps.

Other options:

Option B: Advancement flap is a sphincter-preserving procedure that is reserved for high, complex fistulae and recurrent fistulae.

Option C: Ligation of the intersphincteric fistulous tract is a sphincter-preserving procedure and is best suited for trans-sphincteric fistulae. In fistulas involving large amounts of sphincter muscle, as in high fistulae, the initial treatment is focused on controlling the fistula with a draining seton. 

Option D: Fistulectomy involves excision of the entire tract, which creates a large wound and delays healing. Hence, it is not preferred for low simple fistulae.

question.text: Under the National Sickle Cell Anemia Elimination Mission, a 19-year-old tribal male receives a "Sickle Cell Genetic Status Card" after screening. The primary purpose of this card is which of the following:
question.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Facilitating premarital genetic risk assessment

The primary purpose of the Sickle Cell Card is to facilitate pre-marital and pre-conceptional counselling.

Counsellors at Primary Health Centres (PHCs) use these cards to assess genetic risks by matching the sickle cell status cards of prospective couples. This ensures that individuals carrying the abnormal hemoglobin gene are aware of the risks of having a child with sickle cell disease if they marry another carrier.

This card system is a cornerstone of the National Sickle Cell Anemia Elimination Mission, which aims to eliminate sickle cell disease as a public health problem in India by 2047. Since the sickle cell trait is highly prevalent in tribal populations (one of the top 10 priority problems in tribal health), the government has targeted screening in these belts. Issuing these cards supports the mission's "Primary Prevention" strategy, which focuses heavily on awareness-raising and genetic counselling to prevent the transmission of the disease to the next generation.

Patients with sickle cell disease may eventually require treatments like hydroxyurea or blood transfusions (Options A and C), and while the sickle cell trait offers some protection against severe malaria (Option D), these are not the primary purposes of the genetic status cards.
